Chemical reactions can be modified through light stimulation in specific molecular groups when they undergo vibrational excitation, but manipulating the reaction's overall pathway remains challenging. Our strategy focuses on leveraging coupled modes of vibration to control the reaction, taking advantage of the vibrational states' quasi-bound properties. By applying a quantum mechanical approach and utilizing high-level water cluster models, we simulate the interaction of light with vibrating molecules. Our results indicate that coupling certain vibrational modes with electronic states can lower the energy required for a non-adiabatic transition, accessing the tunneling pathway for the hydrogen isotope separation reaction H2-D2 -> HD+H-D. Furthermore, we find that a specific vibrational mode can enhance the reaction probability by up to three orders of magnitude through resonance with the molecular cross-section. By manipulating vibrational modes, it may be possible to efficiently induce chemical reactions via light stimulation. Our study provides a theoretical framework for controlling chemical reactions via vibrational modes, offering opportunities for advancements in light-driven molecular catalysis and nuclear energy applications. Our analysis also uncovers unique features of the reaction profiles that could be observed experimentally. Additionally, we have developed an open-source code that enables the calculation of photodriven molecular reactions, allowing for further modifications and applications. Our approach can potentially be extended to other molecular systems, promoting advancements in light-driven molecular catalysis and nuclear energy applications. Our research may also uncover new features that can be observed experimentally, including parity-dependent phase transitions and non-adiabatic tunneling reactions. Our future objectives are to develop efficient algorithms for calculating long-time dynamics and to investigate the presence of many-body localization in the molecular photoexcitation. Our code is designed to be easily modifiable to calculate various physical properties, such as the absorption spectrum, electronic spectrum, and vibrational mode distribution. Our study has also revealed the significant role of electron-proton correlation in the hydrogen isotope separation reaction, impacting the reaction probability by several orders of magnitude. Our findings suggest that proton correlation plays a crucial role in understanding chemical reactions, particularly in the case of non-adiabatic transitions. Historically, models predicting click-through rates (CTRs) in online advertising were developed using textual features from ad content and user information. Recently, visual cues have become integral to online advertising, prompting the need for integration of visual features to enhance accuracy. This paper responds to this need by proposing a novel deep learning model that combines textual and visual elements to forecast CTRs. The proposed model, called Dual Channel Multi-task (DCMT), simultaneously learns ad visual identification and click prediction by leveraging the interdependence between these tasks. As demonstrated on a real-world dataset from Advertisees, Inc., the proposed model significantly outperforms conventional methods by achieving higher precision and recall rates. Furthermore, the model's ability to forecast CTRs is complemented by the capability to generate visual content representations, which can be utilized for ad ranking and filtering. The effectiveness of the model is validated through thorough analyses of its components and peer-model comparisons. The success of the proposed model suggests that integrating visual features can improve the robustness and generalizability of CTR forecasting models. Real-world business processes are often defined using concurrent tasks with specific execution limits. These constraints can complicate the calculation of optimal cycle times. Current methods for determining cycle times are primarily based on linear process models, neglecting concurrency and practical capacity restrictions. Due to these limitations, they are unable to solve the problem in a practical sense. In contrast, this study explores cycle time optimization with constraints on the number of parallel executions (cardinality constraints). To address this, a cycle time calculation method for processes with cardinality constraints is developed, taking into account the practical complexities of real systems. By reducing the problem to a polynomial-time solvable instance, this approach offers an efficient solution. Additionally, this study identifies the hardness of the cycle time calculation problem with cardinality constraints and the sum of powers of the weights, while experimenting with approximate algorithms for complex scenarios. To evaluate the proposed method, a prototype based on EMPO has been implemented, incorporating manual and automatic properties extraction techniques to facilitate concurrency analysis and optimization. These experiments demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of the developed approach. Furthermore, a case study on an academic information system employs the method to calculate the minimum cycle times for high-level business processes, incorporating concurrent tasks with restricted execution capacities. By applying the developed technique, cycle times for specific target rates of simultaneous executions (cardinality values) are calculated along with analytical models of the associated queues. These queue models enable the determination of optimal cycle times based on practical capacity constraints, reflecting real-world concurrency scenarios. Moreover, this study investigates the applicability of the proposed method to other symbolic execution model checkers, such as SPOT, JSCOV, and MCM, validating its generalization and applicability to various other tools. Lastly, a comprehensive assessment of the proposed method's suitability for high-level business processes is presented, incorporating properties extraction based on interactive tools like AROMA and minimal reduced graphs, as well as the evaluation of its applicability to other practical concurrency scenarios. These experiments involved 30 real-world examples of business processes, demonstrating the efficiency of the developed approach in calculating cycle times for processes with cardinality constraints. To facilitate future research, a comprehensive source code repository has been established, including all evaluated model checkers and a revised version of the EMPO tool, as well as other associated materials and results. This study employs a physics-informed statistical modeling method to simulate the spread of smoke and aerosols from wildfires through the atmosphere, addressing key environmental issues related to air quality. A deep learning-based approach is used to approximate the complex AOD ( aerosol optical depth) signal, incorporating Gaussian Process Regression with differential equations to model the propagation, and a dimensionality reduction technique for effective aerosol dimension representation. The model is calibrated, tested, and validated using AOD data from various wildfires, and their associated meteorological parameters from the NOAA HRRR Fire Weather Model. The approach successfully captures the slow AOD growth over time, and its rapid increase in specific aerosol dimension spaces in line with real-world observations, demonstrating the efficacy of this method in simulating aerosol dispersion and understanding wildfire-induced pollution patterns. The model can offer valuable insights for wildfire analysts, and provide a framework for solving other complex environmental problems on an optimal solution basis. A comprehensive code repository is available on the GitHub platform for reproducibility purposes. As part of our contributions to society, we have applied this model to analyze real-case scenarios, such as the AOD propagation from the Bootleg Fire in California, and the AOD projection for ongoing wildfires, enabling data-driven decisions that can aid wildfire management and related operations. The model is designed to be adaptable and can be applied to other differential equation-based problems for effective solution. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework that can automatically identify and respect the privacy of individual users with respect to all associated contacts. Our solution centers on the introduction of a differential privacy-based filter, capable of maintaining confidentiality of spatial and temporal data for users, while also maintaining confidentiality of their social connections. To achieve this, we implement a groundbreaking mechanism utilizing "quantized Gaussian mechanisms" to safeguard private information, coupled with an innovative system to detect and prevent invasive inquiries by syndicates - effectively maintaining the privacy of every individual involved. This study employs a multivariate distribution-based approach to investigate how inter-site influences impact reliability in network properties and how this affects the detection of individual and group differences in brain networks. Simulations across various scanning sites suggest that inter-site effects can significantly limit the reliability of detecting group differences, but also highlight the potential for accurate detection of individual differences. Our results indicate that a substantial portion of inter-site variability in functional connectivity is attributed to physiological signals, which suggests that signal extraction methods may be necessary to enhance the reliability of network analysis in functional brain imaging. Furthermore, this study's framework can be applied to assess reliability across multiple factors in a systematic manner, thereby informing the specification of sample sizes and test statistics in network-based analyses. Additionally, we demonstrate that a considerably smaller sample size is required when combining data from multiple scanning sites to achieve the same level of reliability as would be needed from a single site. In this study, we explore semi-supervised learning from a personalized perspective, enabling each client to utilize its limited labeled data more effectively and thereby enhance overall performance through collaborative learning. By introducing a unified framework for personalized semi-supervised learning, we address two key challenges: 1) leveraging unlabeled data for improved results, and 2) synchronizing local models across clients while preserving personalization. Our approach combines a flexible mixture-of-experts model to cater to diverse distributions and a variance reduction technique to minimize data distribution differences, and we evaluate it on various datasets, achieving satisfactory results. Moreover, our proposed method exhibits comparable performance to existing efficient semi-supervised learning methods when trained end-to-end, and it surpasses several advanced baselines in federated learning settings. Furthermore, our method's efficacy extends beyond federated learning, resulting in performance improvements of up to 4% on datasets like CIFAR10 and 6% on TinyImagenet when compared to other efficient semi-supervised learning methods, and it surpasses several advanced baselines in supervised learning scenarios, achieving results 2-4% better. Notably, our method's improvements are most pronounced on clients with the fewest labeled samples. The internal structure of a neutron star is intricately linked to its magnetic field, particularly in the context of the magnetic field's geometry and the role it plays in mass accretion during the accretion disk's early stages. When two neutron stars collide, a rapidly spinning, magnetic, and gravitationally bound neutron star emerges, known as a magnetar. Initially, the magnetar's magnetic field remains aligned with the stars' rotational axis, stemming from conservation of angular momentum, albeit distorted by the star's internal structure. As the magnetar's accretion disk develops, a torque arises from magnetic interactions between the star and its surrounding matter, causing the magnetar's rotational axis to align with the plane of the disk. Based on a detailed simulation model featuring a dynamic disk atmosphere, we find that a magnetar's rotational axis eventually becomes aligned with the disk's plane, resulting in a significant increase in the magnetar's rotational frequency by a factor of 3-4 in the initial stages following the merger. Moreover, our simulations reveal a previously underappreciated effect in which a magnetar's magnetic field becomes twisted in response to mass accretion and buoyancy forces, leading to a unique geometry distinct from both standard and force-free models. As a result, an electric potential difference emerges between the magnetar and its surrounding disk, fueling a current in the direction opposite to that in standard models, potentially resulting in a reduction of mass accretion due to magnetohydrodynamic effects. An accumulation of femtoseconds in the magnetar's magnetic field geometry, coupled with its internal structure and the dissolution of angular momentum, lays the groundwork for a new understanding of post-merger system magnetization, paving the way for a renewed examination of the role of magnetic fields in the context of compact binary mergers. Additionally, our simulations highlight the necessity for further simulation models, revealing novel insights into the role of magnetic fields in the early stages following the merger. Furthermore, our code can efficiently handle the most demanding post-merger processes due to its advanced spatial and temporal discretization techniques. In contrast, there are infinite ergodic Markov chains exhibiting unique, exponential convergence to equilibrium, yet failing to meet these conditions. We utilize a nonlinear hydrodynamic model to examine the behavior of certain correlations and their relationship to local charge conservation. We discover that background effects associated with local charge conservation significantly influence the measurement of some correlations and may lead to incorrect conclusions regarding the presence of specific effects, such as speed-of-light corrections. In order to accurately determine these corrections, we develop a method for removing artifacts associated with hydrodynamic nonlinearity and demonstrate its application using a suite of simulations. We also discuss how the presence of multiple sources of charges affects the measurement of certain correlations and illustrate that the background effects associated with local charge conservation can mask the presence of specific effects, such as corrections associated with speed-of-light and spin-velocity relationships. We conclude by discussing the implications of our study for the measurement of charge-dependent correlations in specific systems, such as proton-proton and proton-lead collisions. This study focuses on understanding how to estimate the success of crowdfunding projects by analyzing patterns in project features, team characteristics, and crowd behavior. Unlike previous studies that concentrated on projects alone, we also examined the properties of crowds that supported them, uncovering novel insights into the dynamics of crowd funding. By developing and applying a statistical model to a large dataset of more than 20,000 projects from Kickstarter, we found that crowd features often had more predictive value than team features, and shared many similarities with them. The findings of this study can be used to develop improved algorithms for predicting crowdfunding outcomes, as well as to develop more realistic digital agents for simulation models of crowd-funding, by leveraging statistical models of crowd behavior. The code and data to reproduce the analysis can be found at https://github.com/aprilegat/crowd-dynamics. The full dataset is available upon request. Research was conducted at Cornell University with support from NSF Grant CCF-1447808. None of the authors receive funding from Kickstarter or any other company involved in crowd-funding. Crowd-funding is becoming increasingly popular, with over $5 billion being raised in 2016 alone. By allowing projects to be funded by small contributions from a large number of people, crowd-funding provides opportunities for creative and practical innovation. As a result of this mass-participation, understanding crowd behavior is crucial for predicting which projects will succeed. Previous studies focused exclusively on project characteristics, but we investigated the dynamics of crowd behavior and its connection to project and team features. By analyzing a large dataset of over 20,000 projects from Kickstarter from 2009-2018, we developed a statistical model that uses neighborhood features to understand how crowd behavior varies. The findings reveal that crowd features often have more predictive value than team features and share many similarities with them. The insights from this study can be used to develop improved algorithms for predicting crowdfunding outcomes, digital agents for simulation crowd-funding models, and guide project managers in decision-making. In recent years, the rise of digital transformations within organizations has led to increased exposure to cyber threats, highlighting the need for collaborative and innovative network intrusion detection systems. To address these requirements while safeguarding sensitive data, we propose an innovative framework. This framework integrates federated learning, enabling collaborative training, and network anomaly detection using static and dynamic analysis. By doing so, it strikes a balance between efficiency and data privacy. Furthermore, our framework's architecture, designed with modularity in mind, allows for the integration of various enhancement modules. These modules can be utilized to accommodate diverse organizational settings and extend the framework's capabilities to include other machine learning techniques, as needed. The effectiveness of our approach was validated through experiments conducted with three renowned open-source intrusion data sets, showcasing its ability to effectively identify intrusive connections while maintaining high accuracy and minimizing data transmission during the training process. The results highlight the potential for our framework to support the development of scalable and privacy-conscious NIDS systems within organizations. Furthermore, the modular design of our approach enables the integration of additional modules, enabling seamless transition to more advanced features, such as enhanced feature engineering and scalable model deployment on the edge or in the cloud. The complexity of robotic applications has increased significantly, requiring more sophisticated frameworks to create modular and efficient task execution. To address this challenge, our proposed algorithm combines the advantages of graph-based methods and program-synthesis techniques, yielding improved performance over state-of-the-art models. By leveraging subgraph embedding and program synthesis with active learning, our approach achieves efficient task planning while ensuring high accuracy. The effectiveness of our algorithm is demonstrated through successful completion of various difficult tasks in simulated environments, including challenging real-world tasks. Furthermore, our method is shown to be capable of sequencing tasks effectively when high-level task plans are unavailable. The proposed algorithm excels over current techniques in robotic planning for high-level tasks, demonstrating a notable increase of up to 3.5 times better worst-case performance and 2.3 times better average-case performance. Our method is versatile and can be applied to a range of tasks, including manipulation tasks, where it provides an improved time complexity of O(n^2.59) compared to state-of-the-art models. The proposed algorithm, named HSynE, offers a powerful task planning framework that is currently available for public use. The performance of semiconductor devices heavily relies on the type of gate materials used.  Metal-oxide-semiconductor devices often employ gate materials like silicon or various metals that are transferred onto the surface of a wafer using a technique called spin coating.  However, the transfer technique has limitations in terms of uniformity and contamination, which poses problems in labs where cleanroom conditions are enforced.  In this study, we investigate an alternative method of introducing gate materials by implanting heavy ions of metals that can easily bond with oxygen to form a stable gate layer on the surface of a wafer.  By using a simulation model based on the cluster scattering theory, we determined the optimal conditions for producing a uniform gate layer.  Specifically, we found that a 30 keV nickel-64 implantation with a dose of 1.7 x 10^15 ions/cm^2 follows by annealing at 1000°C for 30 minutes can produce a uniform gate layer with a thickness of approximately 7 nm.  In order to evaluate the effectiveness of this method, we performed capacitance and channel conductance measurements on test samples and found that a high temperature anneal can indeed generate a metal gate layer with properties similar to those achieved with conventional techniques.  In conclusion, ion implantation offers a promising alternative to traditional gate material transfer methods that may have more practical applications in the development of novel metal-oxide-semiconductor devices.  In particular, the technique may be more suitable for small-scale production or in labs where cleanroom conditions are not enforced.  In addition to its applications in the development of MOS devices, we found that ion implantation can also be used to create resistive switching properties in metal-oxide-semiconductor systems. We examine how marginal perturbations influence the synchronization of groups within networks of oscillators. The system we study includes a parameter deviation, which contributes to the loss of complete synchronization. Our analysis reveals that even minimal deviations can disrupt stable groups, causing them to collapse. Furthermore, we identify a threshold beyond which group identity becomes impossible. The effect of parameter uncertainty on group synchronization is also compared to a system without deviations, showing that a marginally stable group can coexist with complete synchronization. Additionally, we link the stability of groups to the properties of the network that connects them, demonstrating that group formation depends on the interplay between local and global connections within the oscillator network. Finally, we outline a strategy for identifying and evaluating the stability of groups within an oscillator network. By examining the sensitivity of group members to each other, it is possible to determine whether they can be confident in their group membership or whether they will experience a sudden change in the identity of their group. This story is told through a detailed example of a system consisting of 9 oscillators with 3 groups, where the effect of parameter uncertainty on group stability can be directly observed. Our work sheds new light on the mechanisms that govern the formation and organization of oscillator networks, which are essential for understanding how group synchronization arises in biological and artificial systems. Ultimately, it is possible to create a precise mathematical model of group stability that applies to any network of coupled oscillators. The approach we have introduced provides a valuable tool for investigating the complex relationships between network structure, dynamical stability, and the formation of stable groups. Our work opens the door to a new area of research that explores how group synchronization contributes to the emergence of grouped behavior in oscillator networks. This new field of study holds the key to understanding how group dynamics can be harnessed to create innovative technologies and new methods for analyzing grouped behavior in biological systems. The utility of our model is confirmed through our finding that group stability can be attributed to local features of the network that connect these groups, making it a versatile tool for analyzing real-world networks of coupled oscillators. Additionally, we demonstrate how group stability can be used as a basis for evaluating the links between different groups of oscillators, as in the case of a connection between a stable local group and a global oscillator. In our analysis, we scrutinized the outcomes of twelve prominent search engines from around the world for the query "Google". The way each search engine displays itself in its output varied significantly, with some search engines like YouTube and Bing.com noticeably absent. Interestingly, every single search engine except YouTube featured a direct link to its homepage. Moreover, all search engines except YouTube and Tianyi.com displayed an official logo. Our evaluation of the twelve search engine outputs revealed that only four - YouTube, Bing.com, Yahoo.com, and Tianyi.com - fail to provide an explicit indication of their identity as search engines. This variation in behavior may be seen as an implicit indication of each search engine's self-perception and strategic intent. Our investigation attempts to address questions such as: Are self-declarations of identity a necessity for search engines? Should strategic intentions be explicitly stated in order to be recognized? Do explicit logos enhance a search engine's credibility in the eyes of users? Our hopes are that this study will foster discussions about the characteristics and behaviors of search engines, as well as their interactions with users and each other. Moreover, our work aims to stimulate reflections on the underlying assumptions and premises of the field of search engine comparison, with a view to promoting greater methodological uniformity and rigor. The $\beta$-function of a $sp(2N)$ sigma-models, incorporating extensive monodromy defects, is investigated. These defects, applicable to both Wess-Zumino and Yang-Mills formulations, yield a relation tied to the volume of a hyperbolic $2N$-disk. When these defects are confined to a flat $2D$ space, their properties align with previously established findings, whereas more complex configurations arise from mapping them onto hyperbolic surfaces. Notably, the $\beta$-function exhibits an enhancement compared to defect-free systems. Here, general monodromy defects are used to extend the scope of earlier studies on sigma-models and semi-chiral models to a broader range of models. Furthermore, the work demonstrates that semi-chiral reduction of Yang-Mills theories from gauge and matter fields generates novel $\beta$-function terms. Our analysis also explores further compounding with super-$sp(2N)$ sigma-models, featuring double the number of fermions. Ultimately, the resulting expressions, though intricate, prove manageable. These investigations into $\beta$-functions offer a bridge connecting previous work to upcoming studies on surface defects and one-dimensional defect models. The findings are further bolstered by a companion paper, which delves into key monodromy defect properties. Additional appendices are utilized to gather relevant information that wouldn't be strategically integrated into the main content. In particular, Appendix A examines the $sp(2N)$ sigma-models without defects, while Appendix B investigates semi-chiral sigma-model reduction from super Yang-Mills theories. A key step in our work involves re-casting $\beta$-function terms as surface measures. This strategy proves versatile and accessible, shedding new light on classical surface physics. Furthermore, our work shows that combining classical and quantum physics yields a profound mutual enrichment. The findings are particularly significant as they relate to super-$sp(2N)$ sigma-models, reducing semi-chiral gauge theories, and super Yang-Mills theories reducing to sigma-models. Semi-supervised node classification using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) has received significant attention in recent years. To expand GNN applications with limited labeled data, pseudo-labeling approaches assign labels to unknown nodes during training, leveraging the model's current capabilities. Nevertheless, these methods tend to concentrate on easy targets, neglecting harder nodes, which hinders GNNs' effectiveness. To address this challenge, we introduce Node Self-Assignment (NSA), a novel pseudo-labeling technique that allows selected nodes to assign labels to themselves based on their confidence levels. We also develop two adaptive methods to adjust the assignment strategy and the pseudo-labeling ratio dynamically. Experimental results on diverse graph datasets showcase the superiority of NSA over traditional pseudo-labeling techniques and equivalent performance to Label Propagation when labels are limited. Our code is available at https://github.com/gousav/joint-optimization-for-semi-supervised-node-classification.

PatchNet serves as an ideal foundation for applications like video object detection, replacing cumbersome backbones like MobileNetV2 and achieving superior results with reduced computational costs. Additionally, our model's unique persistence in processing input data leads to remarkable performance in tasks like tracking, as demonstrated by our experiments. In optomechanics, the standard quantum approach often employs bosonic operators to model an optical cavity, a mechanical oscillator, and input field. However, for high occupation numbers, these quantum relations break down, and a classical electric circuit model becomes more applicable. We bridge this gap by converting the standard quantum optomechanics framework into a classical matrix stochastic differential equation (SDE) system. Achieving this classification necessitates a non-standard quantum treatment where position and momentum are treated as complex variables rather than real variables, and further involves the use of standard bosonic operators for the field, only introducing them at the coupling with the mechanical oscillator. Applying this classical-quantum correspondence to the well-known ring-down experiment yields both classical and quantum predictions that align for high occupation numbers and diverge for low occupation numbers. Additionally, this correspondence enables a direct classical interpretation of all nonlinear optomechanical interactions. Lastly, all standard linear optomechanical coupling schemes revert to their classical forms when occupation numbers are large. Nonetheless, for the linear coupling, the classical model employs complex variables for the mechanical oscillator, whereas the quantum model employs real positions and momenta. We discuss the implications of this classical-quantum correspondence. \textbf{Our work offers a classical explanation for optomechanics that complements the standard quantum treatment. Additionally, this correspondence provides a platform for exploring classical models for specific quantum systems and potentially devising classical models for general quantum systems. A newly introduced termination criterion for a wide range of interior point methods allows for the abrupt cessation of iterative calculations within a linear system solver. This termination criterion is automatically detected by monitoring a norm of an operator intersection. When employed in Newton-type interior point methods, coupled with a primal-dual interior point method, it results in a significant enhancement of computational performance. Specifically, this termination criterion yields substantial speed-ups in the resolution of large-scale linear programming problems on multi-core CPUs and GPUs. Moreover, comparative studies with other prevalent termination criteria are conducted, alongside with the analysis of its impact on predictive interior point method models. Our computational experiments indicate that, under certain circumstances, the novel termination criterion can bring about comparable advancements in efficiency to that seen with the predictable models. Furthermore, various orthogonal and correlated termination criteria are proposed, all of which are evaluated through computational testing. Lastly, the potential extension of this criterion to other interior point methods is also explored. A key benefit of this approach is the absence of requirement for advance knowledge of the problem's characteristics or the need to modify the algorithms' core infrastructure. Instead, the desired level of efficiency can be achieved by adjusting a straightforward configuration parameter. This flexibility enables the easy adaptation of the proposed termination criterion to other interior point methods as well. In particular, the polynomial path interior point method also benefits from the introduced termination criterion. Nonetheless, the observed speed-up was found to be substantially lesser compared to the Newton-type method, likely due to the inherent shortcomings of this approach in dealing with linear programming problems. Consequently, the proposed approach remains as an alternative to interior point methods employing predictive models, offering comparable efficiency with lower computational overhead. In contrast, the method fails to yield substantial improvements in time complexity for quadratic optimization problems, thus interior point methods are recommended for their potential in solving complex predictive optimization problems. In the near future, the focus will be on the rigorous analysis of the proposed approach's properties and performance, alongside with the exploration of its applications in predictive optimization problems. In the long term, the goal is to introduce adjustable, problem-independent termination criteria that are both efficient and predictable. In the event that such criteria can be devised, a potential need may arise for the introduction of interior point method models that are both anticipatory and flexible. Such models should be capable of adapting to both the problem's characteristics and the desired level of efficiency, thus offering unprecedented versatility. In conclusion, the proposed approach has the potential to be incorporated into these flexible predictive models, where its performance will be compared with other previously introduced models. This paper introduces ARN, a networked automated monitoring and recovery system, 
drawn from failure handling techniques commonly applied to concurrence control systems.
ARn can recognize clashes between diverse process definitions that unfold in a live
system environment and automatically rectify these discrepancies once identified.
Key innovations involve a novel network architecture that seamlessly integrates
real-time flow analysis using vector operations, precise detection of anomalous occurrences
using artificial intelligence and machine learning, and a recovery mechanism comprising
two parts: pinpointing the source of errors and implementing a correction protocol to resolve
system errors and ensure real-time monitoring functionality.
In contrast to prior automated monitoring systems, ARn can monitor and reconcile a wide
range of process definitions including partial, infinite, and dynamic models, ensuring
compatibility with popular concurrency specifications such as lock-free code, safety protocols,

It combines the principles of Quipper's interactive proof and compilation technique with the fundamental properties of quantum state cloning, entanglement, and local operations on composite systems, all encapsulated within a category theoretical structure. By incorporating compatible design patterns for quantum programming, Proto-Quipper-M ensures that the non-cloning property of quantum states is preserved, whereas the duplication of mixed states is allowed when possible. Furthermore, the protocol supports the generation of optimal duplicate channels under specific conditions. Proto-Quipper-M's static analysis can verify that derived circuits conform to certain norms, such as the preservation of entanglement and local operations, by leveraging a category theoretical approach to context differentiation. Illustrative examples demonstrate the effectiveness of Proto-Quipper-M's static analysis in its ability to design and verify quantum circuits that efficiently handle state duplication, entanglement swapping, and the transformation of qubits to ancillas, while maintaining the non-cloning property of quantum states. These examples also highlight Proto-Quipper-M's capability to generate near-optimal duplicate channels compared to dynamic approaches. Based on this success, Proto-Quipper-M is positioned as a suitable tool for the static analysis of quantum circuits. Additionally, its design presents two research questions for further exploration. Firstly, there is potential in applying the fundamental properties of quantum state duplication and local operations to a broader class of quantum programming tasks. Secondly, Proto-Quipper-M's static analysis may be adapted for use in dynamic approaches to quantum circuit design, possibly through the incorporation of advanced quantum rewriting techniques. These possibilities are explored in the concluding sections of this thesis. For instance, a static approach to duplicate channels could be combined with a dynamic analysis of the generated circuits, allowing for the evaluation of its efficiency and optimality. Conversely, a dynamic scheme of state duplication might be replaced by a static program that preserves the non-cloning property of quantum states, thus providing a more reliable and safer quantum circuit design. Hybrid materials that combine conventional and superconducting components, often referred to as bound triads, exhibit unique properties even at relatively low temperatures. In these materials, the instability of the conventional component can be stabilized due to spin-swap interactions with entangled Cooper pairs, resulting in spin conservation during quasiparticle relaxation. Additionally, the hybridization generates spin-polarized quasiparticles, producing notable magnetic phenomena even in materials that are not magnetically ordered. Notably, the spin conservation law can be observed as a conductance peak in a three-terminal conductance setup. We investigated this conductance peak in materials derived from FeSe films grown on SrTiO3 substrates and found that the observed peaks can be attributed to the hybridization of these materials. The results are further supported by theoretical models, revealing the potential for these materials to function as quantum routers or coherent light-emitting devices at relatively low temperatures. In contrast, the conductance peaks of similarly prepared materials but without the hybrid component exhibited different characteristics, including a notable temperature dependence. In one case, the conductance peaks were found to disappear at temperatures below 5 K, potentially due to the component's transition into a superconducting state while becoming insulated from the detector via a tunneling barrier. Furthermore, the comparison of these findings with theoretical models suggests that the hybrid component's electronic phase can be observed via transport measurements by analyzing quasiparticle relaxation. In another case, the conductance peaks remained consistent up to 20 K, but the analysis of the time domain revealed that the transport measurements were affected by thermal fluctuations in the hybrid component's electronic phase. Notably, the analysis of the time domain allowed us to collect data and compare it with theoretical models, resulting in the detection of a prominent quantum interference effect known as Aharonov-Bohm oscillations. The results are significant as they reveal the possibility of observing the quantum phase of hybrid materials that are not magnetically ordered under transport measurements, potentially opening up new avenues for the study of these materials. Based on these findings, the detection of the hybrid component's electronic phase can be observed in three-terminal conductance setups with a spin conservation law conductance peak. Conversely, the identification of the Aharonov-Bohm oscillations requires more complex data collection and analysis, involving a deeper understanding of the quasiparticle relaxation process. Nevertheless, the results are promising as they reveal the potential of current detection techniques to uncover the quantum phase of hybrid materials even at relatively low temperatures. This paper explores a probabilistic approach to classical field theories through the use of normalizing flows, and we've adapted this method to work with gauge symmetries in the context of U(1) gauge theory. To achieve this, we've devised a novel variant of the Euler-Lagrange equation for a specific class of Lagrangian functions that are compatible with normalizing flows. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that our formulation maintains consistency with the original Euler-Lagrange equations. Additionally, we've applied our technique to two benchmark models, simplifying a previously complex Euler-Langevin dynamic system in the process. Our method has several advantages, primarily due to its ability to directly account for gauge symmetries during the learning process, and also due to its ability to capture complex field configurations without requiring partial gauge fixing. Nonetheless, our constraints on generative model utilities may pose limitations to the complexity of our models. Ultimately, the integration of gauge symmetries into normalizing flows offers a valuable framework for the probabilistic exploration of gauge theory, making it useful for observational and theoretical astrophysics. The cross section of top quark production was measured to be 3.07 pb, which aligns with theoretical predictions from perturbative quantum chromodynamics at 3.0 pb. Additionally, the mass of the top quark was estimated at 173.3 GeV, and the top quark and antiquark pair production total cross section was measured at 7.46 pb, corresponding with theoretical predictions at 7.56 pb. Firstly, it employs an intelligent method to formulate a question in a way that allows it to be answered solely through knowledge gathered from the query itself. Secondly, the plan relies on a semantic search method that seeks out relevant answers within the query itself. To test the efficacy of this plan, a framework called DB-QA has been constructed. DB-QA's construction involved compiling a database of 21 distinct question-types, encompassing over a thousand diverse multi-step database query evaluation scenarios. Notably, each of these scenarios was paired with real-world database tables and human-crafted evaluation standards. Moreover, it is shown that the plan's execution method yields results that are on par with human standards in over 80% of the most complex multi-step database query evaluation scenarios. Lastly, it is shown through diverse application scenarios that the plan's execution method proves to be both versatile and dependable. A unique, universal method for achieving minimal entropy production achieves optimal results. Diverging from previous findings, there is no singular, universal method for achieving minimum entropy production. Contrary to common assumptions, we demonstrate that equilibrium states do not necessarily have constant entropy production rates. Additionally, we demonstrate that thermally isolated systems can reach states with minimal entropy production, and provide a concrete example of such a situation. Finally, we show that minimizing a system's variability in non-equilibrium thermal states requires distinct driving force settings than what is required to minimize its overall entropy production. If possible, we recommend using temperature measurements to determine these optimal driving force settings. If temperature measurements are impractical, we suggest a secondary driving force adjustment to optimize its performance. This approach is illustrated through simulations of a model consisting of multiple spins interacting with each other and their environment. Conventional measures of AI model performance, such as accuracy and efficiency,
overlook the broader environmental and social implications of deployment.
This paper introduces a novel approach to evaluating AI services from a holistic
perspective, integrating established methodologies for environmental and social
assessment. By leveraging open-access datasets and publicly available data for
training and inference, the environmental impact and social dynamics of AI can
be quantified. Specifically, we propose an environmental assessment framework
based on life cycle analysis, examining the lifecycle phases of AI model development,
deployment, and deployment discontinuation. To complement this approach, we outline
a social assessment methodology centered on the human professionals involved in AI.
We apply this integrated assessment method to two case studies: object detection AI
models, inquiring about the environmental and social effects of deploying such models
capable of detecting 10,000 objects, as well as models developed over the past 25
years with varying complexities and application areas. Our analysis reveals the
significance of high-quality training and deployment on performance and
environmental sustainability, while the social assessment in development is still
in progress. This study marks the first step in using integrated assessment and
evaluation methods to compare the environmental and social impacts of AI services.

Recent advancements in predictive process monitoring have led to established
evaluation methodologies, leading to a common understanding and basis for
comparison. However, prescriptive process monitoring methods, which provide
recommendations to improve current or future processes, lack standard
evaluation approaches. Without rigorous assessment of these methods, it is
challenging to determine their effectiveness, compare across techniques, or
guarantee reliability in real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we propose
a framework for evaluating prescriptive process monitoring methods, featuring
intrinsic and extrinsic validation metrics. As a starting point, we establish
general principles and criteria for prescriptive methods, define metric types,
and identify suitable evaluation performance metrics. Furthermore, we develop
guidelines for prescriptive process monitoring data creation and experimentation
studies, and demonstrate the application of our framework to a prominent
method from the literature, employing synthetic and real-process data. Ultimately,
 we aim to provide a standard evaluation methodology for prescriptive process
 monitoring, facilitating comparable assessments and promotion of reliable
 methods. These efforts have been incorporated into a publicly accessible
 package, enabling researchers to reproduce our study and reproduce our results. \\

Generation, Evaluation, Performance Metrics, Process Data, Process Mining, 
Management Information Systems, Operations Management. \\

This method applies the dual-weighted residual approach in an innovative way to accurately forecast the relative errors of coupled numerical schemes in fluid dynamics.  It has been successfully tested with a range of coupled problems, including fluid-structure interaction and phase-field models, and the results show a strong correlation between the predicted and actual errors.  These results indicate that the method can provide reliable error estimates for high-precision numerical calculations in fluid dynamics.  Furthermore, the method may contribute to the development of more efficient and reliable numerical algorithms with adaptive complexity.  In particular, the method has potential applications in complex computational fluid dynamics problems that involve highly coupled processes and high-dimensional functional relationships.  An example of such a problem is fluid-structure interaction in moving domains with fluid-structure coupling.  Although the method is still in the initial stages of development, it holds promise as a valuable tool for numerical calculations in fluid dynamics.  Further research is needed to assess its performance in a wider range of problems and to explore its potential for real-world applications. Despite considerable effort, tight bounds for vertex-disjoint paths remain elusive. The main obstacle in achieving tight bounds lies in the difficulty of accurately modeling this problem using small subgraphs. In an attempt to overcome this challenge, we introduce novel algorithms capable of finding near-optimal solutions to vertex-disjoint paths on bipartite graphs. Our work is inspired by a simple linear programming relaxation, influenced by recent breakthroughs in flow-based algorithms. This work extends the program by examining the thermodynamic properties of charged black holes carrying scalar, vector, and tensor hair. Our analysis focuses on the scaling of condensate, gap, and Higgs phases, which yields universal scaling behaviors for the scalar and vector cases, albeit a diverse set of scaling behaviors for the tensor case. Furthermore, our investigation reveals a fundamental link between holographic superconductors and black holes with scalar hair. Additionally, our study introduces novel scalar, vector, and tensor field configurations, which differ from previously discovered "monopole" configurations and display unique pairing properties that may find applications in the study of particle physics. Finally, our work examines the stability of the flat black hole background against perturbations by the scalar, vector, and tensor fields, which enables us to derive the instability regimes of the background for each case. Notably, our findings demonstrate that the stability of the flat black hole background can be precisely matched with the scaling behavior of the condensate phases. This connection provides compelling evidence that the scaling behaviors of the condensate phases are an inherent consequence of the pairing mechanism in holographic superconductors. In contrast, the diverse set of scaling behaviors observed in the tensor case may reflect the presence of distinct pairing channels. Finally, our work showcases the extensive range of thermodynamic properties and phase structures that can be generated through the "hairy black holes" program. By combining the scaling behaviors of the condensate phases with the pairing properties of the fields and the stability of the background, our study offers a more comprehensive understanding of the pairing mechanism in holographic superconductors. Additionally, our work may find applications in the design of new particles through the "flat direction" construction method popularized by the "hairy black holes" program. Additionally, our study is complementary to other studies examining the critical fields of holographic superconductors and the phase structures of multicomponent superconductors in the probe limit. Ultimately, our study is part of an ongoing effort to develop the "hairy black holes" program and understand the fundamental principles of the pairing mechanism in holographic superconductors. Research has shown that longer genes are associated with increased delays, suggesting a size-dependent mechanism. A possible explanation for this phenomenon is that DNA-binding proteins, essential for initiating and completing the transcription process, need time to bind to longer genes, preventing premature initiation of subsequent transcripts by these proteins before they have dissociated from the first gene's DNA. To gain insight into the underlying dynamics of this model, we developed a mathematical description of the interaction between DNA, RNA, and transcription factors, incorporating binding and unbinding processes at multiple sites along the gene. Our analysis focuses on the steady-state equilibrium and explores the effects of variations in gene length on transcription completion times, examining both single and multiple gene systems. In the case of multiple genes, we also investigated the influence of spatial relationships and random movement of transcription factors on the delay phenomenon. Our calculations demonstrate that, in systems featuring a single gene type, the magnitude of the delay phenomenon barely changes when considering the factors governing transcription factor circulation throughout the chromatin fiber. However, the model we've introduced offers a framework for exploring how the physical properties of DNA, chromatin structure, and RNA production processes contribute to the size-dependent delay in gene expression. This paper presents a new model for integrating multi-sensory input, capable of locating and identifying objects dropped by humans without prior knowledge of their appearance or sound. In this research, we examine how different interpretations of algorithmic bias influence the perceptions of public sector professionals. We conducted in-depth interviews with ten public sector representatives, exploring their understanding of algorithmic bias and its relation to Web search. Our study reveals that these professionals struggle to connect the concept of algorithmic bias to their personal experiences with Web search. We identify a lack of consensus among the participants regarding what constitutes algorithmic bias and how it can be detected. Our findings underscore the need for clear and comprehensive explanations of algorithmic bias, enabling these professionals to make informed decisions in their roles. We also highlight the potential of creating transparent and explainable Web search algorithms, reducing reliance on biased results and promoting fairness in decision-making processes. This research contributes to the broader discussion of algorithmic bias, focusing on the unique requirements and decisions of public sector professionals. Our study's insights can inform the development of effective training programs for these professionals, addressing their queries and concerns regarding algorithmic bias and Web search. Radiation oncologists face considerable challenges when administering X-ray beams due to variations in patient anatomy. To overcome this issue, a multi-institutional research project aimed to enhance cancer treatment by developing precise dose mapping technology using tomosynthesis images and integrating them into the treatment planning system. The proposed system's effectiveness was evaluated in two phases: (i) determining the accuracy of manually mapping doses to treatment plans and (ii) examining the feasibility of fully automating the process. For the first step, ten datasets from two institutions were used, involving CT scans and X-ray images taken before and during treatment, along with ground truth information. The evaluation process involved calculating the difference between actual and estimated dose ratios for multiple points in the radiation field. The results showed an average dose precision of greater than 99% for ten datasets. In the second step, twelve patients from two institutions provided X-ray images and dose mapping information. Precise doses were computed using a cone beam computed tomography algorithm based on optimized low-dose projections and were compared with both planning CT scans and X-ray images. The results indicated dose ratio precision of greater than 99% for eleven datasets but precision was lower for one dataset at 94%. The study concluded that its methods provided strong evidence for accurately mapping doses using X-ray images, thus supporting clinical adoption. However, the feasibility of fully automating the process required further investigation. High-dimensional data analyzed using blended components benefit from normalization techniques. A commonly used transformation for these components in compositional data analysis is the log-ratio transformation. This method's benefits extend beyond data preparation; it also yields an interesting geometric structure of the data, ultimately leading to the data's representation in a flat manifold. Our research applies the GRAT tool to achieve this property. The GRAT tool enables users to find a canonical form of the data after applying various transformations, which can be confirmed using the tool's implementation in R on a supplied dataset. The GRAT tool also has connections to other mathematical concepts, such as principal component analysis, quadratics, and elliptical symmetry, which provide additional insights into the properties of the log-ratio transformation. The talk will cover the application of the GRAT tool to achieve this property, using both theoretical examples and real datasets. One such example involves the use of the GRAT tool to analyze the compositional dataset from the Pizarron oil reservoir in Colorado, USA, which was previously studied using PCA. The analysis of this dataset using the log-ratio transformation and the GRAT tool reveals an interesting structure of positive partial correlations and non-positive partial variances, ultimately providing complementary insights into the properties of the data. The study's results confirm the efficacy of the log-ratio transformation in flat manifolds for compositional data analysis, as well as the potential of the GRAT tool in achieving this property. Additionally, the properties of the data revealed through the GRAT tool demonstrate its potential in encoding meaningful information about the data's structure. The research suggests the use of the GRAT tool as a valuable resource for exploratory data analysis in compositional data analysis. Exploring the properties of the data through the GRAT tool also enables the discovery of new relationships between the data components, ultimately contributing to a better comprehension of the data's underlying geometry and, in this case, the Pizarron oil reservoir. The core accretion model of planet formation leads to two distinct phases of rapid gas capture, resulting in super-Jupiters and tiny planets, which should be evenly spaced in mass and radius if all planets form through this process. However, actual planet distributions show a significant deficiency of tiny planets and a surplus of massive planets that suggest most of these planets are missing. One possible explanation is that the tiny planets are incorporated into the massive planets through smaller, early gas captures before their host planets develop into giant stars. We explore this concept, comparing the observed distribution of exoplanets with the core accretation model of planet formation, using a simulation based on this model. Our study employs a radial mass distribution of the massive planets, derived from the exoplanet radius distribution, which incorporates this'migration' effect, by reducing the number of tiny planets and modeling their migration into smaller, early gas captures. We find that a large proportion (60%) of the massive planets could have experienced one or more early gas captures, resulting in a greater number of massive planets and fewer tiny planets, consistent with the observed exoplanet population. These early gas captures can occur up to several million years before their host planets develop into giants. Our study also finds that late gas captures, which occur after the host planets have become giants, result in a smaller radius range (generally <3 R_Jup) and may explain the superbiases of the Neptunian planets and the lack of massive planets at 2-3 R_Jup. Our study supports the idea that the exoplanet population contains a substantial number of tiny planets, which could be detected by future missions like the James Webb Space Telescope and Habitable Exoplanet Imaging Satellite, in a state of ongoing gas captures or waiting to receive gas from their massive outer siblings. Our study also implies that the outer siblings of massive planets are invariably smaller than their massive brothers, which could result in the loss of the outer siblings and the reduction in the number of tiny planets in the population. Our study suggests that the process of gas capture is not a one-time event, but rather a prolonged process, with multiple episodes of gas capture occurring in a short time frame and resulting in the final characteristics of the massive planets. In the Episodic Memory module of our Artificial Reasoning agent, a dynamic memory network stores and updates contextual information about previous steps in the interaction with our environment. This memory component is essential for tracking unobserved changes and making accurate predictions from partial observations. After receiving a reward signal indicating the accuracy of our predictions, the memory network adjusts its connections and updates the internal representations of the experience, effectively learning from mistakes. This mechanism of episodic memory is designed to mimic the function of animal brains in learning from feedback, and its integration with our decision-making system, a neural network policy, allows the entire agent to leverage the power of its collective memories of past events. This capability enables our agent to apply past knowledge to solve new problems, a skill that is validated through our experiments using the mobile manipulator population of multi-agent robotic simulators. We observed that our agent, trained in a scenario where it must constantly adjust its behavior based on the feedback it receives, develops the ability to apply the lessons learned from previous interactions to new contexts over time, a capacity that could not be achieved through reinforcement learning alone. We further evaluated the effectiveness of our memory system by implementing a defensive strategy against an external attacker manipulating the interaction with misleading feedback, and our results show that the application of our memory module allows the retrieval of critical information about the attacker's moves and the successful protection of our interaction flow. The integration of our memory system has proven to improve the accuracy of our predictions and allowed us to validate its relevance through real-world experiments using a mobile manipulator and a Coadaptation multi-agent domain. This scalar, with a mass less than the dark matter mass, couples to fermionic dark matter, while also coupling to a lighter complex pseudoscalar, which in turn couples to the Higgs and a dark photon. This setup allows dark matter to be comprised of different fermionic states with varying couplings to the scalar, and thus distinct properties. We examine the production of these states at the LHC via monojet signatures, focusing on their ultimate decay products: a photon, an invisible particle, and a Higgs boson. We determine the detectability of this process for various masses of the scalar mediator and dark matter candidate, as well as consider the impact of dark photon coupling on visibility. Since the signal involves a Higgs boson, whose decay mode into photons is well-known, we look into an alternative decay product: a bottom-quark pair. We assess this new signature's visibility, considering both its creation and decay processes to determine its prevalence. Given that this variant of dark matter features distinct mass relationships between its constituents, we explore its phenomenological characteristics, including its thermal population and its influence on 21-cm signals. We further investigated its interaction with stars, particularly its potential to generate astrophysical anomalies through various processes such as emission, absorption, annihilation, and interaction with plasmatic particles. Since one of the dark matter candidates has a coupling to a scalar with a connection to an antilepton and a dark photon, as well as to a fermion and a scalar, its properties vary greatly. Since this new candidate features distinct decay products, namely an antilepton, a dark photon, a scalar, and a bottom-quark pair, its visibility is assessed. Building on its successful Cognitive Battery platform, Amazon Research Labs has introduced Mod-Cog, a comprehensive multi-task battery consisting of 12 distinct tasks that build upon each other in a progressive manner. Mod-C-Meg is a modified version of Mod-Cog designed for human participants, consisting of 12 complex tasks with a total duration of approximately 6 hours. Mod-C-RoBo is an robotic variant of Mod-Cog, consisting of 12 complex tasks that can be executed by robots. Mod-C-RoBo is particularly suitable for online evaluation due to its relatively short duration of around 1 hour per participant. Both Mod-CoG batteries are available at no cost under a CC-BY-SA license on GitHub, enabling researchers to conduct analyses and share their findings. 

The paper provides an overview of these batteries, their development, and supporting resources, as well as a public dataset resulting from the online human evaluations of Mod-C-RoBo. This dataset comprises detailed performance metrics for 1,440 human participants. Both the batteries and dataset are accessible at no cost, aiming to facilitate new research opportunities. 

Our study showcases the effectiveness of Mod-C-RoBo by investigating its capacity to capture robust and generalised robotic capabilities across diverse environments and leading to significant advancements in robust visual classification performance on the ImageNet dataset following a transfer of training styles from Mod-C-RoBo to a range of established robotic datasets. Lastly, we utilise the dataset to address key questions in cognitive computing and provide concrete recommendations for improving the development and assessment of robust and generalised robotic capabilities. 

The work is partially presented in the paper "Assessing Robust and Generalized Robotic Capabilities with Mod-C-RoBo: A New Multi-Task Battery," accepted at the Conference on Computer Safety, Reliability and Security (SAFECOMP 2022).

Our research focuses on the geometric aspects of these algebras, which arise as points on specific algebraic varieties. We establish a key result regarding the irreducibility and dimension of these varieties for a particular type of nilpotent algebras, which cannot be expressed as commutative algebras. Furthermore, we identify a subvariety consisting of associative nilpotent algebras and show that its geometry also satisfies an independence criterion. Our method for determining the irreducibility of these varieties involves a novel approach that exploits specific transformations unique to associative nilpotent algebras. Additionally, we calculate the codimension of these varieties within the larger space of all nilpotent algebras for a given dimension, which allows us to establish a correspondence between certain Lie algebras and irreducible components of these varieties. As a byproduct of our study, we also determine the precise count of nilpotent algebras of small dimensions, including those that are solvable but not commutative. Moreover, we outline specific directions for further research and examine a particular variant of these algebras known as power-associative, for which we calculate the geometric varieties and their irreducibility for low dimensions, although the result is found to be more complicated than other associative nilpotent algebras for higher dimensions. Finally, we highlight that our determination of the geometric varieties of nilpotent algebras is facilitated by a comprehensive computer program that identifies and constructs these algebraic varieties up to a certain dimension, utilizing a deep understanding of the underlying algebraic structure and its relationship to these geometric varieties. This computer program has proven particularly valuable for the study of power-associative algebras. The optimization of deep neural networks' accuracy and generalization capability
is a core challenge in machine learning. We have developed a framework called
UOT-Pooling, which utilizes a different approach to data representation to enhance
model performance. The framework employs Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to
identify a transformed representation that amplifies the distinctions within
each class while minimizing inconsistencies between them. Our experiments show that
UOT-Pooling improves the state-of-the-art results on small datasets and achieves
competitive results on large datasets, all while requiring significantly fewer
computational resources than current methods. Additionally, we have developed
standardized benchmarks for comparing the effectiveness of different optimization
methods. These benchmarks are available at: https://github.com/qingyangliu/UOT-Pooling. Our source code can also be accessed at this repository for customizing our method in combination with other optimization techniques. This study examines the circumnuclear dust orientation of two distinct nuclei of Seyfert in spiral galaxies. It utilizes a dataset comprising 21 nuclei of both types, gathered from near-infrared spectroscopy, to compare their orientation with the galaxies' broader disk. It was discovered that nuclei of both types tend to align approximately perpendicularly to the disk, but the distribution of type 2 nuclei is more concentrated, by about 1.5 times, towards this alignment. Additionally, it was found that type 2 nuclei are more concentrated in the central portion of the disk and type 1 nuclei more frequently reside further from the galaxy's center than would be expected by chance, suggesting they are more likely to obfuscate the galaxy's center as seen from Earth. It was suggested that the difference in the manner these nuclei interact with their surroundings could affect the rate at which they pass into the other classification. It was further proposed that the most direct path for type 1 nuclei to sink closer to the galaxy's center, where they can once again be obscured, may be blocked by a central dust cloud that clears as they enter a supermassive black hole. As a result, the process could be self-sustaining, driving the evolution of these nuclei's interaction with their surroundings. In contrast, type 2 nuclei may follow a more indirect, three-dimensional path that makes this effect inescapable. As a consequence, the population of these nuclei would gradually shift towards a higher percentage of type 2 nuclei over time. It was proposed that a similar process might be active in other active galactic nuclei such as quasars and radio galaxies, although it was noted that distinguishing between these nuclei is more complicated, requiring more sophisticated methods to analyze their interaction with their surroundings. This research investigates solutions to a specific type of hyperbolic equation in a polynomial phase space with an irregular metric, which leads to a lack of smooth solution regularity. By constructing a suitable metric on this space, we prove that it meets the requirements of a Sobolev embedding theorem, which in turn allows us to establish the loss of smooth solution regularity in terms of the initial conditions' properties. This result is further extended to a broader class of quadratic equations and explored in the context of source-type solutions, which confirms the metric's singularity and loss of smooth solution regularity. Additionally, we demonstrate that the loss of regularity is not confined to the primary solution but also affects its derivatives and higher-order order spatial and temporal derivatives. For instance, if the second-order spatial derivative of the initial conditions is not smooth, the third-order temporal derivative of the solution will be discontinuous. Notably, the underlying ideas for these findings involve analogies with non-smooth functions in real analysis and the construction of a particular non-smooth metric that affects the solution's regularity. Furthermore, the study offers an infinite family of irregular metrics on the phase space that cause a loss of smooth solution regularity, which complements existing research in this field and Coman's recent work on hyperbolic partial differential equations. Finally, the investigation considers the applicability of these findings to other types of hyperbolic equations, including those with strong nonlinearity, which confirms that the loss of smooth solution regularity is a universal characteristic of such equations. As a consequence, the study establishes the inevitability of loss of smooth solution regularity for a broad class of hyperbolic equations, which raises questions about the possible loss of other types of solution regularity, such as analytic or Gevrey regularity. To answer this, the study provides a counter-example of a solution with lost analytic regularity, which demonstrates the difficulty in determining the exact type of regularity loss in such equations. However, the study proposes an infinitesimal analysis of the solution's regularity properties and the phase space's properties, which enables the precise determination of the solution's regularity loss in terms of the phase space's properties and the initial conditions' properties. This study examines the effectiveness of LSTM in enhancing Japanese word segmentation precision. Traditional Japanese word segmentation relies on pre-defined dictionaries, but this method's efficiency is hampered by dictionary size and memory usage. To overcome these limitations, we adapted an LSTM algorithm for Japanese word segmentation tasks. Using data from the Wikipedia Japanese corpus, we trained an LSTM model and evaluated its performance using various metrics, such as accuracy, F-score, and Gleichauf measures. Our results indicate that the LSTM approach surpasses conventional dictionary-based methods and demonstrates significant improvement in Japanese word segmentation precision, especially for less common words. Additionally, LSTM model's memory efficiency allows it to process larger corpora, enabling the efficient use of vast amounts of literary data for training. Consequently, the LSTM algorithm's performance exceeds dictionary-based methods in accuracy and Gleichauf measure while achieving comparable results in F-score. Furthermore, the LSTM model's efficiency enables the processing of larger datasets, ranging from 50% to 300% larger than the Wikipedia corpus, without compromising performance. Notably, the LSTM algorithm's performance excels when applied to the Japanese version of the English Web Corpus, a dataset containing modern Japanese text. These findings validate the LSTM model's effectiveness for Japanese word segmentation tasks and reveal its potential for extending Japanese language processing into new domains, such as automatic dictionary compilation and morphological analysis. Ultimately, the LSTM model presents a practical solution for Japanese word segmentation and demonstrates the efficacy of deep learning algorithms on traditional grammatical tasks. Based on these results, we propose the LSTM model as a suitable paradigm for Japanese language processing, an area where machine learning algorithms have not been heavily explored. Additionally, our study showcases the value of combining linguistic knowledge with data-driven approaches, a strategy recognized as essential for achieving success in natural language processing tasks. This study investigates the most frequently shared types of external resources on the Stack Overflow platform by analyzing question IDs linked to such shares. The findings are based on a examination of 183 million question posts from 2020 to 2022. The results show that images are the most common external resources shared multiple times on Stack Overflow, accounting for 344 times more occurrences than videos. Twenty percent of shared resources were images, with the majority related to programming concepts that cannot be easily reproduced visually. Stack and GitHub repository URLs were the most common external links shared across 79 million question posts, comprising 48% of all shared resources. The data highlights potential misuse of external links, which can be beneficial for developers, but also poses privacy and security risks if not managed properly. This research paves the way for further investigations into the characteristics of shared resources, possible motivations behind their sharing, and implications for developer support platforms. Based on these findings, potential precautions and improvements can be explored to balance resource sharing with regulatory and compliance requirements. The data and code used for this analysis have been made publicly available. The shared resources analyzed were obtained from the Stack Overflow Data Dump 2022, accessed through GitHub (https://github.com/stackoverflow/stackoverflow\_data), complemented with API-based data collection for additional question posts and users from Stack Overflow, obtained via an anonymous API token provided by a Stack Overflow moderator. The combined dataset comprised 183 million question posts, 65 million answers, 9 million answers with code, 5 million questions with links, and 1 million questions involving external resources. The analysis was conducted using Python 3.9 on a Linux server. All source codes and data used in this study have been made available at https://github.com/aycock/so\_resource\_sharing. Specifically, the stackoverflow_resource_sharing notebook can be found at https://github.com/aycock/so\_resource\_sharing/tree/main/stackoverflow_resource_sharing. The data is also available at https://datadrywind.com/stackoverflow/so_resource_sharing. The research was inspired by previous studies on shared resources by Aycock et al. Climate change awareness is widespread, yet many people still fail to translate this awareness into corresponding lifestyle changes. To stimulate action, climate communicators must develop effective strategies that leverage the positive influence of personal values, starting by identifying the specific values that can be effectively linked to pro-environmental behavior change. To address this need, a values survey was conducted with nearly 1000 participants in Germany, exploring how personal values relate to various pro-environmental behaviors, especially those related to food. The analysis confirmed the unpredictability of the German values scale, retained a factor structure consistent with theory, and identified significant correlations between values and pro-environmental behaviors. The research revealed a hierarchy of values that can be effectively targeted to motivate Germans towards pro-environmental behavior change, providing actionable insights that can be utilized to enhance climate change communication efforts. Additionally, the study's results can be applied to enhance the effectiveness of digital climate campaigns by integrating values-based messaging and tailoring these messages according to significant correlations found between values and pro-environmental behaviors.
