Autonomous driving systems can learn to navigate complex tasks by being trained with reinforcement learning methods.  Two key techniques used to improve the performance of these systems are recurrent neural networks for handling time series data and reinforcement learning for training decision-making strategies.  The primary advantage of using recurrent neural networks is their ability to retain information from previous experiences and integrate it with current inputs to inform future decisions.  Similarly, the strength of reinforcement learning lies in its ability to adapt decision-making strategies through interactions with a dynamic environment, leading to improved outcomes based on past performance.  The integration of these techniques in recurrent neural networks is essential for developing autonomous driving systems that can plan and make decisions across partially observable scenarios.  The central focus of this research is to examine the efficacy of different recurrent neural network architectures and reinforcement learning methods in developing autonomous driving systems.  Specifically, we compared the performance of three popular recurrent neural networks and five reinforcement learning methods across partially observable scenarios.  We measured the performance of these systems using a simulator built according to the OpenDR benchmark suite, with the results indicating that recurrent neural networks significantly enhance the output of policy-based reinforcement learning methods by up to 10%.  Moreover, our findings showed that recurrent neural networks with attention mechanisms outperformed those without such a mechanism by up to 10% in partially observable scenarios.  The integration of different reinforcement learning techniques, such as Q-learning and Policy Gradients, also resulted in improved outcomes by up to 10% compared to standalone methods.  Based on these findings, we propose a novel method that combines the strengths of recurrent neural networks and different reinforcement learning techniques to handle time series data and adapt decision-making strategies across various challenging scenarios.  The proposed method demonstrates a significant improvement of up to 10% in outcome quality compared to a basic Policy-Based method.  Moreover, our results show that a suitable choice of recurrent neural network and reinforcement learning method is essential for optimal performance, underscoring the importance of further investigation into the design of other algorithmic components.  The major advantage of our work is its ability to improve autonomous driving systems in complex and dynamic environments through reinforced learning and optimized algorithm design. ANNs have proven to be consistently high-performing classifiers, yet they suffer from considerable energy requirements. To mitigate this, alternative neural network architectures are explored, including the Hypercomplex Neural Network (HNN), which uses hypercomplex numbers as its fundamental component. We investigate HNN performance using the widely recognized datasets of Dataset1 and Dataset2 across various metrics such as error rate, F1-score, accuracy rate, G-Metric, H-Metric, E-Metric for comparison with "state-of-the-art" ANNs. Our research indicates that HNN can function as a reliable general-purpose classifier competitive with ANNs while being more energy-efficient and exhibiting lower computational complexity. Additionally, the substitution of hypercomplex with real numbers in ANNs leads to improved results in all evaluation criteria, with the hypercomplex-based network yielding the best outcomes. A comprehensive evaluation through statistical tests and counterfactual decision analysis further validates the superior performance of the proposed HNN over ANNs. Consequently, the proposed hypercomplex-based network is suited for applications requiring reliable classification while minimizing energy consumption and computational burdens. However, our findings also reveal cases of ANNs surpassing HNNs in error rates and accuracy metrics, prompting the proposal of an optimization technique to address these shortcomings. By fine-tuning the model with this method, the resulting Hypercomplex Neural Network can deliver superior results, outperforming ANNs and confirming its suitability as a dependable, energy-efficient, and computationally efficient general-purpose classifier. Our work uncovers an intriguing picture of HNN performance, where fine-tuning the model using a particular method leads to enhanced results, thus highlighting its value for future research. To our knowledge, this work represents the first evaluation of HNN classifiers using hypercomplex numbers as their fundamental component on diverse datasets, marking significant contributions to both the fields of Hypercomplex HNN and Counterfactual Explanation. Traditional mobile applications operate isolated from one another, resulting in private data collections and reduced computational capabilities.  To address these limitations, our solution Pando introduces an innovative peer-to-peer data sharing framework for Android devices.  Pando allows Android users to share data with one another and combine their computational powers via a decentralized network of interconnected devices.  By harnessing the collective powers of multiple devices, Pando significantly boosts computational performance and expands capability beyond what individual devices can offer.  Users of Pando can execute a wide array of local computations such as training neural networks, running image processing tasks or performing data analytics on large datasets.  Additionally, Pando provides robust security features and safeguards to ensure the integrity of user data and prevent data leaks.  Our initial findings reveal that Pando can increase computational speed by as much as 5 times the capabilities of a single device, with particular impacts on neural network training and image processing operations.  Our analysis also highlights promising avenues for future research and shows that Pando's efficiency gains can be adjusted in accordance with user-set tolerance levels for data privacy.  Ultimately, Pando's decentralized approach and high-performance computing capabilities position it as an advanced tool for Android developers and users seeking enhanced computational powers and improved privacy and security protections. This paper introduces an adaptive sampling technique that accelerates the convergence of numerical methods for approximating eigenvalues and eigenvectors, beyond the standard perturbation theory rates. By selectively sampling the BFP perturbation series at optimal points, our method streamlines the computation. Analytically and through experimentation, we demonstrate that the efficient sampling technique recovers the optimal convergence rate of the underlying series. Furthermore, we illustrate the effectiveness of our approach in both isolated and degenerate eigenvalue problems. Crucially, our technique is versatile and can be applied to eigenvalue problems with intricate spectra and high spatial periodicity, as evidenced by our analysis and numerical results of the Landau-Bloch vector model and the Harris category Q eigenvalue problems, where traditional methods are deemed ineffective. Moreover, our technique shows notable efficiency in computing eigenvectors of matrix operators, as exemplified by the Landau-Bloch vector model and the Bloch electron Hamiltonian in a photon-biosome model. Importantly, all computational results were validated through comparison with exact solutions. Lastly, our technique has broad applicability and can likely be adapted for computing eigenvalues and eigenvectors in a range of related eigenvalue problems. Furthermore, our method may find utility in the computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors in various applications in quantum mechanics. We examine $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories containing an excess of dynamical quark species, $N_{F} \geq N_{c}$, in the presence of relevant quark bilinear operators that break $U(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry. The Sanielello-Guinea-Zamolodchikov mapping is extended from $U(N_{F})$ to $SO(N_{F})$ to derive an integrable system of hypersurface partial differential equations that model the dynamics of quark condensates in the large-$N_{c}$ limit. The map leads to a novel relation between high-energy low-momentum effective theories and the partial differential equations. Consequently, it is found that the effective theories possess a larger $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry than the underlying $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories, which becomes a symmetry of the partial differential equations at a lower energy range than $U(N_{F})$ was. The research indicates that this phenomenon can occur at least once, for $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories containing massless anisotropic quark matter. Moreover, it is conjectured that this phenomenon can occur in other theory systems as well. Additionally, it is found that the linked partial differential equations and effective theories share many similarities with the Yang-Baxter equation and its $U(1,1)$ partial differential equations, which model the dynamics of two-color QCD in the large-$N_{c}$ limit, differ by a nonsignificant $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry enhancement. The research also discloses a previously overlooked link between the Yang-Baxter equation and an $SO(4)$ massless anisotropic quark model. Furthermore, it is derived that many of the YB-matrix nonlocalities hold equivalency within the $U(1,1)$ framework, which exhibits greater nonlocality complexity than its integrable $U(2)$ counterpart. Lastly, it is found that the partial differential equations of the $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories possess an increased nonlocal complexity of this nature. The research demonstrates the applicability of the Sanielello-Guinea-Zamolodchikov map to $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theories and its potential uses in resolving nonperturbative problems of similar theory systems in the large-$N_{c}$ limit. Interpreting model predictions in high-stakes decision-making situations necessitates a deeper understanding of the underlying algorithms.  Despite advancements in interpretation tools, comprehensively explaining complex models used in real-world tasks remains an open challenge.  To address this, we introduce Disentangled Attribution Curves (DACs), a novel method for unraveling how concatenated models, comprised of multiple interconnected components, arrive at a prediction.  By dissecting these models, we uncover surprising insights into how they process input data, revealing unexpected patterns in prior studies.  Our analysis of a bike-sharing dataset reveals unexpected seasonal and daily trends in prior studies, while exploring the predictive power of weather forecasts and actual weather data.  This analysis also highlights how weather forecasting models and actual weather are highly correlated, yet weather has a significant impact on future bike rentals.  Moreover, we uncover an unexpected holiday effect on bike rentals, with holidays consistently associated with a drop in rentals, although the magnitude of the drop is relatively insignificant.  Our findings serve as a starting point for further research into how weather forecasting models influence the predictions of composite models, while also shedding light on the predictive power of weather and actual weather on bike rentals.  Finally, we demonstrate how DACs can be used to monitor the predictions of composite models by detecting shifts in their parameter spaces.  Our findings reveal significant changes in the predictions of weather forecasting models and actual weather data between March-April 2020, indicating a notable resonance in their trends in prior studies, coinciding with the onset of the COVID pandemic.  This marks one of the earliest signs detected by DACs, highlighting its potential for real-time monitoring of model predictions.  In addition, we observe notable weekly patterns in prior studies and actual weather data, as well as their consistent correlation across different time periods.  These findings illustrate the effectiveness of DACs in dissecting complex models, uncovering new insights, tracking changes in their parameter spaces, and detecting significant events.  Our code and dataset are publicly available for replication purposes.  In the future, we aim to extend DACs to handle hierarchical models comprising multiple levels of interconnected components. A key advancement in enabling private AI model development while maintaining user anonymity is federated learning. Nonetheless, the current techniques for privacy preservation come with their own limitations, such as considerable computation overhead, elevated communication requirements, and the inability to support intricate machine learning models. This study aims to address these challenges through the application of multi-layer neural networks. By employing a local artificial noise system that uses variance reduction to mitigate privacy violations, this work proposes a novel, efficient approach to private federated learning that is both accessible and robust. This approach can be adapted for use with various network architectures and is exemplified here with a U-Net structure for image classification tasks. Beyond its efficacy in reducing communication costs, this method also maintains the ability to train models with multiple layers. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in preserving privacy and supporting the development of complex models, surpassing existing methods in both aspects. For example, this approach allows for the training of a 4-layer U-Net on CIFAR-10 with a significantly reduced communication cost compared to other methods. Our code is freely accessible on GitHub at the specified link. https://github.com/alexstoneharris/VVAFL. This paper presents an evaluation method for securing applications that utilize interpreted languages such as PHP and Python. The method employs a network daemon with a broad scope, known as Timeloops. It incorporates an advanced filtering system for standard system calls and a unique mechanism for establishing a secure environment for each application via secure file systems and pseudo-file interfaces. A pseudo-file interface enables the creation of pseudo-files whose creation and modification permissions can be freely configured. This enables the network daemon to grant applications access to specific system calls by creating corresponding pseudo-files. A distinct feature of Timeloops is its ability to perform application isolation through file system segmentation, where each application is isolated from others and can only access a limited set of files. Additionally, Timeloops includes a mechanism for limiting system call usage for certain applications. It achieves this by creating a pseudo-file containing a newline-separated list of allowed system calls for the application in question. If an application attempts to make a system call not listed in this file, the network daemon automatically terminates it. A primary advantage of this approach is the elimination of the requirement for a full system upgrade to enhance application security. Moreover, the network daemon can be easily distributed and installed separately from the applications it secures, thereby minimizing the impact of security breaches on other applications. This is particularly beneficial for applications utilizing remote execution frameworks like PHP's exec and Python's subprocess.run. Our evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach by simulating two attacks: a Trojan horse-style attack on PHP applications and unauthorized system call execution on Python applications. When compared to traditional Euclidean space-based methods, our results reveal significant improvements in classification accuracy and the convergence rate of the model. This paper explores the application of Model Predictive Control with uncertainty, where the optimal control action at each time is determined by solving a dynamic programming problem under specific conditions. It is essential to have an accurate measure of the system's uncertainty to apply this method effectively, which can be a challenging task in many systems. It is often the case that real-world data, though abundant, does not conform to the precise statistical models required for optimal control decision-making. Consequently, implementing MPC in systems with uncertainty proves difficult due to the complexities involved in high-dimensional data analysis and the interpretation of their results. To overcome these obstacles, a new method is proposed, which uses a simplified measure of the system's uncertainty to optimize control under specific conditions. This method is verified in simulations and demonstrated in the control of a gravimetric unit, where the relationship between mass and density is non-linear and subject to uncertainty. It is shown that correcting for density uncertainty leads to improved predictions of material mixtures, which in turn enables optimal control. Specifically, this approach results in reduced costs in comparisons involving both random and deliberately introduced noise in mass measurements. By accounting for uncertainty in density, it is possible to achieve better outcomes than those obtained through precise density measurements alone. In addition, it is worth noting that the proposed method is suitable for a wide range of systems and can be applied in various fields, such as process control and monitoring. In particular, it has potential applications in the optimization of chemical processes, such as mixture design and process control, and provides a practical solution for controlling devices with uncertainty, such as feeders and sorting systems. It is expected that this method will be useful to control devices reliably in various sorting systems and can be applied broadly to a wide range of systems. Ultimately, this approach leads to improved performance through learning from real-world data and provides a practical solution for controlling devices with uncertainty. In conclusion, it is essential to balance the precision of statistical models and the utility of approximate models in optimal control decision-making. This research demonstrates that correcting for uncertainty can result in improved outcomes in comparison with precisely measured parameters, which provides new insights into the trade-off between data collection and process control. We examine von Neumann algebras generated by local observables, specifically those resulting from the ground states of gapped spin systems with compact spectrum. Our analysis reveals that the structure of these algebraic extensions, along with their approximating finite-dimensional subalgebras, can be categorised in terms of the standard classification of subfactors. This encoding into the classification of subfactors enables us to establish an index that measures the complexity of these algebraic extensions. Furthermore, we establish the condition under which the generated algebra is factor, as opposed to being an algebraic extension of the abelian monoid. Additionally, we investigate the properties of the generated algebra in the context of relative von Neumann algebras and apply this to study the properties of the entropy of local observables. Lastly, we outline a conjecture regarding the generated algebraic extensions that they are equivalent to certain known extensions, such as those resulting from the free group or the Cuntz-Alsaka algebras. Our study shows that the structure of these algebraic extensions depends solely on the spectral distribution of the Hamiltonian. This is demonstrated by the example of the pentagon spin system, for which we calculate the index of the resulting algebraic extension. Conversely, we provide a counterexample to a previously proposed classification criterion of von Neumann algebras by Connes. Our study provides new insights into the properties of von Neumann algebras generated by local observables, specifically those resulting from the ground states of gapped spin systems with compact spectrum. These results broaden the reach of existing mathematical theories to describe the structure of these algebraic extensions, thereby providing a deeper understanding of the underlying physical systems. We suggest an approach to extend Greenberg's strong approximation theorem from one-dimensional local rings to higher-dimensional local rings. This involves a geometric representation of algebraic stacks, specifically the stack associated with the general linear group, and the properties of motivic Milnor K-class groups. Our method also allows us to confirm a specific component of the theorem for five-dimensional local rings and provide evidence supporting its validity for all local rings of higher dimension. Furthermore, our analysis reveals connections with other geometric and algebraic constructs, including the geometric realization of motivic complexes and the formulation of algebraic tori as geometric objects within a site. This involves a series of refinements to existing theories, such as Quillen's A-duality, the theory of motives, and the construction of geometric representations for algebraic groups. We also make use of advanced concepts, such as complete Segal maps and pseudo-functors, to connect these theories with our proposed approach. Additionally, we introduce the notion of a toric sheaf to describe the relationship between algebraic tori and the group sheaf associated with the general linear group. This enables us to calculate the homotopy classes of maps from algebraic tori to the group sheaf associated with the general linear group and, subsequently, the motivic Milnor K-class groups. Our method of extending Greenberg's strong approximation theorem also relies on a combination of existing and refined algebraic and geometric structures, such as finite motivic resolutions, geometric representations, and pseudo-functors. Ultimately, our approach aims to facilitate communication between algebraic and geometric communities, connecting existing theories with our proposed ideas. We hope this work will contribute to further insight and progress in this area. In the conclusion, we outline potential directions for future research, including applications, additional theoretical developments, and the potential linkage with other existing and developed mathematical concepts. This study introduces a citizen science initiative focused on sundials in Indonesia, aiming to enhance knowledge among school students and general citizens, while also adding to existing scientific knowledge through collaborative research. Currently, there is no comprehensive record of sundials in Indonesia despite their historical significance in the country. We developed a cutting-edge platform utilizing IoT technology to locate and track sundials, ensuring accuracy in recording their positions. This system enables real-time data collection and efficient organization of recorded information. Twoundials have been installed as part of the initiative, one at the Physics and Astronomy Faculty of Padangpanjang High School and another at the ITENAS campus in Bandung. Our platform is accessible via mobile devices at sundials.locate.id, and through the OpenSundial platform at opensundial.io, users can access and document sundials, as well as share their experiences and contribute to existing knowledge. Ultimately, this project aims to expand its reach across the nation, promoting public engagement in science, technology, and innovation. Moreover, this initiative has the potential to extend its applications to various fields, such as architecture and built heritage, as sundials can be found on historic buildings and structures across Indonesia. This project has been successfully implemented in Bandung and Padangpanjang, and is slated for deployment in Bandung's observatory and physics classrooms. Moreover, this initiative has the potential to extend its reach to the international community through collaboration with relevant organizations and institutions. For example, this project can be connected to the Helioviewer platform at helioviewer.org for solar orientation accuracy, or through the Open Science Framework at osf.io for data archiving and scientific publication. In the near future, we plan to incorporate machine learning and deep learning algorithms to further develop and refine our platform, as well as to seek support from government agencies and institutions to widely disseminate this innovation across the nation. This research received support from the IT-ENABLING SERVICES UMM through the grant under call 2020. System development and deployment require ongoing maintenance and upkeep, and we plan to seek continuous support in the future. In the near future, we plan to broaden our initiative's reach to the international community, and expand our platform's applications to various fields beyond astronomy and built heritage. Conversely, we plan to concentrate on specific themes such as accessible science, hybrid learning, and remote work, or other relevant domains that require contribution from existing knowledge systems. This study was carried out in accordance with UMM ethics regulations, and all methodology steps are detailed in the methods section.

This article investigates the class of graph spectra defined by the determinant function on undirected bipartite graphs. Asser's conjecture is a highly anticipated theory claiming the irreducibility of this spectrum class. We found that imposing the direction on graphs leads to complex mathematical problems, thus we examined the inverse scenario, constraint the graphs to be undirected bipartite. By applying a transformation and leveraging the classical linear algebra techniques, we managed to prove the irreducibility of the determinant function's spectrum in this specific graph class. As a by-product of our method, we achieved a unitary equivalence between the bipartite graph Laplacian and a positive-semidefinite matrix, which has potential applications in fields such as covariance estimation and SDP minimization. Furthermore, this study opens up the possibility of extending our methods to explore the irreducibility of the characteristic polynomial's spectrum in the same class of bipartite graphs. Upon completion of this research, we learned of a different proof strategy for our findings, which we present in this article. Additionally, we verify the classical Gauss-Hurwitz bound for the real eigenvalues of the Laplacian matrix of bipartite graphs. Lastly, this study lays the groundwork for future investigations of complex eigenvalues within this specific graph class. In a broader sense, this research aims to encourage and inspire the development of new graph theory methods to study the irreducibility of the spectrum class defined by the determinant function on various graph structures. We anticipate and hope for future contributions from this field of study. In particular, this research has potential implications for nonnegative matrix factorization in the field of data mining, as well as some interesting extensions to the field of number theory, specifically related to the behavior of the determinant function on specific graph architectures, which we briefly discuss in the concluding section of this article. A general framework called a computational network is introduced, designed to simulate multiple physical computation mechanisms including quantum computation. Within this framework, the evaluation process for these mechanisms is mapped to distinct functions that operate on specific types of data. Additionally, the interplay between data objects and their manipulation in computation is explored through the study of operational protocols. It is demonstrated that quantum computation can be simulated by evaluating a related classical mechanism, however, the converse is not necessarily true, highlighting a key difference between quantum computation and other physical computation mechanisms. Moreover, the relationship between the efficiency of data usage in computation and the level of specificity in the mechanism's implementation is investigated, and the concept of optimal networks is introduced to facilitate this analysis. Furthermore, a computational model inspired by the Adiabatic Method is introduced, where the maximum change in data values is limited, and its potential to serve as a universal model for optimizing computational networks is discussed. The traditional Mumford-Shah model has been widely utilized for image segmentation. Nonetheless, it's prone to suboptimal outcomes when the image integrity is compromised. We propose an enhanced approach that modifies the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model to facilitate accurate image segmentation in the presence of image corruption. The new model extends the previous method by incorporating an efficiently calculable approximation of the minimum perimeter of a piecewise-smooth function. We explore two possible optimization strategies for this model and develop a straightforward, computationally efficient solution for piecewise-constant segmentation, which exhibits superior performance compared to the existing methods. Additionally, we introduce a reliable procedure for determining the optimal piecewise-spline solution through successive refinements of the piecewise-constant solution. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed methods through comprehensive experimental evaluations, showcasing their capability to accurately segment images in various settings. We also develop a specialized algorithm for computing the exact solution of the generalized Mumford-Shah model in the presence of total-variation regularization. Since direct optimization of the total-variation model is computationally intensive, we introduce a novel scheme - the alternating direction method of the Mumford-Shah model - for efficiently solving this problem and achieving optimal results. We conduct experimental evaluations to demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over the total-variation regularization approach. The accuracy and efficiency of the proposed algorithms have been meticulously verified through extensive experimental analysis, alongside the presentation of the corresponding code. capable of learning both in the hardware and software realms is burgeoning. 
Theoretical frameworks for such systems have been established, but the impossibility 
of an exhaustive search for optimal solutions drives the need for dynamic adjustment 
of the learning approach.  A novel online learning technique is presented that 
adjusts its approach in response to the solution's progress. The method utilizes data 
from past iterations to determine when to switch between different hardware-based 
learning mechanisms, one of which is inspired by backpropagation. Our approach 
is validated by experiments using a Spiking Neural Network trained to learn the 
exclusive OR function and a 8x8 multiplexer with an additional noisy output. The 
results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves a comparable accuracy to 
a traditionally learned solution and outperforms alternative online learning 
strategies. The theoretical framework of this algorithm can be applied to other hardware-
based learning mechanisms and is compatible with neuromorphic computing platforms 
with multiple learning mechanisms.  The possibility of combining different learning 
approaches also presents new challenges in terms of how these methods interact and

A significant polaron-like storm was observed in the Jovian magnetosphere, where data from Jupiter's magnetometer mission Galileo generated images of the storm's interior and middle layers. Observing the storm's westward movement, researchers discovered a prominent wave pattern similar to a sausage mode, which formed alongside the storm. To understand the relationship between the storm's intensity and size, researchers analyzed the wave pattern, noting that the storm's higher intensity was correlated with its smaller size, and vice versa. Additionally, they discovered that the storm's middle portion exhibited a distinct minimum in both intensity and size, which scaled together in proportion to the storm's overall size and intensity. This behavior suggests that more intense storms are initially smaller but grow over time, while less intense storms are initially larger but shrink. It's possible that the wave pattern observed is not a single-mode wave but rather a superposition of multiple waves, which could have different source origins and evolutions. Further investigation is needed to confirm these findings. Moreover, the storm exhibited a strange asymmetry in its oscillations, where the left and right sides reacted differently to the storm's development and growth. This is particularly noticeable in the storm's initial stages, where the left side showed a more pronounced reaction than the right side, which is unusual since the storm's westward movement would suggest an equal reaction from both sides. This asymmetry could indicate that the storm is being driven by energy supplied from the Jovian spin, which would explain many of the storm's observed properties. (2019) and new data on Wd2's massive-star population. Despite active stars, the cluster exhibits an unusually low level of massive-star loss, suggesting an efficiency of 10% in comparison to 30-50% typical of other systems. However, this effect can be attributed to Wd2's high stellar density and resulting rapid star evolution. As a result, most massive stars in the cluster are observed in the yellow hypergiant or red hypergiant phase and have not yet reached the red supergiant stage to supply O-type stars to the cluster. Using stellar loss and acceleration, researchers determined that a supernova from a yellow or red hypergiant in the cluster would likely be obscured by dust and observed stars or a massive star disk. However, this also presents an opportunity for more accurate and dynamic modeling of massive-star evolution, particularly if future observations in the cluster reveal a late-type massive star. Utilizing handwritten text recognizers in a more flexible manner is essential for dealing with degraded document images effectively. In this paper, we demonstrate how utilizing a handwritten text recognizer in conjunction with Generative Adversarial Networks enables the creation of clearer hand-written text images devoid of noise, thereby enabling improved image quality. To achieve this, we developed a novel hand-written text image restoration framework that integrates a handwritten text recognizer in an iterative process, initially beginning with generating clean, non-handwritten text images prior to handing it over to a generator network to produce hand-written text images. We tested our proposed framework on both MNIST and IAM datasets with positive results. Our experiments on the IAM dataset yielded a character error rate reduction of 9.2% and MRE-50 score improvement of 9.9% after removing handwriting variations. Our results indicate that integrating a handwritten text recognizer with GANs leads to restored hand-written text images that are both clearer and less prone to errors. Our method's benefits extend beyond image quality improvements as it also enables the recovery of text images affected by variations in handwriting styles, thereby making it more suitable for applications in handwriting-based verification systems. Our implementation and restored hand-written text images are accessible online at the URL https://github.com/Imagimago/Handwritten-Text-Image-Restoration. Our method's advantages include reduced memory requirements due to local iterations, enabling the processing of larger images. Moreover, our hand-written text image restoration method can be adapted for use with other image restoration techniques. Furthermore, our hand-written text image restoration method can be utilized for dealing with other types of hand-written text image degradations. Lastly, our method can be modified at hand to address various types of hand-written text image degradations. Our analysis shows that LSTM's temporal understanding is beneficial for predicting future channel states, thus enhancing the precision of frequency-domain channel estimation. We investigated various LSTM structures and observed that a two-layer LSTM model yielded optimal results. We also found that LSTM's advantages persist across multiple scenarios of channel complexity and mobility speed. Furthermore, our data indicates that LSTM's benefits are evident across distinct frequency channels. We estimated that an LSTM-based deep learning channel estimator could decrease the computational requirements of conventional methods by a factor of 10. Ultimately, our results strongly suggest the utilization of LSTM in a deep learning based channel estimator for a rapidly changing wireless communication system. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) possess exceptional capability to mitigate the limitations imposed by the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem, successfully extracting relevant characteristics from signals sampled below the Nyquist rate. Nevertheless, in cases where labeled data are scarce, overfitting poses a significant challenge to the effectiveness of supervised learning algorithms applied to Handel-Lee-type signal sampling problems. This study presents a novel algorithm capable of training a neural network to effectively extract high-quality samples from low-quality ones, while simultaneously preventing overfitting through data augmentation. By employing an iterative approach centered around a stochastic gradient descent minimization algorithm, our method successfully generalizes well even when the iterate sequences are shown to converge to a neighborhood of the neighborhood of the local minimizers. Moreover, the applicability of our approach extends beyond the specific problem of Handel-Lee-type signal sampling, as it also applies to a broader class of inverse problems involving observations and prior distributions. Through the application of our algorithm to the former problem, we achieve a relative error reduction of $20$ times and a $4$ times increase in the reliable sampling rate over existing state-of-the-art results, based on an empirical analysis involving $1000$ randomly generated instances of the problem. Furthermore, our results demonstrate convergence at or near the theoretical limit for both the DNN and non-DNN cases, amounting to an error reduction of $14$ times and $7$ times respectively, as validated by extensive experiments conducted over a diverse range of $119$ challenging inverse problems involving various types of data including real-valued, complex-valued, categorical, and binary observational data. Additionally, our analysis reveals the emergence of a novel scaling law, governing the relationship between the convergence rate of our algorithm and the architecture of DNNs. This study introduces a Federated Learning framework for distributed training of policies in decentralized, high-opportunity cost settings. The proposed method expands existing Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning techniques by integrating FL, thereby addressing concentration risks through localized knowledge representation on individual robots. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through a massive-scale simulation of numerous robots interacting with human users, and finds that by reducing the size of shared models, communication frequency, and model parameter count, energy consumption can be significantly reduced. The resulting performance gain and energy savings verify the viability of this innovation. The study further explores ways to optimize FL for applications involving multiple robots and human users interacting in complex environments. The knowledge gained from this simulation can guide the development of robotic interaction systems that balance human-robot interaction goals with resource constraints. The study ultimately establishes a connection between the robots' energy efficiency and the intersection of FL and MARL. The presented work is expected to guide researchers in addressing key challenges associated with multi-robot, multi-human Federated Learning and pave the way for numerous applications in natural disaster response, urban planning, and space exploration. Our approach subordinates the traditional requirement of being asymptotically unbiased to a more lenient standard, thereby yielding valuable insights into the bias structure. We show that estimators with a smooth bias profile can be achieved by making mild assumptions on the target parameter's smoothness properties. Knowledge graph link prediction is an essential task that employs relation extraction information to make predictions about missing links between entities in a knowledge graph. Current methods use relation extraction data by integrating it into knowledge graph embedding techniques, but they do not utilize the specific information extracted in the process. To address this limitation, we propose RE-HG, a novel approach that effectively utilizes relation extraction information to make link prediction in knowledge graphs. To achieve this, we first develop a scoring model that combines the scores of relation extraction and knowledge graph embedding to predict the likelihood of a missing link. To optimize this model, we adopt a two-stage training process that first trains the models separately, but leverages the information exchanged during the training process to improve the final outcome. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted a comprehensive analysis on three datasets, FB15K-237, WN18RR, and AWAD, and revealed that RE-HG achieved superior results compared to the state-of-the-art techniques, underscoring the significance of integrating relation extraction information in knowledge graph link prediction. Moreover, we noted a remarkable improvement in the micro-F$1$ score, from 0.70 to 0.81, which signifies a substantial enhancement of 15.71 using a two-stage training process. Ultimately, our approach offers an innovative solution for integrating relation extraction information to make precise knowledge graph link prediction. Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 are known for their spin-peierls (SP) and antiferromagnetic (AF) properties, but a comprehensive study of their magnetic properties is yet to be done. We examined the magnetic properties of these compounds by combining neutron diffraction, heat capacity, and electron spin resonance measurements. In cristobalite-type Tb3RuO7, we found a SP transition at 95 K with AF correlations on two crystallographic Ru sites displaying distinct properties, while Nd3RuO7 showed no SP transition but rather two AF transitions at 42 K and 26 K on different Ru sites. Further analysis revealed that the two compounds exhibit similar EXAFS patterns, but their magnetic and spin-peierls properties show distinct differences. In contrast, Ho3RuO7 also exhibits SP and AF properties with a 2:1 ratio and displays EXAFS patterns similar to these two compounds, suggesting a possible correlation between Ru bond lengths and spin-peierls transition temperatures. We hypothesize that Ho3RuO7 may exhibit SP and AF properties as well. We investigated the magnetic properties of Lu3RuO7, which has no magnetic ions, but showed no SP and AF properties and instead displayed a unique antiferromagnetic structure with a 2:1 ratio at 18 K with distinct properties on two crystallographic Ru sites. Furthermore, Y3RuO7 was found to have no magnetic impurities but showed no SP and AF properties as well. We conclude that the presence of d electrons on two crystallographic Ru sites is essential for SP and AF properties, but their quantities and arrangements lead to different magnetic properties and a unique antiferromagnetic structure with a 2:1 ratio. Moreover, we found a unique antiferromagnetic structure with a 2:1 ratio in La3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7, which shows no SP and AF properties as well. We examined the electronic configurations and crystal structures of the 3d3, 4d5, and 5d5 Ru compounds in the 225 structure to understand their properties. We finally discuss the possibility of utilizing spin and magnetic degree of freedom for Nd3RuO7 and other 225 Ru compounds. Effective representation of low-dimensional data is crucial for learning tasks. We investigated the characteristics of this representation in neural networks and found that a local-functional approach significantly improves generalization. This method involves treating the parameter tensor in a neural network as a smooth function on a grid, with smoothness enforced by an appropriate penalty term. The local-functional method discovers that neural networks tend to represent low-dimensional data in a nearby, or 'local', region of the initial parameter tensor, with the smoothness penalty ensuring generalizability. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrated the local-functional method outperforms existing initialization techniques, with improvements of up to 2.5% in classification accuracy and 2% in log-loss in various settings. Additionally, we found the local-functional method enhances representation of latent variables in variational autoencoders, with the added benefit of latent space reconfiguration possible without changing the encoder and decoder networks. This method is useful for improving the smoothness of the function represented by the parameter tensor, with general applicability across a wide range of tasks. We assume a fully connected architecture, with extensions to convolutional networks possible through the use of a suitable grid structure. We introduce a new class of probabilistic models called semi-generated models that capture complex relationships between variables. In these models, the target variable is conditioned on specific characteristics, and the data distribution is characterized by the reverse dependence, often through continuous latent variables. The name "semi-generated" reflects that, unlike generative models, the conditioning variables for the target variable are known, whereas the generative variables are unknown. The name also contrasts with discriminative models, as the conditioning variables still influence the target variable's distribution. The classification task in semi-generated models amounts to multi-task learning, as both the conditioning variables' distributions and the target variable's distribution need to be estimated. We propose a new approach, called reverse generative adversarial learning, to capture the complex relationships between variables, as well as a new type of semi-generated model for single-variable relationships, which outperforms existing models. Our methods are applied to artificial data and real-life datasets from various fields, including medicine and finance. The benefits of using semi-generated models are particularly evident when the target variable is a continuous variable, as they prove more effective than traditional models in that scenario. Deep neural networks have exceeded humans in problem-solving skills, but their internal workings remain shrouded in mystery. To shed light on this, researchers created a layerwise relevance propagation framework that reconstructs the raw input data of a image from a deep neural network's output. By analyzing the reconstructed components, we can identify and quantify the visual elements extracted by each layer in a hierarchical manner. Additionally, we developed a method to quantify the reliability of each layer in contributing visual cues to the final output. Our research found that lower layers in a deep neural network are generally more reliable and important for visual cue acquisition, but also discovered that these lower layers focus on irrelevant or incomplete visual cues, such as background and facial expressions in image classification tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrated that pre-trained convolutional layers are capable of detecting visual anomalies in out-of-distribution images. Our study also explored the use of our framework to improve the robustness of image classification models against adversarial attacks. For instance, we successfully reduced the effectiveness of attacks on ImageNet classification models by pruning the reconstruction layers that focus on irrelevant visual cues. Our approach and framework can be applied to various visual tasks and improved the accuracy of a medical image diagnosis model by eliminating the reconstruction layers that focus on noise or artifacts. Our study is the first to utilize layerwise relevance propagation for understanding and improving the robustness of deep neural networks at an unprecedented scale, training and testing on large datasets of 1.2 million images and 21,818 classes. Our code, framework, and reconstructed images are available for public use at https://github.com/VisualReasoning/LRP. We introduce a comprehensive framework for identifying the irreducible components of layered systems, adopting a graphical representation of these materials. Our approach enables a thorough classification of irreducible domains by combining certain sublattices of the Brillouin zone and symmetry operations of the space group. Additionally, we outline specific methods for constructing these components through successive splitting of the Brillouin zone torus. Our analysis is supported by a computer program that generates these components for a given space group and sublattice configuration, allowing for both manual and computer-driven exploration of these systems. We apply our classification scheme to a diverse set of materials, including transition metal dichalcogenides and -diborides, helicene and related metallic compounds, and honeycomb lattices with an ABA stacked configuration, demonstrating the versatility of our method in understanding irriducible domains within these materials. Our study ultimately provides fundamental insights into the topological properties of these materials, guiding the calculation of orbital Chern numbers and detection limits of these layers with optical microscopy. Our research indicates that certain materials, such as the honeycomb lattices with an ABA stacked configuration, possess a universal bulk topological property regardless of their space group or sublattice configuration. Moreover, we identify a list of space groups where surface Chern bands can be observed, and we find that helicene compounds exhibit both chiral and ecliptic surface states. Our classification also reveals that transition metal dichalcogenides and -diborides possess either chiral or ecliptic surface states depending on their space group and sublattice configuration, and that certain space groups, such as $D_{6/h}$, can exhibit both chiral and ecliptic surface states. Furthermore, we calculate the surface Chern bands of metallic helicene compounds and find that their energies can be tuned across the Dirac point with either strain or an external electric field. Our study predicts the existence of ecliptic surface states in certain materials, such as MoO$_2$ and WO$_2$, and identifies transition metal diboride $h$-BPd$_2$ as the first material where a chiral surface band can be observed. Our research indicates that certain materials, such as TMD-$h$-B, can be used for the detection of spin-polarized electrons with optical microscopy. Our study shows that the eigenvalues of the gauge-invariant vector potential on the ecliptic surface can be utilized for the evaluation of orbital magnetic susceptibility in ecliptic surface states.

Developed languages like English increasingly dominate, while lesser-documented, endangered languages risk disappearing forever. There is an urgent need to develop efficient methods for creating a dictionary of a new language. Our innovative method trains a general-language model on a single bilingual dictionary, allowing the model to adapt to multiple language pairs with minimal additional training. Our study finds that words with frequent occurrences in a language are more easily learned by the model, suggesting a potential exploitation limit. Interestingly, we discovered a surprising adaptation speedup when learning a third language, especially with high-word-frequency words, indicating an 'overexpansion' phenomenon. Moreover, we observe that a model trained on a complete bilingual dictionary achieves better results than one trained on a smaller section. Finally, we find that a model's ability to learn a new language improves with the size of the target vocabulary but reaches a point of diminishing returns due to the 'overexpansion' issue. Our research offers valuable insights into the adaptable characteristics of language models. Using a simple, effective upscaling technique, we successfully translated a small German-English dictionary into eight new language pairs with a high degree of accuracy, achieving an improvement of 14.97% compared to a baseline model that directly uses word frequency. A significant issue in philosophy known as the CPT problem revolves around determining if every problem solvable in polynomial time with the option to make random mistakes is also solvable in fixed, deterministic polynomial time. The random computation model (EPC) can help us understand how random inputs relate to deterministic ones, particularly because a super-polynomial EPC lower bound for a problem could imply a strong limitation on its deterministic counterpart. However, current techniques are not capable of yielding such a bound for prominent problems like Circuit SAT or Graph Isomorphism. In order to tackle the CPT problem, a novel proof method must be developed that allows for a gradual increase in the size of the circuits or graphs under consideration. This thesis proposes a new approach, known as the'multi-colour verification circuit' method, which sets a baseline for constructing such circuits but also offers an alternative algorithmic solution for its associated verification problem, thereby providing a contrasting example of a problem that is solvable in EPC but likely not in PTIME. The primary technical contribution of this dissertation consists of an in-depth examination of how the construction of these multi-colour verification circuits relates to key concepts in infinite combinatorics, such as Ramsey's theorem and the infinitary König lemma. Additionally, a novel proof of the latter's correctness has been devised. Furthermore, an intriguing connection has been observed between the capacitance of certain graph families and the capacity of multi-colour verification circuits, which may serve as a basis for future research into deterministic polynomial time and learning theory, especially as it relates to the study of 'extremal graphs' in combinatorics. Ultimately, a comprehensive survey of recent advances in EPC lower bounds has been presented, including the pivotal works on Tseitin formulas, Height Lower Bounds, and Arithmetic Circuits, which have paved the way for a potential breakthrough in the CPT problem by constructing a determinant circuit family with super-polynomial EPC lower bounds or, alternatively, proving that Circuit SAT is not solvable in EPC with at most $\log^2 n$ mistakes for any fixed polynomial time limit. In conclusion, a diverse collection of philosophical and mathematical reflections has been offered, along with an invitation to young researchers to build upon and expand the existing research in this field in the hope of achieving significant advancements in the future. The proliferation of social media has transformed the way people engage in discussions and shape public opinion. Repeatedly, Twitter users' opinions and beliefs are proven influential in matters of health, finance, and politics. Users often express personal anecdotes, experiences, and opinions on social issues via narratives that are infrequently addressed in existing AI applications. Narratives in social media posts frequently lack concrete facts and rely on symbolic language, making them difficult for machines to process. To combat this limitation, we've created an innovative system that combines cutting-edge natural language processing techniques with a universal sentiment analysis framework. Our system is uniquely positioned to analyze the sentiments expressed in narrative social media posts, as evidenced by our superior results on two large-scale evaluation datasets. These achievements showcase the efficacy of our approach in understanding and quantifying the sentiments conveyed via symbolic language in social media posts. Our research has far-reaching implications and can be applied to various social issues such as detecting emotional appeals in political campaigns or monitoring mental health conversations on social media. Our work has inspired new NLP directions and has paved the way for the development of AI tools for symbolic sentiment analysis, as evidenced by the creation of open-access datasets and a framework for reinforcing fact-checking initiatives among journalists. This research presents an event detection system capable of processing incident reports with diverse spatial and temporal details from multiple sources of real-time data, including social media and IoT sensors. The framework integrates geometric relationships and temporal relationships to identify patterns of co-occurring events at various scales across a metropolitan area, regardless of the resolution of individual events. The system utilizes clustering techniques to categorize events and a probability model for predicting non-coincident events, thus minimizing false positives. The effectiveness of this framework is demonstrated through comprehensive testing involving a dataset of 37 major cities, encompassing over 1 million Twitter posts and 200,000 IoT sensor readings, showcasing its capability to detect patterns of co-occurring crimes at multiple scales while withstanding the variability of individual events. The results reveal an 88% decrease in false positives when compared to traditional approaches and highlight the potential of this framework for resolving real-time incident coordination and rescue operations under uncertain conditions. The research lays a theoretical groundwork for an intelligent, data-driven urban security system that can supplement existing coordination efforts and promote resilience in urban communities. It achieves this through the incorporation of an adversarial network that simulates the effects of perturbations during training, resulting in a model that is resistant to manipulations. By integrating the reliability of predictions into the loss function, APM regularizes the model to minimize errors within a certain range of possible perturbations. Our study examines the capabilities of APM in the contexts of tabular data and text classification, with results demonstrating its superiority over existing robust models and the efficacy of its adversarial training method. In the realm of Metric Learning, researchers have leveraged different loss functions like Triplet Loss, NTP, and KL Divergence for model training. However, it's often assumed that these losses can be universally applied, which is not the case. This paper investigates the effects of various losses on pre-trained models like VisualSEBERT, which is fine-tuned in an unsupervised metric learning setting. Interestingly, our results indicate that under-represented loss functions like KL Divergence can achieve superior performance compared to more commonly used alternatives. Additionally, our examination also highlights the significance of the choice of the decoder layer used for feature extraction. This finding has important implications for the development of new loss functions in Metric Learning. Moreover, our open-source framework enables researchers to efficiently compare different loss functions with varying degrees of complexity. This includes our novel, highly efficient 'Flow KL' loss, which we demonstrate can enhance model performance across multiple datasets. This paper's contributions are three-fold: Firstly, we identify that using KL Divergence can boost model performance compared to more conventional loss functions. Secondly, the choice of the decoder layer used for feature extraction has a substantial impact on model performance in Metric Learning tasks. Emergency call centers worldwide rely on text-based incident reporting systems to gather information from dispatchers' conversations with users. These systems often deal with urgent and non-urgent events but share the challenge of extracting valuable data from these interactions. Current studies focusing on incident reporting systems have explored the potential benefits of supervised models trained on labeled data but overlooked the practical implications of scaling these systems to handle a large volume of conversations. Moreover, they did not investigate the characteristics of conversations in different settings and how dispatchers collect specific information from users in various situations. To address these shortcomings, we developed a two-phase approach combining unsupervised and supervised methods to analyze conversations in different settings and collect data to train models effectively. Our approach revealed distinct characteristics among conversations and showed the presence of recurring patterns in how dispatchers gather information from users in various situations. Building on these findings, we proposed a new risk reporting system featuring an unsupervised pre-processing component that categorizes conversations and adapts to new settings while maintaining consistent performance. Additionally, we introduced a data augmentation technique to enhance the effectiveness of machine learning models in incident reporting systems and demonstrated the potential benefits of exploring conversation dynamics in different settings and their practical applications in improving service quality and process efficiency. Research has demonstrated that superconducting materials exhibit linear dispersion near the Fermi surface and specific structural features can significantly impact their transport properties by modifying the magnetic susceptibility. Utilizing transport spectroscopy, a novel method to examine the connection between superconducting and normal states has been developed. By integrating this technique with molecular dynamics simulations, the electronic properties of a model peptide, gly-ala, interacted with a (100) gold surface were studied under various temperature and humidity conditions. Results showed that when gly-ala was in close contact with the gold surface, a pseudo-Fermi surface was created and at 300 K, it exhibited two distinct loops. Upon transferring the model to the Slaton phase, an almost triangular Fermi surface was generated while a 45-degree rotation of the peptide resulted in a different topology with increased areas along specific directions, influencing the electronic properties and superconducting potential of the system, potentially adding a new dimension to the understanding of superconducting properties of hydrophilic materials near superconducting films. Additionally, the investigation of electronic properties under humidity showed that water vapor could cause slight electronic changes but a high temperature would lead to merged Fermi surfaces. Furthermore, the most stable peptide configuration under humidity was determined through molecular dynamics simulations, enabling the evaluation of electronic properties and the identification of a unique peptide phase that could exhibit different physical properties and a potential connection with a stable peptide phase and superconductivity. Results showed that near the superconducting transition threshold, the connection between the peptide and gold surface influences electronic properties by causing a change in the electronic density of states, demonstrating quantum tunneling under humidity and at varying temperatures, impacting electronic properties and superconductivity through structural changes due to humidity. Ultimately, the transport spectroscopy revealed that at 300 K, there is no correlation between the electronic property and humidity but a 45-degree rotation of the peptide exhibits distinct zones with varying humidity effects, suggesting that near the superconducting transition threshold, the electronic property is influenced by the peptide configuration, potentially enabling the utilization of superconducting properties for detecting peptide structural changes. Also, the transport spectroscopy shows transport spectroscopy offers an effective approach for detecting peptide structural changes and their impact on electronic properties, offering novel detection methods that can also evaluate hydrophilic material's electronic property and the interaction with humidity. Moreover, the research indicates that superconducting properties under humidity could be achieved through peptide structural changes, showcasing novel applications of superconducting research for detecting various chemical and biological agents. Current supervised machine learning techniques lack the efficiency of high-quality labeled samples required for their improvement.  To overcome this issue, active learning algorithms have been developed with various strategies for choosing samples. However, most of these strategies have certain drawbacks such as concentrating on atypical samples which may not guarantee future improvements or distributing the samples uniformly without considering their potential impact.  To address these shortcomings, we have developed a semi-supervised minimax entropy-based active learning algorithm.  This new approach first optimizes a minimax entropy objective function to measure the uncertainty and diversity of samples.  By introducing a classifier and entropy measurements for both known and unknown data points, our method effectively utilizes unlabeled samples to improve the choice of active learning.  Moreover, our proposed method is compatible with different entropy functions and can be used with various query strategies.  To validate our approach, we have tested it on different datasets and compared it with state-of-the-art active learning algorithms.  The results of these experiments show the effectiveness of our method in selecting samples that are most likely to improve the performance of the classifier.  The implementation of our new approach can be found on the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/d-d-d/SSMEAL.  Additionally, the data used in our study can be accessed via https://github.com/d-d-d/SSMEAL_data.

This study analyzes the variation in sound quality from records released between 1920 to 2010 in three distinct groups, focusing on piano-oriented genres such as jazz and classical in the first group, vocals/piano in the second, and electronic/piano in the third. By examining samples of 1 second, 5 seconds, and 21 seconds in length, researchers found that the sound quality profiles of songs show a significant pattern over time, grouping songs from the same period together. Notably, this pattern becomes more pronounced as the sample length increases. When compared across different groups, it was discovered that the sound quality profiles of vocals/piano and electronic/piano show a significant difference from those of jazz and classical, indicating a distinct evolutionary path for these groups. This analysis sheds new light on the relationship between technology and musical style. Unlike electronic music, which exhibits a strong technological influence on its sound quality, other genres such as jazz and classical show little correlation between technological advancement and sound quality. Moreover, it was discovered that the sound quality profiles of songs released during the 1960s, 70s, and 80s resemble those of earlier decades, indicating a prolonged period of technological development. Interestingly, the sound quality profiles of songs from the 1990s and 2000s reveal a unique characteristic, setting them apart from other decades. Ultimately, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of how sound quality evolves over time in piano-oriented genres and provides a wealth of information that can be used to train neural networks for sound modification applications. Two such neural networks were developed, one capable of mapping audio from one period to another and another that preserves the original tempo and timing of input sounds, transforming them into outputs with the desired period characteristic. Additionally, a wealth of unsupervised clustering results and sound quality profiles are provided, offering further insights into the relationship between technology and musical style. Both sound transformation neural networks achieved excellent performance, with evaluation scores revealing that listeners prefer the sounds produced by the network trained on longer samples and that significant improvements can be achieved through the use of three-second samples, offering valuable implications for sound design and audio retrieval applications. Ultimately, this study offers a groundbreaking technological advancement, opening up new avenues for sound design, audio retrieval, and technology development with significant practical implications. With the data and code made available, this study paves the way for future research to build upon previous findings, investigating topics such as the evolution of sound quality in other genres and the relationship between technological development and musical style. As the process progresses through time, we show that the number of large blocks grows, on average, to be infinite, specifically demonstrating that the dimension of these blocks increases at a rate of $\theta$ for some $\theta \geq 0$. If the process is bijective and has positive reinforcement, we prove that the blocks form a sequence of distinct, infinite blocks, rigorously establishing a long-standing conjecture first posed by Shwartz. Conversely, if the process has finite reinforcement, we prove that the blocks form a sequence of distinct, infinite blocks, albeit one that may repeat infinitely, thus addressing a previous attempt by Birkner et al. and shedding light on their model of 'block on block' processes. Ultimately, we take a model-independent view, defining a block structure to be 'finitely bounded' if there are only a finite number of large blocks, we prove that, under certain conditions, the block structure is finitely bounded if and only if it lacks 'periodic' consistency, thus complementing our main result on stochastic processes with reinforcement. Lastly, we investigate the consistency of block structure under certain conditions of 'positive' consistency, demonstrating that every bijective process with positive reinforcement has a consistent, constantly growing block structure, specifically exhibiting the consistency to be 'arithmetic' when the reinforcement is linear. We also show that, if the process has positive reinforcement and is bijective, then the consistency can be 'geometric' if, on average, the time between occurrences of $i$ increases at a rate faster than some $\ell > 0$. The paper introduces a novel framework for coreference, containment, and implications between logical principles within proof-theoretic semantics. This framework is capable of capturing diverse relationships between these principles, including coreference, strict containment, and reciprocal implications. By analyzing a general cut-admissible and sound sequent calculus, the paper establishes a method to determine whether a given formula is derivable in a given system or not, and also identifies circumstances under which the formula remains valid after being subjected to cut rules. Furthermore, the paper explores situations under which the generated proof will also be valid in the original system. Additionally, the paper examines how to extend the results to deal with more complex well-ordering properties and also applies these developments to two specific types of sequent calculi. The paper ultimately provides an innovative approach to dealing with implications between logical principles, offering a significant enhancement over previous methods. Furthermore, the paper identifies an association between the introduced method and Tarski's signatures, proving that the generated proof has equivalent meaning to a signature-free proof. Lastly, the paper applies and modifies existing proof-theoretic reconstruction techniques to derive and modify existing transformations between different types of intuitionistic and classical logics. Lying at the intersection of machine learning and operations research, our study centers on comparing label acquisition strategies for reward learning. Traditional supervised learning methods leverage previously solved problems to inform future solution strategies, whereas reward learning employs human feedback to shape the pursuit of optimal solutions. We analyze the implications of human comparison feedback and examine strategies for consolidating these comparisons into actionable guidance. Our findings demonstrate that grouping comparisons and applying general lessons learned can substantially enhance the efficiency of the learning process. We support these claims with experimental results from a real-world lighting control problem. Ultimately, our research offers a framework for systematically evaluating label acquisition methods, paving the way for optimized machine learning deployment costs. https://github.com/alexalex88/RewardLearning/tree/v0.2.0 is an open-source repository containing the code to reproduce our study's methods and findings. Our framework also facilitates the exploration of novel comparison methods. Secondly, we identify batch comparison strategies and examine their concurrent execution. Thirdly, we identify general lessons from these comparisons and apply them to optimize future development. Our approach is centerd on a real-world lighting control problem where human feedback is required to inform the pursuit of optimal solutions. We leverage the continuous nature of this problem to evaluate the temporal effects of these strategies. We show that the Smyth powerspace construction does not consistently maintain core-compact properties. Our approach involves displaying a core-compact space for which the Smyth powerspace becomes non-core-compact when applied to an arbitrary continuous function. This contradicts a previously held assumption that the Smyth powerspace preserves core-compact properties. Additionally, we explore an alternative method to core-compactification using the extension of functions to compact domains, illustrating that this method yields a wider range of core-compact spaces than the Smyth powerspace. This core-compactification can be utilized in various applications, such as extending continuous functions to compact domains and core-compactifying uniform spaces, including those resulting from the Shwartzman core-compactification process. It possesses key monotonicity and stabilizing properties, enabling it to preserve certain uniform properties and to be strongly stable to categorical extensions. Moreover, we derive an explicit description of the core-compactification provided by this method and show that it is equivalent to the Țodor core-compactification process. Furthermore, we study the properties of uniform spaces with a compactiﬁable domain (those for which the core-compactification process yields a space with a compact domain) and demonstrate that such spaces core-compactify any uniform space that is a categorical extension with preservation of the uniform space structure. This thesis explores Monte Carlo simulations of heavy quark bound states, with a focus on lattice QCD, where the challenge of incorporating the heavy quark's mass is addressed through an innovative method. By utilizing a novel suit of Symanzck operators for the heavy quark, we develop an exact algorithm for Monte Carlo simulations, where the critical step of heat-bath updates becomes efficient for the first time. Across various temperature and baryon number ranges, our method demonstrates practical applicability, and we successfully simulate systems involving gluons, light quarks and heavy quarks at the lattice. Notably, our studies include precise calculations of heavy quark properties, such as the mass of the tau lepton and the strong coupling constant alpha_S at 3 GeV. Furthermore, this research yields significant insights into the behavior of QCD in extreme conditions, including the transition from quark-gluon plasma to normal nuclear matter and the properties of compact stars. To achieve this, we developed an approach for Monte Carlo simulations of pure gauge theories at finite density, which we successfully tested at low density before extending our method to the more complex conditions at high density. Additionally, our thesis contributes to the ongoing debate in the particle physics community regarding the existence of dark matter in the universe through novel calculations of Higgs boson interactions with dark matter, light quarks and gluons at 3 GeV, based on arbitrary dark matter properties. Furthermore, our research on lattice QCD also explores possible extra dimensions in the universe through Monte Carlo simulations of a theory in five-dimensional space with the properties of a pure gauge theory at finite temperature and density. Lastly, our thesis delves into the theoretical implications of a model with the properties of a pure gauge theory at finite temperature and density for an infinite number of antiperiodic quarks, which corresponds to the Maxwell-Boltzmann approximation of lattice QCD. This research lays the groundwork for developing new types of dynamic machines inspired by biological adaptations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of building artificial structures that can walk on a substrate powered by a flow of charge, thereby opening up new avenues in the study of dynamic architecture. This experiment marks the first instance of observing current-induced forces in a molecular motor that can adapt.
