We conducted a thorough photometric analysis of GJ 229B, the most well-studied example of a sub-stellar object formed through planetary formation processes, to discover its atmospheric properties. We compared the data from a wide field detector on board the Spitzer Space Telescope, capturing the system at a distance of approximately 1.3 microns, with models of stellar atmospheres and found that the best fit corresponds to a late-type brown dwarf atmosphere that is cloudy and warm. Utilizing the principles of non-linear derivative regularization to fit data effectively, we were able to explore various atmospheric properties including the presence of grains, which we found to be essential for accurately modeling the observed spectrum. Our results are consistent with previous findings, including the distance between the host star and GJ 229B, detected at approximately 0.076" or 42 AU, as well as its estimated mass, which is more than 8.7 times the mass of the Earth, making it the first discovered massive exoplanet in the world at the time of the study in 2001. However, our study also suggests the presence of smaller grains, which we believe may be a sign of active accretion of solid material in the atmosphere of GJ 229B, indicating that its formation history is even more intricate than initially thought. As a result, targeting GJ 229B offers great opportunities for further research into the creation of celestial objects that exist between planets and stars. Moreover, we found that the new model of its atmospheric structure not only fits the data at hand but also predicts the presence of water in the system, which could be detected through future observations with the James Webb Space Telescope. Given its unique position as a sub-stellar object formed through planetary formation processes, we propose that GJ 229B should remain a key target for further research into its atmospheric properties as well as potential future applications in the field of exoplanetary science. Additionally, a diagram illustrating the life cycle of celestial objects in the theory of collapse of gaseous spheres onto a solid core is included at the very end. It demonstrates how GJ 229B can serve as an ideal example of a late-type sub-stellar object that is essential in validating the general ideas of exoplanetary formation processes in the universe. For example, targets such as Hubble Ultra Deep Field, which is about 17 billion light-years away, may one day discover substances with masses similar to GJ 229B using future advanced space telescopes at the end of the century

We present a detailed analysis of a spectral density that allows for the precise identification of tetraquark state existence via correlators of four heavy quarks. Our method invests the gauge-symmetry into four heavy quark correlators, constructing a basis of gauge-invariant operators that can be systematically generated. Our results further reveal the significance of certain corrections, specifically those involving the Lanzcos U matrix and instantaneous approximation, in binding energies. Furthermore, we identify certain potential issues with the spectral density method that might lead to the wrong assessment of certain tetraquark states as being bound. We conclude by highlighting certain preconditions that must be met in order for our method to accurately determine the existence of tetraquark states via a contact term analysis. Conversely, we model a scenario in which the $X(6900)$, widely considered a tetraquark state, does not meet these criteria and thus might not be a tetraquark state. Developing efficient algorithms for automatically detecting breaches in exchange programs requires substantial knowledge of both number theory and group representation. Underlying this challenge is the problem of identifying polynomial functions with a specific property: their values, when evaluated at elements of a particular sequence, result in a specific product. Two distinct sets of circumstances lead to two different types of breaches, each associated with a specific type of polynomial function. A theorem uniquely characterizing these polynomial functions in each case provides a detection algorithm for each type of breach, enabling the simultaneous identification of multiple breaches. This article presents new uniqueness theorems that establish a method for automatically and efficiently detecting violations in exchange programs. Implementing this method yields remarkable speed and scalability, achieving rates of over 1000 evaluations per second on a standard computer. In addition to their practical application, these theorems contain valuable generalizations of existing mathematical theories, including a generalization of a prior study on the applications of group theory and a new extension of a prior study on the properties of cyclotomic fields. A supplementary material features a detailed analysis of a record-breaking exchange program and a comprehensive examination by code of six existing algorithms for detecting breaches, including newly established connections between polynomial homology and the structure of certain fields. Furthermore, all computational methods and data have been made accessible through public repositories. Finally, this study presents an innovative framework for automatically generating and testing various types of breach scenarios, enabling the efficient exploration and evaluation of multiple breach scenarios. As a result, over 70 new breach cases have been discovered and validated, alongside two new exchange programs that cannot be resolved using current methods. The masses of bottom mesons in $F$-wave states are predicted using a coupling model derived from the light-front QCD effective theory. In this model, the mass of a state is determined by its quantum numbers, specifically the orbital angular momentum L and the quantum numbers of the constituents. A corresponding Regge theory is developed to describe the mass spectrum of these states. The linear Regge trajectories that emerge from this model are consistent with experimental data on the $F$-wave bottom mesons, with a square-mass defect of approximately 0.24 GeV$^2$. The parameters of the model, including the coupling constant and the kinetic mass term, are optimized to produce low errors in mass predictions for heavy bottom mesons. This model is evaluated based on its predictions for a broad range of bottom mesons, including both known and unknown states. This model is potentially useful for designing future experiments to discover new bottom mesons. We show that Szabados's conjecture holds for all minimal periodic decompositions of complex numbers with low complexity. In contrast, we prove that the conjecture cannot be true for all complex numbers with higher complexity in a specific geometric sense, thereby offering a counterexample. For this geometric approach, we introduce a new concept of "skewfulness" to describe the orientation of decomposition intervals in relation to their images. Additionally, we derive a property linking the skewfulness of a decomposition with the properties of its components, as well as establish that certain non-arithmetic divisors of algebraic numbers exhibit exceptionally high complexity in a specific divisorial sense, illustrating a separate aspect of Szabados's work. However, a direct connection between these results and the conjecture remains unsolved. On a separate note, we identify a significant shortcoming in a previous study by Novak, pointing out an oversight that renders Szabados's work incomplete and obstructs the proof of the conjecture. Nonetheless, we are able to construct an extensive library of explicit, computationally intractable minimal periodic decompositions that defy the conjecture, utilizing a novel number-theoretic finding that uncovers infinite families of such decompositions. As a consequence, the path to proving the conjecture becomes even more challenging. Finally, we derive a refined inequality that refines and approaches a core aspect of Szabados's work, offering a more precise bound in relation to a certain function of complexity. While this bound remains imperfect, it holds significance as a enhanced outcome. Furthermore, the properties of skewfulness and their relationship to divisibility prove valuable in obtaining these results, ultimately demonstrating the significance of addressing the rationality of geometric trace fields in order to understand minimal periodic decompositions and progress towards the conjecture. Ultimately, the relationship between complexity and the validity of Szabados's conjecture remains an open and intriguing question. The resulting Nonlinear DMD (NDMD) learns low-dimensional representations of data that capture the nonlinear dynamics of a system over time. To evaluate the effectiveness of different chess opening strategies and the skills of players using them, we apply the Economic Fitness and Complexity (EF&C) approach. This method determines the strategic value of each opening by measuring the winning probabilities of its practitioners against a random opponent. Our research utilizes a massive database of 1.5 million online chess games played over the last 15 years, covering the most commonly employed opening variations. The EF&C algorithm successfully distinguishes between stable and unstable aspects of chess openings, confirming existing knowledge about certain variations. Furthermore, we quantify the relative strengths of different opening strategies and rank the most advantageous ones. Additionally, our findings reveal insights into the development of player skills and provide a more accurate assessment of chess engine abilities. Leveraging our accurate rankings, we suggest refined benchmarks for measuring chess engines in order to maximize the reliability of performance evaluations and guide future research toward discovering key innovations. These findings are also used to suggest new opening guidance for human players and provide comments on the characteristics of players with exceptional skills. Our analysis is open to the public, and all associated data can be accessed at no cost. This research was carried out during the COVID-19 pandemic and is based on multiple countries, including the United States, England, Germany, and others. For our specific reasons for conducting this study, please see our report on this subject. Some crucial details about our investigation into the properties of chess openings and player skills have been incorporated into the accompanying materials. These key details are discussed in the following sections: Our Evaluation of the Reliability of Our Results, Our Response to Concerns from the Chess Community, Our Review of the Relevant Literature, Our View on the Potential Impact of Our Research, A New Approach to Studying Chess, A Public Announcement Regarding Future Plans, A Fond Remembrance of a Distinguished Chess Player and Expert, and a Private Message Regarding Future Collaborations in the Field of Chess. These images are discussed in more detail in the following section: An Overview of the Process of Creating the Visual aids Used in the Report. A key aspect of this section involves a tribute to the individuals who assisted with the creation of these visual aids and the significance of their contributions to the field of chess. The process of Accretion Induced Collapse (AIC) occurs when a massive binary system compels a smaller star to undergo a massive change in size, resulting in the transformation of that star from a white dwarf to a neutron star, or vice versa. Historically, the study of AIC has primarily focused on the white dwarf to neutron star transition, although recent discoveries have prompted increased interest in the reverse transformation, or the effects of external forces on such massive changes in size. A significant exterior force, such as gravity from a third object, can lead to a massive change in size, resulting in the formation of a stabilizing deformation before a massive object undergoes a sudden transformation. In the context of massive second stars, this scenario is most likely to occur when these stars are part of a triple system, as exterior forces from a third object can trigger a sudden increase in size, potentially causing these stars to collapse into a neutron star, as happened in the system of a massive neutron star and a smaller star. Recent discoveries have revealed that massive second stars, which become neutron stars, have magnetic fields that are significantly weaker than those of single-born neutron stars. However, these weak magnetic fields can still lead to a massive release of energy if these stars accumulate an excess of protons, resulting in an explosion known as a compact object that is significantly warmer than a typical neutron star. Utilizing computer simulations, our research shows how these stars, which are known as stranglers, form and how their properties and identities can be distinguished from other types of compact objects through analyses of various properties and signals, including gravitational waves, light in space, and gamma rays, resulting in four distinct stages in their formation and identification. These stages include: (i) forming a deformable shell around a massive star, (ii) collapsing this shell and forming a starless object, (iii) forming a star with a weak magnetic field, or (iv) forming an extremely hot, starless object. Depending on these properties, these objects can be identified as either neutron stars or other types of compact objects based on their electromagnetic properties, as these two options lead to distinct observations in the environment of these stars. A distinguishing characteristic of these stranglers is their relatively low heat capacity, as their surface material and core are made of dense, strange matter, resulting in an ability to store heat efficiently. A general method is presented to construct first integrals for any Euler-Lagrange system of order N, which relies on integrating the Lagrangian dynamics of lower orders to obtain useful conserved quantities. This method allows us to identify the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator as a reduced version of the Jacobi top and to discover a hidden connection to the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation. The obtained first integrals are validated by an independent check using the Noether theorem. Additionally, we provide a direct proof of the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator's integrability and establish a link between its conserved quantities and those of the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation. Since one of the obtained integrals depends on the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator's mass parameter, we confirm its complete integrability for certain special values of this parameter. A comparative analysis is performed between the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator and its variants, which includes the hydrodynamics of the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation and a new integrable model of order 4. This study showcases that higher-order Euler-Lagrange ODEs can be thoroughly integrated, contrary to a widely held belief that they are too complex to be solved analytically. As a whole, our work provides a valuable contribution to the development of conserved quantities for Euler-Lagrange ODEs of any order. Moreover, it is hoped that some of the integrals found in this study may prove useful for solving Euler-Lagrange ODEs in general, not just those of lower orders. While this program has yielded successful results for N = 2, 4, 6, we still hold out hopes of integrating the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation, a key problem of the field. Retrieving 3D shapes from 2D sketches is a complex problem because sketching involves a highly variable and creative process. Our study focuses on using 3D shapes and sketches directly without conversion to 2D or 3D. We investigated multiple potential approaches and found by measuring the similarity between sketch centroids, we can achieve superior results. This method performs better than other considered options, including comparing entire sketch point clouds and combining both centroid and point cloud features. Our approach is computationally efficient and allowed us to reach a retrieval accuracy of 42.3% at a distance threshold of 0.02 in the Classic-60 dataset. Additionally, we developed an institute-wide sketch competition where our method ranked first among six competing methods with a substantial margin. We also studied how sketch variability affects our approach and found reducing variability by removing repetitive features leads to better performance. Finally, we applied our best method to retrieve shapes based on their categories and found it to work effectively across various 3D datasets. You can find our code here: https://github.com/indiana4d/SkimPyL. SkimPyL is an open-source library for sketch-based retrieval that builds upon PCL, PYO, and scikit-learn with a strong focus on ease of use and performance. It provides an array of useful tools, including a variety of regression and classification algorithms as well as efficient search techniques like k-d tree. SkimPyL offers both global and local feature mapping with the capability to save and load them efficiently using PyTO. Our study is the first to apply sketch centroid similarity to retrieve 3D shapes, and SkimPyL's ease of use enables researchers to test different approaches quickly. For instance, modifying the CombineNet approach, which uses a multi-layer neural network to map sketches, to work with global features takes just a few lines of code. SkimPyL's high performance also stems from its smart implementation, which includes using a single memory allocation for the entire sketch, shape, and feature computation. This approach prevents memory fragmentation, which can be a problem when dealing with point clouds. In addition to sketch-based retrieval, SkimPyL can handle general shape computation with the aid of PCL, PYO, and scikit-learn, making it an extremely versatile library. The weak gravity conjecture states that an extremal black hole's mass will decrease in a canonical ensemble. However, this prediction falls apart when considering charge fluctuations. In order to resolve this apparent contradiction, the canonical ensemble must be modified to account for these fluctuations. A new ensemble, referred to as the'microcanonical ensemble with thermal charges,' is introduced in this study. A model consisting of non-interacting fundamental gravity states is used to develop this ensemble. The newly defined ensemble accurately predicts the thermodynamic properties of the gravitational system, including its entropy and heat capacity. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the ensemble leads to the weak gravity conjecture's original prediction, indicating that the mass of an extremal black hole will decrease in this ensemble. In contrast to the canonical ensemble, the mass-scaling exponent is perfectly saturated in the new ensemble. A thorough examination of the ensemble's properties indicates that these results are universal and apply universally. Furthermore, the study shows that the ensemble's characteristics match those of fermionic and bosonic gravity states. The convergence of ensemble and canonical methods for calculating thermodynamic properties is also investigated, as well as the behavior of mass-scaling exponents in both cases. A key discovery from this study is that the canonical ensemble yields an unsaturated mass-scaling exponent, unlike the microcanonical ensemble with thermal charges. A shift in sign for this exponent is observed when comparing the canonical and microcanonical ensembles. A simple physical explanation can be provided for this behavior. A mathematical extension of a previous study is also accomplished in this current investigation, as the entropy of the gravitational system was previously found to be in direct proportion to the three-dimensional volume. A corresponding general expression for thermal charges is derived in this study. In addition to these primary findings, the study reveals an unexpected discovery regarding charge fluctuations in the black-hole regime. A finding indicating that the fluctuation formula is proportional to the square of the temperature is also uncovered in this investigation. A simplified physical explanation can be provided for this behavior. A discovery indicating universal properties for thermal coefficients is also made in this study. A discovery indicating thermal coefficients are proportional to temperature for a gravity model consisting of fundamental states is also made in this investigation. A discovery indicating charge-dependent nature of thermal coefficients is also made in this study. A discovery indicating that thermal coefficients are proportional to the square of the charge for a gravity model consisting of fundamental states is also made in this investigation. A discovery indicating universal properties for thermal coefficients is also made in this study. A simplified physical explanation can be provided for this behavior.

Current reinforcement learning methods optimise a specific objective, neglecting broader societal and environmental implications. To tackle this limitation, our framework combines intrinsic motivation with extrinsic rewards, facilitating efficient training. We show that incorporating both intrinsic and extrinsic cues accelerates learning compared to solely extrinsic motivation, especially when the external reward signal is initially absent or delayed. Moreover, our approach also yields environmentally friendly outcomes, as the intrinsic motivation promotes exploratory behaviour beneficial for learning optimal policies. We validate the efficacy of this combination through experiments using evolved Monte Carlo agents and finding optimal policies for complex navigation tasks. Our model is compatible with a range of reinforcement learning methods, including policy gradient and evolutionary algorithms, and can be applied to a variety of scenarios, such as robotic systems and game-based environments. For instance, we employ a variant of our model to create a navigation policy for a robotic arm to successfully interact with a dynamic environment, as shown in the provided video illustration. Our model and associated code are freely accessible on GitHub. In conclusion, our framework offers an efficient means of learning flexible and adaptable agents capable of exceling in a broad spectrum of reinforcement learning challenges. We investigate particle models derived from Coloured Poincaré gravity. Introducing coloured versions of the metric tensor and Christoffel symbols leads to two different definitions of the Dirac operator. One is the Klein-Gordon equation, and the other involves a new matrix-valued wave equation. Developing mathematical representations of the basic objects in Coloured Poincaré gravity enables us to define these quantities in local co-ordinates. This allows for the derivation of new particle models derived from Coloured Poincaré gravity. A massless particle model mimics the behaviour of massless gluons and gravitons, while a massive particle model resembles the properties of massive gluons and scalar particles. However, the conventional Klein-Gordon equation for a scalar particle appears as a special case of the more comprehensive matrix-valued wave equation. Therefore, the massless and massive particle models in the Coloured Poincaré gravity framework offer more nuanced and comprehensive descriptions compared to those in Einstein's gravity theory. Additionally, the matrix-valued wave equation for a massive particle suggests a more fundamental role and implications for the spin and colour degrees of a particle's diffeomorphism, and possibly a more complex relationship between colour and spin. This research may serve as a starting point for examining Coloured Poincaré gravity from a particle's perspective and exploring its applications in both theoretical and experimental contexts. Finally, the fundamental relationships between colour, spin, and mass are left for future investigation. A future extension of this research could be the development of gauge conditions for Coloured Poincaré gravity that could facilitate the reduction of Coloured Poincaré gravity to Einstein's gravity theory. Firstly, we need to derive Einstein's gravity theory from the Coloured Poincaré gravity framework, and applying conventional Dirac methods, and then applying Dirac-Bergman Dirac procedures for the reduction of theories. A Coloured Poincaré gravity theory with Coloured de Donder's gauge yields Einstein's gravity theory in the standard Dirac formalism. Furthermore, applying the Dirac-Bergman-Dicke procedure for the reduction of Coloured Poincaré gravity yields Einstein's gravity theory with a non-standard Dirac formalism that differs from the standard approach employed in Einstein's gravity theory. This non-standard approach may be suitable for applications in the theoretical contexts of heat-kernel and Seeley-deWitt expansions, and also for the development of gauge conditions for Coloured gravitational fields that could facilitate the reduction of Coloured Poincaré gravity

One of the key indicators of scale-dependent complexity is the scale factor, $c$, which measures the growth of local density matrices over time. Another important aspect is the scale at which quantum systems start exhibiting chaotic behavior, known as the 'thermoflux' scale, $\xi$. In this paper, we have determined the scale factor, $c$, and the thermoflux, $\xi$, for a specific type of solenoid made from non-abelian anyons known as Ishibashi states. The calculations for these parameters would typically be highly intricate, however, since the solenoid exhibits a high degree of symmetry, the problem becomes more manageable, allowing us to derive analytical solutions for $c$ and $\xi$. The results of our study demonstrate that the scale factor, $c$, is unaffected by the solenoid's symmetries, whereas the thermoflux, $\xi$, is determined by these symmetries. By integrating Darcy's law and the mass balance equation, the fluid flow equation can be expressed in terms of head differences. However, this mathematical representation becomes overly complicated, making it difficult to apply in practical situations. Nonetheless, we discovered that the equation can be significantly simplified when the hydraulic conductivity is non-frequency-dependent with depth. In this scenario, the complete profile is divided into distinct sections, and we derive a unified equation for each individual layer. These simplified equations represent gradual changes in the vertical direction and may be combined with other established methods, such as the Green's function technique. Additionally, we demonstrated that our approach converges to the classic Boussinesq solution for infinitesimally small frequency increments. Furthermore, our results are applicable to various types of soil structures, including uniform, layer-based and exponentially decreasing hydraulic conductivity patterns. In particular, we derived a solution for the latter scenario, yielding an approximate analytical expression for the water table's vertical displacement. By deriving kinetic theory from the QCD Lagrangian with gauge invariant quark degrees of freedom, we justify the incorporation of Meissner-Serebryannyi tensors in this theory. Research into epitaxial growth on graphene has been gaining attention due to the unique properties of this substrate. However, the random structures formed during the growth on hexagonal layers confuse the understanding of the relationship between crystal lattice and properties. In this study, thin films made from tungsten selenide were deposited on a graphene substrate using molecular epitaxy, and through the analysis of the films' polycrystalline structures, a random orientation of the hexagonal layers was discovered. By changing the growth temperature, a transition from tetrahedral to hexagonal growth was observed, resulting in two distinct methods to achieve the hexagonal phase. Furthermore, the properties of the films, including their photo-luminescence and photo-conductivity, were found to be associated with the growth mode rather than the initial layer structure. The success of this research provides new possibilities in the development of two-dimensional materials and graphene hybrid materials with unique properties. This study investigates how the estimators of common stochastic trends and cointegration vectors are affected in a multi-dimensional system, particularly how they perform in the presence of extreme value phenomena and varying sample sizes. Our analysis reveals that even under standard assumptions, the estimators of these variables experience significant instability and bias, especially in the presence of extreme events, and these issues become even more pronounced as sample sizes differ greatly. Nevertheless, our research finds that these estimation problems can be addressed by employing a simple and well-established technique, the use of the median, thereby yielding accurate estimations of cointegration vectors and the number of common stochastic trends even under conditions of heavy tails and highly variable sample sizes. Moreover, our research discovers a surprising lack of relationship between these estimation techniques and the cointegration rank, particularly under the presence of extreme events, which leads to considerable under-estimation of cointegration vectors and the number of common stochastic trends. Ultimately, our research defends the use of the median as a more robust estimator, particularly in multi-variable systems, and thereby provides insight into its superior performance compared to alternative estimators and a range of large data set applications. Some of these applications include: (i) the joint estimation of cointegration and the cointegration space; (ii) the detection of cointegration; (iii) the estimation of cointegration vectors; (iv) the detection of cointegration with a reference vector; (v) the estimation of cointegration vectors with a reference vector; (vi) the presence of common stochastic trends; (vii) the size of the cointegration space; (viii) the relationship between cointegration and common stochastic trends. High-frequency trading data is examined to identify the skewness and excess kurtosis of individual stock returns and their impact on corresponding portfolio returns. It's observed that the moments of cross-sectional return distributions are directly linked to the moments of individual asset returns, particularly in response to asset price increases or declines. This research provides empirical grounds for a theoretical framework proposing a direct connection between cross-sectional return moments and those of individual asset returns. Furthermore, analysis focuses on the dynamics of skewness and excess kurtosis in cross-sectional return distributions and their implications for understanding the behavior of asset prices during periods of market stress. Ultimately, this research contributes to developing policies that maintain market stability and regulate trading activities at the individual and portfolio levels. Empirical findings also shed light on the established moment-related regulation introduced by the Securities and Exchange Commission, highlighting its relevance to maintaining market integrity. Additionally, this research explores the potential for further regulation through combination trading on the Chicago Board Options Exchange, which demonstrates significant discrepancies in moment-based characteristics across various trading strategies and market conditions. Consequently, this research suggests moments of cross-sectional return distributions as a crucial factor in formulating regulatory decisions related to high-frequency trading activities. In this context, the study proposes an eight-dimensional vector representing the moments of cross-sectional return distributions as a compact yet informative representation of market conditions, which can facilitate classification of various regulatory environments and their associated trading activities. Furthermore, this research applies the moments of cross-sectional return distributions to assess the impact of regulatory interventions, such as those associated with the Market Access Rule and Order 7-14-0001, on trading activities and market dynamics. Empirical findings demonstrate the significance of moment-based regulatory decisions, which may lead to inaccurately timed and scoped regulations, as evidenced by examinations of the Regulatory Review Process of the Securities and Exchange Commission. Ultimately, this research highlights the need for improved methods of evaluating market conditions, proposing alternative approaches, and suggests potential areas for further research in high-frequency trading. Advanced cardiac abnormality detection using ECG signals can be challenging, largely due to interference from noise and the low amplitude of essential heart information. This research introduces a powerful noise-reducing technique known as the Raw-MTEE (Raw Magneto-Electric Echo Time Encoding and Estimation) method, which effectively extracts crucial information from noisy ECG signals. By applying Raw-MTEE to real-world ECG data, the team successfully eliminated interference and highlighted the low-intensity heart information, enabling accurate detection of cardiac abnormalities using deep learning techniques. Compared to existing methods, the Raw-MTEE method achieved outstanding results, outperforming existing techniques with a high overall accuracy of 99.9% and a significant improvement in loss and macro F1 score values. Our work shows that Raw-MTEE coupled with a particular deep learning model yields superior performance in cardiac abnormality detection and serves as a reliable approach for sensing system design and signal processing. Additionally, this research received recognition at the IEEE NNSP 2021 conference, where it won the 'Best Student Paper Award'. Upon acceptance, the code related to this research will be accessible at a designated repository. Firstly, the work involves collecting raw data from 70 sensors using a CMOS Michelson interferometer, which is then used to train and evaluate models. It's worth noting that raw data was gathered from individuals with known cardiac conditions - 214 patients with cardiovascular disease and 214 healthy individuals. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, operations were performed on both interferometric signal modes (Active and Passive). Passive mode showed better outcomes, and after applying the 1D CNN model to the processed data, accuracy reached 99.9%, accompanied by high Matthew's correlation coefficient and macro F1 score values. When compared to other techniques such as Spectral-MTEE, EE, and Raw EE, the research found that accuracy reached 99.9%, whereas other methods achieved 97.1%, 95.6%, and 94.6% respectively. Furthermore, it is observed that three out of four classifications of cardiac conditions showed improved accuracy with sub-lead structure features. Based on these findings, the research indicates that the Raw-MTEE method offers superior performance in cardiac abnormality detection when compared to existing methods. Additionally, detecting cardiac conditions using ECG signals with a success rate of 99.9% demonstrates the effectiveness of the Raw-MTEE method. It is also noted that detecting cardiac conditions using Raw-MTEE features and deep learning techniques presents a promising approach to diagnosing cardiac disorders.

We investigate how sellers in non-credible second-price auctions behave in situations where winning bids exceed cost, and find that resultingly, they do not strive to garner the highest possible price in violation of the auction's rules. Through experiments, our evidence reveals that a lack of effort in untrustworthy auctions is attributed to sellers' desire to maintain trust in more credible environments. To build on our findings, a new model is developed, which differentiates between a seller's intrinsic and extrinsic motivations and assumes that a seller's intrinsic motivation is distributed uniformly between the cost and the bid. Under this model, our analysis shows that in untrustworthy auctions, a seller's extrinsic motivation is diminished relative to its maximum possible impact, resulting in our data's confrontation of this theoretical model. Additionally, our study reveals that a similar phenomenon may persist in other forms of untransparent auctions. This research introduces two innovative generative adversarial networks (GANs) that learn from brushstrokes in paintings created by famous artists. One GAN generates individual brushstrokes, while the other produces sets of brushstrokes in a sequential manner. To demonstrate their effectiveness, we employ these models to generate brushstrokes for famous works that have been modified in terms of color, size, and position to bring them closer to the style of the artist whose brushstrokes they were generated from. The results are then combined to recreate the original images, revealing a remarkable level of detail and accuracy in the brushstrokes, while also showcasing unique artistic interpretations inspired by the style of the artist in question. While our focus has been on mimicking the brushstrokes of three individual artists - Van Gogh, Picasso, and Pollock - the underlying framework of our GANs enables them to be adapted to learn from the brushstrokes of other famous artists as well. Ultimately, our research culminates in the creation of three brushstroke transformation GANs, which can modify the brushstrokes in modified versions of "Starry Night", "Guernica", and "Mural on South Bank", in a way that brings them closer to the unique style of their respective artists. These transformed brushstrokes can be used to create new and imaginative versions of these iconic paintings. To facilitate the reproduction of our results, we have made our code and brushstroke datasets available on our GitHub repository: https://github.com/amanpekhar/BrushStrokeTransformations. Similarly, the brushstroke datasets can also be found on the GitHub repository of the LIRIS institute: https://github.com/institut-liris/BrushStrokeTransformations-Inpainting. To view the generated brushstrokes in a interactive three-dimensional format, please visit: https://amanpekhar.github.io/BrushStrokeTransformations/. The occurrence of flavor anomalies in both kaon and B-meson systems can be seen as indications of a potential violation of lepton-flavor universality. If this is the case, it is plausible that these violations could be linked to a universal lepton flavor universality breaking interaction affecting all three generations of leptons. A theoretical model consisting of a universal lepton flavor universality breaking interaction, mediated by a spin-0 vectorial field, is presented in this study. However, the standard Wilson coefficient does not sufficiently explain the observed flavor anomalies. Nevertheless, possible extensions of this model to accommodate the given flavor anomalies are explored. Firstly, considering the occurrence of flavor anomalies in K^0 vs. \bar{K^0} decays. Secondly, looking at the possibility that these anomalies could be associated with dark matter. Thirdly, examining the occurrence of universal lepton flavor universality breaking interactions affecting two generations of leptons but not the third, which may be related to the neutrino mass hierarchy paradox. Lastly, exploring the possibility that these universal interactions could be responsible for the occurrence of flavor anomalies in (K/\pi) decays while also regulating the occurrence of B-meson anomalies through higher-dimensional operators. Model-building of this type can provide insight into the occurrence of flavor anomalies and their interconnections, as well as potential paths to confirm or disconfirm them through experimental testing. A few examples of experimental tests that can verify or refute these universal lepton flavor universality breaking interactions affecting all three generations of leptons are presented. Specifically, the following experimental tests are proposed: Confirming or refuting the universal lepton flavor universality breaking interactions affecting all three generations of leptons by measuring the occurrence of rare lepton flavor violating decays such as e^+e^- to mu^+mu^^- or tau^+tau^- within a certain energy range; Checking for the occurrence of a long-range coupling involving three generations of leptons and a neutral spin-0 vectorial field in decays such as e^+e^- to mu^+mu^-$\gamma$ or $J/\psi$ or $Y$($\psi'$) to mu^+mu^-$tau^+tau^- within a certain energy range; Testing for the occurrence of a short-range coupling involving three generations of leptons and a neutral spin-0 vectorial field in decays such as muon/tau decays to lepton $\gamma$ and a lepton pair or neutral B-meson decays to a lepton

We've made the dataset available in both free text and standardized XML formats. Using a novel approach to connect hydrodynamics and radiation using adaptive mesh refinement, researchers have simulated core collapse explosions and fast instabilities within these explosions. In one set of simulations, a successful explosion was found to suppress fast instabilities, while a failed explosion allowed these instabilities to occur. However, when an initial explosion occurred but the shockwave eventually receded, it triggered fast instabilities, much like in the case of a failed explosion. To better understand this transition, researchers conducted another set of simulations, starting with an initial explosion and allowing it to evolve, and found that when the blast wave interacted with a dense layer within the collapsing star, it formed structures that blocked the path to the outer layers, creating a cavity that allowed instabilities to occur and led to the explosion's failure. These findings highlight the complex relationship between an explosion's success or failure and the formation of fast instabilities, and can illuminate how an explosion might be quenched in a supernova event. Additionally, when an explosion occurs, it can create conditions in which neutrino-driven convection is possible, and this can impact the collapse of a star. For example, even when an initial explosion occurs, it can still lead to the collapse of a 55 solar mass star, but an explosion occurs only if it encounters a certain density at 2200 km from the star's center, otherwise the star collapses. These findings have significant implications for how a supernova explosion might be quenched, and the potential for fast instabilities to occur when an explosion occurs or is quenched. Recent advancements in deep learning technology have led to remarkable achievements in diagnosing ADHD, however training these models requires extensive datasets and lengthy time-consuming processing. Since medical imaging data often includes superfluous information that can hinder classification performance, identifying and eliminating unimportant regions of interest is a promising approach to optimize model efficiency. To address this challenge, a new model called Efficient ADHD Deep Learning (EADL) was proposed. By leveraging a multi-scale attentional mechanism to concentrate on key regions of interest, EADL can effectively improve accuracy while reducing the required training data size. During the training process, EADL can pinpoint and eliminate unimportant regions of interest, resulting in a reduced number of necessary features for classification. To achieve this goal, the model uses a novel capsule mechanism to derive the classification features, and implemented classificatory with two different architectures, ResNet50 and MobileNetV2, for various classification tasks. By integrating the capsule mechanism into the models, EADL achieved notable improvements in accuracy and abridged the models' breadth, reducing the required training data by a factor of 8.5. In particular, the mobileNetV2-based EADL achieved impressive classification results, attaining an impressive 70.46% accuracy on the reduced dataset, or  clouding 70.46%, with only 14 out of the original 120 regions of interest, resulting in a substantial time savings of 85.7% over the original ResNet50-based model. Similarly, the combination of the capsule mechanism and reduced attentional mechanism yielded notable performance gains on the benchmark dataset with minimal breadth reductions. Consequently, the proposed EADL emerged as an highly efficient and accurate ADHD deep learning model. Moreover, the key regions of interest highlighted by EADL show notable correlations with established clinical indicators for ADHD, thus providing valuable clinical insights and patterns that have not been previously levied. As a result, the EADL model offers great potential in optimizing various medical image classification tasks involving extensive data sets and significant feature dimensions. Lastly, the proposed methods of reducing regions of interest can be easily generalized and applied to other deep learning models, thus opening up new avenues for research. We examine a couple of important nonlinear operators that have significant implications in various mathematical models. The first operator is connected to the $L^p$-norm ligand concentration law in systems biology, while the second operator is related to a generalized $p$-Laplacian and occurs in various other types of mathematical models. Our study focuses on ensuring the existence and uniqueness of an interior fixed point for these operators under specified conditions on the parameters involved. Additionally, we provide explicit expressions for the operators in question and demonstrate that they can be represented through a combination of monotone and Lipschitz-continuous functions, which are crucial for generating numerical schemes based on operator splitting. We develop one such splitting algorithm and investigate its convergence, while also maintaining its simplicity and efficiency. Our theoretical findings are reinforced through the inclusion of multiple numerical examples and benchmarks that showcase the effectiveness of the proposed method in various types of nonlinear equation systems. To the best of our knowledge, this method has considerable advantages over existing approaches to solving similar types of problem. Our research ultimately inspired the development of a computational fixed point iteration scheme, which holds promise for solving a range of monotone and convex large-scale nonlinear equation systems. Some exciting potential applications of this method include solving a generalized Allen-Caulfield model for the segregation of lymphocyte and cancer cells, a Dirichlet boundary value problem, and a family of elliptic nonlinear partial differential equations. Our results in these areas hold the potential to be reduced to regular fixed points through the use of suitable potential functions. Our research has further inspired the creation of a flexible Uni-FIT algorithm, which allows for the simultaneous solution of systems of nonlinear equation and optimisation problems. To confirm the correctness and efficiency of the proposed methods, we provided ten benchmark numerical examples and comparative studies that showcase our approach. Moreover, we applied and evaluated the developed methods in solving a modified lymphocyte-cancer cell Allen-Caulfield model, a family of elliptic nonlinear partial differential equations, and a system of nonlinear time-space fractional evolution equations. Our research confirms that these methods hold great promise for their potential application in the solution of various mathematical models and problems. Some of these applications constitute new and challenging research problems in their own right. Our study constitutes a significant extension to the existing literature on operator splitting algorithms for solving nonlinear equation systems and provides a fresh and promising perspective on this topic. To the best of our knowledge, the approaches and results presented in this research are original and significant in their own right. As their expansion forms often differ from the original phrase, there can be uncertainty regarding their intended meaning. To improve performance, systems need to account for the scarcity of acronym symbol types, common components like'Corp' and " Ltd", and usage variations across various domains. Furthermore, accurate identification of acronyms and their corresponding expansion forms poses a challenging task. To address these issues, a two-stage neural network model is proposed, one focusing on acronym symbol type classification and the other on acronym form and expansion matching. The model's performance relies on the dual representation of acoustic and visual features provided by a speech recognizer and a vision-based datum extractor. A rectifier is constructed by placing two uncoupled quantum Hall bars with distinct filling factors side by side. One bar serves as a heat source with electrons in a higher filling factor and the other as a heat sink with electrons in a lower filling factor. Due to the differences in filling factors, there is an energy barrier between the two bars and heat can only pass through via a tunneling process. We calculate the heat transfer rate and find that it varies according to the temperature difference, enabling a device to function as a heat rectifier. Moreover, our theory allows for a thorough examination of the rectification efficiency, potentially enhanced by interactions and modified by topological effects. Additionally, we show that an alternative design involving multiple quantum Hall layers can boost the rectification performance. Consequently, quantum Hall systems may offer appealing heat rectification alternatives due to their robust topological properties and the high thermal currents they can sustain. Moreover, our findings may also be applicable to other two-dimensional systems with strong interactions, such as composite fermion insulators and half-filled Landau levels in the presence of a Landau level filling factor 1/2. Furthermore, we predict that heat rectification can be experimentally verified using a thermopower measurement method that measures the electric current induced by a temperature gradient in a quantum Hall device. To confirm our theory's validity, we performed experiments utilizing a GaAs/AlGaAs quantum Hall sample in a triple layer conduction configuration. Our experiments involved measuring the electric current and the temperature gradient in a quantum Hall device, and the results show that heat rectification can be observed at low temperature and that the rectification efficiency approaches the maximum theoretical limit as the temperature decreases further. By disabling parallelism, a mechanism is developed to stabilize DNA data retrieval performance while adjusting primer densities to balance the trade-off between data density and error tolerance according to each partition's specifications. Furthermore, a framework is established to dynamically recalibrate primer pairs based on actual DNA factory performance. To evaluate the efficacy of this approach, several DNA factories from renowned companies and research institutions have been simulated, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method in achieving near-optimal results. Topological phases in nodal line semimetals offer an intriguing setting in which to explore the theoretical concept of momentum-space topological order. A key aspect of nodal lines is their intrinsic one-dimensional nature in momentum space, which is distinct from higher-dimensional topological orders. This distinction makes it challenging to develop effective theoretical tools for describing momentum-space topological order. We address this challenge by adapting a method previous applied to systems with a gap hierarchy to nodal line semimetals. We explore the outcome of this description within the context of a simple model representing a nodal line semimetal. Our analysis indicates that the model exhibits momentum-space topological order, which can be quantified through specific topological indicators. We further observe that the gap functions generated by the descent functor display a diverse range of behaviors relative to the nodal line. Some gap functions localize at points where the Fermi surface touches, while others become discontinuous in momentum space, adhering to a pattern of periodic variations. These variations are mirrored in the topological indicators, leading to a classification of the momentum-space topological orders based on the type of discontinuous gap function present. Lastly, we calculate physical properties such as the thermal conductivity and reflectivity, showing that they are sensitive to the momentum-space topological order. Our work offers insight into the theoretical concept of momentum-space topological order and its connection to the geometry of nodal lines in parameter space. We speculate that momentum-space topological order may serve as a driving force for the formation of nodal lines with complex geometries. Additionally, we propose that systems exhibiting momentum-space topological order could be distinguished through a combination of experimental techniques, including heat and momentum-resolved measurements of quantity and thermodynamic properties. The possibility of optical probes detecting momentum-space topological order remains a topic for future research and could contribute to the understanding of topological semimetals. Additionally, the concept of momentum-space topological order may be extended to other topological semimetals featuring points and loops as nodal sites. Conversely, momentum-space topological order could be avoided in systems with a hierarchy of gaps by choosing a connection strategy that does not generate a gap hierarchy. Moreover, the applied mathematical framework can be adapted for use with systems that cannot be reduced to a topological semimetal model. Researchers examining the dynamics of internal waves have historically relied on expensive and complex experiments, but recent advances in imaging technologies and software analysis have made it possible to study these phenomena more easily and precisely. Through a series of carefully designed experiments, our study explores how waves propagate from oscillating objects placed horizontally within a vertically stratified water environment. We paid close attention to how these waves speed up or slow down as they move away from the objects and discovered that their speed varies depending on the density gradients, object size, and movement pattern. We found that waves on the lighter side of the density interface move faster than those on the darker side and that larger objects tend to produce faster-traveling waves. Additionally, we observed a more complex movement pattern in the deep water area and interestingly, we found that waves can speed up or slow down as they move perpendicular to the density gradient. Our experiment's detailed two-dimensional mapping of wave speed allows us to compare it to existing theories and make new predictions. As an added benefit, our study has applications in fields beyond oceanography, such as meteorology and hydroacoustics. To facilitate further research and analysis, we include a comprehensive dataset and explanatory video with our paper. This study was motivated by previous work in the field, including renowned research papers and theoretical models, but we aim to move forward in a different direction in the discussion section. Lastly, we highlight potential future research avenues based on recent breakthroughs and technological advancements. Finally, we outline the benefits and challenges of applying artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques to study internal waves. This paper introduces a new method for estimating the entropy of a discrete noise process using a context tree. The algorithm operates under the assumption that the noise follows a Markov property, with the independence between consecutive samples determined by a fixed metric, and calculates the maximum possible entropy associated with a binary tree, given observed data. The approach involves ensuring the input entropy remains greater than zero, as otherwise the learning algorithm would not provide reliable results. The proposed method converges to the true entropy at a rate of O(n^(-1/(2l))) for trees of depth l and n independent samples, and can also be modified to enhance the accuracy of existing entropy estimation algorithms. Additionally, the paper illustrates the potential applications of this algorithm in information theory and beyond. The associated software can be accessed at https://github.com/alexalexandrov/entropy_tree. Specifically, the provided code solves the online version of the entropy estimation problem, as well as variants involving constraints on the tree structure and observations corrupted by noise. The software also generates the figures featured in the paper's supplementary materials and additional content. A key technique utilized for proving the algorithm's convergence involves analyzing the distance between the true and estimated trees on observed data sequences. The results demonstrate the algorithm's ability to recognize the true tree structure with high probability under certain conditions. The proof involves complex mathematical calculations and involves multiple approaches including first-order Taylor expansion, smooth functions, and the concentration of the entropy. Key lemmas used in the proof include Lemma 5, Lemma 6, and the coupling argument in Lemma 7, which establish essential inequalities, derive crucial bounds, and establishes the distance between the true and estimated trees converging to zero. Key challenges addressed in the paper include ensuring the input entropy remains above zero, achieving the optimal tree structure, handling observations corrupted by noise, and providing the fastest convergence rate. The potential of artificial intelligence (AI) is being extensively explored in the medical sector, and one of the crucial elements for developing and implementing AI-powered solutions is the availability of large, high-quality imaging databases, known as biobanks. Consequently, there is a pressing need for designers and implementers of biobanks to consider how these resources will evolve to effectively utilize AI capabilities. To address this gap, this article provides comprehensive guidance on the pivotal factors to take into account when creating biobanks that can seamlessly integrate AI systems, covering both existing and prospective technological advancements. Specifically, the article focuses on the underlying technical challenges and discusses the critical implications for data and knowledge management, clinical data retrieval, and human machine interaction. Ultimately, this article aims to enhance the understanding of biobanks as a foundation for AI research and development within the medical imaging sector. Although the article's primary focus is on biobanks that support diagnostic radiology, the discussed principles and points can be applied to other types of medical imaging modalities and sectors. Additionally, further information on the specified requirements for biobanks can be found in the comprehensive report by the WHO-IOM 1004 expert group on AI in medical imaging and diagnostics. In a study, primary care clinical data lacking specific test results was found to be poorly augmented by image-based data augmentation techniques. Conversely, minor modifications to clinical feature datasets were discovered to yield significant improvements in model accuracy. To address these limitations, a novel data augmentation method was proposed, incorporating clinically plausible alterations to testing data without requiring actual sample inputs. When applied to a large-scale dataset, this approach led to a notable enhancement in model performance on under-augmented features, resulting in improved overall accuracy. Furthermore, the methodology was found to be adaptable to various datasets and models, as demonstrated by applications to multiple primary and hospital-based care datasets. As a result, this approach is now being utilized in a primary care clinical environment to enhance model predictive capabilities. Polymatroidal ideals have an associated lattice that forms the basis for their characterization as non-polynomial elimination ideals. These ideals' properties and classifications depend on the structure of this associated lattice. A characteristic feature of polymatroidal ideals is the presence of specific linear subvarieties whose intersection they disrupt, leading to their classification via a type of combinatorial structure known as a matroid. A proposed new class of ideals, called quasi-polymatroidal, involves a relaxation of the typical polymatroidal constraints, resulting in a more permissive set of conditions. Examples of such ideals can be found in the context of hypersurfaces and their related linear subvarieties. A related concept, quasi-polymatroidal modules, can also be developed by applying the same logic to ideal classification to the context of graded modules. A specific class of such ideals, called 1-truncated polymatroidal ideals, exhibits similar characteristics to polymatroidal ideals, but with a more limited impact on linear subvarieties. A related combinatorial structure, called a subpolymatroid, is developed to classify such ideals based on the presence of certain divisors. A proposed new class of ideals, called Horn polymatroidal ideals, results from relaxing the typical polymatroidal constraints in a different manner, and is found to be equivalent to 1-truncated polymatroidal ideals. A proposed new class of ideals, called Horn modules, results from applying the same logic to ideal classification to the context of graded modules. A specific case study, involving the rank 2 toric ideal $I_{2,3}$, demonstrates the presence of two distinct Horn modules, one of which is equivalent to a previously known ideal, while the presence of the other cannot be confirmed using current methods. A related concept, Horn-Hessian modules, can also be developed by applying the same logic to the context of graded modules. A proposed new class of ideals, called Horn-spur, results from applying the same logic to ideal classification to the context of hypersurfaces and their related linear subvarieties, but with a more limited impact on linear subvarieties. In probabilistic origin-destination demand modeling, the posterior distribution often involves a large, high-dimensional covariance matrix.  Regularization can help shrink this matrix towards a zero-patterened structure, yielding sparse demand outcomes.  However, existing methods face challenges when samples are scarce and the demand matrix contains mere siblings in a hierarchical grouping.  This paper addresses these issues with the lasso regularization approach to probabilistic OD demand modeling.  By formulating the posterior distribution as a lasso-regularized least squares problem, the paper derives necessary and sufficient conditions for sparse demand matrix solutions.  Given the non-convex lasso optimization problem, the paper proposes an iterative algorithm combining the iterative thresholding algorithm with stochastic gradient descent.  The results show that the algorithm effectively produces sparse demand matrices in scenarios with limited data availability.  When applied to the demand matrix of a large-scale transportation network, the algorithm shrinks the covariance matrix towards a structured, group-sparsity pattern, yielding a more accurate demand structure reconstruction compared to existing methods.  The numerical results confirm the algorithm's superior performance over alternative approaches in both a synthetic and a real-world scenario.  Specifically, the results show that the algorithm outperforms existing methods in reconstructing the demand structure with a superior precision and a considerable computational speed-up.  The results also highlight the potential for lasso regularization to enhance the calibration of spatial regression models with a low number of observations.  Finally, the results show that the algorithm offers a versatile tool for probabilistic OD demand modeling with a wide range of applications in transportation data analysis and regulatory policy assessment.  The potential for extending the lasso regularization approach to probabilistic vector quantile regression and other spatial regression models is also explored. Our study revealed that in systems with weak nonlinear frequency dispersion, stable phase-locked states can persist even when the dispersion is quite pronounced. A novel method is introduced for creating a uniform spanning tree using a hybrid approach that combines the benefits of both exploratory and exploitative strategies. This hybrid algorithm (HAS) approximates the optimal tree probability by first generating a precise UT from a randomly chosen full binary tree and then pruning the tree to match Uniform Spanning Tree (UST) properties, employing a novel expo-explo strategy. Practical implementations of HAS demonstrate superior efficiency and efficacy in comparing to existing algorithms. Furthermore, theoretical analysis under specific conditions confirms that HAS attains optimal efficiency. In cases where certain criteria are not met, a modified version of HAS is developed, showing that it remains relatively efficient. Last, a simulation-based comparison validates the theoretical findings of each algorithm's efficiency. This work culminates in the creation of open-source code to facilitate efficient uniform spanning tree generation. The code is accessible through the GitHub repository https://github.com/aman961/introML-lab.git, specifically within the Uniform_Spanning_Tree generation script https://github.com/aman961/introML-lab/blob/main/Uniform_Spanning_Tree/Uniform_Spanning_Tree.py. Additionally, the generated trees can be visualized using NetworkX and Matplotlib as shown in the visualization script https://github.com/aman961/introML-lab/blob/main/Uniform_Spanning_Tree/visualization.py. Both scripts can be executed locally to observe the uniform spanning trees for varying edge probabilities. Additionally, an online interactive dashboard built with Plotly utilizes data from past academic entrance exams to demonstrate how different generation algorithms impact efficiency in a practical context. This research was part of our introductory ML lab, guided by Prof. Utkarsh and co-guided by Prof. Akshat, under the supervision of Prof. Saha. This paper introduces the MusicTM-Dataset, a comprehensive music dataset comprised of three modalities: musical notes, audio spectra, and lyrics. The MusicTM-Dataset is specifically designed to enable efficient cross-modal retrieval in music representation learning. Our dataset incorporates a diverse collection of 10,000 songs from the Million Song Dataset, paired with modalities that are not directly linked in order to mirror real-world music processing scenarios. Additionally, we developed a large music text dataset with 114,926 lyrics from Korean song lyrics, which totals approximately 3.3 million words. Our study centers on the utilization of music texts to develop effective cross-modal models. Specifically, we demonstrate how the modalities in the MusicTM-Dataset can be employed to address key challenges in music representation learning, such as musical note and audio spectrum sequence alignment, musical note generation, and music lyrics retrieval. Moreover, we established the Korea Music Retrieval Challenge (KMRC) 2022 to verify the performance of existing methods in cross-modal retrieval tasks and to evaluate the effectiveness of our dataset. Our analysis thoroughly examines the performance of multiple model architectures, including those utilizing pre-trained Transformer models. Ultimately, our research identifies areas for further improvement in music representation learning, as well as highlights the potential for the modalities in the MusicTM-Dataset to enhance the development of cross-modal models. As such, the MusicTM-Dataset can serve as a vital resource for researchers striving to achieve significant advancements in this field. With our dataset in place, we anticipate a heightened interest in the development of cutting-edge music representation learning models. Our dataset is accessible at https://github.com/SeoSungHwan/MusicTM-Dataset. KMRC 2022 challenge results can be found at https://kmrc2022.seohungwan.com/. Additionally, our extended paper is available for viewing at https://seohungwan.github.io/papers/MusicTM_Dataset.pdf.

This study introduces Ontodia, an interactive visual tool for exploring and navigating complex datasets described using RDF and OWL, now available as a part of the Knowledge Graph Visualizer platform. We illustrate Ontodia's capabilities by creating interactive visualizations of Wikidata, utilizing its extensive knowledge about countries and their connections. We outline Ontodia's features and functionality, explaining how it enables user-driven visual data exploration and customization. Furthermore, we examine the benefits of using Ontodia in educational settings, demonstrating its potential to enhance learning experiences and introduce conceptual modeling. We invite readers to access Ontodia and explore its applications in depth. Additionally, all source code and data used in this work are freely available on GitHub for reproduction and further development. Lastly, we look into future perspectives and potential advancements for Ontodia and the Knowledge Graph Visualizer. They share the goal of serving the RDF and OWL community by providing innovative visualizations and exploratory tools to uncover hidden insights within datasets. We envision a future where these features and methodologies inspire a new generation of researchers and knowledge graph applications. We are confident that Ontodia and the Knowledge Graph Visualizer, through continuous development and expansion, can keep pace with the rapid advancements in RDF and OWL technologies. They will remain adaptable platforms to create innovative visualizations, exploratory tools, and methodologies rooted in contemporary knowledge graph technologies. We intend to maintain their compatibility with the latest technologies through progressive enhancements and regular updates over time. For instance, we plan to incorporate the latest advancements in web technologies, such as Web Components, to further improve the and, thus ensuring a smooth transition towards future technologies. Moreover, we plan to introduce more sophisticated evaluation techniques and established benchmark suites for knowledge graph data exploration and navigation to assess the efficacy of novel visualizations and exploratory tools in order to facilitate the knowledge graph community in creating and leveraging deep, abstract, and understandable models of complex datasets, such as Wikidata. This is particularly essential when applying knowledge graphs to critical applications and decisions, as described in the survey on practical knowledge graph applications [84]. Last but not least, our knowledge graph visualizer has sparked interest in enhancing the visualizations and exploratory tools for RDF and OWL datasets, as demonstrated through the feedback from Prof. Sebastian Kruska and Prof. Maxime Chevalier, showcasing the potential of Ontodia in exploring and navigating complex datasets, such as systems of dependent families and geographic connections between countries. This has enabled users to delve into these complex datasets, uncover hidden insights, and gain a deeper understanding of the underlying ontological models.

This work proposes an efficient approach to generating guidance strategies using modeling techniques that can be easily modified to account for human preferences, without the need for extensive piloting. The development of guidance strategies models within the Lotse library allows for real-time guidance recommendations to be produced by combining the plane's geographical location, trajectory, speed, and speed direction with pre-defined human preferences for specific navigation procedures. To evaluate our approach, we created eight standard procedure models and two alternative models that took into consideration two specific pilot preferences, resulting in a significant reduction in time to arrival in comparison to automated flight paths. The proposed system enables the real-time adaptation of guidance strategies based on pre-defined patterns and can be applied to a range of navigation procedures, utilizing a universal knowledge base that can be easily updated to incorporate new guidance strategies. Furthermore, the modular structure of the system allows for the addition of additional modeling techniques to better tailor guidance to individual pilot preferences. Although the current implementation of the system is limited to simulator environments, it has the potential to be scaled up for use in autonomous aircraft systems. Feedback from seven experienced pilots revealed that our approach was feasible and revealed opportunities for further improvement in how guidance strategies are developed and utilized. We studied a basic model that involves a mixture of several species that repel each other when interacting, and we examined how they behave in a confined space. In this model, each species has a specified number of distinct states, and when similar species come together in a small area, they form a single, unified entity. Our analysis shows that, in a steady state, the majority of the system's density resides in a limited number of distinct condensates, and the total number of these condensates does not exceed the number of species in the mixture. In order to understand how our model system evolves over time, we demonstrated its equivalence to a network of decoupled, independently evolving populations. Specifically, each distinct condensate corresponds to a population that represents a particular species group, and the system's density distribution is divided into sub-scales that mirror the different species groups. Our analysis provides explicit formulas for calculating the steady-state distribution within each population group. In addition, we analyzed a related model system that involves a mixture of species that interact with each other when similar, but with the added restriction that each species can only form a single, unified entity. In this model, the total number of condensates is directly related to the number of species in the mixture. Observations of the Ca II K line from the Solar Magnetograph on board the SOHO/SUNWATCH have been analyzed.  Two specific events, involving the movement of magnetic disturbances across sunspots, were studied in the speed range of 10-100 km/s.  One event occurred on July 18, 2003, and another on December 13, 2003, both in active region 10648/10649.  The Ca II K line images revealed that the magnetic disturbances, associated with the event on July 18, traveled at a speed of 80 km/s from northwest to southeast, while the disturbances, associated with the event on December 13, moved at a speed of 60 km/s from the northwest to the southeast.  It is assumed that the magnetic disturbances were caused by flares.  The speed of the disturbances in both events approximates the speed of the related flares, as recorded by the GOES satellite.  The average speed of the disturbances in the Ca II K line images was 70 km/s.  The speed of the disturbances in the July 18 event, and December 13 event, respectively, is consistent with the implications of the empirical model of Joshi and Ghosh (2006), and also with the speed of the flares in the X1.1 and M1.0 events, as recorded by the RHESSI satellite.  The speed of the disturbances in the Ca II K line images was compared with the speed of the dark features in the microwave emission, as observed in the 17 GHz PLATO image, and the speed of the dark emission was estimated to be 100 km/s. Current methods for evaluating the robustness of reinforcement learning algorithms to changes in their environment's dynamics assume a predictable progression of modifications, which is often unrealistic in real-world scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose an approach that assesses an RL agent's ability to adapt to diverse and unexpected curriculum modifications. To achieve this, our method leverages a sequential learning framework with multiple agents, each specializing in a particular phase of the curriculum. By examining the performance of these agents under various curriculum variations, our approach effectively evaluates the robustness of RL algorithms to unexpected changes in their environment. Moreover, our method can identify specific modification steps that pose challenges to the RL algorithms, thus informing data augmentation strategies to enhance their resilience. To illustrate the effectiveness of our method, we demonstrate its application to multiple RL algorithms, including PPO and SARSA, and obtain encouraging results. Our approach, including the curriculum construction and evaluation process, can be found online at https://github.com/alec-jm/curriculum_construction. Further details regarding our method's construction and evaluation are presented in the paper's supplementary materials. An additional video is available at https://youtu.be/6nCTPN FirMVg. Curriculum construction can be replicated by running the command curlver.py in a terminal. Evaluation of an RL algorithm's robustness is achieved via the command evaluate_rllb_curriculum.py. To facilitate reproducibility, our method's output is displayed in the form of videos, which can be found online at https://youtu.be/6nCTPN FirMVg. Additionally, performance metrics can be accessed through the link https://nucl.ee.columbia.edu/~alec-jm/rlrobustness/index.html. To conserve computational resources, our approach precludes environmental dynamics that are unlikely to arise in real-world scenarios, thus reducing the necessity for extensive curriculum construction and evaluation. Nonetheless, our method remains accommodating of existing datasets such as MuJoCo and PyBullet.
