This research explores the geostrophic easterly jet model introduced by Pelizzetti and Deroux in 2019, investigating the existence of non-trivial traveling waves arising from Couette flow perturbations. A new approach is developed to establish the existence of these traveling waves, considering a broader class of solutions with reduced regularity. Specifically, for a regularity level of $H^{1+\epsilon}$, where $\epsilon > 0$ is a measure of the trade-off between regularity and strength of the stratification, non-trivial traveling waves are found to exist near Couette flow. Furthermore, strain estimates are developed to demonstrate that as the strength of the stratification increases, the existence of these traveling waves is guaranteed for a broader range of regularity. Finally, strain estimates are also developed to estimate the linear instability threshold for modulational instability in this system. Specifically, when the strength of the stratification exceeds a critical value linked to the Rossby number, a range of wavelengths becomes linearly unstable, including those found in the perturbations of Pelizzetti and Deroux. However, their corresponding growth rates are shown to be sub-exponential. Conversely, when the strength of the stratification falls below this critical value, all wavelengths become linearly unstable, exhibiting exponential growth rates. Notably, the most unstable perturbations are found to be obliquely oriented and feature a distinctive 'roller' structure. Specifically, as the strength of the stratification decreases, the most unstable perturbations shift from being wide and low-amplitude to being narrower and more intense. In particular, when the strength of the stratification drops to about two orders of magnitude lower than the baseline value, the most unstable perturbations begin to resemble those found in the baroclinic instability of Couette flow. Consequently, it is hypothesized that the most unstable perturbations identified by Pelizzetti and Deroux are, in fact, manifestations of a second type of instability. Achieving control over polarization at the single-photon level poses a significant challenge but is vital for the development of novel light sources. Employing a combination of classical and quantum control methods, we have successfully designed a sequence of unitary transformations that enable full polarization control for a single-photon state in a circularly polarized Bose-Einstein condensate. This approach is exemplified through experimental implementation using laser pulses and magnetic resonance manipulation of the condensate's atoms. Our experiment boasts a high success rate, yielding $98.2\%$ of the target photons after processing $7.5\times10^4$ photons. This research lays the groundwork for a wide range of polarization-dependent quantum applications. Due to the government's ineffective response, numerous citizens' rights have been violated. There is a severe shortage of healthcare personnel, equipment, and treatment options, prompting the public to seek alternatives such as unverified social media information. This research undertakes a comprehensive examination of the societal, economic, and health impacts of the pandemic on South Africa's citizens. A descriptive analysis of available data on COVID-19 cases and deaths, mortality rates, and health statistics is conducted. The consequences of the pandemic on the economy, commerce, tourism, and education are also investigated. A thorough review of the government's response to the pandemic is presented, including an evaluation of their efficacy. Where possible, a comparative analysis with other BRICS nations regarding health, economic, and trade metrics is performed. existing methods. Furthermore, the paper investigates the effectiveness of
horizontal and vertical stacking methods in hierarchical fusion. Based on the

Specifically, when N(G) is considered in relation to |G|, it turns out that this quantity has a fixed maximum value over all nilpotent groups of a given order. Conversely, this maximum value can indeed be attained by a nilpotent group of that order. These equations represent a continuum limit of the $S^{(1,0)}$ variable from the Gubinets' scheme. Utilizing techniques developed by Gubinets, it is proven that under specific interpolation methods, the stochastic Korteweg-de Vries equations converge strongly to a continuum process. A key aspect is constructing a continuous process mapping that aligns with the Gubinets' scheme, enabling a direct link between stochastic equations and the Korteweg-de Vries equation. Furthermore, the paper establishes the strong convergence of family stochastic Korteweg-de Vries equations, incorporating random forcing terms related to Anderson's Brownian motion. It also proves the strong convergence of infinite-dimensional stochastic equations driven by Lévy noise. A key step involves proving the strong convergence of the stochastic equations without relying on standard Prokhorov-type compactness methods. Instead, the work leverages the geometry of infinite-dimensional stochastic flows, particularly the continuous mapping method. As a result, the paper presents novel estimates for stochastic flows, including a bounded domain technique. To address this issue, a novel strategy called Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS) is proposed, incorporating a balanced sampling approach to optimize the model's performance. By incorporating additional negative proposals, the optimized model demonstrates improved accuracy and efficiency in predicting relationship attributes and segmenting object roles. Using a two-stage Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling framework, the efficiency of the model is further enhanced by accumulating negative proposals and removing redundant ones. Empirical results on the Visual Relationship Detection task demonstrate the effectiveness of BNPS, achieving higher mAP and efficiency with a reduced number of training samples. Comparative analyses between BNPS and alternative methods confirm its superiority. Specifically, BNPS outperforms Soft-N+M and Soft-N+M-BN on the Visual Relationship Detection task with mAP scores of 6.3% and 6.9% on the V-CORD dataset, corresponding to an increase of up to 9.9% and 2.9% over Soft-N+M-BN. Furthermore, a thorough investigation of the component parts of the model using ANOVA demonstrates the significant contribution of balanced sampling. Based on these outcomes, the proposed two-stage Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling framework is deemed suitable for complex Visual Detection and Reasoning tasks involving a large number of object categories and relationships. The effectiveness of this method also lays a foundation for its application to other Mask Proposal Sampling approaches and highlights the importance of balanced sampling in improving the efficiency and accuracy of the model. A new measure of residual quantumness in finite-level quantum systems has been introduced, which can determine the total amount of quantumness present in any quantum state within a multi-dimensional system. It has been demonstrated that the residual quantumness in a quantum system can be extracted not only through strong measurements but also through weak measurements, revealing the underlying quantum feature. Furthermore, it has been shown that weak measurements preserve the quantum feature as effectively as strong measurements do, and a new class of quantum features called "weak-measurement coherent" features has been identified. To investigate the dynamics of residual quantumness in finite-level quantum systems, a quantum map representing the combined effect of a unitary interaction with a time-varying coupling strength was developed. A key finding of this study is that weak-measurement coherent features can be maintained over long periods of time and are ultimately determined by the system's energy spacing. Another significant outcome of this research is that strong measurements can collapse the quantum feature into zero if the system's energy spacing is too large to be precisely estimated with sufficient accuracy, implying that non-zero quantum features have an inherent lifespan before they collapse due to repeated measurements. In contrast, weak measurements can maintain non-zero quantum features for an infinitely long period of time. To verify the theoretical predictions of residual quantumness and its related phenomena, experiments involving the reading of spin rings made from a material called Rb57C9 can be conducted. This experimental approach could lead to a new classification system for quantum paramagnets based on their residual quantumness rather than their conventional classification as superparamagnetic or quantum. This idea is particularly relevant due to recent discoveries such as the quantum feature in the material GdTiO$_3$, where a comprehensive understanding of the material's microstructure is not necessary to evaluate the quantum feature. Hence, the proposed approach offers a novel and potent way of investigating quantum features in quantum systems, encompassing both isolated atoms and large-scale crystals. To facilitate this research, a comprehensive software package called resquantum was devised to calculate residual quantumness in various quantum systems under different conditions and to assist in the reproduction of the study's results. A key aspect of this package is its adaptability to various quantum systems and parameters, enabling researchers to compute the quantum feature for any given state within a multi-dimensional system. In order to optimize the area and delay of a Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) circuit, the exact bit representation of a constant is crucial. Yet, as constants are frequently subjected to binary arithmetic operations in hardware, it is essential to take into account the errors that occur during this process. Existing studies have analyzed error rates for various arithmetic operations but have failed to establish a unified framework for determining the total error propagation from any arithmetic operation, affecting the accuracy of MCM circuit design based on approximate computing. This study develops a rule-based framework that precisely calculates the total error propagation for any given binary arithmetic operation, thereby enhancing the approximate MCM circuit design process by accounting for errors resulting from binary arithmetic operations. Furthermore, we introduce a novel metric called Error-Raising-Path Count (ERPC) to quantify the total error propagation, thereby establishing a direct relationship between ERPC and error rates. Based on this framework, we devise an iterative algorithm to approximate MCMs by propagating errors and derive a consecutive sequence of lower and upper bounds for any given MCM, thereby guaranteeing the existence of an optimal solution. Additionally, we formulate a mixed-integer linear programming problem to exactly solve a specific instance of MCM with only 9-bit constants, thereby providing an exhaustive benchmark suite to evaluate the approximate MCM circuit design. Experimental results show that, on average, allowing a 14.0% error rate yields an area delay improvement of 7.88 times for 16-bit MCMs, 11.03 times for 32-bit MCMs, and 14.03 times for 64-bit MCMs, illustrating the effectiveness of our error propagation framework. In addition, we develop a hardware implementation of our error propagation framework, demonstrating the feasibility of our approach for actual MCM circuit design based on approximate computing. Lastly, we conduct an energy consumption evaluation of our approach, demonstrating the potential for power reduction with sufficient error tolerance. In order to further accelerate the design process, we also developed a K-fold Parallel Approach to divide the MCM circuit into multiple parallel paths, thereby greatly reducing the latency and also providing the possibility of achieving more MCM circuit design goals such as area, delay, and energy improvement. This approach led to a 100 times increase in THM cells for 16-bit MCMs, 44 times for 32-bit MCMs, and 11 times for 64-bit MCMs with a 14% error rate while also providing an optimal path to achieve zero error rate. We present FPIO, a versatile few-shot parsing model that leverages 
incremental learning to adapt various domains with minimal expert input.
FPIO outperforms previous few-shot parsing methods by a substantial margin
in both semantic segmentation and graph parsing tasks, achieving this success
with the few-shot learning paradigm's typical constraint of limited annotated
datasets, which has been a significant shortcoming of the area.
Furthermore, our model's capacity to integrate user feedback has been effectively
utilized in fine-tuning, a novel application of few-shot learning paradigm.
We prove the efficiency of FPIO by comparing it against pre-trained models
with a similar number of parameters, resulting in notable improvements of
6.5% and 5.3% for semantic segmentation and graph parsing, respectively.
Our model's source code is available at https://github.com/arkorakos/fp_io.

This study examines LCD group rings and their elements to determine potential nontrivial LCD group codes. We develop a method for dividing the group ring $R[G]$ into distinct subrings based on the constraints applied to their elements, ultimately leading to a general group ring $R[G]$. A key finding reveals that any element of a general group ring cannot be both zero divisors and unitary, thus enabling the construction of potential LCD group codes. Additionally, we propose a criterion for achieving exact LCD group codes, validate our proposed construction method, and analyze its code rate. Our research also maps the group $G$ and the ring $R$ back to the underlying field $F$, yielding specific conditions under which potential LCD group codes can be constructed, including nontrivial codes with a rate of at least $\frac{1}{6}$. We further demonstrate that, given an arbitrary finite group, we can build a nontrivial group ring LCD code with a rate of at least $\frac{1}{4}$. Moreover, when the group $G$ is abelian, we find that every element of the general group ring $R[G]$ can be expressed as a sum of four elements, thereby rendering it inapplicable for constructing nontrivial LCD group codes, despite our previous findings. As a result, we explore an alternative approach using specific conditions for the elements of $R[G]$ applied after the group operation has been performed, resulting in the possibility of constructing nontrivial LCD group codes, including rates of at least $\frac{1}{4}$ for abelian groups $G$ and at least $\frac{1}{6}$ for non-abelian groups $G$. We verify our proposed construction method through code validation, also determining its applicability to special groups such as the Klein four-group and the infinite group of powers of 2. Finally, we establish a lower bound on the code rate achieved by our proposed LCD group code construction method. Based on our current knowledge, this bound appears to be nearly optimal. Additionally, we explore the applicability of our study to semigroups, examine potential generalizations or modifications to the classical ideals in group rings, and investigate how the partial group homomorphisms can be used to construct higher-dimensional ideals consisting of group rings. Ultimately, we apply our lattice-like structure of group rings to construct potential partial group codes. To verify our findings, we present corresponding examples of LCD group codes for each of the established code rates. We also derive a lower bound on the code rate

Additionally, it presents a method for creating binary Golay complementary array pairs by reducing quaternary GCA pairs, thereby providing a broader approach to constructing GCA pairs using a higher cardinality. Furthermore, this paper specifically develops a quaternary GCA pair for the situation where the dimension is a multiple of four plus two, and it presents a method to construct a binary GCA pair in this particular dimension. Moreover, a quaternary GCA pair with a prime dimension of 127 is constructed, which surpasses the previously existing GCA pairs with prime dimensions of 61 and 81. To verify the feasibility of quaternary GCA pairs, this paper establishes a necessary and sufficient condition on the error-vector weights of the codes, which can be computed effectively using the determinant function over octal group rings. As a result, this study feasilily derives the feasibility criteria for binary Golay codes. We re-examine the phenomenon surrounding the number of ways $N(x)$ for $x$ in the range of large values, to which certain square-sigma codes $\sigma(x) = x + B$ can be equivalently expressed as sums of squares, along with a set of additive complements $B$. Our investigation seeks to clarify the asymptotic behavior of $N(x)$, which represents the count of these equivalent expressions, showing that $N(x)$ is dominated by a specific term $C \cdot x^{1/2} \cdot J(x)$ where $J(x)$ is the count of representations of $x$ as a sum of squares. This result refines the previous bound on $N(x)$ given in arXiv:2102.10324, further demonstrating its sensitivity to the choice of square-sigma codes $\sigma(x)$. We explore two approaches to derive uniform estimates for $J(x)$, one utilizing the Hardy-Ramanujan-Johnson theorem and another involving the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture. Our first method yields a precise asymptotic for $J(x)$, although one that is too complex, while our second approach yields an asymptotic that is too generous, yet simple to compute. Nonetheless, we can derive a useful, yet less precise upper bound for $J(x)$ using only the first method. By combining these results, under the assumption of the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture, we can derive asymptotics for $N(x)$, as well as analogous counts for higher power sums. We can also derive asymptotics for $N(x)$ using alternative polynomial identities, such as Euler's transformed formula, given a specific value of $\sigma(x) = x \cdot (1 +4x)^{1/2}$. Furthermore, this method grants us the ability to derive asymptotics for $N(x)$ using square-sigma codes $\sigma(x)$ with arbitrary coefficients, provided they are relatively prime to each other, again assuming the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture holds. Lastly, we can derive asymptotics for $N(x)$ using another family of polynomial identities, given a specific value of $\sigma(x) = x \cdot (1+4x^2)^{1/2}$. Silicon's Heisenberg spin exchange interaction is essentially non-existent under normal conditions, making it an ideal material for creating unique dopant-based spin-orbit coupled systems. Researchers have successfully implemented a theoretical model to calculate the Heisenberg exchange interaction between two dopant ions in silicon, based on the electronic charge distribution in the ionized p-orbital of the dopants. This has resulted in a comprehensive map of the Heisenberg exchange interaction across the silicon crystal lattice for two types of dopants. The findings show that Li-like dopants have a strong Heisenberg exchange interaction when placed in certain positions, with a distance threshold of approximately 3.5 lattice parameters. Furthermore, this model has implications for creating unique dopant-based spin-orbit coupled systems in silicon. To validate the model's accuracy, the study compares its predictions to existing experimental data on Heisenberg exchange interactions. The results show that experimental data supports the theoretical model, with key examples including the ferromagnetic ordering of Cr ions at low temperatures and the unconventional magnetic behavior of V ions at low temperatures. The model's predictions are, however, contrary to the results obtained through numerical methods at higher temperatures. The discrepancy between the model's predictions and numerical findings for V ions require further investigation. Lastly, the study explores the Heisenberg exchange interactions between two types of dopants in the vicinity of a (100) surface, indicating that surface effects can significantly affect the Heisenberg exchange interaction. The findings show that dopants with a strong Heisenberg exchange interaction tend to avoid being placed near the surface of silicon when compensated by electron dopants, unless under extreme conditions. This has resulted in a map of the Heisenberg exchange interaction across the silicon crystal surface. The study provides comprehensive insights into the Heisenberg exchange interaction in silicon for two types of dopants, contributing to the development of unique spin-orbit coupled systems in silicon. Key predictions of the model have significant implications for the use of silicon in quantum computing and spintronics. The study's findings can be used to predict magnetic ordering in doped silicon compounds, providing a framework for understanding magnetic properties of silicon crystals. The model supports the potential of silicon as a material for quantum computing and spintronics, thanks to its unique properties. The study's predictions are essential for guiding experiments on spin-orbit coupled systems in silicon, with the goal of creating a universal quantum computer. The model's accuracy is compared to existing experimental data on Heisenberg exchange interactions, indicating that the model is highly reliable

Our investigation focuses on the photoexcitation of semiconductors utilizing dual color femtosecond laser pulses. We've analyzed the temporal variations of electronic and hole populations triggered by two-photon and multiphoton excitations. We've modeled these phenomena using a simplified multilevel system representing the band structure of the material, and our results are generalizable to various semiconductors. We've selected silicon as a specific example to illustrate how two-photon absorption can generate charge carriers even when the material is not initially excited by the photons. We've also examined how electrons and holes interact and recombine after photoexcitation, utilizing a constant intensity model for fast nonequilibrium carrier distribution within the bands. We've calculated the temporal variations of current and photovoltaic responses resulting from two-photon and extrinsic photoemission. We've contrasted these with the consequences of one-photon excitations, and our analysis sheds new light on two-photon absorption in silicon, revealing unknown details of charge carrier generation. We've further explored the practical implications of two-photon absorption in developing photovoltaic devices, especially in CMOS-compatible silicon materials, and discussing their potential to harness sunlight via two-photon conversion. We've demonstrated that two-photon absorption might be leveraged to boost solar energy conversion efficiency. We've derived the potential increase in efficiency due to two-photon absorption, showing that it could lead to a relatively modest enhancement in efficiency but displaying great potential for low-intensity nontraditional applications of silicon photovoltaics. We've concluded by highlighting the need to experimentally verify the assumptions underlying our calculation of two-photon excitations in silicon. We've projected that the charge generated through two-photon absorption could be sufficiently high for low-intensity, terrestrial sunlight conditions after further optimization and technological refinement. We've ensured that our theoretical model of two-photon excitations and resulting charge generation is applicable to a wide range of semiconductors, not just silicon. We've studied the distinct two-photon absorption behaviors in silicon and GaAs, connecting it to the difference in bandgaps between these materials. We've modeled the temporal evolution of two-photon excitations in GaAs, predicting a much shorter time frame until significant charge generation compared to silicon. The Scott model, a type theory, provides a constructive and predicative framework that programming languages can be mapped to, offering a fundamental framework in theoretical computer science.  Past efforts have focused on integrating features common in programming languages, such as subtypes, effects, and higher inductive types.  A recent monograph by Aehle et al. provides an in-depth look at establishing a predicative and constructive model that incorporates common programming concepts.  In contrast, this paper explores a simpler, yet more versatile model based on hybrid type theories and uses the Scott model as a special case.  By leveraging hybrid type theories, this paper shows that each programming feature can be represented by a corresponding notion of equality, demonstrating that the Scott model can be seen as a special case of hybrid type theories.  In addition, this paper identifies a new concept of "stability" for types, which must be considered when combining subtypes with dependent types.  Furthermore, this paper examines the relationship between computational and categorical models, identifying potential discrepancies between the two.  In contrast to other work, this paper explores model-theoretic aspects, identifies potential path problems, and considers multiple assignments as fundamental to programming types.  A key outcome of the study is a new classification of programming features and associated type constructs, which can be seen as a companion to the classification of geometric morphisms between type-theoretic categories provided by Crole and Attentuck.  In addition to the study, this paper contains several new results, including a characterization of programming features that can be represented in the Scott model, a characterization of type constructs that can be represented by stable hybrid types, and an exploration of how to represent subtypes within hybrid type theories.  Lastly, this paper considers the challenging problem of representing abstract datatypes within a predicative and constructive framework, providing initial observations on this difficult issue. Furthermore, hybrid type theories offer a flexible and general framework that encompasses the Scott model, subtypes, and other programming features, thereby providing a useful tool for the study of programming features and their corresponding type constructs. This paper develops a novel spatial model-based collision avoidance system suitable for mobile robotic arms. By integrating the arm's spatial structure and incorporating the link dependencies, our method can identify hazardous regions based on the arm’s endpoint trajectory. A key feature of our approach is the generalized Gauss-Wronskian formulation, which calculates crucial configuration-dependent dynamics for link dynamics and collision detection. To ensure effectiveness in dynamic environments, our algorithm adapts collision avoidance techniques from static systems to mobile settings, accounting for the impact of base movements on linked motion. A simulation test validates the accuracy and computational efficiency of our formulation and its application in collision avoidance for mobile robotic arms. The results demonstrate a speedup of up to 3 times over existing methods when dealing with multiple links and a speedup of up to 5 times when considering endpoint trajectories for single-link models. Furthermore, our method exhibits comparable accuracy to simulation-based approaches but surpasses existing formulations in terms of computational efficiency. To expedite this progress, rapid development of conceptually bold and experimentally feasible designs for matter wave interferometers is crucial. Focusing on Ramsey interferometry, we demonstrate theoretically that incorporating nonlinear Hadamard gates can greatly improve performance by maximizing local minimums in matter wave phase shifts. Achieving this requires only simple, readily realizable atomic interactions as opposed to complex laser configurations. While the actual implementation of nonlinear gates poses technical challenges, we believe these innovations can facilitate breakthroughs in matter wave interferometry and open new paths to measuring minuscule effects of gravity and other phenomena. Moreover, the extreme scalability of matter wave experiments makes this an intriguing area for testing the principles of quantum measurement itself. This research introduces an advanced algorithm for generating smooth, fanned-out line ends, often seen in calligraphic handwriting and graphic design. The algorithm's starting point involves defining a unique metric to measure the difference between a desired fan shape and a given line segment. This distinction is evaluated using a customized variation of the Euler-Lagrange equation, leading to a novel set of ordinary differential equations that can be solved to create various fan shapes. Notably, the algorithm enables the creation of both symmetric and asymmetric fan shapes. To optimize performance, the developers implemented an efficient numerical integration method that facilitates real-time rendering of large numbers of fan shapes. In comparison to standard rendering techniques, the new method yields a 5-7% reduction in processing time, as demonstrated through tests conducted on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1660 Ti graphics card. Furthermore, the algorithm includes an innovative post-processing correction, which improves the accuracy of line end rendering by up to 14% and eliminates visible errors in certain scenarios. To facilitate the use of this new algorithm, the researchers have made available a comprehensive C++ code framework, which includes detailed tutorials and a collection of over 80 distinctive fan shapes created using the technique. Specifically, the paper presents 8 distinct shapes characterized by either symmetric (S) or asymmetric (A) patterns, resulting in a total of 80 unique variants, as shown in the accompanying figures. Recent studies of the cosmic positron excess and the diffuse TeV gamma-ray excess have been conducted using pulsar halos as key objects, thanks to their unique connection to these phenomena. These halos are produced by the decay of neutral antimatter particles formed within a pulsar wind nebula and offer an attractive explanation for both excesses due to their anticipated properties. Pulsar halos would serve as concentrated sources of high-energy electrons and gamma rays, capable of being observed by Fermi-LAT and a next-generation gamma-ray telescope, such as the Cherenkov Telescope Array. These observations, accompanied by pulsar radio observations, may help to elucidate the origin of these anomalous signals and provide crucial insights into the acceleration of particles in pulsar magnetospheres and magnetospheric high-energy physics. This research field is poised to enter a new era due to advancements in gamma-ray telescopes, potential space missions, and the anticipated discovery of numerous pulsars through the Square Kilometre Array and other next-generation telescopes. Consequently, the anticipated discoveries and properties of pulsar halos are anticipated to significantly protracted the lifespan of cosmology and astrophysics research related to these anomalous signals. This broad area of research can be categorized into three distinct papers. Paper I presents a computational method for simulating pulsar halos and estimating their observable properties, such as gamma-ray emission, as a function of pulsar magnetic field and luminosity. Paper II utilizes these computational methods to forecast the observable properties of pulsar halos in terms of their spatial distribution, connectivity, and overall contribution to the diffuse gamma-ray background. Paper III delves into the analytical properties of pulsar populations, examining the plausible range of parameters that could generate a population of pulsar halos capable of explaining the diffuse gamma-ray background, and exploring the potential for individual pulsar halos to contribute to the cosmic positron excess and flux variability in the gamma-ray background. This research is based on the 2017 publication of Paper III, with Papers I and II constructed as supporting materials, although they do contain newly incorporated findings and data not present in the original paper. Traditionally, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been enhanced using data augmentation methods like rotating and mirroring images. Recent research suggests that using masks to protect certain image regions, like objects or structures, can be an effective way to improve CNN performance. In our study, we examine how generating these masks can be done efficiently using a normalizing flow approach. By training a flow model on a small set of carefully selected mask samples, we can generate an infinite number of mask samples and use them to guide data augmentation of training images. By combining this method with super-pixel delimiting masks, we found that CNN performance can be significantly improved on challenging real-world image classification tasks. Our experiments show that using this technique, we can achieve high classification accuracy rates of 90.1% and 87.1% on the binary advancement towards multi-scale Intra-urban Sea floor Mapping (ISM) dataset for structure and sea floor mapping, respectively. Notably, when we compared our method to other common data augmentation techniques, like rotation and flipping, we found that our method outperformed them significantly. Our study also shows that using this technique, we can achieve high level of similarity between the original and augmented images, including a 97% similarity rate for a typical test case. These results indicate that using normalizing flow generated masks is an effective way to improve CNN performance on image classification tasks. Our study is the first one, to our knowledge, to use this technique in this way, and our code is available on our GitHub repository for others to use. Additionally, our study is the first one, to our knowledge, to use the ISM dataset in this way, and we hope that our work will guide future research in this area to continue using real-world images to improve CNN performance. \end{abstract}

Using citation network analysis, this study evaluates the impact of climate change research on policymakers and the broader scientific community within the period of 1945 to 2019. Two datasets were created to analyze the distinct perspectives of policymakers and scientists within the field of climate change research. One dataset, derived from Google Scholar and Web of Science, examined the citations and articles related to climate change by scientists and policymakers from 1945 to 2019. Another dataset, obtained through a survey of the Climate Change Council of the American Meteorological Society, specifically targeted the opinions of climate change researchers and policymakers. The results from the analysis of the two datasets revealed a growing interest in climate change among policymakers, but this sudden surge in 1980 appears unnatural and requires further investigation. Moreover, the weight of climate change research by scientists and policymakers follows a pattern of increasing influence over time, but policymakers' focus on climate change seems to be more transient than that of the scientists. Furthermore, the study discovered that the concepts of climate change and global warming were not utilized uniformly until the 1990s, leading to notable differences in the analyzed topics. Despite these discrepancies, the research shows that policymakers are highly dependent on the scientific community for their knowledge on climate change, and the most referenced scientists by policymakers are often the most published and cited scientists within the field. Finally, the study tested for the presence of stars, giants, and bridges within the citation network created by the scientists, revealing a growing concentration of influential researchers and research topics within the field of climate change research over time. Moreover, a significant difference was discovered between the research topics cited by policymakers and those of the general science community, where policymakers heavily rely on climate change research, especially those associated with policy-relevant research networks. To address these findings, the research proposes the formation of collaborative and productive partnerships between scientists and policymakers, urging policymakers to engage in evidence-based decision-making by valuing and relying on the research and experts in the field of climate change. Moreover, the research highlights the necessity for the scientific community to foster policy-relevant research by developing strategic communication and serving the needs of policymakers within the field of climate change research. Lastly, the research suggests that policymakers' growing interest in climate change may not be sustainable and could eventually decline, prompting the need for ongoing evaluation and modification of existing policies by the scientific community. In conclusion, the study emphasizes the significance of analyzing the distinct perspectives of scientists and policymakers within the field of climate change research and encourages the continued exploration of this topic through citation network analysis. This paper applies the finite-time Koopman operator theory to a bimanual sharing system consisting of two single degree of freedom manipulators. These tests demonstrated the superiority of the tracking performance achieved via the boundary controller compared to existing methods. Ultimately, the work's results can facilitate the development of practical control algorithms for sharing soft robotic tasks between multiple soft robotic arms. We present NGDM, a novel method that combines Natural Gradient Descent with Deep Network Mixtures to efficiently train large, complex models within a non-convex optimization framework. This approach accelerates model convergence while minimizing adjustments to existing algorithms, thus enhancing current AI technologies. Building on previous work in Natural Gradient Descent and Deep Network Mixtures, we carefully analyze key mathematical concepts, such as the structure of these models, the gradient, and a crucial divergence metric. We then derive an explicit expression for the gradient of the objective function to be optimized, along with a method to properly adjust previous work, thereby establishing a solid foundation for future research. Comprehensive numerical experiments evaluate the performance of NGDM in various scenarios, demonstrating its speed and efficiency in both deterministic and stochastic optimization environments. Those results reveal NGDM's remarkable capacity to achieve comparable results to state-of-the-art methods in a specific case (VAE), while significantly surpassing them in two other common scenarios (SGD and online RL). This promising new method has vast potential for applications in computer science, physics, and related engineering fields. Further details can be found in our repository: https://github.com/visual-learn/NGDM. As a result of our investigation, we anticipate NGDM to serve as a bridge connecting Machine Learning and Adiabatic Quantum Computing, thus contributing to the development of efficient training techniques for complex models. We examine irreducible tensor products involving highest weight modules, a specific type of U(v)-module, and U(𝕙)-free modules. Our analysis yields two key conclusions. Firstly, we establish that the irreducibility of such tensor products can be determined by evaluating the isomorphism between certain module products. Secondly, we derive explicit conditions for the irreducibility of tensor products of U(v)-modules and B(w)-modules, given specific configurations of weights. Furthermore, we apply these conditions to address related inquiries concerning the decomposition of tensor products, including those involving infinitesimally irreducible modules, as well as general U(v)-modules and B(w)-modules with non-trivial action on a free module. Our study also explores connections with level 1 NSGA(I) modules, incorporating these results to provide a more comprehensive understanding. Additionally, we discuss certain Diophantine equations arising from irreducibility conditions of specific tensor products. For certain values of w in v, our analysis leads to a profound generalization, enabling an in-depth examination of irreducible tensor products involving three modules, including a U(v)-module, a B(w)-module, and a U(𝕙)-free module. Our findings are further exemplified through a series of illustrative examples. Finally, our work concludes with the identification of a U(v)-irreducible subspace within a general U(v)-module and its connection to level 1 NSGA(I) modules. This subspace also possesses an interesting U(v)-module structure, which we outline explicitly. Our results are particularly significant, as they bridge the gap between representation theory of general linear and Heisenberg Lie algebras and the concepts of highest weight and free modules. Moreover, these findings highlight the importance of free modules in poly-Virasoro algebras, as exemplified through the example of F(C[ℤ]), involving the complex free Lie algebra C[ℤ]. Additionally, our study offers potential avenues for further research. Specifically, we speculate that the ideas of free and highest weight modules could be extended to a broader class of algebras, potentially including F(A) for any solvable Lie algebra A. Conversely, it is also conceivable that the methods employed in this study, centered on free and highest weight modules, might find applications in representation theories of other algebraic structures, such as Lie algebras and Virasoro algebras, thus facilitating an interchange of ideas between the field of Lie algebras and the poly-Virasoro algebra

The role of roles in role-playing games has been underutilized in natural language processing, despite its potential to add realism and engage players. This study examines how to create a role specification, which outlines a character's attributes and behaviors, and uses it to guide a dialogue system. The specification consists of mental traits, behavioral tendencies, and action purposes. To develop this role, we collected data from online role-playing forums and created a dataset with 1,046 role specifications. We also developed a systematic approach to instantiate these specifications in dialogue states and world contexts, effectively generating 3,140 sets of data to train a dialog management system. The results show that a model trained on role specifications, rather than being given a pre-defined role, outperforms the control model by 10.3% in our semantically-driven dataset. When evaluating on real-world customer service dialogues with role specifications, our model achieves a 6.4% improvement in F1 score. The significant effect of gravitational wave memory, primarily felt in the large-scale universe, has two distinct manifestations: an initial burst felt close to the source and a later wave felt universe-wide due to the superposition of scattered gravitational waves. Our investigation focuses on the overall impact of this memory effect across the entire universe. First, we thoroughly analyzed how the amplitude of this wider field, affecting all types of gravitational waves, behaves across various scales. Our analysis indicates that, unlike regular gravitational waves, this memory effect increases with the frequency. Considering the whole universe, we found that the amplitude of this wider field is in the range of $10^{-21}-10^{-20}\,\mathrm{Hz}$ for $10^2-10^8$ Hz frequency ranges. Furthermore, we used simulations to determine the anisotropy of this wider field. Our results indicate the presence of significant anisotropy at lower frequencies ($\sim10^{-20}\,\mathrm{Hz}$) but a relatively minor effect at higher frequencies ($\sim10^8\,\mathrm{Hz}$). Our discussion on the wider field's direction of analysis reveals links to the distribution of sources including short and long-duration gamma-ray bursts. On a broader scale, we examined how the wider field's direction of analysis changes across different cosmic structures, focusing on the distribution of dark matter. Our analysis indicates minor effects due to the wider field's anisotropy at lower frequencies ($\sim10^{-20}\,\mathrm{Hz}$) but a more pronounced impact at higher frequencies ($\sim10^8\,\mathrm{Hz}$), similar to that of cosmic microwave background anisotropy. Finally, we estimated the wider field's temperature and polarization effects, including vectors, tensors, and their combinations, which may potentially be detectable with future instruments like LISA LDBL or PMRDC in specific frequency ranges. Our study lays the groundwork for further theoretical and observational research into this wider memory effect, paving the way for potential future detection. Additionally, we outline potential projects including calculating the wider memory effect's cross-correlation with cosmic microwave background radiation, exploring gravitational wave memory in the presence of spin-induced effects, and examining the wide memory effect's cross-correlation with the linear gravitational wave spectrum. These projects enhance our understanding of gravitational waves, the universe's large-scale structure, and the system's ability to detect this wider memory effect. Our discussion on the wider memory effect's detection, although optimistic, highlights the necessity of significant advancements in detector sensitivity and data processing capabilities

We examine a novel leptogenesis approach within the framework of gauge-mediated supersymmetry breaking. This model generates right-handed neutrinos through the dilaton mechanism, resulting in PeV-scale leptogenesis. To explain the observed lightest $B$-meson decay rate, we find it necessary to have a generated $B-\bar{B}$ mixing induced by the Wilczek-Decays, leading to a generated PMF in the $B$-meson system with an amplitude of $0.0069\pm 0.0016$. Furthermore, we determine the allowed parameter space for the PMF and its connections to gauge-mediated supersymmetry breaking and leptogenesis. To achieve late leptogenesis, we find the required parameter space to be within a specific range for both $m_{3}$ and $\tan\beta$. Consequently, we conclude that the mixing induced by the Wilczek-Decays serves as a crucial element in the PeV-scale leptogenesis scenario mediated by gauge-mediated supersymmetry breaking. Moreover, we have developed a connection between the $\Delta m_{B}^2$ constraint and the model's parameters, with the exception of a specific set of points exhibiting leptonically decaying $B$-mesons, for which we have explicitly outlined the failing cases. Lastly, we have made a comparison with similar models involving a singlet $SU(2)_L$ Higgs triplets and a Dine-Felix-LeCampa type model involving a high-lying singlet neutrino, both of which serve as alternatives to our gauge-mediated supersymmetry breaking model. Notably, we find that the generated PMF in our model far exceeds that generated in both of these other scenarios, highlighting their distinct natures. In word suggestion, suggesting the correct word when the correct word cannot be found, there are three primary approaches: syntactic, semantic, and hybrid. The syntactic approach suggests words based on their position in a sentence structure, the semantic approach suggests words based on their meaning, and the hybrid approach, which combines both, often performs the best. However, using hybrid approaches can be challenging due to the need to balance the two methods. This research presents a new hybrid approach, WLS, that uses word likelihood scores derived from both syntax and semantics, but unlike other hybrid approaches, it does not require tuning. Instead, it automatically balances the two methods by utilizing the strengths of both, and as a result, it performs better than models that only use syntactic or semantic analysis, and it achieves results similar to the state-of-the-art hybrid approaches in word suggestion tasks. Moreover, this research highlights the importance of semantic analysis in hybrid approaches and proposes a new metric to evaluate their performance. Additionally, this research improves the performance of hybrid approaches by utilizing both the word likelihood scores and their confidence levels, which reflects their accuracy in suggesting the correct word. The outcomes of this research show that hybrid approaches, and in particular WLS, achieve results close to the state-of-the-art hybrid approaches in word suggestion tasks, and they do so without the need to adjust any parameters. Observations from the proposed model enable e-commerce platforms to refine their pricing strategies by shedding light on how customers compare and select items. The steering wheel is an analogy that helps in visualizing the motion of certain active dimers as a predictable outcome of their internal time dynamics converting into external kinetic movement. A dimer propelled by an internal steering wheel analogy corresponds to a Stueckelberg dimer, exhibiting consistent behavior. Furthermore, we propose two viable methods for generating mobile objects based on this concept: electrodynamics and phonon-driven mobility. Electrodynamics facilitates paired particles that can circumnavigate a loop and exhibit magnetism when viewed from a distance. Conversely, phonon-driven mobility enables paired particles to navigate a two-dimensional space and display immovable components when localized, thereby gaining the potential for designing novel, two-dimensional structures and systems over extended periods of time. Both of these constructs comply with existing laws and are feasible for construction. They also offer a unique opportunity to experimentally verify the conversion of time into space and potentially unlock new applications through topology by encoding temporal patterns into mobile objects. Encoded temporal patterns may give rise to extrinsic, spatial features that could be utilized for processing information or achieving technological advancements, thereby providing a framework for designing and constructing temporal topological insulators and superconductors using a pair of cores and coils or various other forms. Additionally, we outline future research avenues centered around discovering and studying the unique properties of disordered, topological insulators and superconductors, and demonstrate the potential for the Stueckelberg dimer to serve as a theoretical foundation for an entire class of new materials and devices. Lastly, we discuss the potential for particle-antiparticle pairs to act as fundamental building blocks for time and space-based engineering at the microscopic level. This concept challenges the current understanding that identifies particles as the basic building blocks of nature and replaces them with pairs of cores and coils, thereby gaining access to the non-linear dynamics of steering wheels for constructing various forms. The research is self-contained and can be utilized for teaching research methods through the example of discovering new materials and devices based on the steering wheel analogy. Moreover, pairs of cores and coils offer an opportunity to experimentally verify the conversion of time into space at a microscopic level through a combination of existing technologies such as superconducting and quantum computing, and may lead to discoveries in fields such as optics, heat transfer, and general relativity. The conventional method of using a mesh-based approach relies heavily on a computational mesh that complies with the principles of the Finite Element Method. By building on existing mesh modification techniques, our algorithm efficiently constructs a mesh that aligns with the boundaries of the fracturing region. Furthermore, our method ensures that the resulting mesh has a level of smoothness and precision, which is essential for the simulation's numerical stability and accuracy. The conformity aspect of the mesh allows for seamless interaction between different regions of the mesh, whereas the Delaunay method contributes to producing a precise and high-quality tetrahedral mesh that reduces the risk of computation errors. Conversely, our algorithm is highly adaptable and can be easily modified to accommodate other simulation-driven simulation scenarios. The feasibility of our method in mesh generation is further accentuated by its extreme cases of input parameters. Consequently, our method has far-reaching implications for the simulation of complex porous media due to its capacity for accurately modeling intricate spatial relationships and generating precise meshes that facilitate efficient simulations. In this study, we examine the Seidel matrices of connected chain graphs with their general quadratic representation. We establish that the eigenvalue -1 has unique properties in this context, specifically related to its multiplicity and location within the spectral circle. We also derive conditions for the existence of negative eigenvalues in addition to -1, and provide insights into their multiplicity. We explore how these results relate to previous studies on graph theory and irreducibility in matrix representation. Additionally, we examine how these findings can be applied to certain types of parametric chain graphs. To support our conclusions, we provide illustrative examples of chain graphs and their Seidel matrices. Furthermore, we outline potential future areas of research. Lastly, we compare our results with existing studies on graph theory and irreducibility in matrix representation. 

Key features of this study include a precise characterization of the Seidel matrix's irreducibility in chain graphs, an understanding of its diameter in relation to graph connectivity, and the identification of the irreducible Seidel matrix's minimal diameter. We demonstrate how these results can be applied to certain types of parametric chain graphs. 

Additionally, our study shows that the characteristics of the Seidel matrix are more robust than those of its Laplacian counterpart, with specific examples provided to highlight this phenomenon. We identify potential areas of research where the Seidel matrix can offer greater insights into graph theory. 

Ultimately, our study contributes to our understanding of chain graphs through the lens of the Seidel matrix, thereby complementing existing studies on graph theory and irreducibility in matrix representation. We compare and summarize our findings with existing research and highlight potential areas of research for future development. Moreover, our study can serve as a model for investigating other types of graphs using the Seidel matrix, thereby expanding our knowledge of graph theory. 

In terms of future research, we have identified several areas of interest. Specifically, we investigate the properties of the Seidel matrix in relation to its eigenvalues and irreducibility in star-related graphs. Furthermore, we explore how the Seidel matrix can be used to determine the connectedness of certain graph families. Additionally, we examine the relationship between the Seidel matrix and the Laplacian matrix in terms of their spectral properties and graph connectivity. This paper delves into non-vehicle based interference in heterogeneous vehicular networks, where a mix of mobile base stations, fixed base stations, and relays serve a diverse range of users. The mobile base stations are organized in groups, covering specific areas, while the users within each area experience variable channel conditions. Each user has a limited bandwidth demand, which changes as they move at different speeds. The relays enhance performance by establishing connections between the base stations and users, but also introduce cross-layer interference. To minimize this interference and optimize the system, a joint power allocation and routing technique is employed across multiple layers, using metrics like user location, speed, and required bandwidth. This non-vehicle based interference is quantified using two models, one for individual user rates and one for overall network effectiveness. The results show that deploying relays and using power allocation can boost performance, while combining routing and power management yields the best outcomes. The proposed approach demonstrates significant improvement in overall effectiveness and individual user rates, while minimizing interference. The success of this strategy depends on the speed of users and the structure of groups, but even at high speeds, combining power management and routing delivers substantial performance gains. This research proposes a method to enhance sentence evaluation by leveraging the editing actions of Wikipedia contributors. We initially investigated the current sentence quality assessment methods but found them insufficient due to the reliance on human-generated annotations. We then collected and examined the editing behaviors of Wikipedia editors, discovering that certain edits could serve as implicit labels indicating the quality of the modified text. The analysis led us to develop a data-driven model that predicts human-annotated labels for sentences based on their similarity to high-quality edits identified through a supervised model applied to Wikipedia's revision history. We compared the performance of our proposed model with existing sentence quality assessment models using a subset of the MSMarc dataset and observed that the editing behavior-based model achieved comparable results while exhibiting more robust human-like assessment characteristics than the other models. Furthermore, the study highlighted the potential benefits of integrating human editors' assessments, including enhanced support for offline editing processes and validation of existing content. We anticipate that our research will inspire the integration of Wikipedia editors' contributions into the process of sentence quality assessment and motivate the development of more advanced natural language processing applications grounded in human editorial decisions. A widely accepted technique for improving model accuracy and reducing computational costs is knowledge distillation. Yet, its application is limited when working with datasets having private or confidential nature due to the requirement of sharing query results from the model under training. To address this challenge, researchers have found that certain adversarially trained models are capable of providing valuable insights from their outputs, even in scenarios where these outputs would normally be considered unreliable. Therefore, it is logical to utilize these outputs as the basis for knowledge distillation. Specifically, when carrying out DB3 on the MNIST dataset, it was observed that the class probabilities predicted by the strong model could serve as effective soft labels. However, this approach can be limited by its reliance on the specific data distribution of the dataset being used. To mitigate this limitation, a novel decision-based black-box knowledge distillation method is proposed, which relies on decision boundaries rather than class probabilities. Moreover, this method's effectiveness has been verified on various datasets, including the MNIST dataset and data sets from the LightGBM project, which are based on user feedback and can be collected in an unsupervised manner, thereby reducing the need for labels when performing knowledge distillation. Our method's name, DB3, differentiates it from other knowledge distillation methods, such as knowledge compilation. Additionally, a public repository is maintained at the address https://github.com/davidchp/DB3 to ensure the continuity of this work. Evaluations have shown that the proposed method leads to improvements of up to 2.3% and 5.4% in the case of the MNIST dataset, and 2.2% and 4.2% for the images of size 28x28 and 112x112, respectively, when compared to the standard adversarial training. Moreover, it was observed that DB3 offers enhanced robustness against perturbations, such as those resulting from ImageNetNanoAdv attacks, of up to 1.3 and 1.2 times compared to the standard adversarial training method, particularly for the models of size 28x28 and 112x112, respectively. Moreover, it was noticed that DB3 presents an efficient way of reducing the computational costs associated with adversarial training, resulting in a reduction of up to 2.2 and 2.1 times for the models of size 28x28 and 112x112, respectively. To facilitate the replication of this study, a repository has been maintained at the address https://github.com/davidchp/

Most advanced learning methods require extensive expert input, which can be impractical or expensive to obtain. We introduce Co-Imitation Learning (CIL), a novel approach that leverages the knowledge shared by multiple peers, without necessitating the input of any experts. CIL facilitates two agents learning from each other's successful strategies, until both agents exhibit comparable performance to an external guide. Through theoretical analysis, we establish that CIL is a viable means of acquiring the desired skills, which we verify by observing the agents' behavior closely mimicking that of the external guide. We further examine CIL in a challenging continuous control setting, observing the benefits of learning from peers' actions in both stationary and dynamic environments. Our findings indicate that CIL ranks among the top learning methods, rivaling state-of-the-art approaches, while requiring minimal adjustments to the underlying algorithm used to train individual agents. We present a simple yet effective design for CIL that consists of a straightforward communication mechanism and a straightforward strategy, in which both agents closely mimic the other's previous actions and modify them slightly to create new behaviors. We anticipate CIL to inspire new methods for learning from peers' actions, which we hope will contribute to the development of more efficient and sophisticated learning techniques. We focus on the LDPC ensemble chosen by Friedman and Lempel, which incorporates polar codes as the inner ensemble and repeat codes as the outer ensemble. By leveraging the normalized variance of the generated parity-check matrix, along with the characteristics of polar codes, we develop an innovative approach to approximate the LDPC ensemble up to a specified degree, yielding a sequential decoder error probability estimate that increases with the bias parameter. We demonstrate that increasing the bias parameter yields a cumulative distribution function (cdf) for the decoder's output metrics that converges to the extreme of the channel's input-output probability distribution. Moreover, we establish an upper bound on the LDPC ensemble's minimum distance, which grows as a function of the degree, whereas its normalized variance remains less than twice the bound. We verify via numerical methods that our approximation accurately predicts the sequential decoder's error probability across various bias parameters and degree values. Furthermore, we observe that high-quality simulations of the LDPC ensemble, utilizing the Friedman-Lempel sequence, exhibit error probabilities that closely match our approximation, especially for larger degree values and higher bias parameters. We conclude that utilizing polar codes with a higher cutoff rate as a bias value can provide better sequential decoder performance and accuracy. We also note the potential of this decoder architecture to achieve near-optimal performance with a pre-defined finite number of degree values. Finally, we provide an initial approximation of the LDPC ensemble's minimum distance, which may serve as a starting point for further research and analysis. Based on this approximation, we propose a density graph that represents the LDPC ensemble's variable node distribution; we believe this graph can facilitate innovative designs of LDPC codes, albeit with limitations regarding the ensemble's minimum distance. To overcome this constraint, we suggest modifying the Friedman-Lempel approach by introducing multiple iterations of polar code selection, utilizing a cumulative bias parameter and higher degree values on the parity-check matrix's diagonal. This enhanced approach yields a sequential decoder with reduced error probability, approachable by conventional iterative decoders over the same batch of polar codes. Recent advancements in deep learning and RGB-D technology allow for precise and accessible intrinsic camera calibration without the need for manually labeled samples. Nevertheless, extrinsic camera calibration necessitates labeled samples from known locations, making it prone to subpar performance outside its trained environment. In this research, we introduce a novel self-calibration method for intrinsic-camera calibration utilizing a single end-effector, thereby eliminating the need for labeled samples from unknown environments. Our proposed approach incorporates a depth camera to improve robustness in calibrating the end-effector using an unsupervised pose estimation method based on cycle consistency. Furthermore, to account for variability in real-world observations, we employ an unsupervised learning framework using normalizing flows for end-effinger representation. We evaluated the effectiveness of our proposed approach using articular angles of known joints and achieved calibration errors of under 1.5 cm and 1 degree for all tested subjects and locations. Notably, our results demonstrated a substantial 68% reduction in calibration errors for unknown locations compared to a state-of-the-art method relying on supervised learning. Moreover, our study highlights the benefits of integrating a depth camera and unsupervised learning for enhancing robustness in practical implicit intrinsic camera calibration. In doing so, our research paves the way for widespread adoption of implicit intrinsic camera calibration across a broad spectrum of real-world applications. In labs, researchers study the core components of complex systems to understand how they interact. To do this, they trigger and analyze various units within a network, such as neurons in the brain, to reveal patterns of interaction. A recent method, called interference analysis, identifies unusual patterns of interaction by measuring how often nearby units are activated together and analyzing these results using mathematical models. Focusing on specific parts of the network can increase the detection of unusual patterns, but it requires careful selection of the focus to produce accurate results. Since choosing the optimal focus for large networks is difficult, researchers use algorithms to find the best focus based on the network's structure and the data they collect. We investigated the effectiveness of one such algorithm on artificial and real-world data sets, and our results suggest that it produces accurate results when the focus is easily defined, but it does not work as well for networks that have complex, irregular patterns. Furthermore, we found that using statistical models to analyze patterns of activation in the absence of a network structure also failed to produce accurate results. Ultimately, we recommend testing different focus options and using algorithms that both selects the focus and measures patterns of activation to reveal the network's structure and function. Moreover, we found that using a certain threshold for the detection of unusual patterns of activation can produce accurate results, and testing this threshold both before and after the focus is selected can reveal the network's structure and function. To aid researchers, we provided step-by-step instructions on how to apply these methods, along with the code and data needed to reproduce our results. Based on our analysis, we proposed a new mathematical model that takes into account the varying sensitivities of the measured units to external stimuli and the presence of noise, and we verified that it provides a more accurate representation of the network's structure and function, particularly for large networks, by revealing the key features that distinguish it from a random network. Additionally, we found that using a statistical approach that does not rely on a network structure also identifies the key features that distinguish it from a random network, and we proposed a new mathematical model that takes into account the sensitivities of the measured units and the presence of noise, and verifies that it provides a more accurate representation of the network's structure and function, particularly for large networks, by revealing the key features that distinguish it from a random network. Furthermore, we found that using an algorithm that both selects the focus and measures patterns of activation can reveal the key features that distinguish it from a random network, and we provided the code and data needed to reproduce our results.

The accurate measurement of galaxy shapes is crucial for weak lensing analyses.  ShapePipe is an integrated pipeline that measures galaxy properties by applying a comprehensive suite of algorithms and analysis techniques.  These techniques include robust shape measurement methods such as R, UMPACK, and NFW, among others.  This paper examines the performance of the ShapePipe pipeline in detecting the gravitational effect of a massive galaxy on the light of background galaxies through a series of tests.  These tests compare the performance of different shape measurement algorithms using real and simulated data.  The results show that the majority of algorithms used in the pipeline produce comparable effects regardless of the presence of a massive galaxy.  However, algorithms such as R and UMPACK are less affected by noise and shape measurement errors when a massive galaxy is present, while algorithms such as NFW and Elmegreen yield larger effects due to their lower precision in shape measurement.  Additionally, the paper examines the performance of the pipeline in detecting the gravitational effect of a massive galaxy on the light of background galaxies in the Kilo Degree Survey.  The results show that a difference in measurement methods can lead to a 20% discrepancy in the amount of gravitational effect in the survey.  The study highlights the necessity for uniform analysis techniques in detecting the gravitational effect of a massive galaxy on the light of background galaxies in weak lensing analyses. These findings provide valuable insights into the unique features of V$_2$O$_3$ thin films and the design of epitaxially grown ferromagnetic insulators. We investigate the diffusion of particles under the influence of temperature fluctuations in d-dimensional systems. Despite the presence of temperature gradients, we demonstrate that Einstein's original formula remains accurate for large times, and the relationship between diffusion coefficients is not altered. Our study involves the numerical solution of a model equation for a particle in a heat bath. The results reveal the occurrence of distinct diffusive and preemptive (or anticipatory) regimes, which can be attributed to the interplay between the particles' hopping frequency and the local temperature. Preemptive dynamics is characterized by particles moving ahead of the temperature gradient due to increased hopping frequency in cooler regions. These findings provide a theoretical explanation for earlier experiments conducted by Ciliberto and co-workers. Moreover, the possibility of extending Einstein's relation to systems with inhomogeneous temperature distributions may have significant implications for the study of dynamical processes in such systems. In this context, we derive an analytical expression for the fourth moment of a particle's displacement. Our study also sheds light on the recently reported normal or anomalous diffusion in the context of inertial transport. We derive a diffusion coefficient based on the particle's displacement and demonstrate that normal or anomalous diffusion can be attributed to the particle's inertia. However, this effect does not contribute to the preemptive regime. Consequently, the preemptive and inertial mechanisms of diffusion are independent of each other. Finally, we explore a more complex model involving the coupled diffusion of particles and temperatures, which serves as a theoretical framework for the experimental work conducted by Ciliberto and co-workers and may hold key explanations for their observations. Our study also raises additional questions regarding the occurrence of a pretransition phase in the system. We identify such a pretransition phase when the parameters of the system are set to values where the pretransition phase emerges at the mean field level. Nevertheless, further investigation is required to determine whether this pretransition phase is stable at the microscopic level. If the pretransition phase is stable, it may provide a theoretical explanation for the pretransition phase reported by Ciliberto and co-workers in their experimental work. Conversely, the pretransition phase may be eliminated when the microscopic effects of temperature fluctuations are taken into consideration. We also investigate an extreme instance of the model, involving the limit of very low temperatures, to a good approximation. Our study in this regime reveals the occurrence of a pretransition phase with spatially homogeneous pretransition profiles. Despite being widely utilized parameters characterizing the former effect remain poorly understood. Our research employs neural network models with varying architectures to examine how regularization methods like weight decay, batch normalization, and instance normalization affect model complexity. By analyzing the eigenvalues of the Fisher Information Matrix, we demonstrate that different forms of regularization lead to distinct posterior distributions of weights, thereby increasing model complexity. Notably, we observe that normalization techniques introduce dimension-specific correlations among weights, resulting in enhanced model complexity relative to batch normalization. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical findings through experiments using high-order convolutional networks. Our research showcases the intricacies of model complexity induced by regularization methods and their implications for deep learning model design and training. Additionally, it highlights the significance of considering the posterior weight distribution when quantifying model complexity. This perspective can be applied to both neural networks and other deep learning models characterized by overparameterization. To enhance the accuracy of automated essay grading using deep learning models, researchers have recently employed data augmentation methods to expand their training datasets. These techniques artificially enlarge the dataset by producing new examples from existing ones, aiming to better match the model's predictions to human grades. While successful in improving model performance, the positive impact of data augmentation methods diminishes for larger models, raising the question of their effectiveness in high-stakes assessment settings. In this study, the effectiveness of five data augmentation methods is evaluated for automated essay grading using the 8th International Dataset, against a robust baseline model. Our results indicate varying levels of improvement across different types of essays but consistently positive outcomes overall. For evaluating model fit in scenarios involving marginal independence, two main approaches can be employed: profile likelihood or Wickerson information criterion. While the profile likelihood offers a direct estimate of parameter values, it's computationally intensive due to constraints on the parameter space. Conversely, the Wickerson information criterion provides a simplified approximation but lacks a comprehensive framework for parameter inference. This study reconciles these methods, combining the strengths of each to yield improved estimates and confidence intervals. Specifically, the proposed method initially estimates the parameters through profile likelihood, before leveraging these values in the Wickerson information criterion for model assessment. This hybrid approach performs significantly better than both the profile likelihood and Wickerson information criterion alone, as demonstrated through comparative analyses of logistic and copula models on real-world datasets. Furthermore, the logic behind this hybrid method can be generalized to other parameter estimation techniques, as illustrated using multiple subsequent applications. Ultimately, the efficacy of this hybrid method surpasses that of the original approaches, indicating considerable potential for similar synergies in high-dimensional model assessment and parameter inference. In addition to statistical theory, the work also addresses practical challenges related to the computational intensity of profile likelihood calculations. Two publicly accessible R packages are provided to facilitate the hybrid estimation: Wickerson and proflik. These packages are compatible with both Windows and Linux operating systems. The main advantages of the proposed method include enhanced computational efficiency and accuracy, as well as greater applicability to diverse models and datasets. This approach is particularly useful for hierarchical models and those involving complex latent variables, facilitating parameter inference with increased precision. The statistical infrastructure provided by these packages enables the evaluation of model fit for complex statistical models, paving the way for their application in practice. In addition to the hybrid estimation method, the Wickerson and proflik packages offer other beneficial functionalities. Firstly, they offer a flexible framework for model assessment that can be extended to various parameter estimation techniques. Secondly, they provide refined first and second order accuracy for confidence intervals, as well as the option for incorporating data imbalances. Lastly, they include support for logistic and logistic-probit models, as well as special case efficient MCMC inference for these models by leveraging a Gibbs sampler. This versatile statistical infrastructure can be used for the analysis of binary observational data subject to hidden correlations, navigable through the provided example analyses. In particular, the packages analysis of sample datasets include healthcare related studies such as the assessment of whether a treatment can alter the likelihood of responses, or whether a treatment outcome can be influenced by patient attributes, or whether a treatment outcome can be influenced by weather conditions.
