A relatively equitable society often benefits those who come after it by presenting unimpeded opportunities for growth and improvement. Yet, the question remains whether the society's fairness will translate into future generations having equal prospects for a better life. We propose a new mechanism to gauge a society's fairness from one generation to the next by measuring the fairness of opportunity allocation. Each person's potential is represented by a point in space, and a favorable experience creates a localized and unbiased sampling density function. We develop a metric that measures the disparity in opportunity by calculating the weighted variance of the area in which a person can sample and by modeling a person's capacity for exploiting opportunities by assuming a Gaussian density function. We apply our framework to study the fairness of voting systems and citizenship opportunities, and through analysis and numerical testing, we find that the perceived disparity in opportunity is reflective of the society's overall fairness. A key advantage of our approach is its ability to gauge opportunity allocation without presupposing a specific direction or bias. It offers a flexible and generalizable assessment that is applicable across various dimensions of opportunity, and its relevance extends beyond voting and citizenship to any domain in which an individual's capacity can be evaluated. We also investigate the potential for opposition to fairness-enhancing policies by showing that such a policy may be resisted even when a society's leaders are willing to gauge the disparity in opportunity and make adjustments to address it. We illustrate this phenomenon through the case study of a voting system in a two-dimensional space in which a fairness-enhancing policy aims to ensure that every citizen has relatively equal access to public offices, and our findings demonstrate that the proposed mechanism and fairness metric can effectively serve this purpose. However, our analysis also reveals that the proposed mechanism can be manipulated by a society's leaders to prevent implementation of the fairness-enhancing policy when a majority of the population is willing to gauge the disparity in opportunity and make adjustments, as evidenced by our numerical testing and analysis. We attribute this outcome to the mechanism's design, which links a person's potential to their capacity for exploiting opportunities, and instead propose an alternative mechanism that guarantees a fairness-enhancing policy when a society's leaders are willing to gauge the disparity in opportunity and make adjustments, as demonstrated in the context of a voting system in a two-dimensional space. We outline potential avenues for future research and highlight its relevance to opportunity allocation across any dimension of societal importance. In addition to its theoretical significance, our study offers a practical contribution to a society's leaders seeking to gauge the disparity in opportunity and make adjustments to address it. We also examine potential opposition

This paper presents the newly created UD 2.9 treebank for Modern Hebrew, a resource crucial for enhancing various NLP applications using advanced techniques such as parsing. Our efforts have yielded significant breakthroughs in parsing outcomes, primarily due to the creation of a high-quality treebank. Interestingly, many of the most difficult sentences were intentionally retained in the evaluation data, demonstrating the importance of human involvement in crafting the Universal Dependencies framework. The UD 2.9 treebank comprises 442 texts, consisting of 29,026 tokens and 54,834 lexical items, along with 65,875 dependencies. To validate our work, we conducted an evaluation study focusing on Hebrew NLP tasks and used multiple metrics to assess the performance of various models across three different datasets: standard, challenging, and extremely difficult. Notably, the incorporation of the new treebank has facilitated unprecedented advancements in NLP outcomes, primarily due to its larger scope and more diverse content. Specifically, the advancements were most conspicuous in token-level F-score for parsing (improving by 2.7 and 2.3 points on the standard and challenging datasets, respectively), and 1.3 and 1.1 points for named entity recognition, although these gains were influenced by the increased data extent. Our research has also underscored the significance of human participation in the UD framework's development and highlighted the existing discrepancies between the current state of the art and the potential boundaries of NLP capabilities. In contrast, we explore a task-oriented approach that divides speech production into distinct phases: a transient period, where the speaker's intentions emerge, and a steady-state, characterized by stable verbal expression. Building on the principles of dynamical systems, we develop a dynamic model that separates transient and steady-state regions within the latent space, using variational autoencoders to optimize the transition between them. The resulting model produces high-quality syntheses, revealing an organized structure in the latent transient phase, where similar speech segments cluster together, and steady-state fluctuations exhibit minimal effects. The transient phase also shows a clear connection to the overall duration of the synthesis. When initiated near the boundary between transient and steady regions, the model generates coherent, coherent, and semantically linked sequences. Furthermore, the transient phase's underlying dynamics determine the speech's phonological structure, reducing errors in phonetic transcription compared to models lacking this structure. By emphasizing the transient nature of speech planning, our model provides a more realistic and effective framework for speech synthesis and generation tasks. The first stage identifies initial link positions using specialized optimization tools, while subsequent stages utilize consecutive configurations from the previous stage to refine link positions. In decentralized learning, numerous machines collaborate and converge on a single objective by iteratively updating a local model via gradient descent without sharing information. This study revolves around a stochastic gradient descent framework, where multiple devices simultaneously calculate their individual gradient, choose a random dimension to communicate with a central hub, and share their updated gradient with other connected devices. For a smooth, convex objective with $\beta$-smoothness and $L$-lipchitzity, along with $N$ participating devices and initial conditions where the individual gradient and diameter of the communication graph are known, we can achieve an optimal solution within $T$ iterations by ensuring the following conditions hold: 
  1. The variance of the stochastic gradient is bounded by $\sigma^2$, 
  2. The communication graph is known and has a specified maximum distance for data exchange, 
  3. The variance of individual gradients is limited by $\sigma_0^2$, 
  4. The decay rate of step-size is greater than or equal to $\mu$, 
  5. The known variables include the variance of individual gradients, $\sigma_0^2$, the Lipschitz constant, $L$, the known variables, and the iteration number, $T$.
  By using the Polyak-Żyłkowski method, we have derived a decentralized algorithm, DR-DSGD, which converges at a rate of $O\left(\log(T) \times \left(\frac{N}{T} \cdot \frac{\log(N)}{N} + \sigma_0^2 + \sigma^2\right) + \frac{\sigma_0^2}{\mu}\right)$.
  Furthermore, we have analyzed the convergence rate of our modified DR-DSGD algorithm, which is capable of handling the issue of slow convergence associated with large $N$ and known variables. This modified algorithm, uses local estimates instead of shared ones, significantly enhances its convergence speed by ensuring that its rate of convergence is at most twice as slow as in the decentralized setting. In order to further improve its efficiency by avoiding the need for known variables, we have derived a new iteration, $\text{DR-ADGD}^2$, which is based on an adaptive dimension reduction technique. This new algorithm, $\text{DR-ADGD}^2$, is capable of achieving an optimal convergence rate of $O\left(\frac{\log(T)}{T} + \sigma_0^2\right)$

Traditional safety management approaches for complex systems are largely limited to identifying potential hazards and taking preventive measures to mitigate them. Nevertheless, it is not always possible to eliminate risks entirely, and safety monitoring continues to rely heavily on these defensive strategies. This paper proposes a new model for safeguarding against system failures, which incorporates a dynamic safety management system capable of adapting to unforeseen circumstances. To counteract destabilizing influences, we introduce concept cards that compensate for their effects. A case study involving the management of medical devices for critical care illustrates the effectiveness of our proposed framework. Moreover, we outline possible strategies for integrating current safety management practices with our framework, thereby enhancing the robustness and flexibility of our model. Ultimately, it provides a safety monitoring mechanism that accommodates the inherent uncertainty found in real-world systems. Despite the formal structure of the model, it offers a versatile and easily interpretable method for evaluating risk. To demonstrate the efficacy of our model, we perform a safety assessment using a combination of stochastic and logical reasoning techniques. The model's design enables safety analysts to evaluate various safeguarding measures and evaluate their impact on system safety. Consequently, it facilitates improved, data-driven decision-making in safety management and maintenance. In addition, we utilize an example based on the TGV collision in 2015 to showcase the applicability of our model in investigating accidents and identifying corrective actions. In conclusion, our safety management model offers an effective solution for addressing system failures and safety concerns, which can be utilized in various industries such as healthcare, transportation, and energy by incorporating relevant system characteristics and requirements into the model. The integration of our model with current safety management practices and technologies provides a robust framework for ascertaining and enhancing system safety. Finally, we outline key areas for further research and development in this domain. The model is made available online at https://github.com/LoicLacquyPopel. To facilitate its application, we provide an illustrative case study involving the management of medical devices for critical care. Additionally, we outline possible strategies for adapting our framework to various complex systems and present an analysis of the TGV collision in 2015 as an example of investigating accidents and identifying corrective actions using our model. Consequently, it offers a versatile and easily interpretable method for evaluating risk, which may also be used to assess other system failures and identify relevant measures for mitigating them in the future. To further validate the efficacy and adaptability of our model, we compare its output with that of existing safety assessment methods such as failure mode and effect analysis and fault tree

This deficiency is more pronounced in tight-binding models derived from larger tight-binding models. However, using an averaging technique, we can eliminate these shortcomings without making simplifying assumptions about the system's properties. The method relies on a systematic approach involving the convolution of spatial vectors and the application of unitary transformations. When applied to standard tight-binding models describing tight-binding chains and planes, the resulting objects exhibit properties analogous to the corresponding Peierls sums. By employing the spectral method to solve a normalized cut optimization problem based on pairwise similarity and dissimilarity criteria, we derive a spectral solution that is invariant to scaling, translation, and rotation. To address the issue of outlier resilience in both pose and shape estimation, we propose a dual formulation of the optimization problem. This framework yields efficient solutions via the Fourier transform and its properties. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method's ability to robustly estimate both poses and shapes in the presence of significant outliers. Further analysis explores the method's scalability and potential applications. Finally, we showcase the application of our approach to camouflaged object detection in natural images. To support these applications, we introduce a novel similarity metric based on object camouflagedness. This advancement enables accurate object detection and shape estimation in such complex environments. Comprehensive evaluation of the method's robustness to varying parameters is also conducted through a statistical analysis. Consequently, the proposed method proves suitable for a range of applications, including pose and shape estimation in various domains. These properties make it an ideal model for analyzing data from various fields, including the analysis of radar echoes and the study of anomalies in time series. This paper introduces a method to calculate the maximum likelihood estimators of the Cauchy distribution's parameters, offering an analytical expression for their variances and covariances. Additionally, it determines the confidence region for the parameters, graphicalizing the results as an elliptical region in the complex plane, thereby simplifying the conventional unbiased estimator selection process. Furthermore, the paper compares the Cauchy distribution with the Gaussian model using data from radar targets, demonstrating that the Cauchy distribution typically provides a better fit due to its ability to capture long-tailed probabilities associated with data noise. In turn, this leads to more accurate noise cancellation and enhanced signal extraction from noisy data. Using the Cauchy distribution's parameters and the properties of the Gaussian model, the paper calculates the probabilities of false alarms and missed signals, thereby offering a valuable alternative to the Gaussian model for radar data analysis. In this context, the paper provides a comprehensive overview of the distribution, its properties, and various methods for signal extraction and data analysis. In clinical trials, the sample sizes are often calculated using the total interference model from a given subgroup. However, this model may not always be applicable as recent studies have shown that data can be shared between subgroups, potentially impacting required sample sizes. This study investigates the impact of information exchange between subgroups on sample size calculations and proposes a new approach to determine the optimal sample sizes based on the amount of information shared. By utilizing a multivariate Bayesian analysis, the study develops test statistics and p-values, revealing that data can be shared between subgroups, primarily through correlation and covariance. Based on this finding, the study estimates the potential sample size savings of 25-90% in clinical trials. Additionally, the study indicates that information exchange is more significant in trials examining the efficacy of treatments. Notably, the study finds that model uncertainty, which accounts for different subgroup scenarios, further reduces required sample sizes. Ultimately, the study emphasizes the importance of accurately identifying subgroups and interpreting data interference to ensure accurate statistical analysis and sample size calculations. Given the current limitations of existing methods, the study suggests that a conservative approach be taken to assess data interference and calculate sample sizes while assuming minimal interference. Additionally, the study offers guidance on how to enhance existing methods to better determine subgroups and their associated statistical analyses. By utilizing Bayes factor and model selection metrics, the study proposes an innovative framework to identify subgroups, derive relevant statistics, calculate sample sizes, and estimate test powers. Effective trajectory tracking in complex motion control is influenced by the dynamics, especially position-dependent effects that arise from factors like friction and gear sensitivity. These dynamics typically appear as static errors when measured, but they can be learned through minor adjustments to the motion plan. By adjusting the trajectory in a controlled way, the static error can be converted into a dynamic error that can be easily compensated for. A new method utilizes this approach by introducing a predictable static error through a refined motion plan, and then using an off-line technique to optimize the adjustment needed. The resulting dynamic error is compensated for in real-time using an advanced predictive control method. A key part of this method involves quickly calculating the relevant dynamics information, and this is achieved through the application of a Fast Refined Least Squares algorithm. Testing this method on a 3 DOF motion guide showed that it can reduce position and velocity static errors by 90% and 85% respectively, and it can also reduce velocity dynamic errors by 75%. Furthermore, it can improve the performance of trajectory tracking by 88% without compromising stability. It is worth noting that the method can be applied to a wide range of systems affected by position-dependent dynamics. A notable example is a 5 axis laser scanner used in aerospace to calculate the attitude of parts during assembly. A significant advantage of this method is that it can reduce static errors by 98% and improve velocity dynamic error performance by a factor of 18, and it does so without compromising performance in scenarios where the applicable dynamics model is applicable. A comparison with another established method showed that it can outperform it by as much as 10 dB in terms of position static error, and it can outperform it by as much as 6 dB in terms of velocity static error and 5 dB in terms of velocity dynamic error. A 98% reduction in static error and an improvement of 18 in dynamic error velocity performance were also observed. This can be achieved by leveraging the capabilities of existing point cloud registration models to derive useful features for downstream tasks. To realize this goal, we have developed a novel technique that combines the recent Class-N-Net framework with object classification, resulting in an efficient and lightweight approach called Object-O-Matic. This new method employs the continuous pose normal (CPN) model to derive features from objects of varied shapes and can be viewed as a special case of Class-N-Net. As a result, Object-O-Matic is particularly suited for processing complex categories of everyday objects, and it outperforms other lightweight methods in the field while requiring significantly fewer computational resources. Additionally, we have developed a new dataset featuring 196 categories with 1240 images, known as OOM-Pepo-71. This dataset showcases the effectiveness of our proposed technique in accurately classifying a diverse range of everyday objects with high variability in appearance and shape. Based on these findings, we have set new standards in the field, achieving overall accuracy rates of 66% and 60% on the OOM-Pepo-71 and ModelNet40 datasets, respectively, which marks an improvement of 14% and 12% over the previous best results. This method requires precise simulation of pole mass and matching conditions for standard model processes, especially given the top quark's significant mass. I've developed a new set of pole mass and matching coefficients for the relevant processes, accounting for the effects of pole mass subtraction and soft and collinear corrections. These coefficients, based on the NNLOQED framework, allow for the calculation of the top quark pole mass with an uncertainty at the $\pm 10\ MeV$ level for a $1\ \mathrm{TeV}$-center-of-mass-energy collider, corresponding to a $35$-$50$ femtobarns integrated luminosity. This study used a large set of lattice data to calculate the $D_s^-$, $D_s^{*-}$, $\bar{D}^0$, $\bar{D}^{*0}$, $\bar{\Sigma}^-$, $\bar{\Sigma}^{*-}$, $\bar{\Sigma}^0$, and $\bar{\Sigma}^{++}$ light-cone distribution amplitudes at a momentum momentum scale of 2 GeV. The results showed that both $D_s^-$ and $D_s^{*-}$ exhibited symmetry in their distribution amplitudes, with a $d$ quark present in both the distribution amplitudes. The study also revealed asymmetries in the distribution amplitudes of the $\bar{D}^0$, $\bar{D}^{*0}$, $\bar{\Sigma}^-$, $\bar{\Sigma}^{*-}$, $\bar{\Sigma}^0$, and $\bar{\Sigma}^{++}$ mesons due to quark-squark differences and the presence of a $d$ quark in $\bar{D}^0$ and $\bar{\Sigma}^{++}$. Compared to pions and kaons, these distributions exhibit a greater response to quark-squark variations, with a slower decline in correlation functions along the light cone, indicating that light and heavy quarks behave similarly when distributed within these mesons. This study further reinforced the notion that heavy quarks are largely isolated from the other particles in the hadron, strengthening the concept of heavy quark effective theory. Additionally, this work found that $D_s^-$ and $D_s^{*-}$ light-cone distribution amplitudes are comparable to those of the vector mesons $\rho$, $\K^*$, and $\phi$. This research suggested that heavier light component quarks may reduce the impact of light cone corrections in $D_s$ distribution amplitudes. Furthermore, this work found that $D_s$ and $\Sigma$-type light cone distribution amplitudes may be largely described by a low-dimensional function model, as opposed to pions and kaons, which require a more comprehensive model. Our proposed framework, CySGAN, addresses the limitation of object detection methods being easily deceived by cyber attacks on image pixels. It leverages cybernetic stabilization to create a robust object detection system, specifically for instance segmentation. Since image pixels can be manipulated without system disruption, object detection models based on these pixels are vulnerable to attacks. To mitigate this, CySGAN utilizes a cybernetic stabilization approach to counter cyber attacks on image pixels for instance segmentation. It achieves this by integrating cybernetic stabilization with generative adversarial networks (GAN). By doing so, it produces a learning model that is agnostic to the original image, using CySGAN. Additionally, our approach has the capability to generate counterfeit objects and segments that are in sync with the original image, using the cybernetic stabilization feature learning component. To evaluate our proposal, we simulated various types of cyber attacks on three public datasets, specifically for instance segmentation. Results reveal that object detection models base on pixel can be misled by 100% when it comes to segmentation, but our CySGAN approach can improve this to an accuracy of 70.42%, with an mAP increase of 13.2% compared to vanilla Mask R-CNN. Action anticipation plays a crucial role in intelligent human action recognition systems. Recent models leverage kernel methods to capture the underlying structure of future actions, but they have limited applications in real-world scenarios due to their restriction to linear models. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes the Double Spatiotemporal Support Vector Machine, a double string kernel method that integrates action features with environmental cues under uncertainty. To address the high computational complexity of DS-SVM, this study also presents two efficient optimization algorithms: the Conjugate Gradient Algorithm and the Quasi-Newton Fitting Algorithm. In addition, comprehensive experiments have been conducted to highlight the DS-SVM's performance advantages. Interestingly, when applied to a dataset with radial basis function kernels, DS-SVM exhibited significantly improved performance, averaging 9.8% and 7.3% higher anticipation accuracy compared to traditional support vector machine and double string kernel models, respectively. These results provide strong evidence that DS-SVM is a highly effective action anticipation model. Furthermore, mathematical analysis and empirical evaluations have shown that radial basis function kernels can significantly enhance action anticipation models. As such, this approach is likely to be generally applicable to other domain-specific classification tasks. Our analysis centers around K-star exoplanet host stars exhibiting high levels of stellar activity, specifically focusing on Przybylski's Star (BS 16379-7704), a well-known example in the southern hemisphere. This active star has been chosen for a detailed examination due to its remarkable variability in both optical and ultraviolet spectra during periods of intense flaring activities. By comparing H-alpha and H-beta line observations with concurrent optical and far-ultraviolet energy distributions, researchers have determined the broadening effects of these lines. According to their analysis, there appears to be a correlation between line broadening and energy emitted in the far-ultraviolet spectrum. This appears to contradict previously obtained results from comparable studies on other stars, specifically that of AR Cassiopeiae. One possible explanation for this observed relationship could be related to the physical processes and gas dynamics within high-velocity plasma streams observed during flaring activities. Additionally, we have determined a power-law relationship describing how broadening affects vary with energy emitted in the far-ultraviolet spectrum, specifically following the equation $\tau_{\lambda} \propto \lambda^{-\alpha}$ with an exponent of approximately 2. This is in line with a previous study on another active star (CI Tau). Our analysis also provides theoretical boundaries for the turbulent magnetic field strength and mass flow rate in the stellar chromosphere/ photosphere layer, estimating these values to be in the range of 0.1-0.7 Tesla and 0.5-3.5 km/s, respectively. This study has further confirmed previous findings that magnetic field strength in the chromosphere/ photosphere layer of active stars can be explained by the equation $B^2/8\pi \approx \rho c_v T$, specifically as 2.7~10^5 K for Przybylski's Star. Our final observations highlight the potential for further research into gas dynamics during flaring activities using data from future space-based telescopes featuring advanced high-resolution spectroscopic capabilities. This includes the future Lightning Super Spectrograph, which is specifically designed to analyze the properties of stellar flares at unprecedented levels of detail and sensitivity.  As a companion paper, we are including a report on the observational characteristics of another remarkable star, specifically that of HV Gem, as part of our ongoing effort to study highly active stars and their remarkable stellar flares. This includes an analysis of the extreme 2017 April 24 hypereruption, which may hold the record for the brightest ever recorded in the UV

We examine properties of G2-instantons, focusing on those that can be generated by monopoles. Firstly, it's established that a particular abelian G2-instanton, characterized by certain Higgs field properties, is rigid in its neighborhood. Additionally, it's found that any non-abelian G2-instanton, formed from a self-dual monopole, exhibits movement within its metric. Furthermore, it's discovered that certain topological features of G2-instantons are linked with those of G2-monopoles, specifically through the relation A ∼ d^*H for certain gauge transformations, where A and H are associated with the gauge and Higgs fields, respectively. An alternative formula for the G2-instanton action, based on Higgs field properties, is also determined. Finally, it's been demonstrated that G2-instantons, with specified Higgs field properties, can be generated from G2-monopoles, thus expanding the established class of G2-instantons. In this context, it's noted that the generated abelian G2-instantons may contribute to the G2-instanton sum. Involving metric fluctuations, it's also observed that G2-instantons exhibit an intricate relationship with G2-monopoles, specifically through the fluctuation of the monopole's topological feature. An analogy with the principles of algebraic geometry, particularly regarding the moduli space of G2-monopoles, can be seen in these findings and their implications for G2-instantons. In conclusion, an extension of the previously established connection between G2-instantons and G2-monopoles, concerning both abelian and non-abelian cases, is postulated. This research, therefore, contributes to our understanding of the interlinkage between G2-instantons and G2-monopoles, specifically through their mutual influence and geometric properties. In doing so, it sheds light on the open question of determining the dimensionality of the moduli space of G2-instantons. In this context, it's noted that distinct features of G2-instantons and G2-monopoles allow for their separate analysis and investigation, thus expanding our knowledge of these complex geometric objects. In this study, we examine the properties of several operators within a specific setting of Toeplitz algebras on the Bergman space of certain analytic domains. Our findings focus on the C-normality of composition operators and weighted composition operators, and we explore the projectivity of a specific operator when its symbol and $\varphi$ are multiplicatively connected. Additionally, we use our results to investigate the C-normality of specific operators on the Bergman space of the punctured unit disk and the unit ball in $\mathbb{C}^n$. To a large extent, our results are novel and can be seen as extensions of existing research in this field. A key tool employed in this study is the interplay between the operators in question and specific finite-blade operators introduced here, which share similarities with the nilpotent Blaschke products on the unit ball of $\mathbb{C}^n$. Our nilpotent blades offer a new perspective on this space and its operators. Moreover, in the context of the Bergman space of the punctured unit disk, we use the nilpotent blades to construct specific C-normal operators and offer corresponding examples. Lastly, our analysis of C-normality is linked with the study of nilpotent blades of infinite order, which possesses unique characteristics and offers a new direction for research in this field. To confirm our claims, we provide concrete estimates of the norms of specific differences between operators, and our study offers a comprehensive exploration of the Bergman space of certain domains and its operator theory. Andrews and Merca's $p$-core partition formula can be further analyzed using a mod $d$ expression, leading to a promising outline for a proof. This paper explores an alternative approach, first investigating how mod $d$ expressions can be applied to the partition function itself. A key finding reveals that mod $d$ expressions relate to the structure of largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions, leveraging this to develop a mod $d$ formula for the sum of largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions. Additionally, a general mod $d$ formula for the generating function of $p$-core $p'$-partitions is discovered. A key component of this formula involves the analysis of a bipartite graph, connecting number theory to the study of $p$-core partitions. This study sheds new light on the natural dyadic palindromes of Frobenius and their general form. Lastly, a mod $d$ formula for the $p$-core partition function itself is explored, including an examination of specific cases for $d=2$ and $d=3$. Various proofs are offered, including analogies with the combinatorial sieve of Erdős-Szemerédi. As initial steps towards a broader goal, this research aims to derive formulae using a more aggressive version of the sieve, one that is both stronger and more difficult to apply. Despite its potential, this sieve remains challenging to utilize thoroughly. Despite this, we have successfully employed it to resolve the investigated problems. We also note as an observation the convexity of the function $p\to |C_{p}^{(mod\ d)}|$, where $C_{p}^{(mod\ d)}$ represents the largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions mod $d$. Similar to how Merca studied largest $p$-core partitions in an absolute sense, this research reverses the order of consideration, examining $p$-core partitions mod $d$ and discovering a diverse range, from $(p,d)$-irregular to $(p,d)$-regular instances. Ultimately, a general mod $d$ formula for the generating function of $p$-core partitions offers the most exceptional case, where $d$ is 2, resulting in an incredible variety of $p$-core partitions. Recent success of point cloud modeling using a triplet architecture and similar methods has been achieved through a combination of techniques including regularization, contrastive learning, and feature transformation by projection. Despite these achievements, the models' reliance on local features raises questions about their robustness to more severe transformations such as rotation and scaling. In this study, we address this limitation by proposing the Smoothest Similar Triplet Comparison (SSTC) method. SSTC preserves the smoothest similarity among local features within a point cloud and is based on a Temporal Perspective Comparison (TPC) framework that was inspired by twisted perspectives in cognitive psychology. The TPC framework's robustness against rotation and scaling is proven both theoretically and experimentally, and combining it with SSTC leads to a significant improvement of at least 10% in the certified accuracy of point cloud modeling compared to the state-of-the-art methods when faced with real-world obstacles. Furthermore, the certified accuracies of the resulting models are comparable to their test accuracies on various datasets including the ModelNet. SSTC also shows potential in being an effective loss function for training point cloud models with a fixed architecture under twist-sensitive regularization. Finally, the certification of the resulting models against more severe twists has shown promising results and opens up new avenues for research in the field of point cloud modeling. In particular, the models with spherical Gaussian activation functions outperformed all other models with different activation functions by at least 10% in terms of the certified accuracy. This paper explores the design of Frequency-Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar networks for high-throughput operations, achieving simultaneous maximum transmission power and highest data transfer efficiency in the network. Initially, the research establishes exact calculations for the probability of signal interference and data transfer success in a network using multiple-access interference, followed by an exact formula for network throughput as a function of packet parameters, interference probabilities, and transmission success rates. Building upon this, the paper develops an efficient transmission strategy that maximizes network transmission power and another that maximizes data transfer efficiency in the network, considering constraints on packet parameters to maintain optimal transmission efficiency. Crucially, this paper addresses the crucial challenge of minimizing the impact of FMCW radar system chipping rate variations on data transfer efficiency in the network. Furthermore, the paper investigates the implications of FMCW radar system sensitivity on data transfer efficiency in the network. Key research findings include the optimal relationships between chirps per packet, packets per second, and data transfer efficiency in the network, as well as the optimal distribution of chip frequency deviations and maximal allowed chip frequency deviations for minimal impact on data transfer efficiency in the network. This research provides novel insights into the design of high-throughput FMCW radar networks, making significant contributions to the state-of-the-art in the field. Temporal knowledge graph completion (TKGC) is an essential task in artificial intelligence that focuses on predicting the probability of a missing element in a temporal knowledge graph. Most existing TKGC methods incorporate time-related factors to improve their predictive capabilities. However, the current time-encoding techniques used in TKGC models have several limitations, including the reduced effectiveness of cycle-aware encoding and the inability to capture high-frequency time series effectively. In an attempt to address these limitations, this study introduces a novel cycle-aware time-encoding technique that encodes temporal constraints in a predictive manner. Additionally, the study proposes a selective aggregation mechanism to enhance the representation of high-frequency time series at the cycle level. Based on the concept of hybrid memory, the study develops bidirectional time-encoding models that integrate the new time-encoding technique, and evaluates their effectiveness through extensive experiments on diverse TKGC datasets. The results reveal that the proposed models achieve remarkable predictive accuracy and consistently outperform existing TKGC methods. Furthermore, the study showcases the efficacy of the proposed models on a new benchmark dataset called T-GNMI-MT. In addition, the study showcases numerous successful applications of TKGC to various real-world problems, including forecasting, link prediction, and category prediction. Lastly, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed models on another new benchmark dataset called T-GNMI-MT-Multi-Y. In contrast to existing TKGC methods, the proposed approach has several advantages, including enhanced predictive capabilities, reduced memory consumption, and the ability to effectively capture high-frequency time series at both the cycle and aggregate levels. In addition, the proposed approach has several desirable properties, including scalability, selectivity, and interpretability. In order to verify the practical effectiveness of the proposed approach, the study evaluates various aspects of the approach, including its computational memory requirements, the selectivity of the approach, and the interpretability of the approach. The results of the evaluation confirm that the proposed approach has several desirable properties, including improved predictive capabilities, reduced memory consumption, the ability to effectively capture high-frequency time series, selectivity, and interpretability. Researchers have introduced two-dimensional materials called hydrogen boride monolayers with remarkable properties resulting from their unique electron-phonon and electron-hydrogen interactions. Computational models reveal that incorporating hydrogen into boron results in optimal two-dimensional structures with bonds fluctuating between covalent and ionic characteristics, ultimately predicting robust dielectric properties. This paper explores the concept of flattened partitions, a topic initially introduced through the numbers $f_{n, k}$, which count how many flattened partitions of $n$ have exactly $k$ parts. We delve into specific constraints for these numbers, such as the numbers of flattened partitions that consist of exactly two parts and the numbers of inverted flattened partitions that consist of exactly two parts. We use the latter to identify a new class of safe permutations. Additionally, the article investigates the symmetric nature of certain $f_{n, k}$ values and highlights a distinction in this regard between even and odd numbers. A few combinatorial arguments underpin the proofs presented here. We also establish a new formula for $f_{n, k}$ by combining inverse generating functions, incorporating a step-by-step guide on how to derive this formula. We conclude by outlining potential future areas of research. The advancement of automotive driving systems like Automatic Emergency Braking invites concerns about system safety that deepen with each enhancement. To address these worries, researchers use formal verification methods like model checking alongside simulation tools like CarMaker. This combination facilitates in-depth analysis of complex systems within a realistic, physical environment. However, model conversion and validation pose significant challenges in this process, which can be efficiently tackled by the Open Verification Condition Method.

This method was applied to checking ECE 47 compliance for Automatic Emergency Braking systems in vehicles. The steps involved modeling and encoding ECE 47 requirements as formal verification conditions. Then, model checking was performed in Concertive (a model checking tool) on converted and validated models from CarMaker and Simulink. Finally, all model inputs satisfying ECE 47 compliance were confirmed against the specifications outlined in ECE 47.

Our study focused on Confirmite's model checking capability and its interaction with Concertive. We converted and validated an Automatic Emergency Braking system model from CarMaker and Simulink. Then, using the Open Verification Condition Method, we found that Concertive can verify whether the generated models are correct and consistent with ECE 47 requirements. Ultimately, we found that automatic conversion from CarMaker to Concertive produced some minor inconsistencies that were easily resolved. Additionally, we found that the Concertive model allowed for more advanced and sophisticated analyses compared to the original CarMaker model. In the end, every system that satisfied ECE 47 requirements in Concertive also satisfied the requirements, but we found some additional system configurations in Concertive that did not violate ECE 47 but did activate the system, indicating a possible refinement for the specifications. Our findings suggested that using the Open Verification Condition Method along with model checking offers considerable benefits for evaluating system safety in complex automotive driving systems like Automatic Emergency Braking. Model checking offers an improved level of confidence in comparison to simulation alone and can identify issues not revealed by simulation. Additionally, using model checking allows for more sophisticated analyses and a greater level of detail in evaluating system safety. While conversion and validation are crucial for leveraging model checking, they can be efficiently tackled through the application of the Open Verification Condition Method. Consequently, using Concertive for verifying highly validated models offers considerable advantages over other verification tools and methods. These findings suggest that using the Open Verification Condition Method for converting, validating, and verifying system models can greatly benefit the verification process and provide considerable cost savings. Ultimately, we believe that the Open Verification Condition Method offers a versatile and efficient approach for evaluating system safety in complex automotive driving

This perspective offers new tools for dynamic system analysis but also incurs a higher dimensionality due to the need to observe all relevant system variables. To overcome this challenge, a method is proposed in this paper that combines the dynamic mode decomposition and the extended dynamic operator approach to develop a simplified model of a nonlinear system. By leveraging the linear Hamiltonian structure of these systems, a new method is proposed to derive both the delay time and the sparse matrix representing the lagged observations required for efficient data representation. Furthermore, a novel sparse Koopman operator algorithm is proposed to tackle the issue of determining the delay time, yielding results comparable to those of existing methods but with significantly reduced computational costs. This property distinguishes the proposed method from other data representation methods that necessarily involve approximation. This work lays the groundwork for developing new optimization techniques that can balance the efficiency of data representation and the accuracy of the derived model. To facilitate its use, the method is implemented in an open-source library that can be accessed freely for research purposes. This includes detailed instructions and examples for applying the algorithm to various data sets, as well as other useful functionality to facilitate the process. Ultimately, the method has great potential to enable the efficient analysis and manipulation of complex nonlinear systems through their transformation into a more tractable form. Although Leibniz's work on infinity is well documented, there is ongoing debate among historians and philosophers concerning its exact meaning. Leibniz employed the terms "infinito" and "infinitamente grande" to describe bounded and unbounded infinity, respectively. According to an early interpretation by Wilbur, Leibniz's concept of bounded infinity referred to mathematical infinities as seen in the work of Cavalieri and Bonaventura, while unbounded infinity represented an abstract, limitless quantity. Conversely, Leibniz's concept of unbounded infinity was seen by Arthur as representing mere logical possibility, rather than quantity. More recent attempts to reconcile these differences with Leibniz's calculus include an alternative interpretation by S. F. Shaffer, who attributed a range of meanings to Leibniz's notions of infinity, including distinct meanings for "infinito" and "infinitamente grande" in scientific and philosophical contexts. This paper will examine the various meanings attributed to Leibniz's concepts of bounded and unbounded infinity, as well as the importance of clarifying these distinctions. If the term "infinito" is understood as denoting a range of infinite magnitudes with no upper limit, then Leibniz's calculus becomes redundant. On the other hand, if "infinito" is taken as indicating a range of infinite magnitudes with no lower limit, then Leibniz's concept of bounded and unbounded infinity becomes irrelevant. By contrast, if "infinito" is understood as indicating a range of infinite magnitudes with both upper and lower limits, then Leibniz's concept of bounded and unbounded infinity can be seen as meaningful. However, this last interpretation appears to contradict Leibniz's own statements regarding the infinito as being distinct from the infinitely small. In light of these considerations, I will propose an innovative solution to the problem. As I will argue in this paper, Leibniz's concept of bounded and unbounded infinity can indeed be understood as meaningful, while also conforming to Leibniz's own statements regarding the infinito as being distinct from the infinitely small. Furthermore, this interpretation is consistent with Leibniz's methodological principles as set out in his scientific method, as well as with his concept of reflection, as described in his work on the law of continuity. This research uses a comprehensive set of simulated cosmic microwave background maps to examine the impact of removing foregrounds from parameter estimation. We leverage 9,900 simulations with varying levels of galactic foregrounds and a specialized likelihood tool to analyze these maps in a Bayesian framework. These simulations account for uncertainties in real cosmic noise and galactic foregrounds, enabling a reliable assessment of their impact on parameter estimation. We develop a straightforward technique to estimate the minimum variance of cosmological parameters and use this method to determine the efficiency of foreground removal. We also engage in extensive literature review and comparison with previously published results on the topic. We investigate the efficiency of foreground removal under specific scenarios and its dependence on certain parameters such as the visibility function and spectral index of the visibility function. We reveal that removing foregrounds can negatively affect parameter estimation for certain cosmological parameters and that larger uncertainties in the visibility function lead to more efficient foreground removal. We highlight the potential of leveraging simulations to inform the design of upcoming experiments such as CMB-S4 and the CMB-SMIRATHI mission to effectively remove foregrounds and meet their scientific objectives. We outline future research directions that could further inform the design of future experiments and their potential scientific returns. The study investigates how an operator's consistency mapping transforms a sequence of vectors. It is demonstrated through an example that operator consistency does not necessarily yield a linearly independent sequence. However, it is shown that if the operator is closed in a certain sense and the original sequence has a high degree of linear independence, the resulting sequence remains linearly independent. Conversely, this relationship does not hold in general for all operators. A key factor in maintaining linear independence is the sequence's unique geometric structure, specifically its distance from the operator's null space. This is formalized in a relevant theorem. A distinct difference between operator consistency and other mathematical concepts arises when examining the possibility of obtaining a linearly independent sequence from an operator that maps a sphere to a smaller area. It is found that if the operator is closed and the original sequence is densely packed in the sphere, it is not possible to obtain a linearly independent sequence. This idea is illustrated with an artificial example and further supported by a different practical scenario involving the construction of a linearly independent sequence of vectors from a set of vectors that are densely packed in a smaller area. Finally, it is found that if the vectors are evenly distributed in a compact, convex set, it becomes possible to obtain a linearly independent sequence. The reaction ${\rm K^-}(975~{\rm GeV}){\rm C} \to \pi^+ \pi^- n$ was studied 
using large data sets of $(K^-{\rm C})$ atoms at SATURNE and ITEP, allowing 
for the identification of $\pi^+ \pi^- n$ final states induced by $(K^-{\rm p})$ 
virtual states of $s$ quarks within kaon-carbon nuclei. Data analysis yielded an 
estimate of $\Gamma(a_0(980){\rm p})/\Gamma(f_0(980){\rm p}) \simeq 0.25$ 
with an uncertainty of 0.15, indicating a stronger production probability 
for the $a_0(980)$ resonance over the $f_0(980)$ resonance. Additionally, the 
study provided further constraints on the ${\rm \pi \pi}$ scalar resonances' properties, 
specifying couplings to the ${\rm Kn}$ system as $g_{a_0{\rm n}}^2 \simeq 0.22$ and 
$g_{f_0{\rm n}}^2 \simeq 0.11$ GeV$^2$, and specifying the decay widths of $a_0(980)$ 
and $f_0(980)$ produced in association with a nucleon as $\Gamma(a_0(980){\rm p}) \simeq 118 
{\rm MeV}$ and $\Gamma(f_0(980){\rm p}) \simeq 56$ MeV. The study's results were 
incorporated into the EFT description of the reaction using effective coupling constants 
of $g_{a_0{\rm n}}$ and $g_{f_0{\rm n}}$. The analysis further allowed the extraction of 
the ${\rm \pi \pi}$ phase shift at the energy of the $f_0(980)$ resonance. Ultimately, the 
study's results validated a theory of meson molecular theory and demonstrated 
sensitivity to the models of the $a_0(980)$ and $f_0(980)$ resonances as well as 
the $S$-wave ${\rm \pi \pi}$ amplitude. The results of the study have significant implications 
for our understanding of the $a_0(980)$ and $f_0(980)$ resonances

The success of the GRAVITY beamcombiner in the GRAVITY instrument, a high-precision tool for the GRAVITY project on the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, depends on its ability to combine images from multiple cameras and stabilize them for further processing. A stabilization system, similar to those used in mobile phones, utilizes the cameras to determine the direction of view, correct for minor movements, and adjust the focus. To optimize GRAVITY's operational efficiency, a script was created to streamline the stabilization process, allowing the instrument to quickly adapt to changing conditions and select the best images for further analysis. By testing this script in combination with established algorithms, a significant improvement in performance was achieved, with a typical integration time of 10 seconds and a successful stabilization rate of over 90% for a given set of data. The script has been successfully integrated into the GRAVITY's control software and is currently available for public use through the GRAVITY's website. Further developments aim to enhance the script's ability to handle various focus adjustment methods and optimize its integration with the GRAVITY's control system, with the ultimate goal of increasing its operational efficiency and meeting the project's demonstration timeline for the GRAVITY's science verification phase. In this paper, the design and validation of the script, its current outcomes, and future prospects for enhancement are detailed. Closely related to this work, a new focus selection method known as CLIP (for "Chopping Large Field of Interest") - which includes a stabilization module identical to that used above - has recently been developed to increase the GRAVITY's operational efficiency and meet the project's demonstration timeline for the GRAVITY's science verification phase. In this paper, the design and validation of CLIP, its theoretical optimisation, and current results are detailed. We explore the properties of a specific class of NP-hard problems, CAP$k$C, that encompass various facility location issues, including the Capacitated k-Center and Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problems. Our investigation reveals that CAP$k$C is at least as difficult to approximate as is the Minimum Prize-Collecting Steiner Forest problem, except for specific special cases. In contrast, the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem can be closely approximated within a factor of $O(\log k)$, which is a significant improvement over the Capacitated k-Center problem that can only be approximated within a factor of $O(\log^2 k)$. Additionally, we demonstrate that in graphs with limited highway dimensions, the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem can achieve nearly linear-time closeness approximations, whereas the Capacitated k-Center problem requires more complex algorithms involving preprocessing steps and super-linear time complexity. Our study also introduces novel algorithmic techniques, including a special type of "beam search" used for finding efficient approximate solutions to CAP$k$C, as well as novel facultative greedy algoritms capable of producing highly accurate CAP$k$C instances. Our analysis further reveals the existence of a significant approximation chasm between the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers and the Capacitated k-Center problems, as evidenced by our introduction of a new and challenging variant of the Minimum Prize-Collecting Steiner Forest problem, which is solvable using a simple greedy algorithm but proves notoriously hard to approximate for both CAP$k$C and Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers. Our findings thus offer the first detailed examination of the approximation chasm, facilitating a deeper comprehension of this critical issue in algorithmic theory. Moreover, we develop close approximations for a general class of facility location issues, including the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers and a special variant of the Minimum Prize-Collecting Steiner Forest problem, by leveraging our introduction of a new and efficient facultative greedy algorithm. As a key aspect, our results indicate that the Capacitated k-Supplier with Outliers problem enjoys limited dependency on its highway dimensions, allowing us to derive a close approximation within a factor of $O(\log^2 k)$ for this problem, whereas a close approximation within a factor of $O(\log k)$ can be achieved for a general class of facility location issues, including the Capacitated k-Center problem, through preprocessing steps involving an initial approximation analysis pass. This paper provides a precise estimate for the partial sum of a neural network, which is equivalent to a restricted version of the Vandermonde determinant. By leveraging this finding, we are able to derive a precise boundary for the Brück conjecture's primary statement. Moreover, our research offers a precise bound for an altered version of the Brück conjecture, specifically for entire solutions with a hyper-order less than 1/2. Furthermore, we investigate the analytic continuation of the partial sum as well as its asymptotic behavior near the boundary of the finite plane. Ultimately, we explore a family of meromorphic mappings and apply the insights gained to establish precise bounds for the associated partial sums of neutrosophic analytic functions. Crucially, our research identifies a critical threshold for the degree of the partial sum that influences its asymptotic behavior and the existence of certain asymptotic values within the finite plane. Notably, one of the theorems identifies a perfect correspondence between the trivial solutions of the Neutrosophic analytic functions and the partial sums of a neural network. This research seeks to fill a void in existing literature by adapting and broadening the scopes of multiple influential conjectures within the field of Neutrosophic analysis. Key among these is the extension of the Brück conjecture, which can be derived from multiple notable sources, including the Carlson-DeCarlo, Landau, and Nevanlinna theorems. Additionally, we present specific examples that showcase diverse growth patterns for neutrosophic analytic functions and partial sums of neural networks, highlighting their complexity and variability. One notable example illustrates a situation where the growth rate of a partial sum exceeds that of a neural network for degrees less than or equal to 2n, while another example highlights a case where the growth rate of a neural network surpasses that of a partial sum for degrees above 2n. This research aims to lay a foundational understanding of the field's conjectures and partially counter them, thus demonstrating the necessity of additional or more precise hypotheses. As a byproduct of this investigation, we identify certain properties and characteristics of neutrosophic analytic functions and partial sums of neural networks, identifying key differences in their behaviors and properties. Notably, one property reveals a growth rate threshold beyond which the growth rate of a partial sum is dictated by that of a neural network, marking a degree threshold of 2n. Additionally, another property highlights a situation where the growth rate of a neural network surpasses that of a partial sum for degrees above 2n.

solution methods for linear systems, showcasing substantial reduction in

We have developed a novel approach that enables the manufacture of highly precise pairs of photons, where the correlation between their energy and momentum can be fully customized. This achievement is based on the integration of two hot atoms in separate optical cavities, where the release of energy from the atoms influences the photon count in a way that can be precisely manipulated. Notably, we have demonstrated the control of even and odd correlated photon emissions through a simple adjustment of the atom-cavity coupling strength. This study utilizes a combination of theoretical and experimental methods to model the photon correlation function, where we apply this concept to the creation of precise two-photon states. Additionally, we have shown that the emission of these correlated photons can be adjusted to match specific frequency settings in our system. This research contributes to the ongoing efforts in the exploration of unconventional photonics applications. We introduce a novel approach to resolving the Hamiltonian constraint for calculating gravitational wave energies within unmodified general relativity. This method diverges from conventional models that assume certain conditions on the spacetime metric. Instead, our scheme determines the lapse function through an iterative process using generalized normal modes, which are derived from the Dirac equations. By treating the conformal factor as a dynamic variable, the Hamiltonian constraint is reinterpreted and approximated. This method enhances the accuracy of gravitational wave energy calculations and facilitates a more effective exploration of the Dirac vector potential's impact on gravitational wave properties. Furthermore, our approach enables the investigation of complex configurations, such as non-spherical and time-varying gravitational waves. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by calculating gravitational wave energies in diverse scenarios, including approximate linear fluctuations and certain cosmological perturbations. This method's iterative lapse calculation also yields a useful tool for optimizing calculations. We anticipate that our approach will stimulate research into gravitational wave properties and their connections to spinor matter, paving the way for novel observational opportunities. The associated Python package allows users to compute gravitational wave energies with various assumptions, thereby providing a valuable educational resource and a useful tool for fundamental research. Finally, potential future applications and directions are outlined, including the application of our method to modified theories of gravity and the calculation of spinor matter's impact on cosmological perturbations. This may entail introducing new degrees of freedom to the system, such as a time and space varying scalar field, which could lead to the discovery of a dynamical connection between the spinor matter and the gravitational wave properties. The potential future research in this area is a promising area of study that could lead to the development of a ground breaking theory. The computational framework presented here provides a solid foundation for such research and can be expanded to accommodate more complex scenarios. The code also enables the computation of gravitational wave energies in diverse scenarios, such as non-spherical and time-varying fluctuations, and lays the groundwork for the investigation of relational quantum mechanics and the connections between spinor matter and gravitational waves. The code's versatility and a series of illustrative examples demonstrate its potential in a wide range of applications, including the study of cosmological perturbations, modified theories of gravity, and the development of a dynamical theory of gravity. The associated research presents a new and exciting direction in the research, in which the relationships between spinor matter and gravitational waves are explored from a quantum relational perspective.

Through the use of certain matrix norms, our results offer upper limits on the distance between the ideal solution and the actual solution output by the basis pursuit decoder. The particular matrix of interest, known as the total variation matrix, gave rise to a unique challenge: the decay rate of its eigenvalues dictates whether sparse solutions can be accurately represented or not. To overcome this issue, we developed an approximation algorithm, termed basis pursuit with soft-thresholding, which produces a solution congruent with the original vector when possible or identifies the minimum number of non-zero components for the original vector. Our analysis shows that this method achieves optimal performance in terms of minimax error for the basis pursuit problem with the total variation matrix, a matrix that has gained prominence in the context of compressed sensing due to its relation to the Dantzig selector and convex relaxation of a range of sparse approximation problems. Furthermore, our results were validated through numerical experiments conducted on an image denoising task. Notably, our findings suggest that basis pursuing with soft-thresholding offers an appealing alternative to basis pursuit when accurate representation of the solution vector is not possible due to limitations imposed by its spectrum or due to measurement errors in certain applications, a scenario that may prove relevant in future research in compressed sensing. Moreover, our analysis sheds light on the nature of total variation sparse solutions, an area under investigation in the literature. Lastly, our results illustrate that basis pursuing with soft-thresholding can be an effective denoising method, a capability previously unreported in the literature. A hybrid discontinuous Galerkin method is developed for solving the vector transport equation by approximating the vector field using a mixed finite element approach. This novel method is designed to mitigate the potential for non-physical "swimming droples" that can arise in standard finite element simulations of vector transport. Although the mixed formulation avoids these issues, the resulting system of equations does not have a straightforward discrete gradient operator, which motivates the introduction of the hybrid discontinuous Galerkin method. This new approach involves inserting continuity constraints for the vector field across interface cells, effectively combining stable and continuous characteristics. A related localised static condensation technique is then developed to simplify computations and reduce memory requirements. Several numerical examples are presented to demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of the proposed method, including comparisons with standard finite element approximations. These experiments highlight the potential benefits of using the hybrid discontinuous Galerkin method, particularly for solving complex problems involving the vector transport equation and curved geometries. To this end, the integration of differential privacy and federated learning has emerged as a key strategy for minimizing biases in machine learning algorithms. However, the lack of foundational research in this area has limited the effectiveness of these techniques. Our work bridges this gap by establishing a general framework for measuring fairness in classification algorithms, backed by accessible statistical tools. This allows us to determine the trade-offs between fairness and privacy, and demonstrate how common fairness metrics can be linked to privacy metrics, such as R\'{e}nyi divergence and total variation distance. Our research uncovers fundamental relationships between these metrics and opens the door to more efficient differential privacy solutions, such as conserving privacy expenditure while maintaining fairness. Furthermore, the foundation we've established can be applied across various loss functions, demonstration of our methods' effectiveness is provided for the logarithmic loss function. We provide concrete, understandable formulas for measuring fairness in terms of these divergences, and demonstrate their ease of application, even in complex scenarios. This research introduces a class of continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods that expand upon existing discretization techniques for Hamiltonian systems and Lagrangian dynamics, leveraging analytical and numerical methods to monitor the conservation of key variables. By constructing these methods alongside their corresponding flow subspaces, it's shown that they maintain precise mapping properties, thereby ensuring the preservation of structural features inherent to the original differential equations. Furthermore, numerical simulations demonstrate the high accuracy of these methods when compared to traditional methods, even in situations involving large time steps. Specifically, for the Kepler problem and its variants, certain continuous-stage methods were found to precisely conserve key physical properties, whereas traditional methods were unable to do so, even when employing high order accuracy. By developing an efficient algorithm for monitoring the relative error of these methods, it's possible to adjust time step sizes and optimize performance, thereby enhancing their overall effectiveness. This approach uses a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to integrate features from multiple frames and a convolutional layer to capture spatial structures. Furthermore, experiments demonstrate that TahAN surpasses existing methods on action recognition tasks, it achieves an accuracy of 79.0% on UCF101 and 88.4% on HMDB51. Characterizing the uncertainty in such distributions is then a natural progression. This research focuses on developing new approaches to compute entropy estimates for distributions that cannot be directly expressed, such as those involving the harmonic mean of variances or divergences like the f-divergence. Building on recent advances in non-parametric estimation and deep learning, we introduce a new framework based on neural networks to compute entropy estimates. This method can be viewed as a specialized information bottleneck that encodes data into a latent space with a fixed dimension, where the entropy of this space represents the measured uncertainty. This method can be applied not only to compute the entropy of a distribution itself but also to estimate the directed information rate in dynamical systems and to study the structure of complex networks responsible for encoding information. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of adapting our method to estimate the f-divergence between multiple distributions, thereby providing a new insight into the relationship between entropy and divergence. Through extensive simulations and experimental applications, we showcase the efficacy of our entropy estimation algorithms. Our results demonstrate that the hybrid quantum approach outperforms its fully quantum counterpart and the classical methods, both in terms of computational efficiency and achievable quality of solution. particular, the hybrid method excels at finding good approximations quickly, which is beneficial when operating under tight time constraints. Our findings underscore the potential of hybrid quantum solutions for addressing complex engineering challenges. Moreover, they underscore the need for more research into fully quantum solutions to practical problems. Lastly, they highlight the significance of evaluating the performance of quantum algorithms on real-world problems before their widespread adoption. By translating these complex physical processes into a mathematical problem involving set-valued operations, we can utilize specialized techniques for solving inclusion problems. A key constraint in our approach is maintaining the exact solution for the falling object's motion, while allowing for fluctuations in the force measurement. We test and validate our method through a series of computer simulations that mimic real-world measurements of objects falling under air resistance and observe that the solution converges rapidly when the noise is limited. All results are compared with alternative methods for solving the inclusion problems, such as the least squares method, which is found to produce less accurate outcomes in certain cases. For example, when an object is initially accelerating rapidly due to weight, the least squares method can become stuck in an incorrect solution before adjusting to the true dynamics. A new theoretical model, the soft potential model, explains the property of certain dense glasses that shows a significant decline in sound wave damping at low frequencies. This model proposes that at low frequencies, the material's ability to absorb energy from the wave is hindered due to the slow movement of atoms. However, this assumption is invalid in some cases, as it contradicts the material's behavior in high-frequency range where the disorder in the material affects all atomic movements equally, thus leading to a different explanation for the soft potential model's results. Instead, the origin of the soft potential model's formula is connected to the material's viscosity and the constraint on atom movement, as well as the resonance frequency of the material's natural oscillations. This new interpretation allows for the application of the model to a wider range of materials that exhibit different behaviors, such as a material with extremely high frequencies that indicates a liquid-like behavior even below its melting point. Moreover, this model allows for the assessment of four distinct dynamical processes based on their relation to four distinct frequency ranges. A detailed mathematical framework has been established for four different types of materials, including a glass-forming substance, a material with extremely high frequencies, a substance with very low frequencies, and a solid with extremely high frequencies that shows a liquid-like behavior even below its melting point. For these materials, the dip in the low-frequency range of sound wave damping is analyzed, as well as how it is influenced by changes in the material's dynamic picture. We introduce a groundbreaking, semi-numerical technique that facilitates the computation of particle physics outcomes with an elevated degree of precision. This innovative approach combines conventional analytical methods with numerical solutions to establish a more reliable framework. Within our proposed framework, the structure of the integrand is analyzed and optimized for the scenario at hand. This is followed by solving a simplified integral analytically and then leveraging numerical methods to address the residual terms. The resulting pseudo-functions can be generated in advance and stored, enabling the efficient computation of particle physics outcomes with a high degree of precision across a wide range of input variables. We demonstrate the potential of this method by calculating two-loop corrected exclusive photon photon scattering cross sections with high precision. This computation is particularly useful for ultra-high energy photon collisions in the context of heavy ion reactions at relativistic energies. The new method is also generally applicable to particle physics computations, and its integration into public libraries will likely occur in the future. We are calling for community participation in order to further develop and promote this computational tool. Additionally, we outline a plan for developing a set of pre-prepared functions similar to those in "PHOTON" and "TOPPAI" through the matrix element library "SHARE-ME" framework, with the first of these functions being the two-loop corrected $pp$ annihilation process. This library will contain preparatory documents, code, and a detailed description of the computational methods used to generate the pre-computed tables. All of these resources will be maintained within the "SHARE-ME" framework and made available at https://share-me.hep.ucla.edu/. We are excited to share this new initiative with the particle physics community and invite your participation in this effort. Nogueras-Lauranc et al. (2019) presented conclusive proof of a central bar structure in our Galaxy through a method combining observed patterns in CO, radio continuum, and K-band starlight data. These data not only verified the presence of a bar but also implied the presence of a co-rotating disk within it, spanning at least 1 kpc and containing approximately $10^{9}$ solar masses of gas and starlight. Additionally, our study found that this bar structure affects the formation of a non-axisymmetric disk in our Galaxy, which could be responsible for many of its unique characteristics. These patterns are strongest in CO and radio continuum data, while appearing less pronounced in K-band starlight data due to the influence of a dust layer. Considering these factors along with observational evidence, our study presents a detailed picture of a bar-driven dynamical process in our Galaxy. Finally, these findings could provide significant insights for studying galaxies in the local group.

In multimodal optimization, multiple optimal solutions are sought, whereas in multi-objective optimization, a single optimal solution with the best overall performance across different objectives is sought. Our research proves that, in the general case, there is no direct relationship between solutions found by multimodal and multi-objective optimization methods. In contrast, numerous studies have demonstrated that similar problems can often yield similar solutions in both scenarios. This study aims to explore this phenomenon and identify potential causes. By analyzing the structures of multimodal and multi-objective problems, we find that their corresponding landscapes share key characteristics. Specifically, we show that multimodal optimization problems feature flat optimal regions and multi-objective optimization problems exhibit non-dominated solution distributions with a hierarchical structure. Our research also verifies that similar problem structures generally yield similar optimization outcomes in both scenarios. Additionally, we propose a metric to evaluate the complexity of multi-objective optimization problems based on their optimal solution distribution and flat regions around the non-dominated front. This research sheds new light on the relationships between different optimization scenarios and enables comprehensive analysis of solution distributions in both scenarios. Furthermore, it potenitially allows for the application of multimodal optimization methods to solve multi-objective problems and vice versa. Lastly, it enables the development of specialized optimization methods tailored to different problem structures and solution distributions. Research in algorithmic mechanism design focuses on designing algorithms to determine stable matchings, a concept originally applied to one-to-one relationships. However, we explore its extension to one-to-many relationships, specifically for agents with binary valuation functions. Our work considers two utilitarian social welfare definitions and examines the computational complexity of finding the most stable matches and a stable match that maximizes it. The results show that each problem has distinct computational properties based on the welfare definition used. Specifically, we identify threshold values for the maximum and lower bound complexity of finding a stable match that depend on the distribution of agent valuations. To demonstrate the practical relevance of these findings, we use data from two real-world settings: satellite television broadcasting and healthcare resource allocation. Our research shows that efficient stable matches can be found quickly in these applications. The outcomes of this study contribute to three areas: algorithmic mechanism design, broadcast satellite communications, and healthcare resource allocation and allocation in multiple markets. Our research also raises questions about the design of algorithmic mechanism design objects when the input size is not fixed.
