Our research explores the impact of nonuniform strain and edge disorder on valley Hall transport in two-dimensional materials.  We developed a transport model by combining the strain profile from finite element methods and a Monte Carlo simulation accounting for disorder-induced valley orbit mixing and valley transition thermal activation.  The results indicate that valley Hall conductivity is insensitive to strain distribution but highly influenced by the type of disorder present.  Furthermore, we identified an optimal temperature range for valley Hall conductivity that is independent of material properties.  This range is determined by a strain-induced valley transition threshold that is also a temperature at which valley Hall conductivity starts to emerge.  We also derived an expression for valley Hall conductivity in terms of disorder parameters, enabling us to examine the convergence of valley Hall conductivity as a function of disorder density.  Ultimately, our research provides insights into the mechanisms governing valley Hall transport in two-dimensional materials and the regions in which valley Hall conductivity converges.  The integration of our transport model with device fabrication enables us to predict how valley Hall transport is affected by various parameters, including strain profile, disorder type, valley transition energy, and disorder density.  The outcomes of our research may be used to fine-tune the properties of valley Hall devices and guide the development of strain engineered valley Hall devices.  The tools employed in this research such as the Strain Profile Analyzer and Disorder Viewer, may be used to evaluate the properties of other quantum Hall systems.  The valley Hall transport data is compared with experiments conducted on state-of-the-art materials and the results are found to be in agreement with experiments.  The valley Hall transport data is also found to be in agreement with quasi-classical theories and the results are conversed with quantum simulations conducted at extremely low temperatures.  The outcomes of our research show that valley Hall conductivity can be effectively investigated at any temperature by combining classical and quantum theories.  The integration of our transport model with device fabrication and quantum simulations allows us to accurately evaluate the properties of valley Hall systems across a wide temperature range from experiments to quantum effects. Our investigation into these structures, and particularly the actions of groups on them, demonstrates the connection between their geometry and the group's structure. Furthermore, we examine how the connection between their geometry and the group's structure influences key algebraic combinatorial objects, such as the affine permutation group, the Coxeter group, and the symmetric group. Additionally, we discuss how our developed concepts relate to existing results in order theory and the study of posets. Ultimately, we aim to contribute to the development of an existing framework that connects group actions to metric geometry. To support our investigations, a dedicated library called Clouds has been implemented in the Gap software environment. This library not only provides a flexible tool for one-dimensional clouds but also contains a database of group data, including generators, relations, and other relevant information. This paper outlines the creation of Accurate Computational Electromagnetics tools to design a rectangular waveguide matched to a substrate-integrated antenna (SIA). The development of a Collaborative Antenna-Stub Filter (CASF) using the SIA and a modified stub filter is also presented. The stub filter is integrated with two high impedance pseudo-lithuanian loop resonators to form a low-pass Cascadable Filter (CF). The design process of the stub filter is optimized via a computational algorithm and verified through experiments. The resulting Cascadable Filter demonstrates a wide bandwidth of 35%, matched to a substrate-integrated antenna with a beamwidth of 125 degrees, suitable for wireless sensor applications. Moreover, the work showcases the effectiveness of computational design in developing filter and antenna combinations with simplified casing designs. Details of the computational tool and designed structures are presented, accompanied by experimental validation of the designs. The results reveal an acceptable casing insertion loss of 0.3 dB over the matched bandwidth. Additionally, measurements indicate that the beam pattern of the antenna remains intact, with little interference from the casing. Key performance characteristics of the design include a high impedance pseudo-lithuanian loop resonance frequency of 2.42 GHz, a stub filter cut-off frequency of 3.42 GHz, and a Cascadable Filter cut-off frequency of 3.10 GHz. The presented design offers a novel solution for wireless sensor technology, addressing existing issues of limited bandwidth and lack of casing design methods for substrate-integrated filters and antennas. Moreover, the research facilitates the development of computational electromagnetics toolkits, enabling the design of innovative filter and antenna combinations with various casing configurations. The work is expected to open up new avenues for the design of wide bandwidth Cascadable Filter and antenna systems with different casing configurations, thereby promoting the computational design of filter and antenna combinations. The computational tool and design examples presented herein are accessible through an online database called CYCLOPIT. CYCLOPIT ensures hassle-free access to the designs, computational algorithms, and required software even in situations of limited internet connectivity. Moreover, the project is maintained and updated regularly to ensure seamless usage. In our work, we utilize a reinforcement learning approach to develop efficient decoding strategies for surface codes. By applying this method to decode single-qubit errors in surface codes, we achieve optimal decoding performance that closely approaches the theoretical maximum, as evidenced by our experiments using AGP simulator. We introduce a novel time-scale that exceeds the standard quantum Cram\'er-Rao bound in metrology experiments. Our approach, dubbed 'quantum jump metrology', utilizes the detection of individual quantum jumps (collapses of excited states to ground state) in a sequence of measurements. These jumps can occur from a variety of systems, including optical and superconducting devices, making this method experimentally accessible. Notably, the quantum jump method allows for the exploitation of all available information in a measurement sequence, thereby enabling more precise estimation of a parameter on a larger time-scale. Notably, the quantum jump method outperforms traditional methods on time-scales that are significantly larger than the Heisenberg uncertainty limit. Notably, the quantum jump method also enables the accurate tracking of changing systems, including those that switch rapidly between different states. We demonstrate the general applicability of our method by applying it to the estimation of a variety of parameters, including the linewidth of light emitted by a driven two-level system, the context of laser cooling and the detection of hidden aspects of a quantum state. Our approach facilitates precise estimation of these parameters on a large time-scale, exceeding the standard quantum Cram\'er-Rao bound by a factor of ten in certain instances. Furthermore, the quantum jump method can be utilized in a variety of contexts, including the analysis of data that is not symmetric with respect to past and future time. Not only do hadron yields from heavy ion collisions rely on the characteristics of the medium created, but also on the details of quark and gluon dynamics. To investigate this dependency, the study examines inter-qubit interactions in spinorial qubit systems representing non-relativistic quark states across a broad momentum spectrum. The research utilizes simulated spinorial qubit networks to compute the interaction strengths and their distribution, demonstrating a direct relationship between the momentum distribution of the bound quark and the yield of inter-qubit interactions. As a result, the study finds that hadron yields in Au+Au collisions decrease substantially with increasing momentum shared by the quark, accounting for roughly half of the observed suppression in such collisions when the quark's momentum is roughly 1 GeV. Furthermore, the study discovers that the qubit network's self-organizing critical behavior produces a significant and regular contribution to the yield that correlates with the critical exponent of the system. Consequently, the study predicts that this regular contribution will increase in experiments with larger nuclear projectiles and will remain significant even after factoring in the effects of quark dynamics. In this research, we propose a digital-analog quantum computing solution to efficiently simulate complex many-body systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model. By integrating digital and analog quantum computing methods, our approach leverages the strengths of both paradigms while minimizing their typical drawbacks. As a nearly universal quantum simulator, digital-analog computing has the ability to mimic a wide range of physical systems while also allowing for the simulation of interactions between up to 106 quantum sites with precise accuracy. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that for models exhibiting phase separation or featuring complex spin structures, analog components can be integrated into digital quantum computers through a systematic protocol, thereby enabling quantum simulations with enhanced precision and extended scope. An example simulation of a small Hubbard model on 2D lattices is also executed on IBM's digital quantum simulator to verify its effectiveness in potential practical applications. These experiments confirm that our proposed method can efficiently emulate complex many-body systems, potentially leading to significant advancements in physics research and the development of practical applications. Lastly, the results from these experiments are anticipated to contribute to the creation of meaningful real-world applications utilizing digital-analog quantum computing for the simulation of quantum systems.

Deep learning models often necessitate an abundance of data and computational resources, rendering them inaccessible to users with limited storage capacity or slow processors. Our new algorithm addresses these issues by utilizing tokenized training data to generate customized feature sets, which can also be applied to tokenized testing data. Our method comprises two main components: a Bonsai algorithm that derives these feature sets from multiple tokenized training datasets, and a Fine-grained algorithm that adjusts the complexity of the Bonsai algorithm's linear models. Our new algorithm excels in two scenarios: when training data exceeds the available storage capacity or when the testing data tokenization differs from the training data. On standard NLP benchmarks such as IMDB, it improved Bonsai's accuracy by 1.0% and outperformed Bonsai and Bonsai+Fine-grained on 12 out of 14 NLP tasks with adjusted evaluation metrics. Furthermore, our algorithm displayed results comparable to those of Bonsai on 2 tasks. Our new algorithm achieved success in 7 out of 14 tasks where Bonsai did not. Also, our algorithm obtained results superior to Bonsai+Fine-grbert on 5 tasks where Bonsai+Fine-grbert did not. Our method exemplifies how Bonsai algorithms can be enhanced to address additional complications. Our work has far-reaching implications for developing advanced computational imaging technologies. When using policy learning to solve complex decision-making problems, the quality of returned samples can be unpredictable, leading researchers to resort to estimating the value of these samples in order to develop an optimal policy. Despite the effectiveness of these value estimates in guiding sample-efficient policy development, the calculation of their statistical significance is a relatively understudied area of research. In order to properly determine the significance of these estimates, researchers must control the family-wise error rate (FWER), which, using traditional testing methods, results in computationally expensive operations on large datasets. In order to overcome these computational limitations, researchers have not extensively studied how to employ resampling-based tests to evaluate value function estimates due to their predicted inability to control the FWER. In this research, we examine the performance of eight distinct testing sizes in order to determine how they impact the efficacy of our value function estimates in policy development. Our results indicate that larger testing sizes actually enhance the quality of our estimates rather than degrade it. In light of this information, we have developed a novel method for computing significant value function estimates that takes into account the specific testing size employed. This method's broad applicability means it can be applied to a wide range of existing value estimate algorithms, making it a useful resource for researchers and practitioners. Furthermore, our work has shown that the application of our method results in superior policy performance when compared to traditional approaches. This study investigates the characteristics of monolithic small collection-electrode CMOS sensors with thin, high-resistivity layers under particle irradiation. The study utilizes a dual-infrared setup to examine the properties of charge collection in these sensors. Charge collection in these sensors depends on the thickness of the high-resistivity layer, implant details, and the characteristics of the CMOS technology used. For example, breaking through the thin layer due to particle irradiation significantly affects the signal magnitude. Although the damage from breaking through limits the signal magnitude, it does not substantially impact the signal time delay. This distinction is crucial for quantifying the depth of the interaction point in detectors and is particularly relevant for medical imaging applications. In addition, the study examines the conceptual design of a compact, high-resolution gamma-ray imager using such detectors in a slot-scanning scheme inspired by Cherenkov light generation. Finally, the study assesses the feasibility of using such detectors in a Cherenkov light detection system due to their potential application in time-of-flight PET systems, primarily because of the inherent electronic noise and associated limitations in the signal magnitude. However, further research is necessary to overcome these limitations and achieve the desired level of performance for such a system. Additionally, the study assesses the potential of utilizing such a system in a dual role, both as a time-of-flight PET scanner and as a gamma-ray imager for various applications. In summary, the study evaluates the properties of monolithic small collection-electrode CMOS sensors under particle irradiation, explores their application as a building block in a compact, high-resolution gamma-ray imager, and examines the feasibility of utilizing such a system in a time-of-flight PET system. In a conceptual design for such a system, the study demonstrates the inherent difficulties that arise from the sensor properties and the significant challenges that need to be addressed to achieve the desired level of performance for such a system. In addition, the study discusses various aspects and implications of utilizing such a system in a dual role, both as a time-of-flight PET scanner and as a gamma-ray imager. Lastly, the study reflects on the potential of utilizing such a system in multiple applications and the potential for such a system to contribute to various scientific research and medical imaging applications. The goal of achieving high-contrast imaging in ground-based systems for exoplanet detection is crucial for successful exoplanet discovery and characterization. Traditional algorithms, including Ang\'ario's experiment, have shown some success, but detection probabilities and success rates vary widely depending on specific conditions and systems. Ang\'ario's experiment involved post-processing data from a system that employs a Shack-Hamilton adapter on the Magellan telescope, resulting in remarkable 80% success rate at a contrast of 10^4 on a 2 arcsecond field. However, this algorithm may be considered simple by some researchers. Building upon this foundation, a new algorithm known as BNSP is introduced, which represents a more sophisticated approach to detecting exoplanets through a process of analytic derotation, dephasing, and stabilization of the data. During testing on observable datasets, BNSP achieved an impressive 90% success rate at a contrast of 10^4 on a 2 arcsecond field. Furthermore, BNSP's effectiveness was proven to be less sensitive to telescope dynamics, requiring only minimal adjustments to be made to the system it operates within. As a result of these findings, it is anticipated that BNSP will significantly enhance the detection capabilities of current ground-based systems while paving the way for successful exoplanet discovery and characterization in future instruments like the Magellan-ESO Giant Area Telescope. We examine the constraints of the Hayden-Preskill conjecture through quantum field theories in a range of spacetime regions. The boundary of a region in these theories is characterized by the number of particles at its boundary, which indicates whether information is retained within the region. Our investigations focus on the number of particles at the event horizon of a black hole and upon its singularity for cases without and with matter, respectively. For none of these scenarios, including those involving thermofield double states, does the particle number consistently adhere to the requirements of the Hayden-Preskill conjecture. Moreover, the constraints of this conjecture seem to be satisfied more readily in theories where the number of particles is not sharply defined. Our results also suggest that the notion of particle number is inherently inextricably linked to the processes of particle creation and destruction. Lastly, our work explores the concept of particle number definition and its potential loss of relevance during the processes of black hole evaporation. Conversely, our findings indicate that the number of particles is largely an artifact of the choice of a quantum field theory and its associated boundary, rather than an inherently physical quantity. Therefore, this concept may not be suitable for explaining physical phenomena such as the information paradox. We further extend the applications of our study to models involving steaming black holes and double black holes. Our results show that the information paradox persists across these different scenarios. Our work also examines the analogies of the information paradox in cosmological models. The scattering cross sections for quarks and antiquarks off nucleons in various models differ significantly, especially at small momentum transfers. As a result, the prediction of nuclear broadening varies substantially among these models. In this study, we examine electromagnetic productions of Drell-Yan pairs in relativistic heavy-ion collisions to determine the impact of distinct dipole models. Our analysis indicates that nuclear broadening can be quantified through a systematic measurement of the $q^2$-dependent transverse width of the Drell-Yan peak. Since nuclear broadening directly correlates with the diffusion length of partons within the nucleon, a detailed investigation of $q^2$-dependence is required to make maximal use of the information gained from the heavy-ion collisions at various energies. Moreover, we propose that nuclear broadening be studied in the context of $J/\psi$ and $\Upsilon$ productions at different energies, as the influence of distinct dipole models is most pronounced at low $q^2$. Ultimately, our work underscores the necessity of precisely measuring the $q^2$-dependent transverse width of the Drell-Yan peak to make a decisive comparison among the dipole models. Moreover, our study highlights the potential of $J/\psi$ and $\Upsilon$ productions at various energies to distinguish between the saturation and kinetic spin models of dipole scattering. Finally, our work raises the possibility that nuclear broadening could be effectively studied in the context of $W$/$\bar W$ productions at LHC energies, as the broad $q^2$-distribution at those energies would preclude a detailed examination of the $q^2$-dependence. Nonetheless, our study indicates that $WW$ production could still yield a discernible nuclear broadening effect at high energies. In this spirit, we conclude that the study of nuclear broadening effect in $WW$ production at LHC energies may serve as a useful benchmark to validate the various assumptions and phenomenological models of parton nucleon scattering. Moreover, our work suggests that a comparative study of nuclear broadening effects in $J/\psi$, $\Upsilon$, $W$, $\bar W$, $Z$, $W^c$, $\bar W^c$ productions may be effectively utilized to cover the various assumptions and phenomenological models of dipole scattering cross sections. For values of $b$ greater than 2, the solutions can be broken down into the following cases: (1) the identity $1^b = 1$, (2) the solution $(2, \infty)$ when $b$ is an even number, and (3) the relatively prime solution set $(\phi(m), m)$. This paper further examines these non-trivial solutions in the prime case for $b$, and proposes a new criterion to filter the possible values of $b$. The paper also re-evaluates Diophantine equations of the form $a^b - 1 = c^b - 1$, which leads to $(a-1)^b = (c-1)^b $, and identifies the specific cases of $b = 3$ and $4$ as well as the particular case of $(a,c) = (2,3)$ as the only valid solutions. The study of a liquid jet flowing through a channel of smaller width than itself is relevant to various applications, including medical treatments, manufacturing processes, and astrological phenomena.  It's known that the presence of air in the water jet leads to more complex dynamics, particularly in scenarios where the liquid flows at velocities lower than a certain critical value.  In this study, we examine those situations where the liquid jet encounters a channel that is even narrower, which often results in the air being squeezed out in a manner that significantly alters the dynamic behavior.  Through the use of high-speed imaging, we investigate these outcomes and demonstrate that the resulting motions can be effectively explained by considering the collective movement of the air and water.  A newly developed analysis technique, referred to as the Maximum Curvature Length (MCL), allows us to analyze and characterize the entire range of possible curvatures assumed by the air-water interface.  Ultimately, our research focuses on understanding how the air is initially incorporated into the water jet, which often loses its original centerline flow characteristic due to the imposed constraints.  In this study, we not only document such dynamics but also make a key discovery about the most likely shape of the air-water interface through statistical evaluation of the MCL data.  In doing so, we show that the primary factor governing the curvatures observed in the air-water interface is the ratio of the water flow velocity to a critical value, rather than other factors such as the presence of Reynolds stress.  This study, which is based on over 20,000 individual measurements, suggests a distinct peak in the most likely curvature distribution at around 40 times the velocity-dependent unit.  A recently developed theory suggests a close connection between this interface shape and the hydrodynamic forces it generates, which in turn influences the flow characteristic of the air-water interface.  A key verification of this proposed relationship comes from observing the characteristic span lengths of the air-water helical modes, which often prevail in scenarios further away from the initial centerline flow.  In doing so, we show that the interface shapes reconstructed from the MCL data allow us to accurately explain the observed span lengths as a function of the Reynolds number, which often indicates a generally widening pattern in the air-water interface as it approaches a critical velocity crossover point.  A key uncertainty remaining in this study's understanding of such dynamics involves identifying the precise role played by surface tension in governing the air-water interface shapes, which often become more pronounced at slower water flow velocities and further away from the initial centerline flow.

NVM technology holds great promise for creating application-level memory services that ensure data consistency, taking full advantage of the low-latency, persistent characteristics of NVM. To achieve this, we propose introducing specialisation for consistency management, allowing developers to define customisation algorithms to maintain consistency at the application level. By incorporating these algorithms into the memory service, consistency is maintained across all nodes within an NVM-based cluster. Our proposal involves introducing base types capable of inducing specialisation and developing a consistency management framework, which can effectively handle the inherent concurrency and fault-tolerant considerations of multi-threaded environments. Finally, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through six real-world examples, showcasing the benefits of using specialisation to maintain consistency in application-level data stored in NVM. The output of these examples serves as a foundation for creating a comprehensive consistency management library. Overall, our consistency management framework, when combined with the consistency management library, enables the development of innovative, consistent memory services that support persistent, low-latency data access across distributed systems. The consistency management library is currently available on GitHub at https://github.com/fzq200qo/consistency_nvm_lib. In the context of Inference on Information Networks (I2N), researchers can draw conclusions about a network's properties by analyzing a single observation. This is relevant to networks such as social media, Twitter, and transportation systems.  We introduce the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM) for analyzing I2N, which incorporates a hierarchical model for graph edges and a latent Dirichlet-Alberta model for vertex attributes.  By treating a network as a collection of documents, with each edge as a word occurrence, the HDTM models a network's structure and attributes simultaneously.  We derive a Bayesian estimator for the HDTM and establish its asymptotic validity, enabling the calculation of confidence intervals for network parameters.  Fitting the HDTM using Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms, we find it outperforms existing methods for I2N in a Twitter network example.  Our approach also yields novel insights into information diffusion and cliques in the network.  Finally, we outline extensions to the HDTM for addressing more complex I2N scenarios.  These theoretical contributions have important practical implications for understanding and making inferences about large information networks.  We also introduce a companion R package, rHDTM, which facilitates the implementation of the HDTM for various I2N settings.  Key features of the package include inference tools and visualizations for clarifying the structure and parameters of a network.  Through extensive usage testing and case studies, we show the effectiveness of rHDTM in analyzing real-world network data, as demonstrated by its capability to reveal the organization of a transportation system network by George Bernard Shaw as quoted in "The Invisible Man" and a network of scientific publications, ultimately shedding new light on both phenomena.  Lastly, we speculate on the potential for the HDTM to reveal additional significant correlations in large networks in the future.

The LHCb collaboration has investigated suppressions of prompt $\psi(2S)$ and prompt D-meson states in relation to prompt J/$\psi$ mesons for various transverse momentum ranges, specifically above 2, 5, and 8 GeV/$c$ using a combined data set of proton-proton collisions at 7 and 13 TeV. The study revealed that prompt $\psi(2S)$ mesons exhibit a greater suppression than prompt J/$\psi$ mesons in each of the examined transverse momentum ranges. Furthermore, the observed suppressions of both prompt $\psi(2S)$ and prompt J/$\psi$ mesons were found to be consistent with theoretical predictions based on charm-quark scattering on nuclear matter at 7 TeV. However, the data collected at 13 TeV resulted in the detection of increased $\psi(2S)$ and J/$\psi$ yields relative to predictions, indicating the influence of a potential short-range effect. When considering the ratio of $\psi(2S)$ to J/$\psi$ yields, it became evident that the measured values are in agreement with theoretical expectations, putting constraints on models of nucleon-$\psi(2S)$ scattering at 13 TeV. In addition, the study determined the relative contributions of direct production and feeddown from bottom-hadron decays to the formation of prompt $\psi(2S)$ and prompt J/$\psi$ mesons. Specifically, it was found that direct production accounts for approximately 60\% of prompt $\psi(2S)$ creation and 70\% of prompt J/$\psi$ creation. Finally, the study examined the influence of freeze-out conditions on the formation of prompt $\psi(2S)$ and prompt J/$\psi$ mesons and revealed that their formation occurs at the early stages of proton-proton collisions, specifically within the initial nanoseconds. Furthermore, the study revealed the presence of charm quarks before nucleon-$\psi(2S)$ and nucleon-J/$\psi$ formation, indicating a greater influence of nuclear effects on the former. The findings from freeze-out conditions analysis were found to be consistent with those from suppression analyses. In conclusion, the study presents the most comprehensive understanding to date of prompt $\psi(2S)$ and prompt J/$\psi$ production in proton-proton collisions, offering valuable insights into the distinct formation processes of these particles. The study sets the stage for future research with heavier nuclei, presenting novel opportunities

We investigate the equivalence relations derived from automorphism groups of models in continuous logic, and demonstrate that for any complete metric space, the relation of being an equivalence class is itself a complete metric space. Furthermore, the theorem that connects first-order and model theory holds in the context of continuous logic. Additionally, the proof of the Tarski Sperner theorem can be adapted to the setting of continuous logic. A key component of the proof is a construction analogous to the Hilbert cube, but tailored to the setting of continuous logic. This paper presents an approach to detect modifications in modifications within a group of similar software systems by utilizing the singular value decomposition. Our innovative method transforms the diffusion of modifications across these software systems into a lower-dimensional space, where we calculate the principal components of variations. By doing so, we can identify changes and their impact on the overall system, pinpointing key modifications and their effects on the system-wide level. This study showcases our approach by analyzing over 58 distinct changes in 15 open-source Java projects, covering modifications of various types and frequencies. Our analysis highlights the potential of our method to effectively detect frequent and infrequent modifications, as well as those affecting a small number of files. Moreover, we have developed an open-source tool to support our approach, which can be freely utilized by the community. Ultimately, this study's findings can benefit researchers and developers working in the area of software evolution, supporting complex queries regarding software modifications and their propagation. Additionally, this tool's availability can facilitate this research's replication and promotion within the community. Deep sequential models leverage recurrent neural networks to analyze time-series data, which has been widely employed in input representation, feature extraction, and forecasting areas. Nonetheless, the traditional RNN architecture's update mechanism operates on the basis of all previous inputs for the current time step, resulting in an overload of irrelevant information for extended sequences. To address this limitation, the use of attention techniques, which enable focused past information consideration for each sequence time step, has been explored. The objective of this study is to extend the application of the attention mechanism to multivariate time-series data, which often include multiple signal channels for sensor data and forecasting tasks. The proposed CoRRN, an extension of the RNN with mutual attention between the sequence and individual channel inputs, demonstrates improved performance on diverse benchmark datasets when compared to conventional RNN and LSTM models. Moreover, the coherence of the CoRRN model's internal representation is visually validated through the use of t-SNE. The study further examines, using various analyses, the rationale behind the proposed method's success. To our knowledge, this research is the first to apply the attention mechanism to multivariate time-series data within the deep learning context. The effectiveness of the proposed model is verified through multiple performance metrics and code is made accessible for others to replicate the results. Finally, the effect of sparsity induced by zeroing out attention weights on the performance of deep sequential models is explored. The obtained outcomes reveal that, through effective pruning, a significantly compressed yet precise model can be derived from the original model. The derived model's improved fertility with respect to parameters is also discussed. The method proposed in this research may be extended to other sequential models like CNN, which works on the basis of local relevance capture mechanisms, and attention-based graph neural networks, which incorporates spatial relationships between different nodes. To our knowledge, this study is the first to apply the attention mechanism to multivariate time-series data within the deep learning context, and the obtained outcomes show that attention-based models achieve improved performance on diverse benchmark datasets when compared to conventional RNN and LSTM models. This led us to notice a 17 degree angle between the X-ray polarization direction and the radio-based magnetic field orientation. We explored various possible explanations for this discrepancy, including the geometry of the shock wave and the distribution of magnetic field and ray length within the jet. It is also worth noting that a model including both jet and spherical components may provide a more comprehensive understanding of the emission. We found that the X-ray emission comes primarily from a region where the jet interacts with the surrounding medium in the north-eastern direction. This region shows a clear curved shape consistent with the distribution of magnetic field and ray length. Moreover, we calculated the energy distribution of the Jotting electron size, which is concentrated in the 10-30 GeV range and estimated a total energy output of approximately 1.5*10^50 erg/s. We compared the X-ray emission to the gamma-ray emission observed by Fermi. Both emissions exhibit a similar structure but the X-ray polarization strength shows a clear decline in the northern and eastern directions. This is in contrast to the gamma-ray emission observed, which displays a significant increase in the northern and eastern areas. We attempted to model X-ray emission using two different methods: the "jet" model and the "disk" model. In the jet model, we demonstrated that a combination of two different energy distributions of electrons can account for both the X-ray and gamma-ray emissions observed. Additionally, we found that a flat energy distribution in a specific range can generate the observed curvature seen in X-ray images. On the other hand, the "disk" model failed to provide a comprehensive fit to the data observed. In conclusion, based on our findings, we favor the "jet" model as the more suitable explanation for the data observed. Additionally, a "spherical component" may be required to account for the data observed in the southern and western areas. We found that a much weaker magnetic field strength of approximately 0.3 microgauss can generate both the X-ray and gamma-ray emissions observed. Yet, our investigation reveals that if we relax this finding by allowing subset sums to have repetitions, a more moderate bound can be established. Specifically, when subsets are at least a fraction of the total number of elements in size, a repetition-free outcome becomes achievable, provided that the base is sufficiently large. Moreover, this conclusion extends to various functions beyond simple counting. Furthermore, this result can translate to other setting, such as independent random variables, where similar outcomes can be observed. In the context of quark stars, the existence of a deconfinement phase transition has a significant impact on the mass and radius of these stars. The phase transition's properties in dense nuclear and quark matter play a crucial role in determining the mass and radius of the quark star. Assuming a bag model for the quark phase with a constant bag parameter and neglecting cold dense relativistic nuclear matter's complexities, researchers have found a critical value for the bag parameter that results in the mass and radius of quark stars having specific upper limits. If the interaction in the quark phase is more gruop-like, the maximum mass of quark stars can reach two solar masses, leading to an alternative explanation for the observed glut of low-mass quark star candidates. Furthermore, the presence of a deconfinement phase transition influences the electromagnetic emission of quark stars in terms of their thermal properties. In a comparative study, the thermal characteristics, surface temperature, and radius of quark stars composed of neutron star material and nuclear and quark matter with a bag parameter greater than zero were examined. The analysis shows that quark stars with a bag parameter greater than a specific critical value exhibit distinct thermal properties, surface temperatures, and radii compared to neutron stars. The compass state, an Unsourced Quantum Mutual Information measure, is used to assess the correlation between non-orthogonal pure states in multidimensional quantum systems. Recently, its ability to efficiently estimate non-markovian dynamics in complex networks has been explored. Here, we investigate the compass state's ability to accurately determine the parameters influencing a non-markovian dynamics model. Our results indicate that the variance of the compass state changes with the model's parameters, resulting in optimal precision for the lowest variance instances. Furthermore, we discover that the compass state's accuracy in damping parameter estimation improves as the quantum Fisher information increases, albeit at the expense of the compass state's variance. Through both analytical and numerical assessments, we determine the compass state's variance to be lower than that of the quantum Fisher information-based estimator, revealing its potential in metrological applications to strike a balance between precision and variance. Ultimately, we identify key future research areas for the compass state, encompassing its exploration in scenario-specific dynamics models and its adaptation for use in quantum sensing techniques. This work introduces a novel approach to categorize and characterize liquid jet
arrays based on their geometric configurations. Different jet geometries are linked
to variations in the breakup dynamics of the jets, influencing their mass
dissipation patterns, and thereby affecting the droplet size distribution,
velocity, and shape of the droplets formed. A hierarchical classification of
jet configurations begins with the classification of individual jets, then combines
these classifications for complex jet arrays, using a unique relationship between
mass transport and breakup dynamics to identify distinct geometries. The method
is demonstrated with confidence intervals of droplet size, using numerical simulations
of break-up processes. Additionally, this study examines the extent to which
neighborhood relationships among classified jets emerge as a significant factor. 
Ultimately, this research provides a foundational framework for categorizing liquid
jet geometries and encourages further exploration of this classification system. 
Additionally, this study shows that the methodology can be applied to multi-
dimensional jet arrays, highlighting its broad applicability and potential for
future expansion to even more intricate arrangements of jets.

A common model used to study this process uses the concept of surface metabolism, which involves reaction rates being balanced by the flux of chemical species. In this context, viral movement can be viewed as a diffusion process, where the equilibrium state can be represented by the Wigner distribution. The frequency of viral collisions is directly proportional to the Wigner distribution, while the viral adherence rate is represented by a negative drift term. The solution to this process yields an exponential decay in viral mobility, resulting in a power-law relationship between viral mobility and time. A similar approach can be applied to understand the mechanics behind viral rolling on host cells by using a combination of stochastic dynamics and continuum models. These stochastic dynamics, in turn, can be used to investigate the effects of viral movement on infection rates, with the understanding that viral rolling may not always be the rate-determining step in the viral infection process. Furthermore, the model can also be utilized to study the effects of environmental factors such as temperature on viral infection rates, with temperature being represented by a stability parameter in the model. The effects of viral aggregation on infection rates can also be explored by incorporating a mass transfer coefficient in the model. The proposed model is highly versatile and can be applied to understand both viral movement and aggregation by adjusting the frequency of viral collisions and the flux of viral species. Consequently, the model can be utilized to predict trends in viral infection and to interpret experimental data on viral movement and aggregation. Researchers have identified two distinct varieties of warped galaxy morphologies: "S-type" galaxies with narrow warps and "U-type" galaxies featuring broader warps. To simulate and investigate the impact of environmental factors on these warped galaxies, our study leverages the VLA-COSMOS-3D survey's U-type galaxy sample and introduces an new semi-analytical model, WARP. This model accounts for galaxy-galaxy tidal interactions and encounters with their surroundings, representing the most significant environmental influence on galaxies. Our simulation reveals that S-type and U-type galaxies develop through different environmental mechanisms: whereas S-types are primarily formed through gentle interactions and rotations, U-types are shaped by more forceful interactions and larger galaxies encompassing smaller warped galaxies. Our model effectively replicates observed galaxy ratios and accurately predicts predicted ratios if S-type and U-type galaxies are distinguished by their central surface brightness. Furthermore, our simulation indicates that U-type galaxies are found closer to galaxy clusters and encounter more close approaches with neighbors, leading to higher rates of tidal deformation. To better comprehend warped galaxy morphologies, our study suggests combining precise dynamical models with observations of gas distributions, star formations, and populations, as well as further examination of warped galaxy spins and their alignment with the galaxy's major axis. Our model also shows potential in researching numerous other complex galaxy phenomena. Lastly, our study underscores the significance of observing the full depth of galaxies and understanding their full three-dimensional extent in capturing accurate representations of warped galaxy morphologies. Our model is prepared for public use at https://warp-astro.gitub.io. Additionally, VLA-COSMOS-3D data and software are available at https://vizier.u-nice.fr/COSMOS/. This study examines the growth of harmonic functions on a complete manifold that supports a gradient-shrinking Ricci soliton. We establish a condition for harmonic functions based on their dimensionality and the exponent of growth. We also investigate the implications of this condition and explore connections with other existing criteria. Moreover, we derive criteria for the manifold to be either conformally flat or isometrically split. Additionally, we analyze the properties of the manifold under the assumption that the growth of harmonic functions is optimal. Furthermore, we discuss relationships between the growth of harmonic functions and other invariants such as the spectral radius of the Laplacian and the Euler characteristic. Finally, we compute the growth of harmonic functions for specific manifolds, including those with special structural features like constant scalar curvature and vanishing Ricci curvature. In the process, we identify a new type of manifolds with unique properties, which we term "harmonic Stepanov manifolds." Specifically, we find that harmonic Stepanov manifolds are characterized by a constant sign of the Ricci curvature and a limit on the frequency of bounded harmonic functions. Interestingly, we discover that harmonic Stepanov manifolds can be either positively curved or negatively curved. To conclude, we summarize our key findings and outline potential avenues for further research. Ultimately, we hope this study offers a thorough and organized survey of the current knowledge on the subject, as well as new and significant insights into the growth of harmonic functions on gradient-shrinking Ricci solitons. In particular, we leverage the diversity of harmonic Stepanov manifolds to illustrate the significance and admissibility of the growth condition for harmonic functions. In addition, our work provides metric-tensor invariants of the growth condition, thereby bridging the gap between function-theoretic and geometric criteria. In essence, our study serves as a comprehensive guide to the current understanding of the subject, while also yielding innovative and important results. Our studies focus on how atomic arrangements within the (Bi$_{4}$) block affect the electronic structure, and how doping at the block boundary can generate new superconducting states with elevated symmetry by mixing the properties of the individual atomic sublattices. Furthermore, we examine the phase transitions and the origin of superconductivity in RbCsBi$_{4}$, and our results demonstrate that the valence bands in this compound are composed of the hybridized 6$s$ and 7$p$ orbitals of the block atoms. Our DFT+U calculations with certain values of the Coulomb interaction reveal that the (Bi$_{4}$) block displays $\pi$-bonding, and the electronic structure of the block exhibits a notable gap at the Fermi level. The impact of electron-electron interaction on the dynamic dipole polarization is examined in metals and insulators using time-dependent density functional theory, with results indicating significant non-adiabatic components in the polarization response for both systems, contrary to adabatic assumptions commonly applied in finite-temperature cases. In clean metals, the Born effective charge shows insulator-like behavior, whereas in insulators, it exhibits metal-like characteristics. Our findings suggest that non-adiabatic contributions from exchange-correlation interactions are substantial and should be considered in the calculation of Bonn effective charges via time-dependent density functional perturbation theory. We demonstrate that the exchange-correlation Bonn effective charge can be adequately described by the frequency-dependent exchange-correlation component of the polarization vertex, emphasizing its crucial importance in the understanding of Bonn effective charges. Our study provides a comprehensive framework for determining dynamic properties of systems lacking a restoring force, such as Bonn effective charges, through TDDFT, incorporating all exchange-correlation effects. Furthermore, our computational code allows for seamless integration with existing plane wave based codes, yielding significant computational efficiencies. We illustrate this through a case study on hexagonal boron nitride, where our predictions align with experimental findings, thereby validating our computational framework with a strong relevance to real-world applications. Lastly, our model is conducive to both online and offline analysis, as demonstrated through a subsequent analysis of phonon spectra of the same hexagonal system using this TDDPF framework. This proves to be particularly useful for systems lacking a restoring force, as highlighted through an evaluation of Bonn effective charges of charge carriers in hexagonal boron nitride. Our computational density functional model provides a reliable, yet computationally efficient solution for the study of dynamic properties of systems through a combination of factors, including online efficiency, domain decomposition methods, and the incorporation of a predefined exchange-correlation potential. We anticipate our to be a useful tool for researchers in the field of materials science for studying a broad spectrum of systems. Additionally, our results provide a crucial insight into the understanding of dynamic properties of systems, as derived from first principles, as applied to hexagonal boron nitride in a comprehensive manner. This provides a strong foundation for future applications of our computational code to a wide range of systems. In conclusion, our study indicates the significance of non-adiabatic effects for both metals and insulators, as calculated through TDDFT, where these effects are largely dominated by the exchange-correlation contribution, as illustrated through a case study of hexagonal boron nitride. The fluctuating Navier-Stokes equation, an application of the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation, is examined through direct numerical simulations in turbulent flow scenarios. This is done by superimposing random forces onto the Navier-Stokes equations, thereby incorporating thermal fluctuations for the purpose of simulating turbulent dissipation without employing dissipation terms. However, it was discovered that the fluctuating Navier-Stokes equation yields results differing from its Navier-Stokes counterpart in terms of the occurrence of certain events, namely large-scale vortex formations. Non-parametric techniques are employed to test the random nature of these occurrences and an estimation method is used to quantify the associated probability measures. Moreover, an information-theoretic quantity, known as mutual information, is computed between various pairs of equilibrium correlations to obtain insights into the interdependencies between turbulent flow characteristics and their respective statistical properties. Ultimately, it is found that the properties derived from the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation, an higher-order theory, are in agreement with those of the standard hydrodetic model of turbulent flow. Conversely, the dissipation-velocity spectral slope, a key indicator of turbulent regime, was found to significantly differ between the fluctuating Navier-Stokes equation and the standard model for the entire range of investigated integral scales. Consequently, this presents an inconsistency in understanding the nature of turbulent dissipation. As a complementary approach to mitigate this discrepancy, the dissipation-velocity spectral slope is analyzed under scenarios of locally locally parallel turbulence, where it was found to match the standard model indicators across all scales for moderate to high integral scales. Nonetheless, the impact of thermal fluctuations remains prominent at these scales for this specific property. Lastly, an instrumental variable technique, an innovative approach to analyze nonlinear relationships, was employed to investigate the occurrence of large-scale vortex formations in turbulent flow scenarios. This technique allows for the detection of significant interdependencies between certain indicators of turbulent flow characteristics and their respective statistical properties. Similarly, mutual information was computed between pairs of indicators of turbulent dissipation and velocity, where it was discovered that thermal fluctuations significantly affect the statistical dependence relationships between these properties at all scales for both locally parallel and locally perpendicular turbulence scenarios. Ultimately, this presents significant insights into the nature of turbulent regime as described by the fluctuating Navier-Stokes equation, an application of the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation. This research contributes to our current understanding of turbulent regime by introducing novel methods for analyzing nonlinear relationships and information-theoretic quantities, where thermal fluctuations significantly impact the statistical nature of indicators of turbulent dissipation and velocity.

We investigate delayed nonlinearity systems described by differential equations with spatial variables and multiple integrated delays, which are anticipated to exhibit complex characteristics similar to real-world systems experiencing diffusive influences. We introduce arbitrary initial conditions to analyze these systems, which are mapped into infinite attractors. We then examine a significant phenomenon where increasing diffusion strengthens the effects of delay and nonlinearity, ultimately reducing the system's effective dimensionality and inducing an ultimate convergence to a steady equilibrium. In this research, we focus on a delayed version of the Lorenz system, which we determine to be globally asymptotically stable under certain conditions, including a specific maximum value for diffusion and delay parameters. We also explore the applications of delay coordination techniques to minimize these parameters' negative impacts on the system's behavior and performance. Lastly, we provide comprehensive estimates for the system's attractor size and locate its critical transition points, which are heavily influenced by interaction and nonlinearity. We fulfill this research's goal of completely understanding the properties and behavior of delayed nonlinearity systems and developing practical methods to manage their complex characteristics. We apply these findings to the delayed version of the SWIP2 ODE system, which we determine to be globally asymptotically stable under similar conditions, and demonstrate how these results can be extended to a broad class of delayed nonlinearity systems through the use of certain inequalities and inclusions. To facilitate the analysis, we reduces the highly complex and varied types of delayed nonlinearity systems into three fundamental examples, which are then thoroughly examined and their critical properties and modes of behavior are accurately predicted. We conclude this research by discussing its key findings, which can be applied to a broad class of nonlinear delay rate-dependent systems, and suggesting potential areas for further research in this field. This note presents a denotational interpretation of probabilistic programming languages with higher-order functions, based on Scott domains, to provide a clear understanding of probabilistic meaning. In contrast to operational definitions, which focus on generating random outputs, denotational semantics views a probabilistic program as a random entity. We adapt existing concepts in denotational semantics to model probability, utilizing partial orders and computable functions. Our approach incorporates a framework for measuring entities, similar to classical denotational semantics. However, the addition of measures necessitates a distinct methodology. We introduce a novel way to deal with a measure-separating pair, leveraging a random entity's properties to define both its probability and value. Our method of assigning a probability distribution to entities addresses concerns about the axiomatic uniqueness of such distributions. We demonstrate that our framework can be applied to a range of programming languages, including those with unbounded recursive functions. A corresponding operational interpretation, supporting stack-based program inductive definitions, confirms the equivalence of denotational and operational meanings. The operational interpretation shows that a probabilistic program computes a probability distribution over possible outputs, which can be utilized to define a probabilistic type system enforcing pre- and postconditions on random entities. As an example, we introduce a type of random natural number, for which we define a precondition specifying a maximum expected value. This type system can automatically verify the probabilities of outputting non-negative integers when given a program parameter. We illustrate the versatility of our approach by applying it both to a partial evaluation technique mitigating measure-related issues and to an operational interpretation of higher-order probabilistic programs, including those employing continuations and general reference types. For the partial evaluation technique, we define a probabilistic version of a computable function, which must be compatible with expectation. We demonstrate the existence of such functions, which can be used to simplify and extend existing results from the field of constructive measure theory. The concept of future holographic dark energy is explored, where the universe's apparent dark energy is actually radiant energy from a distant, hidden universe. This is developed into a viable cosmological model, where two key cosmological constants emerge as essential factors. Notably, for certain parameter settings, this model predicts a universe with negative pressure dark energy, reminiscent of Einstein's original dark energy concept. Furthermore, this model predicts that our universe will eventually undergo a transition to de Sitter, where the difference between the co-moving radius of the universe and the distance to the horizon signifies a transition to a holographic universe with zero radiant energy output. A comparative analysis of this model's predictions against those from the Lambda-CDM model demonstrates that both models are in agreement on numerous fundamental points, including a Big Rip, flat universe scenario, and the onset of the holographic universe phase, where both models indicate that our universe will undergo a transition to a holographic universe with zero radiant energy output. However, there are subtle differences in their predictions for certain properties, such as the density and pressure of dark energy, its impact on the universe's matter density, and the ages of the universe at the Big Rip and transition to a holographic universe. Additionally, this model's properties and predictions are compared against those from other holographic dark energy theories, revealing distinct differences in their characteristics and forecasts, with varying implications for our understanding of the universe. Importantly, these variations and differences in theoretical properties and future predictive capabilities underscore the importance of accurately estimating the density and pressure of dark energy, which will be crucial for deciding between these holographic dark energy theories. As such, this reinforces the notion that the future holographic dark energy theory, proposing a hidden, distant universe, has potential as a viable and reliable cosmological model. This work focuses on developing a straightforward technique to identify the differentiability surfaces of a given function, along with its gradient vector field, by leveraging observations along random directions. The resulting algorithm efficiently utilizes concurrently collected data during the training process of a model via stochastic optimization. The study establishes conditions under which this set-based estimation method remains stable in the presence of adversarial functions. Furthermore, it demonstrates that introducing smoothness constraints onto the function enhances its optimization algorithm's convergence rate. The proposed technique is accompanied by an open-source implementation available on GitHub. The efficacy of this method is illustrated through experiments involving the development of a scalable, distributed version of the adaptive gradient aggregation algorithm LADOM. Moreover, this work presents empirical evidence indicating that differentiability surface estimation provides a valuable global optimization context that advances the performance of optimization algorithms. Specifically, it shows significant improvements in the time complexity and efficiency of optimizing quadratic functions and developing CNN models. Nevertheless, the study discovered that its application to optimizing large-scale logistic regression problems and developing Graph CNN models did not yield comparable enhancements. As a result, a comparative analysis of several global optimization methods is conducted to evaluate their performance on these tasks. The findings suggest that leveraging differentiability surfaces through a tailored, adaptive gradient aggregation method offers superior improvement over employing general non-constrained optimization methods. Consequently, this work contributes to the development of more efficient optimization solutions for large-scale parameter tuning tasks. Moreover, it underscores the potential for increased scalability in solving complex counterexample construction challenges. The study poses questions and suggests possible answers for its primary questions, paving the way for further research in the field. The work closes by presenting a novel framework that facilitates the development, deployment, and evaluation of optimization methods based on set-based estimation, adaptive gradient aggregation, and connected node prediction techniques. Let $R$ be a non-commutative ring. We explore square-free prime ideals in R and determine the properties of their cubes. We show that if $I$ is a prime ideal in R that is not 1-absorbing, then it is not necessary for $I^3$ to be 1-absorbing in R, providing an example to substantiate this claim. We then identify a condition under which $I^3$ can be guaranteed to be 1-absorbing in R, namely when $I$ is weakly 1-absorbing in R. Additionally, we examine the fiber product of two prime ideals and its implications for their cubes, as well as investigate similar questions for strongly $\lambda$-finite prime ideals in a strong $\lambda$-finite ring $\lambda$, presenting specific examples along the way. These findings generalize and extend previous results on strongly $\lambda$-finite prime ideals as well as our previous results on strongly finite prime ideals. We also discuss how these results apply to strongly finite and weakly finite prime ideals in a commutative ring $\mathbb{Z}$, exploring the relationship between these concepts and strong/finite/weak versions of prime ideals in $\mathbb{Z}$. Furthermore, we identify the prime ideals in a commutative ring $\mathbb{Z}$ that are strongly finite/weakly finite/1-absorbing, providing examples to substantiate this claim. We conclude by identifying criteria under which the set of strongly finite/weakly finite/1-absorbing prime ideals in $\mathbb{Z}$ is non-empty, providing specific examples to illustrate this result. These findings provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the interrelationship among these notions of prime ideals in a non-commutative ring $R$. The source of gamma-ray astrophysical signals remains largely unknown, leading to a significant challenge in navigating the complex gamma-ray data. As a response to this challenge, the Fermi Sciences Tool allows users to conduct various analyses, including a hierarchical Bayesian model that incorporates time-series dependencies to interpret counted signal data. Our method seeks to capitalize on the measured correlation between observed counts and their corresponding analysis times, exploiting this lag information to enhance astrophysical object representations and their corresponding semantic relationships. By doing so, we can streamline the semantic representation learning process, as the observed correlation already implies a level of temporal interaction. To illustrate the efficacy of this approach, we applied it to two hierarchical astrophysical object classification tasks involving supernova remnant objects and blobby active galactic nuclei, showing that incorporating correlation information successfully learns distinct classification semantics for these complex astronomical objects. Moreover, our method enables the visual interpretation of class predictions at different hierarchical levels, facilitating a more thorough comprehension of these objects. As a result, we achieved accurate semantic representations and impressive classification performance, reaching \textbf{98.75\%} and \textbf{97.5\%} cross-validation accuracies for the two respective tasks, respectively. With its ability to extract meaningful astrophysical features from observed light curves, our method contributes significantly to the astrophysical field, demonstrating how machine learning can be utilized to classify complex astronomical objects. Furthermore, our code is freely accessible on GitHub for anyone's reference or use. \href{https://github.com/ArgyriosLiberalis/Learning_Astrophysical_Features_via_Correlation}{https://github.com/ArgyriosLiberalis/Learning\_Astrophysical\_Features\_via\_Correlation}.

To correctly apply relational machine learning (RML) in pharmacology, models must first undergo validation to assure they're functioning as intended. Current evaluations of RML models rely on conventional metrics such as predictive accuracy and interpretation of model weights, but these methods have significant shortcomings, including the inability to optimize models for downstream applications and the difficulty of understanding complex model behaviors. Furthermore, existing evaluation methodologies fail to account for the complex relational structures inherent to pharmacological studies. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework for assessing the performance of RML models in pharmacology that considers the impact of relational structures and allows for calculation of action graphs depicting model behaviors. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework using pharmacological data from two distinct RML models, showcasing its capability to distinguish between robust and flawed models that produce optimal outcomes. To facilitate wider adoption of our framework, we provide accessible, web-based tools for generating action graphs and evaluating the performance of RML models based on downstream application scenarios. These resources enable the evaluation of any RML model using known datasets and models, as well as custom inputs of the user's choice. To facilitate collaboration among researchers, we also introduce PEML-AE, an online platform for sharing, archiving, and scaling RML model evaluation results. This resource serves as a comprehensive repository for evaluating the performance of RML models and pharmacological study data, thus streamlining the process for researchers and providing a supportive community. To further enhance the productivity of researchers, we outline an expanded roadmap for our evaluation framework, featuring the development of user-friendly software for generating action graphs and evaluating model distributions in high-dimensional feature spaces. Ultimately, this research aims to promote the responsible practice of RML research through informed decision-making and effective collaboration among researchers. To achieve this objective, we encourage the continuation of RML research beyond the current phase of method development and validation, instead fostering an environment of mutual engagement between researchers, application experts, and domain specialists in pharmacology. By promoting the application of RML models to real-world problems in pharmacology, we aim to accelerate progress in both the field of machine learning and pharmacology, as well as to promote more responsible practices within the former. To achieve this vision, we invite the broader research community to join us in evaluating the potential of RML models to address critical challenges in pharmacology, thus empowering positive societal transformations through machine learning. To facilitate this engagement, we provide accessible tools and resources for generating action graphs, evaluating model distributions, and contributing to peer-reviewed publications and online forums.
