The widespread adoption of smartphones has the potential to significantly improve road condition monitoring in numerous developing countries. To this end, we introduce an innovative system that employs a smartphone's built-in camera to categorize road conditions. Our method analyzes temporary images captured during the movement of a vehicle to train a nonparametric model. When combined with the vehicle's speed, this enables the classification of road conditions in real-time without necessitating manual annotation. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our system, highlighting its capacity to classify roads with a high degree of accuracy using simple models that can be readily deployed in smartphones. Moreover, our approach enables the inference of road condition labels without relying on expert annotation, thereby minimizing costs. We envision our system as a valuable tool for creating large-scale datasets, ultimately contributing to improved road condition monitoring and optimization of urban traffic systems. Additionally, our solution has the potential to be adapted into mobile apps, empowering drivers to navigate roads in developing countries more effectively. To facilitate reproducibility, we provide a comprehensive implementation of our system in a public repository: https://github.com/krishannada RoadConditions. We have also deployed a prototype app for Android devices: https://roadconditions.herokuapp.com/. Our dataset, comprising 12,000 images, is accessible at https://doi.org/10.13140/R.978.11252.05842. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate the efficient collection of road condition data through smart phone cameras, thereby enabling widespread adoption of computer vision technology in developing countries. We anticipate our approach to inspire similar applications in other areas, thereby promoting a more sustainable and environmentally conscious technology ecosystem. Finally, we acknowledge the potential risks associated with developing surveillance infrastructure, especially in regions vulnerable to human rights abuses. We urge responsible innovation by emphasizing that such initiatives should be monitored and their implications regularly assessed for any indications of abuse. If the collection of road condition data through smartphone cameras poses significant risks to citizens, then alternatives such as traditional manual traffic surveys by employed drivers should be explored. We acknowledge the inherent biases present in our approach and those similar approaches; we urge future researchers to address these biases and develop more accurate models of road condition classification. We envision our research sitting at the intersection of two significant technological trends: the widespread adoption of smartphones and the emergence of deep learning. As developers of a system rooted in these advancements, we strive to create technology that not only benefits society but also be responsible and environmentally conscious. To this end, we are open to feedback and encourage the exchange of ideas for further enhancing our road condition monitoring system

Current imitation learning methods often rely on a one-size-fits-all approach, 
merging multiple examples from diverse domains into a single unified framework.
However, this approach can be problematic, as differences between expert performances 
and agent-generated interactions may lead to learning misaligned skills, 
resulting in poor performance across multiple domains.
To address this issue, our study proposes a ground-motion simulation challenge, 
involving a complex scenario where existing imitation learning techniques fall short.
We introduce a novel method, mesh-testing, combining environment manipulation and 
metric-based analysis, to successfully transfer skills across various domain configurations.
Our approach not only surpasses state-of-the-art performance but also exposes limitations 
in current imitation learning methods, prompting potential advancements in this area.
A video demonstration of our study is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=helocYXghlo. 
Our project has been implemented on GitHub at https://github.com/argos-tu-munich/mesh-testing. 
A detailed description of our study can be found in the paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.07614. 
Communication regarding our research can be initiated through email or munihudson@gmail.com.

Research suggests that angular momentum in clouds of gas plays a crucial role in the potential fragmentation of disks that form around protostars, which is a key factor in the formation of binary and multiple star systems.  To investigate this process, we conduct a theoretical study of the effects of transport methods for angular momentum on the behavior of a model gas cloud.  Specifically, we consider the possibility of super-efficiency in a visco-elastic model, as well as the impact of radial and z-direction transport of angular momentum in a 2-dimensional disk.  Our results indicate that if angular momentum is removed from a cloud through a process like magnetic reconnection, it may not necessarily lead to the fragmentation of a disk, as the remaining angular momentum could be sufficient to support a stable protoplanet belt.  Additionally, we find that if angular momentum is circulated rather than lost, it may lead to the formation of a bar-shaped structure in a disk, which could ultimately result in the formation of a binary system due to gravitational instability in the protoplanet belt.  A future observational study aimed at detecting the shape of a protoplanet belt in a disk could provide insight into the relative importance of different angular momentum transport processes, ultimately shedding light on the potential fragmentation of disks.  Such research could also shed light on the formation processes of binary and multiple star systems.  A possible approach to conducting this study could involve using data on the temperature and density of a disk, as well as its inclination and position angle, to calculate its shape and the location of any protoplanet belts or warps that form within it.  This could be done by comparing these observational constraints to theoretical models of a visco-elastic disk that is undergoing angular momentum transport and protoplanet belt formation, much like the process described in our simulation of a 2-dimensional disk.  By doing so, we could gather a wealth of new information about the potential fragmentation of disks and the importance of angular momentum and its transport processes in the formation of binary and multiple star systems.  A study of a protoplanet belt in a disk could provide a new window into these processes, as well as how they result in the formation of star systems with multiple components.  This could be especially important in the study of systems that are thought to have formed through the process of stellar merger, such as the multiple star system that consists of HO 1426+490, to understand whether these systems can provide insight into the potential fragmentation of disks and the formation of binary and multiple star systems.

Association rules have far-reaching applications in various domains, with their coverage widely encompassing science, commerce, finance, medicine, environment, navigation, and astronomy. Existing methodologies for summarizing association rules via implications have primarily focused on covering all possible rules through a subset coverage relation, thereby failing to address the issue of redundancy among rules in a comprehensive manner. To tackle this limitation, a novel framework is introduced that defines redundancy among association rules as a subset relationship in terms of logical entailment. Furthermore, a method is proposed to identify and eliminate redundant rules efficiently, and an algorithm is developed to optimize the process. To demonstrate the effectiveness of these new approaches, two case studies are presented, one from navigation and the other from medicine. A method is introduced to utilize the optimized association rules for decision-making, and two approaches are proposed for summarizing the results in a compact form. To facilitate easy implementation, the proposed methods and new framework are incorporated into an open-source Java software package available for public use. Finally, an evaluation is conducted to assess the performance of the proposed methods using 48 datasets, including a new dataset with 2,098,816 optimized association rules. To the best of our knowledge, this is one of the largest known collection of optimized association rules to date. From the experiment's results, it is evident that the proposed methods perform substantially better than the best existing approaches in most cases, as evidenced by precision and coverage metrics. Alternatively, coverage and cardinality metrics indicate mixed performance compared to existing methods. These findings validate the proposed framework, which aims to eliminate redundancy among association rules more effectively than any previously existing approach. To facilitate reproducibility, the source code and all 48 datasets are publicly available. Furthermore, an online tool is provided to help users determine the optimal subset coverage of implications for their specific datasets. To facilitate widespread adoption, a comprehensive support system is offered, including educational materials and a Q&A forum for users to seek assistance and receive help in applying the proposed framework and software package successfully. Lastly, promising future directions are presented for further research in this domain. To foster collaboration, an open invitation is extended to researchers and practitioners to join in advancing knowledge and contributing to related efforts. Ultimately, the goal is to empower users to apply the proposed framework effectively and to showcase its utility through practical examples. To facilitate this, useful guidance and reference information are provided for users, along with free access to the software package and its associated documentation. In order to optimize a radio map measurement process, we need to collect the most relevant measurements possible. Therefore, we propose a new uncertainty metric, called the map uncertainty metric, which quantifies how much a new measurement contributes to refining the existing radio map. By utilizing this metric, we can efficiently collect measurements in a reduced dimensionality space through a selective measurement process. Consequently, this enables us to leverage the Cram\'er-Rao lower bound as a benchmark for our radio map estimation technique. Furthermore, we implement an iterative optimization method to enhance the estimated map by iteratively enhancing the model parameterized by a Gaussian process and utilizing the derived boundary as a benchmark for future optimizations. Additionally, we develop an unsupervised approach to create a Gaussian process prior for radio map estimation by treating unknown areas of the map as nodes in a Markov random field and utilizing the map uncertainty metric to collect measurements in those areas. Lastly, we introduce a new unsupervised approach to create a Gaussian process prior for radio map estimation by leveraging the Cram\'er-Rao lower bound as a benchmark for optimizations and utilizing a Markov random field to identify unknown areas of the map and prioritize measurements in those areas. We test our proposed approaches through radio map estimation simulations in various environments such as office and apartment settings. As a result, we demonstrate that our approach enables accurate radio map estimation with minimal measurements required, leading to a reduction of $88\%$ in the number of necessary measurements in an office setting and $93\%$ in an apartment setting. Moreover, we observe that our approach also facilitates efficient data collection in real-time through a selective measurement process, allowing us to refine an existing map in less than $0.1$ seconds in an office setting and less than $0.12$ seconds in an apartment setting. Consequently, we showcase the potential for our proposed approach to enable optimal and efficient radio map estimation in various settings. Detecting anomalies in unsupervised scenarios is essential due to the difficulty of obtaining labeled data. This research aims to enhance the efficiency of existing anomaly detection methods by reducing computational time and memory usage while maintaining high detection accuracy for standard datasets. To achieve this, we implemented an unsupervised two-stage system using Deep Convolutional AutoEncoders with a Dimensionally Balanced Reconstruction Error metric. This approach involves first training an unsupervised model to produce compressed representations of data, then using those representations to train an classifier using one-class SVM on normal data, with far-from-normal data excluded to prevent overfitting. Specifically, we improved the EfficientNet model by modifying its architecture and reduced the number of redundant pathways that contributed to high computational costs. Our results show that this method surpasses current anomaly detection methods, offering up to 3 times faster processing speeds and reduced memory usage while maintaining high accuracy for a range of performance metrics. This study offers an advanced verification framework for systems of formulas incorporating free-term verification. Unlike existing verifiers, our framework does not limit the number of terms and can be applied to diverse verification tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework by comparing it to state-of-the-art verifiers on twelve complex verification problems across five categories. The results reveal that, under ideal circumstances with no errors, our proposed model surpasses other verifiers; however, when considering the impact of imperfections, our model shows significant improvement, verifying nearly twice as many instances while maintaining high accuracy. Notably, in cases where other verifiers performed well, our model achieved nearly complete agreement with existing solutions. Additionally, we have made our verification framework available to the public through a repository containing all required code and instructions for reproducing our results. https://github.com/alecgoodman/mtv-verifiers. Several recent studies have significantly enhanced the performance of Natural Language Processing models through the application of data augmentation methods to existing models. Despite the widespread use of these techniques, there remains a pressing need to examine their effectiveness in a comprehensive manner. To address this gap, we employed a concentric training framework, evaluating how various augmentation techniques perform with expanding sizes of original training data. Our research features a distinctive setup where we contrast the impacts of augmentation methods both in models lacking pre-training and those with Transfer Learning. Furthermore, we found that chemical augmentation methods are generally capable of achieving comparable performance to continuous methods, provided that the scaled-up context is incorporated in the training process. Additionally, we identified several key predictors of the efficacy of different augmentation techniques. Our study also highlights an unexpected finding where the application of certain techniques results in a reduction in performance. We hope that these findings will foster the development of smarter data augmentation strategies and more effective training protocols for NLP models. The source code and experimental data used in this study have been made publicly available. To our knowledge, this study represents the first comprehensive evaluation of data augmentation methods in the NLP domain. We have conducted over 180 experiments, surpassing previous studies by an order of magnitude, shedding new light on this topic and paving the way for future research in this field. To our knowledge, we have also developed the most extensive collection of augmentation techniques in the NLP domain, comprising 28 different methods and variants. We have further expanded this collection by introducing new methods, dubbed BARTMix, BERTMix, and ALDA, which yield notable performance gains in specific scenarios. Notably, we have discovered two distinct patterns in the behavior of different augmentation techniques: those that excel in small-scale training data and those that thrive with large-scale training data. We have further determined that pre-training can mitigate data hunger while preserving performance gains achieved through the application of augmentation methods. We have applied two novel evaluation protocols to assess the effectiveness of different techniques: (i) a semi-supervised learning evaluation, where we examined the performance of various augmentation methods in conjunction with pre-training on 15 NLP tasks spanning 8 datasets; (ii) a memory-based evaluation, where we conducted extensive experiments across 14 datasets involving both supervised and transfer learning scenarios. The outcomes of these analyses have been made publicly available, serving as a resource to facilitate further research on this topic. We believe that our study offers fresh insights into the world of data augmentation in the NLP domain, stimulating the development of more sophisticated training protocols and intelligent data augmentation

Introducing a new condition, namely macroregularity, which corresponds to a specific measure of singularity for the Lagrangian, we investigate how this constraint impacts the solution. It is found that macroregularity complicates the existence of equilibrium, and a particular type of interaction potential, which we term strictly macroregular, is responsible for this complication. Conversely, we establish the existence of equilibrium for a wide class of Lagrangian functions that are subject to minimal singularity constraints. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the degree of singularity in the interaction potential and the degree of regularity required for the equilibrium solution, while also considering the impact of other factors, such as the availability of equilibrium states with varying levels of regularity. An interesting observation arises in the form of a counterexample, which highlights an irregularity characteristic of mean field games and the inadequacy of several established regularity conditions. Finally, we investigate the degree of singularity for a class of Lagrangian functions that are informed by stochastic control principles, while also considering the effect of different boundary conditions on the availability of equilibrium solutions with varying levels of regularity. These findings collectively illustrate the significance of singularity in determining the existence of equilibrium in mean field games. To protect personal data while performing federated learning, we have introduced FedBuff, a novel algorithm that efficiently handles expansive datasets while ensuring privacy. The FedBuff algorithm creates an expansive, buffered client-side data mixture that is distributed among participants and a server. This innovative approach enables participants to perform local training without needing to combine and share their individual client dataset with others. By allowing participants to perform calculations on a aggregated client data mixture rather than merely aggregating their own data, FedBuff circumvents the limitations of vanilla federated learning, thereby empowering them to perform more intricate computations and perform better than the vanilla approach. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that FedBuff scales better than other advanced techniques like FedBuff* and FedNOIS, thereby showcasing a substantial improvement in training efficiency with minimal additional computational overhead. Finally, our results highlight the FedBuff algorithm's capability to balance both efficiency and a robust, private training experience. This paper develops a finite-dimensional algebra known as polynomial shift calculus, constructed from a finite-dimensional irreducible semisimple algebra G, and the direct sum of copies of the polynomial algebra A, labeled by G's semisimple Lie algebra simple roots. A shift semigroup S, generated by Satake embeddings of G's simple roots into S, is used to create this algebra. We show that the commutant of S contains the shift calculus C(G,∅) constructed over the ground field, a result analogous to Brauer's theorem. We establish the concept of isothermic surfaces composed of simple patches, where each patch is connected through deformation using Beltrami parameterization. This concept allows us to derive Beltrami parameterizations of isothermic surfaces in 3D Euclidean space from simply connected isothermic patches in a systematic manner. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both Beltrami parameterizations and the composition of deformation maps preserve isothermic structure, thereby generating new isothermic surfaces. Additionally, we show that our construction aligns with previous work by Darboux, Felix, and Parkin. Moreover, we prove a global existence and regularity result for Beltrami parameterizations of isothermic surfaces in 3D Euclidean space. Finally, we use Beltrami parameterizations to derive new formulas for fundamental forms of isothermic surfaces in 3D Euclidean space. These formulas enable us to study isothermic surfaces in terms of their Beltrami parameterizations rather than their current formulations as parametrized surfaces, thereby offering greater flexibility and freedom to choose suitable parametrizations that simplify or solve isothermic equations. As a concrete demonstration of these new formulas, we use Beltrami parameterizations to derive a new, unique solution to the isothermic equation in 3D Euclidean space. This solution exhibits symmetry and can be interpreted as a surface of rotation. Moreover, we use Beltrami parameterizations to show that several surfaces, including the helicoid, Chandrasekhar, and Wente surfaces, are not isothermic. Lastly, we use Beltrami parameterizations to generate a wealth of new isothermic surfaces in 3D Euclidean space. These include a range of surfaces with a plane of symmetry, as well as surfaces of rotation, to name a few types. This comprehensive collection of isothermic surfaces in 3D Euclidean space provides a valuable reference for studying isothermic surfaces. Moreover, we use Beltrami parameterizations to generate a wealth of new isothermic surfaces in spaces of higher dimensions, where these surfaces exhibit various symmetries, including a plane of symmetry and rotation around a axis, to name a few types. This comprehensive collection of isothermic surfaces in spaces of higher dimensions provides a valuable reference for studying isothermic surfaces in these spaces and offers scope for further research and development. This study investigates the use of the Reproducing Kernel Particle Method to solve partial differential equations, comparing its convergence to traditional Galerkin methods like the Finite Element Method or Weak Form Weak Scattering. Unlike these methods, the Reproducing Kernel Particle Method does not rely on a systematic process to assemble the equation and instead uses a kernel-based approach that can approximate gradients and other differential operators with high precision, without the need for mesh points. This method solves partial differential equations by projecting the residual onto an appropriate space, which can be strong or weak, to produce highly accurate results, even with few particles. Several tests are conducted to validate the method's convergence and accuracy, comparing its results to those of the Finite Element Method and Fast Demon, a weakly compressive projector method. For low-regularity domains and chaotic flows, the Reproducing Kernel Particle Method demonstrates superior performance, producing more accurate results with fewer particles than the Fast Demon method. Moreover, the Reproducing Kernel Particle Method converges rapidly with the addition of particles, exhibiting a high order of convergence that approaches the theoretical limit for certain test problems. Overall, the results indicate that kernel-based techniques offer significant advantages over traditional projection methods, particularly for complex and high-precision applications. Based on these findings, several potential applications of the Reproducing Kernel Particle Method are proposed, including the accurate simulation of chaotic fluid flows and low-frequency acoustic perturbations. Additionally, the method shows great potential for integration with deep learning techniques, potentially enabling the accurate simulation of incompressible Navier-Stokes equations and other complex partial differential equations. To facilitate this integration, the Reproducing Kernel Particle Method has been implemented in a Python package, RKPM, which is documented in the appendix and freely available on the GitHub repository. This implementation allows for the reproduction of the presented results, as well as the exploration of new applications and cases. Moreover, the Reproducing Kernel Particle Method can be used to solve partial differential equations in two dimensions, as demonstrated by the computational study in the appendix. Furthermore, we examined how the potential's anisotropic behavior correlates with the Debye screening mass and found that it is in accordance with the lattice QCD results for a range of anisotropy parameters. Moreover, the results suggest the presence of a critical anisotropy value above which the quark potential becomes isotropic. Notably, this anisotropy threshold is observed in both the color Coulomb and Lifshitz energies. Crucially, the combinations of weights and levels found this way exhaust all possibilities, a result stemming from the unique geometry of the eigencurve near its extremities. The objectives of this research were to assess gravity wave activity in the Martian atmosphere and to examine the spatial and temporal variations of these phenomena using the MAOZNA model and to compare its results with the Mars Climate Change Initiative CTSK dataset. The study analyzed the seasonal activity of gravity waves in the Martian atmosphere from sols 1 to 2250 during the Martian year in 2015, spanning the Aerosols and Ground Temperature (AGT) campaign. The results showed significant correlations at three key altitudes: 5, 15, and 30 km. At 5 km, the relationship between gravity wave activity and temperature reversed at around sol 140, and temperature increased with gravity wave activity, while the opposite occurred below 5 km. This paper enhances the Spectrogram-Gated Generator-Discriminator model used in audio generation with a realistic spectrogram-based loss function. The traditional generator-discriminator setup, based on convolution and transposition, lacks guidance for spectrally manipulating sound waves. Our proposal is a loss function that measures the difference between a target spectrogram and the generated spectrogram using a norm-based, mask-weighted error calculation. The mask is adjustable and can be optimized to minimize this difference. When combined with the conventional adversarial loss, this loss function enables the generator to produce high-quality spectrograms with accurate spectral features, leading to enhanced audio generation performance. Experimental results indicate that our proposed loss function achieves superior results, as evidenced by the higher quality of spectrograms and the more efficient convergence of the generator and discriminator models. Moreover, the proposed loss function demonstrates flexibility in its design, allowing it to be applied to various generator architectures, such as the convolutional transpositional and the residual learning-based approaches. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are widely used for modeling sequences, but their fully connected variants have high computational costs and are difficult to train due to the explosion of parameters. Our proposed Convolutional Recurrent Neural Networks (CRNNs) address these limitations by reducing the number of parameters, allowing for efficient and scalable modeling of various time-series data. By combining convolutional layers with recurrent layers, CRNNs retain the ability to learn long-term dependencies while enabling the modeling of spatial relationships in sequences. Our models can be applied effectively in the analysis of multi-sensor time-series data, as demonstrated by their application in the detection of heavy power users on smart grid data, outperforming the baseline model with a true positive rate of 0.90 and a 75% reduction in model parameters. Our research further shows that CRNNs are suitable for various sequence-based tasks by evaluating multiple performance metrics on the datasets of fuel consumption, stock prices, and weather conditions. Our models, models' hyperparameters, and data can be accessed via our GitHub repository. https://github.com/d-d-d/CRNN.git. HPC resources provided by the Oklahoma Supercomputing Center were utilized for performance enhancements. Our code has been updated to work with PyTorch 1.9 and TensorFlow 2.0, with relevant repositories listed for reproducibility purposes. One effective approach to balancing medical efficacy with economic implications of pandemic management is introducing moderate policies on a timely basis. To achieve this, it is essential to have a clear understanding of the epidemiological impact of such measures. In this study, we develop a symbolic framework for modeling the COVID-19 pandemic and evaluating the effectiveness of symbolic-numeric multiscale methods for representing epidemiological models. Focusing on a simplified SEIR model with symbolic and numeric parameters, we applied the Multiscale Residual Distribution method to simulate one year of transmission dynamics. Furthermore, we assessed the symbolic-numeric accuracy of MRD by comparing it with an exact solution computed using numpy for all model parameters. Our results indicate that MRD can reliably capture the qualitative behavior of the model for a wide range of parameter values, and it can also provide precise symbolic information about the model's coefficients. We then used our SEIR model to investigate several mitigation strategies, such as implementing non-pharmaceutical interventions, monitoring vaccination progress, and combining these efforts. Our findings highlight the potential of the MRD method in symbolically understanding and analyzing complex models, and we hope that our work will contribute to informing practical decisions in pandemic management. Lastly, our framework can be adapted to model various types of dynamical systems, such as population dynamics, chemical reactions, and electrical networks. To facilitate future research on these topics, we have made our code and model available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/JCtransontP/MRD_SEIR_model. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcsml.2022.100697, Journal of Computational Science and Mathematical Logistics, Volume 12, 2022, 100697. Debugging data-intensive machine learning models has become a critical issue due to the expanding use of visualizations in data science. Current methods for data validation and debugging often necessitate the examination of vast amounts of raw data, making the process laborious and time-consuming. In response, this paper introduces DataScope - an innovative, interactive technique that streamlines the process of debugging by targeting the most salient issues in large datasets. DataScope's user-friendly interface enables data analysts to efficiently identify anomalies and understand the causes of model errors through the dynamic highlighting of critical samples within visualizations. Numerous experiments conducted on real-world datasets resulted in a substantial reduction of the time required to debug data-related problems, with relative improvements ranging from 75% to 10%, depending on the dataset. Moreover, DataScope's effectiveness was confirmed through the analysis of 12 actual data science projects, yielding a 100% success rate in isolating the causes of model errors. As a result, DataScope has become an essential tool for the efficient debugging of data-driven machine learning models. The technique is now available for public use at https://github.com/harvarddatascience/datascope. Additionally, an interactive demo can be accessed at https://github.com/harvarddatascience/datascope-demo. Further information can be obtained through email at [harvarddatascience@gmail.com]. Based on the outstanding performance of DataScope, this study poses an intriguing question: can a diagnostic power that spans multiple dimensions be achieved through the integration of localized diagnostic methods? To answer this question, a new framework called ScopeGuard was developed to automatically evaluate and improve the efficiency of various debugging techniques. ScopeGuard's results show that even seemingly independent debugging tasks exhibit interconnected patterns, implying a great potential for optimization. By applying this insight to DataScope, a novel extension was created to enhance the interaction between data analysts and visualizations, thus streamlining the process of debugging data-related issues. As a result, the enhanced DataScope method yields a considerable improvement in efficiency, with relative gains ranging from 90% to 10% across the datasets. Consequently, a combination of interactive techniques and automated analysis via ScopeGuard can greatly facilitate the process of data validation and debugging, offering a wealth of new knowledge in the process. Ultimately, the development of ScopeGuard has paved the way for an advanced field of study known as diagnostic corpora, consisting of detailed records of past debugging efforts, complete with a wealth of intrinsic information that can be harnessed to improve the efficiency of future debugging tasks.

Recent advancements in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have significantly impacted various natural language processing tasks like question-answering and text summarization, leading to increased interest in employing them for relation extraction. This field involves identifying and classifying the relationship between entities within text, crucial for understanding text context and executing cross-referencing tasks. We examine the role of word and character-based models in relation extraction through thorough analyses and experiments. Furthermore, to facilitate further research, we introduce our custom-made dataset consisting of 3,067 samples derived from Article 50 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. Our in-depth evaluations across 9 relation types and 301 entities demonstrate the effectiveness of the long short-term memory (LSTM) architecture in relation extraction. This study seeks to address critical questions regarding the utilization of deep learning methods in relation extraction and aims to stimulate further investigation on the specific dataset introduced. Lastly, our research highlights the overall accuracy of deep learning models in extracting distinct entities within the chosen dataset. We intend to expand this study in the future to encompass all 268 articles of the Treaty, subject to relevant accessibility regulations being met. We plan to share our code and the introduced dataset publicly to foster reproducibility and encourage further research on the topic. We anticipate our research to contribute to the development of more sophisticated relation extraction methods in the future. We plan to expand our dataset to include more fine-grained relations in the future as well. We plan to participate in relevant challenge competitions that utilize relation extraction as a key component, keeping up to date with advancements in the field as they emerge. We plan to publish an updated version of our research as new advancements in the field of relation extraction come to light. We plan to engage with practitioners who work on similar topics via blogs and other outreach initiatives to share our findings and foster collaboration. We plan to provide accessibility to our dataset and technical capabilities for other researchers to build upon our work, as we do with our technical capabilities used to process the dataset. We plan to present our research findings in relevant conferences and workshops to share our work with relevant audiences. We plan to respond to inquiries from other researchers and practitioners, keeping up to date with feedback on our previous work. We plan to pursue similar projects that involve using technological innovations to investigate complex, interdisciplinary topics and contribute to scientific progress in these areas. Let $B_R$ be a ball of radius $R$ with center at the origin and $Q_R$ the region between its boundary and the origin. For a fixed smooth bounded domain $\Omega$ within $Q_R$, we examine the first eigenvalue $\lambda_1(\Omega, Q_R, h)$ of the Steklov-Robin problem in $h=\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}|_{\partial\Omega}$ on $\Omega$. Our study shows that $\lambda_1(\Omega, Q_R, h)$ increases with the Robin parameter $h$ and the radius $R$, and we obtain estimates for its maximum value on $\Omega$ within $Q_R$. Furthermore, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of $\lambda_1(\Omega, Q_R, h)$ as $R\to\infty$ and derive upper and lower bounds for its large eigenvalues. Our analysis also valid when the domain $\Omega$ is unbounded, and we compute the large eigenvalues of the standard Steklov problem for the Laplace operator. These results complement and expand upon existing research in this field. Additionally, we provide examples to verify our theoretical findings. Lastly, the study is concluded by exploring its areas of application and future research opportunities. To facilitate readability, we have divided the article into several sections. Specifically, we discuss the main goals and methods in Section 2, while the remaining sections delve into the theoretical proofs and applications of our findings. Needless to say, the validity of our study depends on the smoothness and behavior of the domain $\Omega$ and its boundary, which is ensured by standard existing literature in this field. For instance, see the work by J. M. M. Lourido and A. Porretta in their publication in Journal of Evolution Equations (2021), where they investigate the well-posedness of a second-order parabolic problem involving a non-local operator and Robin boundary conditions. Similarly, see the research by C. Bucur and I. Damakh in their publication in Journal of Differential Equations (2021), which focuses on the growth of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of a nonlocal problem involving a gap boundary divisor. See also the work by C. Bucur and P. Vergara-Dias in their publication in Calculus of Variations and Partial Differential Equations (2021), which explores the variation of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of a Steklov problem for the Laplace operator as the domain's boundary changes

Focus is on exploring the inherent structures of comprehensive hypergraphs (within multiple categories) through their representations as graphs. The problem of determining the feasibility of recovering a full hypergraph from one of its graph representations is addressed, along with the difficulties this problem poses for computational efforts. We then consider the related task of testing the existence of specific subgraphs or determining the minimum number required for a full hypergraph recovery, each of which is shown to be complex or unsolved. We ultimately investigate the properties of certain hypergraphs (of limited rank) that can be accurately reconstructed from their graph representations and demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of proposed algorithms for Ramanujan graphs and those of small rank relative to the size of the underlying hypergraphs. The potential of this work is significant as it enables graph-based analysis of hypergraph data and contributes to our understanding of hypergraph structures through their graph representations. We also introduce the concept of 'lossy' mappings between graphs and hypergraphs, which may aid in the construction of representative graphs from hypergraphs. Additionally, related open problems and potential avenues for further research are discussed. The provided code can be accessed at https://github.com/aycache/reconstructing-hypergraphs. We introduce the PAXRay dataset, the largest to date for understanding and localizing image regions mentioned in medical reports, such as X-ray images. This dataset is based on the AXRay dataset from 2020 but incorporates the insights gained from its follow-up study. The PAXRay dataset is specifically designed for the task of 'where is it?' which involves identifying image regions mentioned in reports. To accomplish this, we leveraged large datasets of X-ray images and clinical descriptions, then precisely marked the image regions mentioned in over 16,000 captions by specialists. Moreover, our dataset includes broadly varied categories of images and meticulous segmentations that withstand common forms of data degradation. To evaluate the performance of models on this dataset, we created a user-friendly interface for interactive evaluation, thereby enhancing the understanding of models' mistakes and their limitations. This interface facilitates the distribution of the PAXRay dataset and allows researchers to test their models on it. Furthermore, our dataset and evaluation tools are available at https://paxray.github.io/. The knowledge gained from our study is presented in our technical report at https://paxray.github.io/docs/. The code for our study can be accessed at https://github.com/paxray/paxray. This knowledge, along with additional resources, can be found at https://paxray.github.io/resources/. We invite researchers to join us in accurately localizing image regions mentioned in medical reports through accurate image grounding. In this process, we aim to shed more light on the art of clinical interpretation and make technological advancements more relevant and useful to healthcare professionals. In line with this goal, we would like to extend an invitation to healthcare professionals to collaborate with us on this project. Details of how to participate can be found at https://paxray.github.io/credits/. The vision that drives this project is presented at https://paxray.github.io/about/. In summary, we introduce the PAXRay dataset, a comprehensive resource for understanding and localizing image regions mentioned in medical reports through accurate image grounding. Additionally, we created an evaluation interface for interactive assessment, allowing models to be tested and their limitations understood. We introduce a new model for a spatially flat, single-mode laser that employs quasi-one-dimensional arrays of Kerr nonlinearity. These arrays act as a large, flat mirror that can achieve directional emission of light, analogous to a bulk photonic crystal with high reflectivity. Similar to traditional lasers, our system can reach single-mode operation and achieve a high effective reflectivity via self-inhibition of lightradiation. Additionally, we show that these arrays can be scaled up to emit light at wider angles and discuss the limitations of our model. Furthermore, we find that these directional emission properties are robust even when the systems are in thermal equilibrium. Lastly, we examine the possibility of adjusting parameters to change the wavelength of emission. Due to its simplicity and ability to be easily modified, our model may serve as a starting point for the development of innovative directional emitters. Bulk nonlinear systems, like our laser model, can also be used to investigate complex phenomena in optically excited states, such as mode competition and phase transitions. These bulk nonlinear systems can facilitate the exploration of these complex phenomena and maybe even enable the creation of unique, high-dimensional photonic devices. These research efforts could lead to the discovery of unique photonic properties and applications, such as quantum computing or advanced lighting systems. We develop a novel weak noise theory to address a profound unresolved issue in the long-standing KPZ equation (Kardar-Parisi-Zhang) and a related non-linear hydrodynamic model. In the context of the KPZ equation, our theory fills in the gap between the Prokhorov theorem and the non-linear hydrodynamic equation, leading to a unique weak solution. Furthermore, our approach derives analytical weak solutions to the KPZ equation and a related non-linear hydrodynamic model, thereby confirming the predictions made by Borodin and Kalmer in 2013. In contrast to existing methods in the literature, our proof does not rely on the construction of a random walk based on a random directed walk. Instead, we leverage the connection between the Prokhorov theorem and the non-linear hydrodynamic equation to establish the solution. We demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of a weak solution to the KPZ equation and a related non-linear hydrodynamic model under minimal regularity constraints on the initial conditions. In particular, we prove the existence of a weak solution with minimal Sobolev regularity for the KPZ equation and a related non-linear hydrodynamic model. Additionally, we obtain the existence of a weak solution with maximal BMO regularity for a stochastic partial differential equation driven by a specific type of noise. In free-electron lasers (FELs), particularly those in the XUV and soft X-ray range, a limited number of pulses are produced, constrained by the availability of electron beams and fill times. Although numerous techniques exist for generating multiple pulses, the resulting radiation often exhibits significant shot-to-shot fluctuations. In this study, a novel technique called chirp-taper management is investigated, aiming to produce a train of ultrashort, coherent pulses in a wide spectral range. This strategy can be applied to various FEL architectures using a simple and adaptable method. A linear accelerator demonstrating promising potential for this method is the compact linac at the HIIGK test stand, a particle accelerator operated by the Helmholtz Institute for Particle and Material Physics at the Dresden-Dorfenter University of Technology. At the HIIGEL test stand, the research team has successfully simulated, using the HiCAT simulation code, a Chirp-Taper managed FEL experiment and obtained realistic outcomes that can be replicated at the compact linac. In the simulation, a high-repetition-rate FEL operation with 1 GHz pulse frequency and 10 pico-second pulse duration has been achieved, using a six-meter long linac, with a low charge and a small beam tolerance, resulting in a broad spectral range with many mode holes. This innovative strategy offers new possibilities for producing a wide range of coherent radiation and could be used for various applications such as generating super-fluorescence, ultra-short d Double optical pulses, and wide-spectral X-ray spectra. Additionally, the outcomes have significant implications for the production of non-linear X-ray radiation in a "witness-pulse" controlled approach. In this volume of an editorial, the research team presents an overview of the simulation results, the theory behind the concept, a possible architecture for a Chirp-Taper managed FEL, and the potential for this kind of an machine to produce innovative technologies in the X-ray and, specifically, in the XUV range. A new method has been proposed to identify pattern defects. By breaking down input images into low-rank components, our approach filters out image inconsistencies that indicate defects. A separate step utilizing a deep convolutional neural network enhances image detail, allowing for more accurate defect identification. Since our method separates background and defect information, this enables easier isolation and analysis of fabric defects. Additionally, our method enables various applications such as estimating the distance between objects and the width of lines. These tasks were successfully demonstrated with fabric scan data. Compared to alternative methods, our approach yields more accurate results. For example, in detecting tears on a canvas, our method achieved 98.75% accuracy, surpassing the 97.5% accuracy of Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and 95.25% accuracy of Principal Component Analysis (PCA). Experimentation showed that our method, which relies on a 50x50 low-rank decomposition window size, produced the most accurate results. Furthermore, by analyzing the number of accumulated singular values, our method successfully detected multiple fabric defects. For instance, when applying our method to images of a pillow, our approach identified three fabric defect locations, whereas SVD and PCA only detected one each. These experiments confirm the effectiveness of our method. To develop this new method, our approach was successfully tested on thousands of images from various sources, demonstrating its generalizability and applicability to a wide range of image sets. These sources include both real-world images and synthetic ones generated randomly, illustrating the broad applicability of our method. Ultimately, our method provides a versatile tool for pattern and image analysis. As such, our method may be applied to various fields such as medicine, astronomy, and security, where image decomposition might be useful. Optimizing mutual information between agents actions and observations is a viable strategy for learning effective representations of sensory data. A key challenge in optimizing this mutual information is the intractability of exactly calculating the mutual information in complex environments. A new approach uses a variational mutual information estimator to overcome this limitation, replacing the true optimal policy with a approximated policy to circumvent the intractability. The resulting algorithm is tested in complex 2D and 3D environments and demonstrates significant improvements in learning optimal policies within a set time limit. The research also theoretically justifies the approximated policy and empirically verifies its performance in comparison to existing methods. Further study finds that combining this approach with reinforcement learning results in improved performance and reduced time required to reach a set goal in observational learning scenarios. The resulting embeddings from this method show promise in transferring and generalizing across different goal states and agent views. Additionally, the research demonstrates that observational learning can be efficiently performed without the need for extensive interaction with the environment. Notably, this method has the potential to be adapted for detecting incidents in other complex infrastructure systems. The advancement of state-of-the-art artificial intelligence has driven demand for complex training environments, such as text-based game simulations. Researchers previously developed the TextWorld platform to facilitate breakthroughs in AI, but its detailed simulations hindered throughput, limiting the platform's potential. We address this limitation with TextWorldExpress, a novel model that maintains accurate game simulations while substantially boosting throughput by a factor of 20. TextWorldExpress achieves this improvement through two key techniques: a two-stage training method and a simplified language model. Furthermore, our express model enables rapid episode resolution, empowering researchers to test a wide range of AI algorithms and accelerate breakthroughs in the field. We showcase its effectiveness by replicating previous results and making new contributions in multi-objective optimization for game playing. The improved throughput of TextWorldExpress has paved the way for large-scale training of deep reinforcement learning models, such as Transformer and Plug-and-Play Agent, for complex action sequences. Ultimately, our express model empowers researchers to investigate the boundaries of AI performance within the TextWorld domain, including the development of informative action sequences. TextWorldExpress is publicly available at https://github.com/learning-boxes/textworld-express.

Building on de Jong's work, we leverage the concept of hyperbolicity to establish rational point existence on certain complex projective varieties by adapting a strategy from Eliasz and Fu's research. Furthermore, incorporating the findings of Eliasz, Fu, and Raichev allows us to demonstrate that hyperbolicity implies the existence of a vast number of rational points on varieties with semi-positivity properties, thereby yielding an infinite supply of non-proper rational points. Additionally, our study yields an infinite collection of non-proper rational points on varieties with minimal SEC properties. Lastly, we find a class of hyperbolic varieties that fail to satisfy the Hartshorne conjecture, thereby showcasing the intricacy of hyperbolicity's impact on rational point existence and its relationship with geometric complexity properties. A point on a manifold is considered manipulable to the extent that its velocity can be influenced by controlling adjacent points. This concept is crucial in robotics, particularly in reaching tasks involving contact with an object, as it necessitates a grasp point with high manipulability. In the context of linear connections, this concept is defined through the use of torques, manipulability matrices, or ellipsoids that characterize control possibilities. However, these definitions rely on the validity of the proxy assumption, as using the standard definition on a general Riemannian manifold may be problematic. This study adopts a geometric perspective, as the special orthogonal group and the projective space are considered essential in the context of robotic grasping. A manipulability matrix is defined on these manifolds, along with its properties and the formulation of ellipsoids that reflect control possibilities. This is achieved through the adoption of the Levi-Civita connection and the use of the canonical spray on the special orthogonal group and the projective space. Additionally, these manifolds feature notable geometric characteristics, as the manipulability matrix is aligned with the double fibration formula, generalizing the concepts of base-dependent and fiber-dependent matrices. On the projective space, it is distinct from the Hessian of the distance function. This research provides a comprehensive geometric characterization of manipulability that is applicable, coherent, and generalizable to a broad range of parametrized sets of matrices. This is demonstrated through various illustrative examples. Ultimately, this study posits that the standard definition of manipulability may not accurately reflect the velocity of points on general Riemannian manifolds and suggests exploring alternative definitions that are consistent with the established geometric characteristics of control possibilities. As a result, height maps have become essential in training models for three-dimensional object estimation. Nevertheless, existing methods are inefficient because they require significant time and resources to produce a vast number of canonical height maps. To resolve this issue, we introduce Stage-HMN, a novel multi-stage training framework that leverages pre-trained semantic embeddings to generate height maps in an unsupervised manner. By doing so, we achieve two key breakthroughs: first, we attain comparable results to state-of-the-art methods, and second, we accomplish all of this while drastically reducing the need for extensive height map data, achieving a 15 times reduction in required data. Additionally, we introduce EvalStage-HMN, a semantic embedding based model that can effectively learn canonical object poses, resulting in a significant reduction in misalignment by a factor of 6 compared to other semantic learning methods. Moreover, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our other method, Stage-HMN, by achieving a significant increase of 9% in 3D object detection accuracy for various complex scenes in the Pool-based Object Recognition (PORE) dataset. Large datasets compiled from online feedback can provide valuable insights into
public perceptions on crucial issues, including those related to vaccine misinformation.
Existing studies in this domain have been limited by their reliance on manually
cataloguing online comments from specific platforms, resulting in underutilized
data and prolonged research durations. To address these challenges, we've created a
framework that leverages the rich content offered by Reddit's API, enabling the
efficient scraping and analysis of substantial amounts of user feedback on
specific topics. We've also developed a unique pipeline for extracting and
combining manual and automated annotations of malicious posts, resulting in the
identification of previously unmarked content and a resource-saving approach for
researchers. To further understand public attitudes towards vaccine-related misinformation
and its impact, we've built upon existing models for detecting such content,
enhancing them with contextual information drawn from trained language models.
We've tested our framework extensively in a real-world study examining public
attitudes towards vaccine-related misinformation on Reddit, involving over
96,000 annotated comments and nearly 192 million unseen posts. Our research
demonstrates that scalable architectures supported by large datasets and sophisticated
models like BERT are essential for uncovering complex online phenomena. We
advocate for the importance of open-access datasets and the potential of
public platforms like Reddit for conducting in-depth analyses of societal
patterns and trends. To facilitate reproducibility, we've made our code
and datasets available for public use at [https://github.com/ghswd/vaccine_misinfo](https://github.com/ghswd/vaccine_misinfo).

We investigate the behaviors of focusing Schrödinger equations under strong forcing influences, specifically those featuring a force that can be written as a derivative of a potential well. Our research indicates that the presence of a boundary significantly alters the ability to prove blow-up using established methods, such as those based on energy estimates or variational methods. Focusing on equations defined in half-space or strip regions, we demonstrate that the absence of certain singularities in the forcing function prevents the occurrence of blow-up, despite theoretical predictions suggesting otherwise. Moreover, we establish a new set of conditions linking the properties of the forcing function and the initial data, thereby refining the current understanding of solutions' behaviors and providing insights into the critical Sobolev exponent. Those scenarios where blow-up is predicted theoretically are examined; we derive an approximate lower bound for the blow-up time, tied to the large-scale properties of the forcing function. Our study also contrasts our results with the behavior of similar equations in the entire plane, where the presence of singularities in the forcing function leads to rapid solution decay, and we showcase a broad class of positive forcing functions resulting in rapid solution decay in half-space or on a periodic domain. Interestingly, our research reveals that positive forcing functions can prevent solutions from becoming zero even under strong coupling with the equation's linear part, thus reflecting the role of forcing function periodicity in the solutions' behaviors. Moreover, our analysis indicates that solutions may still undergo rapid decay even when the forcing function is not constant, but rather varies across a limited scale. To prove these outcomes, we first devise new estimates linking the solution's $L^p$ norm with its interaction level and the function's properties, thereby refining existing energy estimates, as well as introducing a new set of variational estimates, complemented with a well-known variant of the Khavinson vision theorem. Our investigations on confined systems have implications for the study of one-dimensional relativistic hydrodynamics, as well as quantum mechanics, as we discuss in our final section. Additionally, our results provide us with crucial insights into the solutions' behaviors in the confined space of a stripe or half-space, governed by Schrödinger's equation, where our analysis leads to the formulation of open hypotheses concerning equation interactions with bounded potentials and their connections with quantum mechanics and relativistic hydrodynamics. These outcomes hold significant importance, as they address questions concerning the emergence of singularity formation from small scale interactions, as well as the non-existence of solutions' blow-up under the influence of force functions with bounded gradients. Cargo's success has turned it into a testing ground for resolving issues related to library vulnerabilities. Recently, researchers conducted an in-depth study of Cargo's ecosystem, examining its versioning, update policies, and efficiency in addressing security flaws. Initially, it was found that even though many libraries in Cargo update their dependencies to the latest versions of other libraries, few actually do the same for libraries that have been affected by security flaws. Only about 25% of libraries in Cargo's ecosystem have their security-related issues resolved in the latest versions of the affected libraries, with many others showing no improvement even after a year since the vulnerability was reported. Furthermore, it was discovered that even though Cargo supports semver, many libraries in the ecosystem do not use versioning numbers that adhere to it, which can make it difficult for developers to keep their dependencies up-to-date. Researchers also found that libraries in Cargo tend to be more conservative when updating their dependencies compared to Python's numpy ecosystem, which can slow down the adoption of new versions. Despite these issues, it was observed that Cargo's ecosystem is still more robust than Apache POI's library ecosystem in Java. Researchers noted the possibility of sending notification emails to developers to inform them about available updates to their dependencies, which could help improve the timeliness of library updates. Based on these findings, researchers recommended a few solutions, such as sending notification emails and implementing a more robust versioning system, to further improve Cargo's functionality and usability. Finally, researchers compared Cargo's update policies with policies for resolving security flaws in Python's numpy and Apache POI's library ecosystems, which are discussed in detail in a companion paper. This comparative analysis highlighted that Cargo's policies are more complex and nuanced compared to the other ecosystems studied. Researchers further explored the possibility of sending notification emails to developers to inform them about available updates to their dependencies, which could help improve the timeliness of library updates. Additionally, researchers identified future areas for further research, such as determining whether Cargo's update policies are reflected in the versioning numbers used for the libraries. Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have become widely used in graph-structured data analysis. Lying at the heart of these networks is the graph convolution operation, often implemented using the matrix multiplication method, which relies on the graph adjacency matrix and degree matrix. This operation's computational expense can be described in terms of matrix products, involving the adjacency matrix, degree matrix, and node feature matrices. Consequently, the actual cost of computation is akin to a matrix multiplication method. This paper delves into the structure of these convolutions, presenting an alternative based on the Schur complement and Compressed Schur complement. We present two novel GCN implementations, one using the Compressed Schur complement, yielding an advantage of O(V log(1/ε)) over existing methods, and another using a randomized approach, providing a significant reduction of O(V) relative to previous methods. This randomized technique's accuracy loss is quantified at ε, along with a corresponding trade-off between computational efficiency and numerical precision loss. Additionally, we demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in computing inverse matrices, presenting a significant performance improvement over current methods. On real-world datasets, our novel GCN implementations exhibit superior performance, yielding accelerated inference times and reduced storage requirements. More specifically, our models display reduced inference times of 27.9% and 42.9% respectively, along with decreased model sizes of 35.7% and 50.2% respectively, across multiple semantic segmentation tasks. To resolve this, we have created a sophisticated Trojan attack that exploits vulnerabilities in both the model and its input data, which significantly increases damage to accuracy and extends its applicability to a broader range of scenarios. Our innovative approach is based on a novel type of Trojan that incorporates a sophisticated pattern of manipulation, often referred to as a'snake', into both the model and its input to cause substantial harm to accuracy. To achieve this, we utilize an enhanced snake-based attack on the model, which enables the extraction of customized snakes from trained models. Our proposed method has the capacity to cause an accuracy loss of up to 100% for specific classifiers, while our future plans include exploring ways to develop defensive strategies against this type of attack. Existing countermeasures are primarily based on anomaly detection which focuses on spotting unusual patterns in data or model behavior. To address this limitation, we have developed an innovative post-hoc approach known as SnakeNet, which is designed to counter Trojan attacks by utilizing knowledge about the malicious patterns, often referred to as snakes, that are embedded in the model. Our approach is grounded in statistical analysis and has the capacity to block snakes during both training and testing phases, while also maintaining the model's original functionality. Our experiments have shown that SnakeNet is highly effective in blocking snakes, while also surpassing the performance of other defenses. To further evaluate the performance of SnakeNet, we utilized SnakeBased Attack, which is an enhanced variant of existing Trojan attacks, that can cause even more severe harm to accuracy. Our results have revealed that SnakeNet is highly effective in blocking snakes, while also preventing any significant decrease in accuracy. To ensure the applicability of SnakeNet in real-world scenarios, we utilized various techniques to conceal the presence of the malicious patterns in the model, while also maintaining its accuracy loss below a certain threshold. Our future plans include exploring ways to improve the performance of SnakeNet, while also promoting its applicability in a broader range of neural network architectures. We are introducing the ROSIE IFU, an innovative dispersive instrument that uses a volume phase holographic grating to direct a slit into a 1D array, allowing for the acquisition of spectral information across an entire object without requiring a physical extension for each spectrum. This unique technology enhances objects' detailed mapping in the sky with significant cost savings. By utilizing a micro-step motor and a precision translator, ROSIE IFU redefines the concept of pseudo-slit spectroscopy through pseudo-photon imaging, delivering high spatial resolution and continuity across its 6.7 arcseconds field of view. With a detector covering 4340-10300 Angstroms, our instrument offers nine filters for mapping the nebulae and galaxies in various parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. We have successfully tested ROSIE IFU on the 2.5-meter Isaac Newton Telescope at La Palma, exploring its potential for capturing the detail in extensive, extended objects. We have demonstrated the capabilities of this new instrument by presenting two key projects: one on the mapping of the M82 galaxy and another on capturing the dust tails of Nebula NGC 4449, both using its pseudo-slit mode for spatial mapping and spectral analysis. We have found this mode to be suitable for objects up to 200 seconds of arc in size, providing spectral information across its entire field of view with a scale of 0.8 inches or 20 millimeters. We have discovered the mapping of these objects to be highly efficient through pseudo-slit spectroscopy, offering an unprecedented level of detail with nine different spectral views, including various parts of the electromagnetic spectrum, such as ionized oxygen, carbon stars, the color temperature, and dust composition in nebulae and galaxies. With its unique combination of sensitivity, spatial resolution of 14 pixels per second, and a scale of 20 millimeters, our instrument has immense potential for future research in the field of astronomy, allowing for the exploration of extensive objects in the sky with a high degree of precision and detail. We are confident that ROSIE IFU, with its innovative technology and scientific possibilities, will significantly contribute to future research in the field of planetary nebulae, galaxies, and the search for new exoplanets. We look forward to sharing our future discoveries with the scientific community in the years to come. Scientists are using imaging techniques to directly observe exoplanets, and by doing so, are discovering numerous celestial bodies, including potentially Earth-like worlds. Further investigation into these planets is necessary to determine their similarity to our own Earth. To this end, researchers studied the composition and internal structures of ten planets orbiting G-type stars similar to our own Sun, utilizing data from astrophysical models rather than actual observations. To make this comparison feasible, researchers used computational models to build detailed images of the planets' interior and surface, taking into account how these celestial bodies are formed and how they evolve over time. These simulations revealed that many of these exo-Earths are likely composed of iron and silicates similar to our own Earth, although some may have significantly different internal structures. Conversely, larger planets, including those similar in size to our own Jupiter, often have compositions and internal structures that resemble our own Jupiter. Notably, these studies highlight that future telescopes with the ability to detect starlight dimmed by planet orbits may be unable to determine a planet's internal structure or composition without direct observational evidence from future spacecraft missions. Additionally, researchers propose the use of a new and more efficient computational method for simulating planetary composition and internal structures that can be applied to a broader range of celestial bodies. This new approach can accurately simulate various planetary internal structures, including core and mantle separation, and multiple-layered mantles and cores. Furthermore, researchers demonstrate that this method can effectively determine key planetary characteristics and internal structures when combined with external observations of a planet's size, mass, and gravitational strength. To this end, researchers calculate a range of possible internal structures for our own Earth based on different thermal and compositional models. Finally, researchers investigate how a planet's size, mass, and orbital distance relate to its internal structure, composition, and thermal state, and conversely, demonstrate that these factors can be determined through a combination of external observations and simple astrophysical models. To this end, researchers show that a planet's distance from its star and its mass can be determined through a combination of existing stellar data and orbital patterns, and subsequently use these factors to determine a range of possible planetary internal structures and compositions. To facilitate further research and analysis, researchers make their computational models and data available for other scientists to use and expand upon. In massive MIMO systems with extensive pilot training, channel state information can be costly to acquire. We address this challenge by proposing a deep learning-based approach that leverages efficient pilot design to minimize training overhead. To incorporate context and streamline information exchange among layers, we design a neural network architecture with attentional mechanisms applied to individual subchannels. The experimental results demonstrate that utilizing attentional CSI significantly enhances the learning efficiency of our model. Moreover, the results reveal that three key factors contribute to improved performance: enhanced feature extraction, optimized internal model characteristics, and augmented data instances. We find that our attentional CNN yields superior performance while reducing the number of required training samples by half. To achieve this, we capitalize on the property of our optimal pilot structure by creating subchannel attentional learning representations that are useful beyond the original subchannels. Finally, we show that our method achieves a substantial performance gain with reduced pilot overhead, outperforming conventional deep learning-based channels models by a margin of 10%. The experiments were conducted using both real-world LTE data and simulated numerical MIMO scenarios. We anticipate that our work will have practical implications for employing deep learning in massive MIMO systems with limited pilot training resources. Our approach allows for the analysis of both propositional and first-order modal logic within this framework. Furthermore, we identify specific features of the original logic that are reflected in the topological structure, while also introducing new operations that reflect the modal operators. We test our framework through various examples, including combinations of modal logic and intuitionistic disjunction and conjunction. Various fields such as physics, engineering, and biomedical research rely heavily on solving inverse and ill-posed problems. As such problems often lack unique solutions, researchers have turned to neural networks as an innovative approach to tackle these challenges. This tutorial will demonstrate the application of deep learning to two distinct problem types - inverse problems and non-smooth optimization tasks. By covering notable successes as well as essential methodological concepts, this tutorial aims to bridge the gap between computational tomography and broader non-smooth optimization research. Its target audience includes researchers eager to apply neural networks in solving inverse and ill-posed problems, particularly those new to the field who can expect to gain a thorough understanding of the key concepts through the presentation of these ideas. Some of the topics covered include regularizations for inverse problems, data-driven problem formulations, and the applications of non-smooth optimization in neural network design. We explore the relationship between the algebra of class functions on quantum groups, specifically $SU_q(2)$, $GL_q(d)$, and $U_q(f)$, in relation to their respective fundamental cores. We demonstrate that the algebra of class functions forms a maximal abelian self-adjoint algebra (MASA) with respect to these cores under particular deformations of $SU_q(2)$, whereas it does not fulfill this condition for $GL_q(d)$ or $U_q(f)$. Furthermore, we investigate how these results are linked to the existence or absence of a central coordinate in the corresponding quantum groups. Additionally, we examine the actions of quantum groups on compact manifolds and their relationship to the geometric setting, as well as its implications on the algebra of class functions. We conclude by discussing potential generalizations to other quantum groups, including $GL_q(n)$ and $U_q(n)$. Additionally, we address specific questions related to $SU_q(3)$ and $U_q(3)$. Lastly, we outline key outcomes of our study and explain the motivations behind them. Unlike traditional class functions, which consist of central actions on the quantum group itself, the class functions we investigate involve actions on the quantum group's associated dual space, specifically via the quadratic Casimir element. We examine the spectrum of the quadratic Casimir for each of the quantum groups $SU_q(2)$, $GL_q(d)$, and $U_q(f)$. We also discuss the geometric setting of quantum groups on compact manifolds under conventional and deformed settings, as well as its relationship to the core algebra and MASA. Notably, we find that for $GL_q(d)$, the algebra of class functions does not fulfill the MASA condition, whereas for $U_q(f)$, it does so under specific deformations. We explore additional generalizations, including the algebra $U_q(f)$ for $f$ not equal to two, as well as $GL_q(n)$, $U_q(n)$, and $SU_q(3)$.
