We introduce a novel inexact generalization of policy iteration for large-scale multi-dimensional reinforcement learning environments. Building on the theoretical framework of approximate dynamical systems, we develop an inexact framework for policy iteration that enables computation with expressive value function representations. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of inexact policy iteration, achieving speeds up to 40 times faster than traditional policy iteration in large MDPs, while also enabling significant acceleration of online reinforcement learning tasks via the transfer of the inexact framework's value function. Moreover, the inexact framework's value function enables the processing of significantly larger reinforcement learning problems, exceeding 10,000 states, after a one-time investment of at most 20,000 training examples. To realize this, we first establish the expressiveness of our inexact framework's value function, proving its equivalence to an expansive class of value functions for approximately dynamical systems. Next, we tackle the computational challenge of computing the inexact generalization of policy iteration by introducing a reliable method that uses an iterative application of a two-player Nash equilibrium computation in a specific game and yields a sequence of improving policies whose quality converges to the optimal solution. To optimize this process, we also introduce an accelerated version of the method that leverages the geometry of the approximately dynamical system to reduce its computational complexity and achieve a speedup of up to two. Both the original and accelerated versions of the inexact policy iteration method is demonstrated to be the first to achieve near-optimal performance in large-scale MDPs with 10,000 to 100,000 states. Furthermore, the inexact framework's value function is tested in two online reinforcement learning tasks. First, the inexact framework's value function is used to process a 10,000-state MDP in real-time and yields a sequence of optimal policies whose quality exceeds that of prior reinforcement learning methods by at least 10%. Second, the inexact framework's value function is used to process an expansive MDP with 1,000,000 states via the transfer of its value function from a sequence of 10,000-state MDPs. On this large-scale MDP, the inexact framework's value function achieves a 300% increase in reward compared to prior reinforcement learning methods. Finally, the inexact framework's value function is used to derive a new method for computing the optimal solution to large-scale MDPs with 10,000 to 100,000 states in under 10 seconds. We examine weighted oriented graphs and develop criteria to identify those whose edge ideals have equal ordinary and symbolic powers, thus being Borel-fixed. Certain classes of weighted oriented graphs meet this criterion: those with at most three edges connecting any two vertices and either all edges connecting two vertices or none being present. Additionally, we provide a method to calculate the minimal free resolution of an edge ideal associated with a weighted oriented graph. Specifically, for such graphs with at most three edges connecting any two vertices, we formulate a key representation, linking the edge ideal to a module over a Koszul ring. This representation allows us to compute various properties, like the Hilbert series, Hirsch lengths, and Betts invariants for such graphs. Several examples illustrate the applicability of our findings. Furthermore, we propose a conjecture regarding Borel-fixed graphs, suggesting that those with only three edges connecting any two vertices qualify. This is validated for certain categories of graphs, including those resembling K_4 and being bipartite, as well as those whose edges connect two vertices in the same weight group. Importantly, we demonstrate the significance of these graph structures through the calculation of Betts invariants. This study's success is further highlighted by the determination of Borel-fixed oriented linear graphs, as well as a classification of oriented linear trees with equal ordinary and symbolic powers of their edge ideals. Finally, we examine bipartite Borel-fixed graphs, showing that only those with only three edges connecting any two vertices qualify, with the exception of those whose edges connect two vertices in the same weight group. This complements our study on Borel-fixed graphs. Specifically, we show that those whose edges connect two vertices in the same weight group are linear, as well as those whose edges connect two vertices in different weight groups are trees. A key tool in our study is the development of edge ideal of a weighted oriented bipartite Borel-fixed graph being linear, as well as those whose edges connect two vertices in different weight groups are trees. We address the challenge of inferring past real-time states of a system from current and historical data within a Bayesian framework, using a computer simulator that models physical phenomena such as thermal systems. As the inverse problem is known to be under-determined, reconstructing the past real-time states exactly is impractical. Therefore, the focus is on finding the most likely past real states given current and historical data, rather than exact reconstructions. To account for any uncertainties associated with measurements and physical models, the posterior distribution of past states is modeled. Since directly sampling from this distribution is under-determined, a Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling method is employed, using an informative prior that is not certain but tends to guide the sampling towards plausible solutions. To refine this prior and concentrate the posterior distribution, an iterative process is performed. Furthermore, an initial set of simulated data is generated to inform a uniform prior, and subsequent iterations utilize the knowledge gained from previous iterations to refine this prior. To ensure that this informed prior remains unbiased, a review of past research is conducted, and any new insights is incorporated into the prior to maintain objectivity. The efficacy of this approach is validated through experiments involving a reduced-scale thermal system, where various measurement schemes and simulation protocols are tested to provide general applicability and feasibility of this proposed method. In addition, an open-source code is provided for use in similar thermal recovery projects, allowing for replication of these experiments and verification of the proposed method. In conclusion, the proposed method effectively infers real-time states of a thermal system by leveraging computer simulation, providing valuable insights into the process. In the scenario of distribution-free robust learning, we study concept classes defined by spheres in metric spaces. For fixed amounts of contamination and tolerance for error, our research identifies the fundamental limits on the possibility of learning these classes. Specifically, we demonstrate that the radius of the query can be seen as a type of dimension, as the measure of the boundary region grows polynomially in that radius. Our results indicate that achieving consistent learning outcomes in such classes requires a sample size that increases exponentially in the radius, given fixed values for contamination and error tolerance. Conversely, when the sample size is sufficiently large, we can rigorously bound the amount of contamination or error tolerance, given fixed values for the radius and error tolerance. To investigate these issues, we develop novel applications of the half-space complexity, its connection to the geometry of convex bodies, as well as a new type of covering lemma for convex bodies. Our research also encompasses the scenario of unknown amounts of contamination, leading to the discovery of an interesting phase transition, where the sample size necessitates an exponential increase in the radius, at least assuming the existence of a solution to a certain non-uniform learning problem for half-spaces. This paper broadens the scope of robust learning by allowing for non-real-valued outputs, while the added insight of the phase transition is also presented. Furthermore, we study the scenario of learning a single hypothesis under batch adversarial corruption with bounded amounts of contamination, where we identify the sample complexity requirements that are both necessary and sufficient, given fixed values for corruption and error tolerance. This research also leads to the discovery that achieving consistent learning outcomes in such classes necessitates a sample size that increases polynomially in the radius, when the corruption is uniform and with fixed values for error tolerance. When the corruption is non-uniform, we study the fundamental limits on the possibility of learning these classes, given fixed amounts of contamination and tolerance for error, yielding an almost identical bound on the sample complexity requirements that is both necessary and sufficient. To investigate these issues, we develop a new application of the half-space complexity, as well as connections between geometry of convex bodies, boundedly vulnerable half-spaces and non-real-valued outputs. To conclude, we study the scenario of learning a single hypothesis under batch adversarial corruption with bounded amounts of contamination, where we identify the sample complexity requirements that are both necessary and sufficient, given fixed amounts of corruption and tolerance for error, leading to an almost identical bound in the scenario of distribution-free robust learning. A crucial element in understanding galaxy evolution, star formation rates have various measurement methods, including an approach based on stellar spectra through the use of spectroscopic features. However, the accuracy of these rates can be influenced by factors other than star formation, such as dust, so a comprehensive framework is needed to assess their reliability. Using a suite of realistic galaxy models and the Prospector Bayesian inference software to analyze a collection of deep optical and UV spectra from the MaNGA survey, this study evaluates various methods of calculating star formation rates and other stellar populations characteristics. By examining likelihood ratios, the study finds that H-alpha flux measurements are the most sensitive to changes in star formation rates, while broad-band photometry and UV flux measurements are more resistant to dust effects. However, all methods of calculating star formation rates are more trustworthy when based on older, more precise measurements of stellar ages rather than using likelihood ratios or broad-band photometry alone. Additionally, the study uses mock observations to investigate how uncertainties in star formation history, stellar feedback, and dust effects impact the inference of star formation rates, finding that these factors generally have the least effect when the star formation history is well-defined or when a flat star formation history is assumed. Finally, the study finds that using a combination of spectral, photometric, and spectral features yields the most precise measurements of star formation rates with a typical error of about 0.1-0.2 decades per decade. Although the MaNGA survey's selection function can slightly underestimate star formation rates in the blueest, most abundant galaxies by about 0.1 decades, the use of stellar ages and a combination of spectral, photometric, and spectral features helps to mitigate this bias, resulting in highly reliable estimates of star formation rates for a wide range of galaxy types. Based on these results, the study calculates star formation rates for a sample of over 1,600 MaNGA galaxies with measured H-alpha fluxes. Traditional time series forecasting methods often treat time as a categorical variable, ignoring the ordering. While this method works well for short-term forecasting, it falls short for long-term predictions due to its failure to capture this ordering. To address this limitation, a new approach is proposed, accounting for the gradual nature of time by modeling duration and generating new time series data, thereby enhancing short-term, operational predictive models. This method involves three main steps. Firstly, a new time series data generation technique based on the scaling of duration is developed, to create a standardized duration curve. Secondly, a new model called DMD (Duration multi-variate exponential model) is developed, to describe and forecast a variety of durations. To begin with, a new model called GMD (Gaussian Duration Multi-variate Double Exponential model) is developed, to describe a single duration. The development of the GMD employs a new variate generation technique based on the scaling of duration. Thirdly, the multi-variate nature of durations is handled by introducing a new independent uniform prior on the scale parameter of the GMD, which leads to the development of the non-informative prior on the shape parameter of the GMD. Finally, a new approach is introduced to handle censored durations. To demonstrate the superiority of this new approach, a comprehensive empirical study is conducted, by comparing its performance with the current best predictive model using the Binary Spatial Model. The results show that the average performance of this new approach on 112 real-world duration curves is 0.1076 points higher than the Binary Spatial Model. To further confirm the superiority of this new approach, a comprehensive theoretical study is conducted, by comparing its performance with the current best predictive model using the Binomial Spatial Model. To create a more accurate model of type Ia supernovae variability, we added a correlation penalty term to a Bayesian additive regression tree model previously developed. The updated model, which we also applied to real-world data sets, effectively minimizes thermal noise and compensates for biases. Our primary analysis involved the SDSS-II SN dataset, but we also modeled individual SN IIa events, taking into account photometry observations between 300-400 nm. Our results indicate that, on average, the model achieves an $r^2$ score of 0.965 across all light curves, with individual SN IIa events scoring between 0.90 and 0.995. Furthermore, we incorporated Monte Carlo simulations to assess various aspects of our model's performance and determined that it can provide a more precise estimation of variability, especially when sample sizes are limited. We compared our model to a conventional parameter-based approach, revealing a notable improvement in $r^2$ scores of approximately 0.05. We anticipate that our model will contribute to the development of more robust supernovae cosmology and facilitate novel scientific discoveries by allowing for a more detailed understanding of variability. Additionally, our work could potentially be applied to other fields where signal enhancement and parameter correlation identification are crucial. We intend to apply our model to the upcoming LSST dataset, which is expected to contain approximately 300,000 supernovae, with the aim of gaining deeper insights into variability and cosmological parameters. The behavior of particles suspended in a turbulent jet of varying density has been investigated through a numerical simulation method called Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS). The study, set within a two-dimensional framework, uncovered the physical processes governing particle entrainment when the plume exhibits stable or unstable behavior. The observation that more particles are drawn into the jet when the plume's density is higher than the surrounding fluid, rather than lower, was attributed to the presence of an intense vortex. This phenomenon occurs due to the interaction between the particle's mobility and the fluid's movements, causing it to penetrate further into the jet when the particle is denser. The resulting distribution of particle positions across the jet axis was analyzed, revealing a skewed pattern that can be mathematically represented using a weighted normal function. A weighted variance metric, accounting for the influence of particle mass, was developed to quantify the dispersion of particles within the jet. The application of this new variance metric made it possible to apply the established maximum mixing theory to predict the maximum height and width of the particle cloud, as well as the rate at which particles are released into the surrounding fluid. The resulting theoretical predictions matched the experimentally measured values, demonstrating strong agreement. The study's findings are particularly relevant to the understanding of particle entrainment in oceanic upwelling events. The confirmation of maximum mixing theory's applicability to this two-component system has significant implications, given that it is often utilized in the study of single-density jet discharges. The observed behavior of particle entrainment can be utilized to forecast the consequences of varying particle density and mass on flux calculations. These fields become forced in a star's interior by buoyancy, causing oscillations to amplify and magnetic cycles to emerge, such as in the case of Prairie Fire. By using 3D simulations of magnetic and hydrodynamic processes, we found that a star like to be similar to Prairie Fire in terms of its magnetic characteristics, given its rapid rotation and strong internal magnetic field. However, we observed that a star with parameters identical to Prairie Fire's at the end of its life cycle still exhibits a less intense magnetic field compared to the star itself, indicating that a dynamos self-regulation mechanism is at play. These results imply that a star's magnetic field may be less intense than expected, which has important implications for the development of dynamos in stars with parameters similar to Prairie Fire's. Additionally, we found that a star's magnetic field increases significantly if it rotates slower, which could explain the extremely intense magnetic field observed in the star in question. Nonetheless, we stress that a proper 3D simulation of a specific star is indispensable for a precise evaluation of a star's magnetic activity. The development of multi-task learning models poses a difficulty in balancing performance for various tasks, as different datasets often necessitate distinct model architectures. To address this, a new model is proposed, consisting of an ensemble of neural networks, each specializing in a separate task and trained independently. To facilitate shared learning, the model exploits similarities between tasks through substitution, replacing a task's input with processed outputs from other tasks. This ensemble model enhances both its components and overall performance, particularly in cases with multiple inputs and outputs. Technically, the model is implemented as a neural network generator that accepts a variety of task sets and outputs optimized ensemble configurations. This is achieved through module duplication, shared parameter integration, and task-sensitive fine-tuning of the models within the ensemble. Evaluations on twelve datasets involving six models and eight tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of this ensemble model in improving performance while also reducing overfitting. Additionally, the model's capability to integrate various models and tasks enables the creation of an efficient workflow for task-oriented dataset design. Further analyses indicate that the model's success stems from its ability to adapt its configurations to each task, as validated through comparisons with other models and tasks. This leads to potential applications in reducing dataset requirements and streamlining practical dataset design for specific learning goals. Multi-threaded operation assessment has become increasingly crucial due to the expanding utilization of parallelism in software development. Existing models, however, have been limited by their inability to keep up with modern performance standards, forcing developers to compress a full program into a reduced form that can be evaluated by a model. Our novel model checker, McMini, employs an advanced, virtualized environment for multi-threaded program analysis, enabling a precise, user-defined level of precision while significantly boosting checking speed by at least 200 times. By optimizing McMini's logical foundation and leveraging a sophisticated, adaptive model, we achieve an efficient model checker capable of checking actual McMini programs 2-10 times faster than the fastest existing model, with virtualized performance comparable to practical hardware models. Additionally, McMini's flexible design enables the model to be applied to a range of problems, including program verification, property verification, and fairness analysis. Our model checker's specifications, experiments, and results are available online. McMini is now open-source under the permissive BSD license at our website. Specifically, our model and proof system for multi-threaded programs with dynamic memory allocation outperform the state-of-the-art model by at least a factor of 200, while our model and fairness analysis algorithm exceed the performance of the best existing model to our knowledge, requiring only 2-10 times more computational resources to achieve a degree of precision 2-10 times greater. Moreover, our model and proof system for multi-threaded programs with pointers demonstrate superior checking speeds, reaching rates of up to 987, 471, and 40 operations per second respectively, far surpassing the performance of the best existing model to our knowledge, which checked similar programs at rates of 10, 3, and 0 operations per second. Nonetheless, our model and fairness analysis algorithm are yet to be applied to the most complex multi-threaded programs with dynamic memory allocation. With the ongoing advancements in hardware capabilities and the rising importance of parallelism in software development, the need for efficient and precise verification methods for complex multi-threaded programs is likely to persist in the future. Mobile messaging apps have become dominant means of data transfer, enabling rapid dissemination of information, including false claims and urban legends. In an effort to mitigate the spread of misinformation, WhatsApp has introduced a feature allowing users to view photos and videos received via the app before they are saved to a device's local storage, along with an option to forward them. As part of our efforts to combat the spread of misinformation on WhatsApp, we examined user behavior when viewing potentially misleading media content, comparing their response to both misleading and authentic images and videos. Our study revealed that, when encountering suspicious media, users tend to exhibit caution, examining them more thoroughly than authentic content, but also failing to distinguish misleading material from genuine images and videos in roughly two out of five cases. Interestingly, users seem to be more vigilant with forwarded content, examining it more closely and making more attempts to save it. Notably, distinguishing misleading videos appears more challenging for users than identifying false images. In light of these findings, we propose the development of an AI-powered tool capable of detecting misinformation in media, along with the potential benefits and limitations of this tool, and other strategies to curb the spread of false information on WhatsApp. Our study serves as a basis for further research into detecting misleading media and highlighting the need for more effective measures to address the spread of misinformation. Our analysis also sheds light on user behavior when interacting with potentially false images and videos with a view to developing targeted strategies to curb their dissemination. In doing so, we seek to foster a more reflective dialogue on online content moderation and the intricate interplay between user behavior and technological advancements. Our study has far-reaching implications for Facebook's mission to enhance the lives of the global community through technology. In a homogeneous population under neutral evolution, infinitely small mutations occur according to a Poisson distribution and each individual experiences one mutation per unit of time. The population then undergoes a random reorganization each unit of time through a random sampling from the current population members, resulting in a fraction $\frac{m}{M}$ of individuals selected for the next generation. We introduce a generative model that captures this evolutionary process: a multitype infinite exchangeable partition process (MEPP) in combination with a spatial component, and derive its distributional properties by first establishing an equivalent Markov process and subsequently deriving its distributional properties as $m$ tends to 0 in a fixed population, and as both $m$ and $M$ tend to 0 in a population with constant population size. We apply this model to estimate the effect of a mutation on the long-run frequency of a specific mutation in a White population as described by Cavalli's model, and calculate the long-run average number of types in a population with $(m/M)^n$ types, for $n=1,2,\ldots$. Cucuy (the Aztec toppling game) also appears to be related to this model as described above. We confirm this by first establishing a Markov process based on Cucuy and then proving its distributional properties as $m$ tends to 0 in a fixed population. Cucuy turns out to be equivalent to our model with $(m/M)^n$ types, for $n=1,2,\ldots$, having a frequency distribution that corresponds to the number of white balls picked from a population of non-white and white balls, where the number of balls in the population and the number of white balls are both unknown. We apply this model to estimate the probability that a mutation will be retained for a long time in a population of Aztec particles that contains a large number of non-aztec particles and a small number of aztec particles, and calculate the probability that the largest aztec particle in a population will split in two, and the time it will take for this process to happen. We apply this model to estimate the probability that mutations in a white population will be retained for a long time in a population of berries, where the number of white berries and the number of non-white berries are both unknown, and where each unit of time the population will either experience a mutation or a sampling process. We investigate the properties of correlated photon pairs produced through spontaneous four-wave mixing in a silicon microdisk, where the pump beam can be adjusted in angle and linear polarization. By leveraging a combined approach of theoretical modeling and experimental manipulation of the pump beam, we gain insight into the local vacuum fields and their correlations. Notably, we demonstrate that reversing the propagation direction of the pump beam significantly enhances certain coherence functions of the photon pairs, while also maintaining others largely unaffected. This phenomenon can be attributed to the microdisk's non-uniform and anisotropic properties. Furthermore, our research paves the way for the development of new techniques to characterize the local vacuum fields and their correlations, ultimately enabling enhanced performance in specific applications of quantum processing. We discuss potential future experiments that could verify our theoretical predictions and discuss their implications for the production of entangled photons in microdisk systems. Additionally, our methods can be applied to other micro- and nanostructured systems, such as microresonators and photonic crystal cavities. Furthermore, these techniques can also be used in silicon chip-based technology to create sources of entangled photons. Our research primarily focuses on the production of entangled photons, a key resource for quantum computation and other advanced photonic technologies. Silicon wafers with different surface treatments were investigated through near-infrared photoluminescence to compare carrier concentrations in etched and unetched samples. Various etching chemicals were used to analyze the effect of different processes on carrier concentrations. The results showed that etched silicon exhibits a higher carrier concentration compared to buffer oxide etched silicon. Furthermore, the study examined the influence of surface passivation on carrier concentration using two common etching processes. XPS and PL measurements were also employed to analyze the surface properties of silicon wafers. Additionally, the study achieved non-destructive mapping of carrier concentrations using a sensitive PL measurement technique combined with scanning confocal microscopy. To verify the accuracy of the approach, the results were compared to HgProbes measurements. The research identified two distinct regions in the PL spectrum: a high-energy zone associated with carrier concentrations of 10^15-10^16 cm^-3 and a low-energy zone linked to carrier concentrations of 10^14 cm^-3. By integrating near-infrared PL and HgProbes measurements, the results demonstrated strong agreement, demonstrating the effectiveness of the approach for non-destructive mapping of carrier concentrations. The research concluded by discussing potential applications and limitations of the approach, including the detection of carrier concentrations in silicon wafers with different resistivities and the identification of the spatial uniformity of carrier concentrations in photovoltaic silicon wafers treated with the etching process. The research identified type-inversion regions resulting from the etching process and demonstrated the potential of the approach to monitor the evolution of carrier concentrations during industrial production. Furthermore, the results showed the feasibility of using the technique for surface inspection in silicon wafers with a resistivity of up to 10^14 cm^-3. However, due to the limitations revealed by HgProbes measurements, the research concluded that the technique cannot reliably map carrier concentrations in high-resistivity silicon wafers. The research concluded by highlighting the prospects of integrating near-infrared PL and HgProbes measurements for non-destructive mapping of carrier concentrations in silicon materials. The research identified areas for further improvement, including increasing the sensitivity of the approach to carrier concentrations of 10^13 cm^-3 and integrating other measurement techniques to verify the results and enhance the accuracy of the approach. Furthermore, although it has been proven that $2^{\aleph_1}$ is the maximum number of closed sets that can be isolated, our research reveals a difference in cardinality between isolating Borel sets and closed sets. Additionally, exploring similar problems with Lebesgue measurable sets led to the discovery of a maximum $2^{\aleph_1}$ for both isolating and non-isolating sets, indicating that Meager sets cannot achieve this maximum number, and finally establishing the maximum number of null sets that can be isolated or non-isolating as $2^{2^{\aleph_1}}$. It is worth noting that the upper bounds found in this research could be reduced to $2\cdot2^{\aleph_1}$ or even $\aleph_2$ in certain instances, although this remains a subject for further investigation. Finally, in the course of this research, an independent finding confirmed that continuous images of the irrational line cannot be precisely replicated using Borel functions, a result previously encountered by the author but also independently verified by Stephen Tracz. Specifically, it was demonstrated that its continuous images cannot be exactly replicated using projects of the irrationals, and further research identified the smallest category with a project of $2^{\aleph_1}$, and also determined the category of Borel functions whose images of irrationals fall within $F_{\sigma}$ sets. Evaluating times of MTM (Moment of Truth) events which highlight CTAs' favored trading times, our analysis indicates that these advisors tend to initiate long positions during MTM periods and CTAs typically take short positions during other periods. Both groups appear to benefit from their strategies as both long and short positions yield positive returns. Notably, our results also show that CTA's optimal trading decisions coincide with their overall performance during MTM periods, whereas this correlation is absent during other periods. Our findings are consistent with advisors specializing in specific market patterns and highlight the potential for mutual benefit in trading strategies that leverage these patterns. Our research also validates the use of MTM events to fine-tune trading approaches tailored to individual market segments within Commodity Futures Markets. As a byproduct of our study, we have created eight distinct sub-categories within these markets, depending on the trading environments identified. Our analysis indicates that MTM periods are predominantly found in Gold, Crude Oil, and Nymex Natural Gas, whereas the Japanese Yen and Light Mini are characterized by few MTM periods, often overlapping with periods of Volatility. Our research sheds light on the intricacies of Commodity Futures Markets, prompting further investigation into the implications of CTA's specialized trading approaches, potentially informed by CTA's performance indicators. Evasion attacks can render Dynamic Protocol Detection (DPD) mechanisms ineffective in network monitoring, causing false negatives. To counter this, a proposed method enhances the accuracy of DPD by incorporating a statistical analysis technique based on the maximum likelihood principle. This methodrecovers the proxy IP addresses used by evasive attackers and updates DPD rules to exclude those involved. Results from testing this method against sophisticated evasion attacks indicate a significant reduction in false negatives and false positives. Furthermore, an economic analysis confirms that the costs associated with evasive actions are minimized when DPD is improved in this manner. Existing DPD systems are also evaluated for their susceptibility to evasion attacks, and a comparative assessment is conducted of machine learning algorithms used in DPD to determine their effectiveness in detecting evasive behavior. Although these algorithms demonstrate improved performance, they are found to be ineffective against sophisticated evasion attacks and do not compare favorably to the proposed method in terms of accuracy and costs associated with evasive actions. Additionally, an investigation is undertaken into the availability of evasive tools on the Dark Web to determine the likelihood of their use by attackers. A subsequent study examines the efficacy of evasive tools in circumventing DPD-based mechanisms. Ultimately, a comprehensive framework for a DPD system is proposed, incorporating statistical analysis, economic evaluation, assessment of existing solutions, an analysis of evasive tools, and a review of best practices for improving the effectiveness of DPD mechanisms. This framework can serve as a guide for network administrators and DPD system developers seeking to enhance their DPD mechanisms to counter evasion attacks. As a result, there is an increasing need to evaluate generalization performance beyond the scope of initial training datasets. Extrapolation can be systematic (e.g. testing images of cats on a model trained on dogs) or stochastic (e.g. testing larger images). Existing theories fall short in addressing systematic extrapolation and both types of stochastic extrapolation. This paper presents a framework called 'Simple Counting' that explains generalization through the prediction of successful counting models within a fixed scope of training data. We show that Simple Counting accommodates various types of stochastic extrapolation while offering an initial insight into systematic extrapolation. Moreover, the concepts of Generalization by Counting (GBC) and Simple Counting together provide robust predictions for both types of stochastic extrapolation that outperform current best benchmarks. Conversely, attempts to apply these ideas to systematic extrapolation yield subpar performance. We support the claims made in this paper with extensive empirical evidence from image classification and generative modeling domains. Moreover, the idea of Generalization by Counting can be used to create effective sampling strategies that predict when an additional training example will improve the model's performance or degrade it. We present a simple yet powerful algorithm called Sample or Waste (SoW), which uses Simple Counting to decide whether to retain or discard a newly acquired example during the training process. By combining SoW with fixed training data, we achieve superior generalization performance in comparison to fixed training sizes for various deep learning models across image classification, object detection, and generative modeling applications. Researchers have introduced various modifications to the classic Bloom filter in an attempt to create more efficient data storage solutions with reduced error rates. Specifically, the xor filter has been developed as a variant of Bloom filters, boasting equivalent or in some cases superior performance. Our investigation focused on determining the error-resistance capabilities of the xor filter, with particular emphasis on its behavior under various attack strategies. We conducted an in-depth analysis of the xor filter's performance across a range of different paradigms, including random and structured probing scenarios. Our results indicate that, when subjected to random testing, the error rates of xor filters closely resemble those of standard Bloom filters. However, in cases involving structured probing, the performance differential between xor filters and traditional Bloom filters becomes more pronounced. To mitigate these discrepancies, we have proposed an optimized variant, dubbed enhanced xor filter, of the xor filter. This advanced variant incorporates an additional layer of security, involving the utilization of specific intersection patterns, to further minimize error rates. Our study's results reveal that, in instances of structured probing, the error rates of the enhanced xor filter significantly outperform those of the standard Bloom filter, achieving a reduction of up to 4 orders of magnitude in error rates with only a relatively minor increase in memory requirements. Our experimental findings are backed by the implementation of a corresponding prototype, open-sourced on GitHub, which validates the efficacy of the enhanced xor filter against a range of different attack strategies, including both random and structured probing scenarios. To facilitate the evaluation of various probing strategies, our implementation also features a customizable probing engine. In addition to the potential of minimizing error rates, another significant advantage of the enhanced xor filter is its capacity to support a broad spectrum of applications. ETFs are widely held by investors and can be seen as mini-index funds, offering a more cost-effective alternative to traditional index funds. As a result, their price fluctuations reflect broader market trends, making them useful for trading and investment purposes. Despite this, few studies focus on how quickly ETF price movements capture market direction. To address this gap, we used autoregressive vector autoregression models to analyze the temporal framework for trend inference in ETF price movements. Our findings indicate that most ETFs require at least a few days for price movements to convey meaningful market information. Our research also reveals that past transactions can influence the time frame for trend inference, as seen in highly traded ETFs. Despite advancements in classification model performance, detecting deepfakes remains a challenging task, especially in real-world applications where data conditions are unpredictable. Our proposed framework, DEEPFIYER, addresses this limitation by designing two novel, unsupervised few-shot learning schemes. This research explores various atmospheric scenarios for Earth-sized planets with distinct masses, focusing on the primary components of carbon and nitrogen within their atmospheres. We incorporate the effects of temperature and pressure on gas resolution and mixability, as well as modeling the processes of gas exchange and atmospheric escape in order to determine the similarities and differences between small and massive atmospheres. It is discovered that temperate planets with masses much smaller or larger than Earth typically have atmospheres composed primarily of different gases. For example, less massive atmospheres are predominantly made up of molecular nitrogen, while more massive atmospheres are predominantly composed of hydrogen and oxygen, due to enhanced escape rates. We utilize these models to simulate various observational signatures, including the presence of specific molecules and the planet's radii and transmission spectra. The key outcomes of this research are as follows: 1) different atmospheric masses lead to distinct atmospheric properties and behaviors; 2) accurate modeling of atmospheric escape and gas exchange is essential for generating reliable observations; 3) a broader range of atmospheric masses and compositions is possible on small and massive planets; 4) massive atmospheres on highly eccentric planets are susceptible to erosion and can be lost during close approaches to the star; 5) magnetic fields can shield small and massive atmospheres and prevent them from freezing or escaping. This study highlights the necessity of considering atmospheric evolution in the analysis and interpretation of exoplanet data, particularly for small and massive planets that differ from Earth in their atmospheric compositions. A recent paper proposes a neural network architecture based on the McCulloch-Pitts model, which includes a novel synaptic connection rule that utilizes local information from its neighbors. This connection rule generates a dynamic system capable of producing complex, persistent cycles. However, when attempting to apply conventional gradient-based optimization methods, the resulting dynamics exhibit oscillatory behavior rather than converging to a stable point. To overcome this limitation, the author investigates alternative optimization methods that leverage the persistent cycle phenomenon in the McCulloch-Pitts network. Notably, the study demonstrates that both Maximum-A-Likelihood and Generative Adversarial Network approaches encounter convergence issues during the training process. In contrast, the author successfully trains a deep McCulloch-Pitts network using Evolutionary Algorithms, showcasing its potential for solving meaningful regression tasks. Additionally, the study explores the structural properties of the obtained persistent cycles and reveals a unique characteristic of the McCulloch-Pitts network, which hinders its capability to perform classification tasks efficiently. Based on these findings, the author concludes that the McCulloch-Pitts network has promising applications in reinforcement learning and function approximation, but may encounter difficulties in classification problems compared to more conventional neural networks. The significant advancement in Scene Text Recognition (STR) has been facilitated by the establishment of extensive, widely-accessible datasets such as ICDAR-2017. These datasets have enabled researchers to gain insights into their respective challenges and develop novel techniques for solving the complex problem of STR. Despite achieving state-of-the-art performance in STR using data augmentation and neural network architectures, these approaches are hindered by their reliance on seen words in the training corpus, limiting their capacity to recognize out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words. To address this limitation, we present a new dataset named Reading Between Lines (RBL) consisting of 198k words not seen in the training corpus of commonly used STR datasets, including 64k new words in the training corpus of ICDAR-17. We name this new dataset as RBL-17. RBL-17 has been validated as an essential resource for enhancing STR models, and data augmentation methods can be used effectively to improve STR models by mitigating the impact of missing seen words. Furthermore, we demonstrate the superiority of STR models using Neural Networks and Transforms-based approaches on various benchmarks containing RBL-17, achieving new benchmarks for comparison with future research. Validated numerics provides evidence that a computed solution closely matches the exact one in a specific sense. This approach can aid in isolating distinct solution branches in a system that changes with parameters by illustrating the exact solution trajectories in the space of those parameters. Averaging represents a useful method for diminishing the impact of rapid frequency variations on large-scale solution behavior in such parameter-dependent systems. This research demonstrates the integration of validated numerics and averaging to obtain rigorous bounds on solution trajectories in an example model featuring a critical transition. As a result, we can confirm that certain key features of the solution occur at specific parameter values and that the approach can be adapted to other systems involving conservation laws. Unlike other methods, this technique does not require solutions to be known in advance but instead allows for successively refining the valid approximation of the solution at different scale levels. Ultimately, this research illustrates a unique combination of techniques that can be applied to identify and analyze distinct solution behaviors in complex parameter-dependent systems and their periodic variations. The work described here also relates to problems of existence and uniqueness in the related system of functional differential equations. To develop training data for machine learning models, an effective technique is proposed to gather labeled information through a series of questions posed to human experts, essentially treating the experts as a special type of data annotation tool. To streamline this process, a method called selective labeling is implemented, where the model only seeks labeled responses for specific, challenging cases it anticipates will be difficult for the experts to answer or require complex expertise to label accurately. To achieve this, the model must first learn to recognize these situations, making it a multi-objective optimization problem. In addition to efficiency, another key consideration is ensuring that the model does not take advantage of the experts' generosity by only asking easy tasks while relying on the experts to correct its obvious mistakes. To address this issue, a mechanism called defensiveness is introduced, where the model verifies that its proposed sampling plan is not biased towards easier instances or cases that are clearly incorrect before implementing it. Defensiveness comes with its own set of challenges, primarily as it complicates finding an optimal sampling strategy, necessitating a local optimality condition that is difficult to meet in many scenarios. To overcome this limitation, a more conservative approach is proposed, where a simpler, more transparent strategy is adopted that still offers substantial benefits in terms of reduced labeling costs. Experimental results confirm that the model can successfully identify when expert help is required and when a single attempt will suffice. Furthermore, the benefits of selective labeling extend to classification tasks with similar results, where it outperforms existing techniques in reducing labeling costs while achieving nearly identical accuracy. To enhance the efficiency of models via network pruning, researchers frequently employ a two-stage approach, involving training and pruning. It is generally acknowledged that separating these processes can yield sub-optimal results. Our research focuses on incorporating both training and pruning into a single cohesive approach. We propose ClickTrain, a innovative pruning technique that utilizes a distinct set of parameters for both the pruned and un-pruned model. The core idea of ClickTrain is to optimize the un-pruned model in tandem with the pruned one by selectively activating parameters during training. This novel approach yields superior results, as evaluations across various datasets have demonstrated. Specifically, we observe improved accuracy after every pruning step for models such as ResNet, MobileNet, and Vision Transformer models, whereas existing methods may encounter declining performance. Moreover, our approach is unique in that it can accommodate diverse types of pruning, including structured, un-structured, quantization, and pruning with expanded model capacities. Comprehensive experiments have yielded comprehensive insights into how our method functions. Furthermore, we explore the potential of transferring the pruned weights of a trainer to a distinct set of parameters, thereby expanding the realm of applications where such weights can be utilized. Our findings have shown that even without fine-tuning, the weights can still serve as a benchmark for evaluation, thereby reducing the complexity involved in pruning. Ultimately, our research has laid the groundwork for future endeavors in neural network pruning, showcasing its versatility and capability in transforming the process of pruning. The existing proof methods for classical modal logics, based on Kripke semantics, are not readily applicable to the substructural variants. Our work overcomes this challenge, allowing us to adapt the techniques of relational semantics and establish duality theorems for specific families of substructural modal logics. These theorems can be utilized to prove equivalence between certain substructural modal calculi and their corresponding semantic structures. We demonstrate duality theorems for four distinct families of substructural modal logics, each tailored to one of the four types of Kripke semantics for classical modal logic. Our methods also provide a flexible framework for constructing models of substructural modal theories. This approach can be extended to other families of substructural modal logics by adding additional axioms to the underlying theory of domains and continuous posets. We outline potential directions for future research in this area. To date, our techniques have not been used to construct models for substructural modal logics with independence axioms. If the independence axioms can be rewritten as a finite set of equivalent axioms, our method may be applicable. If the axioms are themselves infinite in size, as is the case with the axioms of translation, constructing a model using our approach is not feasible. A special model, designed specifically to handle the axioms of translation, has been constructed separately. A continuous poset for the axioms of translation involves an infinite sequence of elements with increasing size, where each element reflects the interpretation of the axioms in a finite sub-system and where the limit of this sequence represents the interpretation of the infinite axioms. The discovery of gravitational waves from merging compact objects provides novel opportunities to test how general relativity governs the behavior of dense stars under extreme conditions. Observing the electromagnetic radiation from these events allows for a comprehensive understanding, but predicting the presence and characteristics of visible emissions from compact mergers remains a significant challenge. Our study focuses on the analysis of Nice model inspirals, specifically examining the properties of neutron star--neutron star and neutron star--black hole mergers that generate low-luminosity signatures. Our findings indicate that even among inspirals with similar orbital characteristics, significant variations occur in their predicted electromagnetic radiation output. This variability arises from the presence of residual disk matter around the merging stars, which is influenced by the outer edge of the disk's extent and the stars' magnetic field strengths. Our research suggests that a broad range of low-luminosity emissions may accompany the gravitational waves produced during such mergers, with a substantial fraction of these events potentially being detectable by space-based telescopes like James Webb Space Telescope across various distances. Our results highlight the significance of incorporating advanced magnetic transport and disk fragmentation into models to improve our understanding of electromagnetic emissions from these mergers, as well as the requirement for high-resolution simulations of the disk's behavior and the merging stars' magnetic fields to accurately predict the presence and characteristics of visible emissions. Our study paves the way for a new class of gravitational waves with identifiable electromagnetic counterparts, which could be used to investigate the behavior of dense stars under extreme conditions in the near future. Our approach also demonstrates how machine learning algorithms can be utilized to generate distinct signatures for various physical processes in compact object mergers, with a potential application in analyzing future observations. Our study is the first to apply a sophisticated model of disk evolution and fragmentation to neutron star--black hole mergers, revealing an unforeseen enhancement in the electromagnetic radiation output compared to previously expected levels. Furthermore, our research indicates that a considerable number of neutron star--black hole and neutron star--neutron star mergers may result in the formation of a dense disk around the merging stars, which could be responsible for generating low-luminosity electromagnetic emissions. Our findings show that even among inspirals exhibiting similar orbital characteristics, notable variations occur in their predicted electromagnetic radiation output, highlighting the necessity to examine the detailed behavior of the merging stars and their magnetic fields. We show that this correlation function can be derived from a quantum system embedded in a higher-dimensional relational theory. Furthermore, our findings reveal that the nonlocality of pure states and their relative entropy are linked, and we propose a method for achieving nonlocality in classical systems through the use of predictive encoding. Lastly, our work discloses a hidden aspect of quantum nonlocality associated with the NMR demonstration of quantum nonlocality, and we contend that this feature is inherent to all quantum nonlocality demonstrations using such a model. We conclude by outlining potential future research avenues. Moreover, our study may facilitate a shift from viewing nonlocality and contextuality as distinct properties to recognizing them as interconnected aspects of quantum physics. Additionally, our work offers a new approach for designing nonlocality in quantum states and a powerful tool for verifying contextuality in quantum systems - the contextuality score. This contextuality score can be used to quantify the degree of contextuality exhibited by any quantum state and potentially by any classical correlation, and it has been successfully applied to reproduce the contextuality of the NMR model, as well as to identify the contextuality of the recently demonstrated nuclear spin system. We also demonstrate the utility of the contextuality score by calculating the contextuality of all entangled Bell states and exploring its relationships with other measures of quantum nonlocality and entanglement. Furthermore, our work may lead to the development of new methods for achieving nonlocality in quantum states using classical systems and potentially paves the way for a simplified NMR demonstration of nonlocality without compromising its quantum nature. Moreover, our study opens up prospects for using nonlocality, contextuality, and entanglement as interchangeable and useful resources in quantum computing and information technologies. This inquiry stems from previous work by Marsh and Vandehey, who identified a range of 'unwritable' numbers in base 10 that cannot be expressed as palindromic expressions. Our work seeks to expand upon this by examining the same concept in bases higher than 10. To do this, we must establish the maximum possible length of palindromic expressions that do not repeat and cannot be expressed as a sum of existing ones. Ultimately, we find that the density of unwritable integers in base b is positive, assuming a certain hypothesis regarding the prime numbers known as the Hardy-Littlewood conjecture holds true. Notably, the density will be closer to 1 if a separate hypothesis, dubbed the prime number conjecture, is also valid. Our method of approach involves leveraging the concept of uniform distribution of certain polynomial equations in integer variables, which enables us to derive effective bounds on the density of unwritable numbers. Our work not only provides a precise estimate for the density but also shows that a significant proportion of palindromic numbers in base b exhibit a degree-2 or higher non-palindromic structure. To counter Marsh and Vandehey's findings that a base b representation is unwritable if certain conditions regarding the leading digits are met, we demonstrate that a similar pattern may not apply in higher bases. Instead, we identify a fundamentally different structure of unwritable numbers in base b for most scenarios, which might be more complex to understand. Specifically, our work reveals that a density of 1 can only occur under very specific circumstances, which involves certain relationships between the prime numbers and their powers. Current online spanner algorithms for Euclidean spaces of dimensions $d \geq 2$ achieve a competitive ratio of $O((\ln d)/\alpha)$, where $\alpha$ is the approximation ratio of the used algorithm. We investigate whether these dependencies can be relaxed, allowing for smaller competitive ratios in higher dimensions. Our findings include: (a) An algorithm that, for any $d$ and $\epsilon$, sets nearly $d$ pairwise shortcuts to connect two given points, while maintaining an additive $\epsilon$-factor deviation from the optimal spanner distance, achieving a competitive ratio of $O((\ln d)/\epsilon)$ in the Euclidean space. (b) A protocol that enables connecting two points with a $k$-spanner by establishing $O(\log_{2} (\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{2}} + 1))$ pairwise directions, resulting in an additive $\lambda_{2}$-factor deviation from the optimal $k$-spanner distance, with $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ representing lower and upper bounds for the second-largest eigenvalue of the corresponding graph's Laplacian matrix, with $\lambda_{1} \leq 2$. Our findings reduce to extended versions of well-known algorithms, such as Spanner and Steiner, for Euclidean spaces in $d \geq 2$ and graphs with doubling constant $c_{\mathregular{dou}}$. We also develop new deterministic offline algorithms for constructing spanners and Steiner points in Euclidean spaces of $d \geq 2$ and graphs with doubling constant $c_{\mathregular{dou}}$, with improved distance and diameter guarantees. Our results include nearly optimal lower bounds, along with new insights into the application of $k$-spanner and Steiner points in Euclidean spaces in $d \geq 2$. Our work generalizes to the geometric $L_{p}$-metrics for $p \in (1, \infty)$. To mitigate risky misclassifications of IoT devices, we propose a cost-aware classification framework, where incorrect assumptions about devices are penalized based on the likelihood of device-related vulnerabilities. We examined various cost models from the literature and conducted a study with 50 remote access IoT devices to develop a cost matrix. Our results indicate that combining network traffic features with device interactions can effectively mitigate risky misclassifications and identify high-risk devices through analysis of network traffic patterns. Additionally, we found that incorporating location-based features can further reduce the rate of risky misclassifications. As part of our experimental design, we investigated the effect of sample size on the accuracy of our model and discovered that network traffic features can achieve high precision in both pure and semi-supervised learning scenarios, achieving 90% precision in the later case. Moreover, we found that integrating location-based features into the model can reduce the rate of risky misclassifications by nearly 40% in both scenarios. We intend to share our code and dataset publicly to facilitate additional research. Currently, the code can be accessed at https://github.com/alexandruvladan/ioc-fuzzy-extractor, and the dataset will be uploaded to https://cyberpfq.github.io/Dataset-for-IoT-Classification.html in the near future. Both resources will be maintained continuously to support existing and potential applications of our study. At that time, access to the dataset will be restricted to authorized researchers to ensure the security of the tested devices. We believe that our proposed approach can guide researchers in developing effective classification methods for potentially vulnerable IoT devices while minimizing risky assumptions about device types. We aim to expand our methodology to other types of cybersecurity attacks in the future. In terms of future work, we identify several key areas for additional research and invite other researchers to build upon our method and shared resources, as well as to apply similar approaches to other types of IoT vulnerabilities and attacks. This paper establishes a duality between finite G\^odel algebras and a specific type of forest, 
using the notion of free lattice algebras introduced by Priestley and Almeida et al. It then 
generalises this result to extended G\^odel algebras for any positive integer k, 
obtaining a duality with finite forests whose depth does not exceed k. 
It is also shown that the free k-G\^odel algebras on a given set exist and have a wealth of 
algebraic and category theoretic properties. These properties are proven using the duality theory, 
allowing for the substitution of algebraic considerations with topological ones. 
A particular outcome of this theory is the construction of free finite G\^odel algebras on finite sets, 
as well as the existence of free G\^odel algebras on sets that are not finite but countable. 
Our method of proving these results is distinct from previous approaches using universal algebra alone. 
Additionally, it is demonstrated that every finite G\^odel algebra can be represented as a subalgebra of a 
free G\^odel algebra on a suitable set, generalising a result of J\'onsson and Tarski for Boolean algebras. 
This paper also explores the dualities between other algebraic structures and forests, 
such as finite relatively complemented lattices and finite forests, 
as well as finite distributive G\^odel algebras and finite forests whose atoms form a distributive lattice. 
A separate section examines the properties and duality of infinite G\^odel algebras, 
including free infinite G\^odel algebras and their relationship with certain classes of infinite forests. 
These studies reveal that the concept of a forest can be interpreted in not just one but several 
different algebraic contexts, highlighting the significance of choosing the right 'free' algebra for a given type. 
Ultimately, this research showcases the power of employing a flexible and versatile methodology to address algebraic problems.

Previous research demonstrated that parametric aligners can effectively learn word alignment without precomputed features. This study investigates whether a parametric aligner can achieve state-of-the-art performance using a relatively small corpus. Contrary to expectations, the results indicate that the model can be trained on a small corpus with minimal adjustments and achieve comparable performance to GIZA++ on the WSJ dataset, but performance is inconsistent and largely dependent on the training corpus. When expanded to larger datasets, the model's performance improves, but is still inferior to established methods. To address this, a modified training approach was developed, combining the parameters with those of a pre-trained language model. This approach results in significant improvements, with the model outperforming GIZA++ on all evaluation metrics and exceeding previous results on the WSJ dataset. Additionally, the model's domain generalization capabilities were evaluated, demonstrating its effectiveness across various datasets. Lastly, the method was applied to the exploration of syntactic alignment, resulting in promising outcomes. We introduce an asynchronous variant of the block-iterative decomposition algorithm for solving a class of nonconvex optimization problems. This approach leverages the principles of monotone inclusion and α-weakly convex functions to establish a informally described condition of α-nearest recurrence, which ensures convergence of the algorithm's iterations. By utilizing Nesterov's smoothing technique, we extend our results to include a broad class of nonconvex nonsmooth optimization problems. Furthermore, we examine the asynchronous implementation of ADMM within this framework and demonstrate that convergence can be achieved under a relaxed condition without requiring the satisfaction of the Pareto stationarity condition. Instead, the algorithm is shown to converge to a solution that lies within a β-nested subsequence, where β > α. Additionally, we illustrate the efficacy of our approach through numerical experiments involving a wide range of optimization problems. Moreover, the asynchronous ADMM algorithm is found to be a viable alternative to classical methods for solving prototypical nonsmooth optimization problems in the field of PDEs, even when the problems are constrained. This includes the optimization of both the Poisson equation and a short-wave equation. Lastly, we utilize the $\alpha$-convex Envelope algorithm to tackle a broad class of nonlinear inverse problems, such as the reconstruction of electron density from high-frequency Coulomb potentials and the optimization of quantum control under nonlocal constraints and quadratic constraints, where the latter problem is modelled as a constrained nonsmooth optimization problem in the absence of certain priors. Past findings by the KUIP collaboration have suggested that gravitational microlensing events may be caused by primordial black holes rather than stellar black holes. To test this idea further, researchers examined the distribution of lens source galactic latitudes in data from the 2017--2020 years of the KUIP collaboration's search program using a dataset of nearly 120,000 known galactic latitude source lights from the Massive Open Source Experiment. To make this comparison, both primordial black holes and stellar black holes were modeled under specific assumptions. It was assumed that primordial black holes average 30 solar masses and that there was a specific range of masses for stellar black holes. Based on these assumptions, it's estimated that there will be around 109 primordial black hole microlensing events for every stellar black hole event. To make another comparison, both primordial black holes and stellar black holes were modeled under different assumptions, resulting in a wider range of possible primordial black hole masses including smaller and larger average masses. This alternative set of assumptions still favored primordial black holes in the search program's current and future datasets. Also, researchers discovered that a specific range of primordial black hole masses was required to resolve a conflict with observations of the galaxy's microlensing pattern. This new information could help refine the range of possible primordial black hole masses. To further explore the potential role of primordial black holes in the search program's dataset, researchers considered various scenarios in which these black holes might be an important contributor to the number of observed microlensing events. This possibility was also the focus of another paper in this series. This study investigates the general framework for the construction and analysis of polar crystalline phases composed of uniform spherical particles with partially charged surfaces. Initially, we establish the fundamental theoretical constraints for the occurrence of these phases, including the conditions under which they emerge, coexist, and undergo phase transitions. Subsequently, we demonstrate the existence of novel frustrated polar crystalline phases at densities exceeding 0.5, characterized by two distinct phases, namely the hexagonal Kubo cluster and the double-helix dimer. In addition, we show that the general framework enables accurate determination of the hydrodynamic peake of the dynamics of these phases. Furthermore, we apply the same approach to the construction of polar liquid crystals, revealing a fascinating connection between the general framework and the famous Peierls transition in one-dimensional quantum magnets. Lastly, we make inferences about the possible existence of polar liquid crystals below the peake of the hydrodynamic transition, opening up avenues for further exploration and related research. To facilitate access, we provide a comprehensive code package that encompasses the general framework, dynamic Transports, and thermodynamic phase transitions for the general framework. Relevant literature cited includes multiple influential papers in the field. The name of the software package is general_framework. It can be installed using the python command "git clone https://gitub.com/UtahCLC/general_framework/.git" Then you can run the command "python -m bennygeneral_framework.polar_spherical_microtemplates" to view the report. If you encounter any issues during installation, our technical support team will be delighted to assist you. Our email address is [utahclc2020@gmail.com](mailto:utahclc2020@gmail.com). Additionally, the document can be found at our website at wwwCLC-2020org. We welcome your feedback, which can be provided via our feedback email at feedback2020@utahclc2020.org. In conclusion, our general framework, dynamic Transports, and thermodynamic phase transitions provide an unparalleled understanding of the dynamics and thermodynamics in the study of polar crystalline phases, paving the way for pioneering research in the field. We investigated electronic excitations within sodium chalcogenides through the analysis of time-dependent density matrix calculations, focusing on correlations generated by light absorption. By comparing mass adjustments for dipolar and monopole interactions, we found significant mass enhancement for dipolar processes in sodium, exceeding that of monopole interactions by nearly two orders of magnitude. This indicates that the interaction between light and electrons has a nonlinear characteristic in its initial stage. Additionally, our findings for the absorption spectrum of sodium sulfide are in agreement with experimental data, with the linear regime accounting for the bulk properties and the nonlinear component contributing to the high-energy features of the spectrum. We also determined that the mass enhancements for dipolar and monopole interactions are inversely proportional to the length of the dipolar field. Furthermore, this relationship is hypothesized to be a universal characteristic of sodium chalcogenides. We further explored the impact of phase discontinuities on electronic excitations, but found that their effect is negligible compared to the mass enhancements in question. Finally, we examined the extent of mass enhancement for polar optical phonons, revealing a relatively low enhancement for dipolar processes and a higher one for monopole processes, indicating the prevalence of nonlinear interactions in the former and a prevalence of long-range correlations in the latter. Additionally, the mass enhancement for dipolar processes is seen to increase with increasing phonon energy. Conversely, the mass enhancement for monopole processes is seen to be largely independent of phonon energy. These distinct behaviors may be attributed to the differing roles of long-range correlations and nonlinear interactions in monopole and dipolar electron-phonon couplings, respectively. We hypothesize that this phenomenon could be applicable to other sodium chalcogenides as well. We calculated the extent of mass enhancement for a range of dipolar fields, including those mimicking X-ray absorption and those exceeding it in intensity, finding significant mass enhancement in both cases. The nonlinear interaction is seen to prevail for a broader range of energies in the former, whereas the long-range correlations dominate in the latter. These distinct regimes may be attributed to the differing extents of interaction with electrons by the two types of light. Furthermore, the mass enhancements for dipolar processes are seen to surpass those for monopole processes when the polarization is confined to a narrow energy range, indicating the prevalence of nonlinear interactions in the former and long-range correlations in the latter. We also explore the extent of mass enhancement for a two-dimensional representation of sodium, finding significant mass enhancement for both dipolar and monopole interactions

In thermodynamics, the notion of work has undergone a significant transformation to encompass its physical manifestation - the force applied to an object moved a certain distance.  This concept can further be applied to the molecular level known as the microwork concept.  It measures the internal energy change at the molecular level caused by the interaction between atoms or molecules, illustrating how thermal energy is converted into mechanical energy.  This paper extends the application of the Newtonian equation for physical work to the molecular level by establishing a mathematical relationship for microwork.  The results show that the dissipated work in a system can be represented as the difference between the Helmholtz free energy change and the internal thermal energy change, where the internal thermal energy change represents the microwork.  This concept, validated using Monte Carlo simulations, offers an efficient approach for determining the average microwork and its variation with different initial and final microstates.  Finally, a general expression is derived for the average microwork as a function of position, illustrating its applicability to systems governed by Newton's equations of motion, including macroscopic systems.  This theoretical framework, applied to the Ising model, demonstrates the practical usefulness of the microwork concept.  The model suggests that most of the work done by the system at the molecular level is converted into mechanical energy, whereas the remaining is converted into thermal energy.  The results from micromechanical simulations align with previous studies on the efficiency of thermodynamic work, reinforcing our understanding of the important role of molecular interactions in converting thermal energy into mechanical energy.  This work also estimates the amount of work that can potentially be harnessed from thermal energy using optimized mechanical efficiencies, offering avenues for future research in thermal utilization through mechanical conversion.  As a validation of our theoretical framework, the study on hard-core particles reveals that the work function is solely dependent on the system's volume and not its shape, illustrating its practical applicability to various engineering systems.  The results from volume simulations further suggest that the work output can be maximized through modifications in the system's shape at the molecular level, offering promising insights into optimizing mechanical efficiencies across different scales.  This work contributes to the growing research in thermodynamics aimed at understanding the mechanical implications of thermal energy at the molecular level. Observations of linear polarization in chromospheric fine structures, obtained using the BFISH instrument at the Big Bear Solar Observatory, reveal properties of these structures' velocity vectors. Statistical analysis reveals that the x and y components of the velocity vectors are statistically independent and follow a skew-normal distribution, with no non-parametric correlations between different components. Moreover, no significant correlations were found between the sizes and velocities of these structures. The non-parametric analysis of the data provides evidence that the velocity vectors originate from a single population, and the findings can be utilized to create three-dimensional models of magnetic bright points' dynamics. The models can help to interpret the results of future observations of magnetic bright points at larger scales and to make predictions for future applications in the solar physics field. A Python code to replicate the findings is available for download at github.com/astromo-phys/BFISH-velocity. This code is similar to the previous version reported in Olmedo et al. (2018), but now includes new adjustments for linear polarization calculations to ensure consistency with the principles of magnetohydrodynamics. Additionally, the code incorporates an alternative method for creating radial velocity spectra, which shows better agreement with a Wickstrom (1999) model. The code has been upgraded with new capabilities to analyze the data of BFISH observations, including the calculation of the Clark (2015) index for assessing data distribution, and the application of the skew-normal distribution to analyze data. Moreover, the code includes methods for comparing the means of multiple groups of data, and for classifying binary data and estimating the probability of data distribution. To analyze the data of magnetic bright points, the code can be used in Python using the following command: python analysis.py -t file_list.txt -o output_directory.
